1001-questions-and-answers-on-orthograph: Benjamin Adams Hathaway offers a question and answer guide to spelling and reading. The book works through letters, sounds, word meanings, and rules for capitals, italics, abbreviations, accents, and punctuation. It also covers prefixes, suffixes, diacritical marks, and the values of letters, with drills in reading aloud. Teachers and learners can use its short items to test knowledge and build clear habits in written English.
10066-gunman-s-reckoning:
Max Brand's 1921 western opens in Jericho Pass, where fifty empty freight cars dance and roll and rattle on the rough roadbed, filling the pass with thunder. The big engine labors at the grade, but five cars back the locomotive's noise is lost, and a brakie talks above the racket in a nasal overtone.

From that noisy start, Brand builds a gunman's story of reckoning: debts, enemies, and a code that must be paid. His hero moves through cattle country with speed and grit. Readers get a classic Brand western, where a train's thunder gives way to a gunfighter's quiet arithmetic.
10120-england-of-my-heart-spring:
Edward Hutton walked the old pilgrim road through Kent in spring for this 1914 travel book, with pictures by Gordon Home. He follows the route toward Canterbury, pausing at Dartford, Rochester, Faversham, and small towns along the way. The book belongs to a series on England, season by season, and treats place as living history.

Hutton links Roman Kent, the Weald and marsh, Rye and Winchelsea, and the field of Hastings to the lanes he walks. Churches, castles, and country scenes prompt notes on saints, kings, and ordinary folk. Readers get a gentle, learned ramble through English spring, rich in local lore and place names.
1016-on-the-improvement-of-the-understan:
Baruch Spinoza wrote this treatise on the improvement of the understanding, also called the Treatise on the Emendation of the Intellect, translated by R. H. M. Elwes. Its contents run from the ordinary objects of men's desires to the true and final good, with certain rules of life and four modes of perception.

Spinoza asks how the mind can rise from confused ideas to true knowledge, and how that knowledge can guide a good life. His prose is clear and searching, though the work breaks off unfinished. The treatise is a fine introduction to Spinoza, and a classic essay on how to think well.
1022-walking:
Henry David Thoreau praises the act of walking out into wild land as a spiritual and political need, not a mere pastime. In this essay, drawn from his lectures, he urges readers to leave town, road, and clock behind and let swamp, wood, and field reset the mind.

Thoreau claims that wildness keeps the world sane, and that a man who walks well thinks well. His sentences stride and halt like a walker, full of jokes, lists, and sudden aphorisms. The piece helped seed the love of wild places in America, and it still calls readers outdoors.
10220-daddy-takes-us-skating:
Howard R. Garis wrote this children's book in 1914, for the young readers of his Daddy series. Brother and sister Hal and Mab Blake ask their father about everything, from red noses in cold weather to steam engines. Daddy answers with patience, turning each question into a small lesson.

When winter comes, Daddy takes the children skating, and the ice brings falls, fun, and fresh questions about frost, skates, and safety. Friends join the outings, and home talk rounds out each day. Readers get a gentle, chatty picture of family life, curiosity, and winter play.
10274-sermons-on-evil-speaking:
Isaac Barrow, a seventeenth-century Cambridge scholar and divine, preached these sermons on the sins of speech. A later editor, Henry Morley, framed them with a life of Barrow, who rose from Charterhouse and Trinity College to wide fame as a preacher. The sermons treat talk not as trifle, but as a moral act with real harm.

Barrow attacks foolish jesting, rash swearing, slander, and gossip in general, showing how each wounds hearers and speakers alike. His arguments are close, learned, and often sharp, rooted in Scripture and reason. Readers get a stern, thoughtful guide to guarding the tongue, still clear on why careless words matter.
10323-the-rover-boys-at-college-or-the-r:
Arthur M. Winfield, a pen name used for the Rover Boys series, published this college tale in 1910. Dick, Tom, and Sam Rover leave school days behind for college, where new friends, sports, and rivals await. The subtitle warns that two roads lie open: the right one and the wrong one.

Hazing, a colors contest, rowing, football, a haunted house, and a charge of disgrace test the brothers in turn. Girls arrive, misunderstandings grow, and evidence at last sorts friends from foes. Readers get a lively, moral boys' story of college fun, fair play, and growing up.
10395-joy-and-power-three-messages-with-:
Henry van Dyke gathered three messages in this 1903 book, delivered at Los Angeles, Princeton, and Harvard within weeks of each other. Van Dyke, a preacher and writer, says the three talks, though shaped for different hearers, point one way and urge one course. Their shared meaning is the best he had learned in life.

Joy and Power treats religion and happiness, The Battle of Life treats struggle and duty, and The Good Old Way treats faith's steady path. Each message joins joy to action, not to mere feeling. Readers get warm, eloquent sermons on living well, useful for students of American preaching.
1046-god-the-invisible-king:
H. G. Wells sets out his own faith in this 1917 book: not the creeds of the churches, but belief in a personal God who strives with men against evil. He rejects an all-powerful, all-knowing deity and pictures instead a finite, striving king who needs human help to win. The book speaks in plain, urgent prose.

Wells sketches a modern religion of conduct, with chapters on sin, prayer, and what a church could be. He wrote amid the slaughter of war, seeking a faith that could face it. The book stirred both praise and scorn, and it gives a frank window on one famous mind wrestling with God.
1049-vanished-arizona-recollections-of-t:
Martha Summerhayes, a young bride from New England, followed her army officer husband to the Arizona frontier in the 1870s and wrote down what she found. Her memoir moves from sea voyages and desert marches to lonely forts, where officers' wives kept house with few goods and much grit.

She writes of Apache scouts, rough roads, childbirth far from help, and the odd kindness of army life. Her eye is sharp and her tone frank, with humor about her own greenhorn days. The book gives a rare woman's view of the frontier army, and it reads as both history and a good yarn.
10630-coming-to-the-king:
Frances Ridley Havergal, a well-known English writer of hymns and devotional verse, wrote Coming to the King as a poem of prayer. The poem takes a text from Solomon's story in the first book of Kings. Its speaker comes alone to the King of Salem, as the Queen of Sheba once came, but with no train and no costly gifts. Only requests and questions are brought to the throne.

The poem follows that meeting: the speaker tells the King all that weighs on the heart and hears answers that bring guidance, victory over doubt, and quiet rest. Short lines and simple images carry the whole piece. Readers looking for gentle, earnest Christian verse will find here a clear example of Havergal's devotional voice.
1075-the-strength-of-the-strong:
Jack London gathers tales of men who live by muscle and nerve: hunters, fighters, and outcasts who test each other in a world where law is thin. The title story pits tribe against tribe in a fable of how the strong rule, and how the weak learn to band together. Other tales range from the sea to the prize ring.

London writes with his usual force, praising grit while showing its cost in blood and pride. His people are blunt, his scenes are stark, and his endings seldom spare anyone. The book gives a compact dose of London's creed, and it suits readers who like short tales with a punch.
1076-the-wallet-of-kai-lung:
Ernest Bramah's Kai Lung, a wandering Chinese storyteller, opens his wallet of tales for Western readers: fables of mandarins, merchants, and rogues, each told in grave, ornate English that mimics Chinese courtesy. The stories turn on wit, fate, and the traps set by greed.

Kai Lung himself frames the tales, dodging robbers and officials with a story at the right hour. Bramah, an Englishman who never visited China, built a whole imagined East from books and fancy. The book charmed a generation, and it gave fantasy its first great Chinese voice, however fanciful.
10794-dahcotah-life-and-legends-of-the-s:
Mary Eastman wrote Dahcotah, or Life and Legends of the Sioux Around Fort Snelling, from her residence at the Minnesota fort, with a preface by Mrs. C. M. Kirkland and drawings by Captain Eastman. Dedicated to Henry Sibley of the House of Representatives, the book records Sioux daily life, customs, and stories as Eastman saw and heard them.

Eastman writes with sympathy, hoping purity of heart and learning will serve the good of others, including Native peoples. Her legends preserve tales told near the fort in the mid-nineteenth century. Readers get an early, firsthand account of Dakota life, valuable despite the limits of its time.
10818-sport-and-work-on-the-nepaul-front:
Writing as "Maori," an indigo planter published Sport and Work on the Nepaul Frontier in 1878, after twelve years in India and a visit home in 1875. A frontispiece of tiger hunting on the return to camp sets the tone. The author found visitors at home ignorant of ordinary Indian life, and wrote a chatty, unpretentious book for friends about daily toil and play.

Chapters cover planting work, sport, servants, neighbors, and the frontier country itself. The tone is familiar rather than grand, full of anecdote. Readers get a planter's-eye view of British India in the 1860s and 1870s, lively and personal.
10850-philaster-or-love-lies-a-bleeding:
Francis Beaumont and John Fletcher's Philaster, or Love Lies a Bleeding, is a Jacobean tragicomedy set in Sicily. Its persons include the King, Philaster the heir to the crown, Pharamond prince of Spain, Arethusa the king's daughter, and Eufrasia, daughter of Dion, disguised as the page Bellario. Lords, ladies, citizens, and woodmen fill the scene.

The plot turns on love, jealousy, and mistaken identity, as Philaster loves Arethusa while Bellario's secret devotion complicates all. The play ends in the mingled tears and reconciliations of tragicomedy. Readers meet Beaumont and Fletcher at their romantic best, in verse of grace and passion.
10916-parent-and-child-volume-iii-child-:
Mosiah Hall wrote Parent and Child, volume three, Child Study and Training, in 1916 for the Deseret Sunday School Union of Salt Lake City. Its introduction calls home-making and child-rearing the fundamental business of the world, needing knowledge as well as love. Loving hearts suffer, Hall warns, from mistakes that loving intelligence might have prevented.

The volume urges parents to study child nature and the laws of development, so they can guide children wisely. Its tone is earnest, practical, and rooted in Sunday school teaching. Parents and teachers get an early twentieth-century guide to raising children with understanding.
10940-manners-customs-and-dress-during-t:
Paul Lacroix, curator of the Arsenal library in Paris, surveyed daily life from the Middle Ages through the Renaissance in this richly illustrated history. More than four hundred wood engravings and nineteen colour plates show clothing, feasts, trades, games, and ceremonies, drawn from manuscripts and artworks. Lacroix argues that art alone cannot explain an age; manners and dress must be studied beside it.

Chapters follow how people lived, worked, and celebrated, from courts to workshops, and how trade and discovery changed what Europe wore and owned. The book speaks to general readers as well as scholars, using pictures as evidence. It remains a lively reference for anyone who wants to see, not just read about, the medieval and Renaissance world.
10969-ski-running:
Katharine Furse wrote this 1924 handbook for British skiers heading to the Alps. A map and photographs from Adelboden illustrate chapters on the history of skiing, the cost of a winter holiday, centres, clothing, equipment, and care of skis. Practical sections teach the elements of the sport, etiquette on nursery slopes, snow and light, falls, tests, and finding the way by map.

Furse traces skis from Central Asian origins and Norse sagas to modern Norway, where races began at Tromso in 1843, and to their use by armies in the First World War. Chapters on avalanches and accidents give plain safety advice. The book suits both beginners and experienced runners, and it captures skiing just as it became a popular British winter pastime.
10977-the-grizzly-king:
James Oliver Curwood's 1918 animal romance follows Thor, a great grizzly bear in the Canadian Rockies, and Muskwa, a small cub who joins him. Thor rules his mountain domain by smell and sound, his eyesight being poor, and he hunts caribou, meets porcupines, and fishes in cold lakes. Hunters with dogs and rifles threaten his world, and a wounded bear's fate hangs on human mercy.

Curwood tells much of the story from the bears' point of view, describing a July den cool as a cellar, a beetle that nips a nose. Illustrations by Frank B. Hoffman picture key scenes. The novel blends adventure with a plea for wild animals, and it remains a favourite among Curwood's stories of the North.
11137-twenty-two-years-a-slave-and-forty:
Austin Steward published this 1856 narrative of twenty-two years enslaved and forty years free, with correspondence from his years as president of the Wilberforce Colony at London, Canada West. Governor Myron H. Clark of New York subscribed to the book in May 1856, and Rochester friends testified to Steward's character as a businessman and Christian, hoping the book would benefit him in declining years.

Steward recalls learning to read from scant books, a friend setting copies for his writing book, and starting in business after freedom. His story moves from slavery to Rochester trade and to Canada, where he led a colony of free Black settlers. The narrative stands as an early African American autobiography, pleading against slavery in the voice of one who bore its scars.
11164-rough-and-tumble-engineering:
James H. Maggard wrote this practical manual, Rough and Tumble Engineering, for engineers of farm and traction engines. Maggard disclaims a scientific work: nice theories suit nice engine rooms, but rough and tumble engineers have everything in their favour today and tomorrow are in mud holes.

Maggard promises plain, unvarnished, practical facts in everyday field terms, with no geometrical figures of circles and angles to explain an eccentric. Chapters explain engine knock: a loose pillow block box, fitted with set bolts and jam nuts, is a good knocker. The book served a generation of threshing and traction engineers.
1118-much-ado-about-nothing:
In Messina, the witty Beatrice and Benedick trade insults while their friends trick them into love, and the young Claudio, fooled by a villain's plot, shames his bride Hero at the altar. William Shakespeare's comedy balances sparkling wordplay with a near-tragedy of honor and slander.

Hero's seeming death and the unmasking of Don John set all right, and the two pairs marry amid jokes and dances. Dogberry, the bumbling constable, steals scenes with his mangled speech. The play's mix of laughter and hurt keeps it among Shakespeare's most loved comedies.
11468-darkest-india-a-supplement-to-gene:
Commissioner Booth-Tucker's 1891 Darkest India supplements General Booth's In Darkest England and the Way Out for Indian readers. arguing that if a cab-horse charter suits England, a bullock charter is no less urgently needed for India. Booth-Tucker calls Booth's gospel of social salvation a resurrection of Bethlehem's message of peace and brotherhood, relieving temporal as well as spiritual needs. Modifications for India, he insists, will be unimportant.

Chapters treat the submerged tenth, beggars, the out of works, homeless poor, debt, famine, pestilence, criminals, and elements of hope, with Booth's scheme of city colonies, labour bureaus, food depots, and brigades. The book shows Salvation Army social thought exported to empire. For Indian historians, it documents Victorian philanthropy confronting Indian poverty.
11667-gentle-measures-in-the-management-:
Jacob Abbott's 1871 book on gentle measures sets out how firm parental authority can stand without violence or anger. Its full title promises methods in harmony with the structure of the juvenile mind, and chapters move from three modes of management to gentle punishment and reward.

Later chapters cover training, sympathy between child and parent, commendation, faults of immaturity, and the imagination in children. Money, truth, and religious training each get a chapter. Abbott argues for reason and affection over tricks, and he gives examples, such as Della and her dolls, to show the method at work.
12312-a-king-and-no-king:
Beaumont and Fletcher play A King and No King turns on Arbaces, king of Iberia, who loves Panthea, believed to be his sister. The cast lists Tigranes of Armenia, Gobrias the lord protector and father of Arbaces, captains Mardonius and Bessus, and the queen mother Arane.

Arbaces, torn between throne and desire, tells Panthea she will blush for him and hang her head like a violet full of morning dew, unless a way to freedom exists. The plot resolves through hidden birth: the lovers are not kin, and the king is no king in the sense the title teases. The play mixes tragic passion with comic captains, and its verse keeps the tension high. It remains the partners most famous tragicomedy.
12512-the-deacon-of-dobbinsville-a-story:
John A. Morrison's story, written some forty-five or fifty years before its reprinting, is based on actual happenings in Dobbinsville. Its publisher's preface draws a sharp line between nominal religious professors and people soundly converted, made new in Christ and rejoicing on the highway of holiness.

The deacon and his neighbours test that line in church life, conduct and talk, as Paul's warning about itching ears and turned-away truth frames the tale. Morrison writes as a preacher-storyteller, earnest and plain, for readers who share his faith. The book documents a revivalist view of American religion, where true conversion, not mere profession, marks the saved.
12571-the-boy-allies-in-the-trenches-or-:
Clair W. Hayes's 1915 Boy Allies in the Trenches, or Midst Shot and Shell along the Aisne, follows Hal Paine and Chester Crawford in France. Chapter one opens with Field Marshal Sir John French, surprised to find the two lads alive, after service with a Cossack regiment in Russia.

French, commander of British forces helping France hurl back the German invader, hears their Russian fighting with astonishment. Trenches, shell fire and boy heroics follow along the Aisne. Hayes writes brisk wartime adventure for boys, patriotic and fast. The book belongs to a popular series that carried its heroes from Liège to the firing line and beyond.
12763-every-soul-hath-its-song:
Fannie Hurst's 1916 story book gathers tales of New York immigrants, shopgirls, and strivers chasing a song of their own. Simon Binswanger first sees Liberty from a steerage deck as a small boy, then swims and struggles toward American life. Other stories follow salesmen, singers, and families in the city's crowded streets.

A Cincinnati tale, Hochenheimer, turns on a bashful suitor at a family table, teased over dumplings and business dealing alike. Hurst's sympathy lies with ordinary people who keep hope alive in hard places. The book shows her early gift for warm, plain tales of city life.
12813-quit-your-worrying:
George Wharton James published this 1916 self-help book as a direct attack on worry as a daily curse. Chapters take on health fears, parents' fears, marriage, envy, jealousy, ambition, and the squirrel cage of work, arguing that most worry is needless, selfish, and harmful to others. Scripture and sages back his case.

James does not deny real danger: he tells of a superintendent threatened by a patient, and asks what attitude fits such a case. His answer is trust and gladness, summed up in a Riley poem, Just Be Glad. The book speaks plainly to readers who feel worry has become a habit of mind.
12817-robert-browning:
Edward Dowden's 1904 life of Robert Browning aims at a biography of the poet's mind, not just his dates. It tracks Browning's poems by date and origin, from early work through his marriage to Elizabeth Barrett and their years in Italy. Paris, the Italian lakes, and London scenes mark the couple's travels.

Dowden shows how Browning's thought grew through dramatic monologues and long poems, with love and faith as steady themes. The editor's preface notes that Browning's events matter less than his spirit's achievements. The book suits readers who want the poems read beside the life that shaped them.
12854-the-master-s-indwelling:
Andrew Murray's Master's Indwelling gathers addresses given at the Northfield Conference of 1895, later rewritten for publication. Chapters move from carnal Christians and the self life through waiting on God, entrance into rest, and Christ our life, to humility, surrender, joy in the Holy Ghost, and prayer. The theme is Christ dwelling within the believer.

Murray opens with Paul's charge that the Corinthians, though in Christ, were still babes fed with milk, not meat. Later he urges readers to put the Kingdom first every morning and all day. The book remains a classic of devotional teaching on the deeper Christian life.
12876-a-young-girl-s-wooing:
E. P. Roe's 1884 novel A Young Girl's Wooing follows Madge Alden, a young woman whose quiet strength unsettles rivals and suitors alike. Graydon Muir courts her, while Miss Wildmere tries satire, patronage, and strategy to win ground, only to find Madge answers with cordial indifference. Mountain climbs, partings, and confessions mark the wooing.

Roe builds the story on effort and achievement, as Madge grows from a crescent of a girl into a woman who makes her own terms. Chapters on veiled wooing, enemies' plans, and checkmate keep the romantic contest lively. The novel is earnest, sentimental fiction of its era, popular with Roe's large readership.
12908-missing:
Mrs. Humphry Ward's Missing, a First World War novel, opens with Miss Cookson ordering tea and supper for lodgers in a north-country house. A maid who dislikes Cookson's poking ways hopes her sister Mrs. Sarratt will prove nicer, while brides and bridegrooms once filled Mrs. Weston's rooms. A telegram frontispiece warns that a husband is reported wounded and missing.

Later the heroine fills quiet days with needlework for a war workroom, sphagnum moss gathering, visits to convalescent soldiers, and Wordsworth, while a restless friend named Farrell reads Shelley and Hardy aloud. Ward traces waiting, grief, and slow hope. The novel is a sensitive portrait of wartime home life.
12991-the-uncrowned-king:
Harold Bell Wright's short allegorical tale, published in 1910, follows a pilgrim who seeks truth beyond the noise of daily life. The pilgrim leaves a city called Daybyday and climbs toward a temple, listening as he goes. Each stage of the climb brings a new voice: the waves, the evening wind, the night, and at last the new day.

Wright frames the journey as a moral fable, not a plot-driven adventure. The pilgrim learns to hear past the fog and din of things, and the voices he meets mark stages of waking sight. Short and plainly told, the tale was meant to be read slowly, as a guide to paying heed to what lies beneath routine and rush.
13001-four-months-among-the-gold-finders:
J. Tyrwhitt Brooks, a doctor, kept this diary on an expedition from San Francisco to the California gold districts in 1849. Sent home at first only for family and friends, it reached print in London the same year as an eyewitness record of the gold rush. The diary form keeps dates, camps, and small facts in the order Brooks met them.

Readers meet tents and plank stores by the rivers, men washing gold dust in tin pans, and one miner showing four hundred ounces valued at fourteen dollars an ounce. Brooks also notes Native visitors who came to his camp, shared the pipe of peace, and spoke of their wants. The book's worth lies in its plain, dated detail, caught while the rush was still new.
13111-the-brain-and-the-voice-in-speech-:
F. W. Mott, a London doctor and fellow of the Royal Society, published this 1910 study of how brain and voice work in speech and song. Mott treats the vocal organ in three parts: bellows, reed, and resonator. He covers breath control, the larynx, loudness, pitch, and timbre, then turns to the brain centers that govern words.

Diagrams show the cartilages of the voice-box and the fibers that join the two halves of the brain. Mott also studies speech defects, deafness from brain injury, and the link between speech and right-handedness. The book joins anatomy, music, and neurology in one short course, and it still reads as a clear first guide to why voices fail and how they work.
13277-stage-confidences-talks-about-play:
Clara Morris's 1902 Stage Confidences, talks about players and play acting, published in London by Charles H. Kelly, opens with a greeting to young girls who honor her with liking and confidences. Morris, author of Life on the Stage, notes she has the advantage of years. Her readers have the advantage of numbers, asking more questions in an hour than she can answer in a week. The book is a veteran actress's memoir and advice.

She tells of a mother in the audience who, seeing her little son stolen by his father's order, cried out in agony and fainted, moving the whole house. Later, she recalls a preacher who, never having seen inside a playhouse, denounced the theatre as the gate of hell, and her amusing letters answering him. The book is warm, frank, and full of stage lore.
1328-the-tinker-s-wedding:
J. M. Synge's short comedy follows Michael Byrne, a tinker who wants to marry his sweetheart Sarah Casey. The priest who would wed them demands a price, and the tinkers' tricks undo the bargain. The play moves through a country roadside with wit and a touch of blasphemy.

Synge writes the tinkers' speech with music and mischief, and the play's joke cuts both ways: priest and tinkers each want their due. The comedy, once banned from the Abbey stage, now stands as a small gem of Irish theatre, funny and sharp.
13342-robert-browning:
G. K. Chesterton's study of Robert Browning follows a life that, as he admits, offers few outward events. It was public yet quiet, crowned by one great test of character, then settled again into work and fame. Chesterton moves from early life and early poems to marriage, years in Italy, and later life.

The heart of the book is criticism, not gossip. Chapters on Browning as a literary artist, on The Ring and the Book, and on his philosophy argue that his tangled verse hides a clear moral imagination. Quoted poems, including a comic roll call of housemaid troubles, show his love of strong speech and strange company. Chesterton makes a hard poet readable without smoothing his edges.
13486-the-story-of-sigurd-the-volsung:
William Morris's verse epic The Story of Sigurd the Volsung appears here condensed in part into prose by Winifred Turner and Helen Scott, with a biographical introduction by J. W. Mackail. Mackail presents Morris, born in 1834, as a Victorian writer who also worked greatly in other arts and lived by beliefs about life and making very different from ordinary people's.

The poem follows Sigmund's son, born to a god of earth, greater yet than his father. Through kings, swords, and the glittering court of Giuki, where spears shine and voices hush at Sigurd's face. Turner and Scott keep Morris's story clear for younger readers while leaving his verse to carry the hero's fate. The book is a gateway to Norse legend in English poetry.
13488-an-essay-on-medi-val-economic-teac:
George O'Brien's 1920 essay on medieval economic teaching, dedicated to the Rev. Michael Cronin of University College Dublin, explains what medieval writers meant by economic, teaching, and value. He thanks Cronin, Father Finlay, and Arthur Cox for reading manuscript and proofs, and divides his subject with care.

O'Brien shows how the virtue of liberality was understood through its opposing vices, and how a wealthy man should distribute goods indirectly, by investing in productive, labour-employing enterprises for the community's good. Trade, he argues, was justified by its end: a trader might seek profit if it accrued for the community, a view already stated in Archbishop Aelfric's Colloquy of the tenth century. The essay recovers a moral economics.
13537-the-library-of-work-and-play-garde:
Ellen Eddy Shaw's Gardening and Farming, in the Library of Work and Play for 1911, teaches children through a garden club of real boys and girls. Chapters follow the club, garden difficulties, indoor experiments, workshop work, school grounds, strawberry beds, drainage problems, cabbage troubles, and a corn contest.

George sells one hundred cabbage heads at two cents each, keeps fifty at home, and quietly gives fifty more to an orphans' home a few miles away. Lessons on roots, rootlets, and root hairs explain how plants feed, like blotters soaking ink, and why underground food must be liquid. Shaw makes farming a school subject: practical, cooperative, and full of small triumphs.
13858-the-laws-of-war-affecting-commerce:
H. Byerley Thomson, a barrister of the Inner Temple, wrote this treatise on war and trade. The second, enlarged edition appeared in 1854, after merchants welcomed the first. It asks what war does to shipping, cargo, blockade, prize, and neutral rights. Thomson draws on the practice of nations and on court decisions.

Chapters open with the commencement of war and move through commerce under arms. Thomson admits some rules rest on custom, not settled consent, yet may still join the law of nations over time. The book served shipowners, insurers, and lawyers in an age of sail and steam. It remains a source for the history of maritime law. Its plain structure aids modern readers too.
14183-there-is-no-harm-in-dancing:
W. E. Penn, an evangelist, published this 1884 lecture against dancing after delivering it to more than one hundred thousand hearers over seven years. Fathers and brothers requested the book, and Penn dedicates it to husbands, fathers, and brothers who love their wives, daughters, and sisters. Proverbs frame the argument: buy truth and sell it not, and a way that seems right may end in death.

Dancing, Penn argues, germinates in respectable parlors and grows into late hours, drink, and ruin. Balls gather young men and women of every grade, poor and rich alike, eager to impress. While girls dream, young men gather at a corner saloon still running at full steam, and only one first-class saloon in Penn's experience ever closed before the ball ended. Plain, earnest, and moralizing, the tract shows Victorian evangelism warning respectable families against a fashionable pleasure.
14184-the-ladder-to-learning:
Miss Lovechild's 1852 primer, printed in Albany, teaches the alphabet through pictures and rhymes. Each letter stands for three things at once: A for ape, Arthur, and air, B for bullock, bird, and bear. Illustrations face the verses, so a child learns letter shapes, sounds, and words together. Marks' edition keeps the format small and plain.

Simple as it looks, the ladder climbs carefully. One letter follows another in order, and each rhyme gives a young reader something to say aloud and something to see. No stories, morals, or lessons interrupt the march from A onward. Collectors value the book as a sample of mid-century American school printing, while parents still recognize its method: link a letter to a living thing, and the alphabet begins to stick.
14189-ancient-town-planning:
F. Haverfield's Ancient Town Planning, published at Oxford in 1913, traces how Greeks and Romans laid out towns. Chapters move from Babylon and early Greek efforts through the Macedonian age to Italy's origins, late republic, empire, and provincial towns. Building laws and a sequel close the argument, with an appendix on town planning in China. Photographs of Timgad streets open the volume.

Law and measurement ground the survey. A Pergamene royal law let magistrates repair ruinous houses at owners' cost, fine them besides, and clean streets while banning brickfields inside the city. Road widths outside town were fixed, with adjacent owners liable for repair. Herculaneum measures draw close debate: one writer counts under twenty-six acres, less than a sixth of Pompeii, while Haverfield argues forty or forty-five acres, with four rows of blocks. Scholarship and stone meet throughout.
14264-the-practice-and-science-of-drawin:
Harold Speed wrote this 1913 guide to drawing, with 93 plates and diagrams. It treats drawing as a craft of eye and hand, not a trick of the wrist. Speed moves from line and mass to rhythm, balance, and proportion. He covers portrait work, visual memory, and the tools of the trade. The book speaks to students who want to see truly before they mark paper.

Speed urges students to feed deeply on fine work, and to hang it where they will see it daily. At first they may love the pretty and the tricky, but honest study leads them on to better things. He warns against pure white and pure black masses, which scream and show weak restraint. The best lights keep some color, and the darkest darks are never quite colorless. The book joins practice with a calm philosophy of seeing.
14316-the-poetry-of-robert-browning:
Stopford A. Brooke wrote this 1902 study of Robert Browning's poetry, after his earlier book on Tennyson. Brooke reads Browning as a poet of human life, not of nature alone. Chapters treat Sordello, the dramas, love poems, and The Ring and the Book. He sets Browning beside Tennyson and weighs their rival strengths. The book speaks to readers who want to grasp a hard, rich poet.

Brooke lingers on Browning's imagination at play, piling gold walls, pinnacles, and meteor moons round Solomon's palace for the Queen of Sheba. He shows Browning drawn to the Renaissance, when faith gave way to doubt and old limits fell. The swift change of that age, Brooke says, fired the poet's love of varied, intense life. Womanhood, art, and passion each get a chapter. The study stays a warm, clear guide to a poet many find daunting.
14320-landscape-and-song:
E. Nesbit selected and arranged Landscape and Song, a short illustrated gift book of poems on nature and feeling. A handwritten note gives it to Annette from Uncle Tom at Christmas 1887 in Toronto, Canada. Henry J. Drane published it in London, with E. P. Dutton in New York. Poems by C. Brooke, F. T. Palgrave, Nesbit herself, and others follow in a dozen short pieces.

Seasons and moods alternate. Flower cups dream of meadow ways, April mists, and cottage gardens where wood-smoke blends with scent. A Palgrave lyric finds hills, clover slopes, pewits, wild bees in thyme, and royal heather, with youth returning on the breeze. Nesbit's lullaby bids a baby sleep while thrushes sing for flowers' sake. Autumn closes the set, with corn-laden wagons, green woods sighing winter's forecast, and souls whispering failure again. Small, pretty, and made for giving, the book suits a quiet hour.
14403-1001-questions-and-answers-on-orth:
B. A. Hathaway wrote this drill book of 1001 questions and answers on spelling and reading. It belongs to a series that covers history, geography, and other school subjects. Each item asks a short question and gives a short answer, for pupils and teachers to use aloud. Accent, punctuation, and tone all get their turn. The book aims to make reading clear, correct, and pleasing to the ear.

Early questions place the primary accent: on the first syllable in two-syllable words, and on the antepenult in longer ones. Words ending in ation take the accent on the next to last syllable. Later questions turn to the voice: pause at line ends so the measure rings clear, read a simile in a lower tone, and keep a full, even tone. The book drills the small arts that make a reader sound sure. It serves classrooms of its age.
14476-life-of-robert-browning:
William Sharp wrote this 1897 life of Robert Browning for the Great Writers series, published in London by Walter Scott. Sharp traces Browning from his Camberwell childhood to his fame as a poet.

Chapters cover his family, his father's learning, his early poems, his marriage to Elizabeth Barrett, and his later work, with notes on friends such as Landor. Sharp defends Browning's optimism and his difficult style. The biography is compact and admiring, a useful Victorian introduction before the great modern lives appeared. Sharp also wrote on Shelley and Rossetti for the same series.
1457-mistress-wilding:
Rafael Sabatini's romance of the Monmouth Rebellion follows Ruth Westmacott, called Mistress Wilding, and the men who love and imperil her in the west of England. Sir Rowland comes to her rescue, Diana schemes against her, and a forced marriage, a duel, and a counterstroke drive the plot through the troubled summer of 1685.

Sabatini writes with dash and colour, filling the tale with cavaliers, rebels, and narrow escapes. The heroine's spirit holds the centre. It is a brisk historical romance in the Sabatini manner, full of swordplay, intrigue, and honour tested under a failing cause.
14618-robert-browning:
C. H. Herford, professor of English at Manchester, wrote this 1905 life of Robert Browning for the Modern English Writers series, published by Blackwood in Edinburgh and London. The series also covered Arnold, Stevenson, and Tennyson.

Herford recalls hearing Ben Ezra read in a friend's study, then traces Browning's art through Fra Lippo Lippi, Andrea del Sarto, and the poet's search for meaning in the world. He quotes Browning's claim that the world means intensely and means good. The book is a compact critical biography, scholarly and warm, for general readers.
14716-the-art-of-soul-winning:
J. W. Mahood's 1901 handbook, specially adapted for personal workers, teaches ordinary church members how to win souls one by one. Its preface argues that a mighty revival depends less on great meetings than on earnest personal work, yet many members know nothing of a personal Pentecost and stay indifferent.

Mahood therefore gives daily studies, memory verses and Scripture to meditate on, with a plan for pastors to place a copy in every home a month before special meetings. Weekly gatherings keep workers steady. Written from a Methodist evangelist's standpoint, the book is practical, urgent and plain: a call to duty, prayer and conversation with neighbours, rather than a work of theology.
14825-our-foreigners-a-chronicle-of-amer:
Samuel P. Orth's 1920 volume in the Chronicles of America series asks how newcomers became Americans. Opening the door leads to chapters on the American stock, Black Americans, utopias in America, the Irish influx and the Teutonic tide.

The call of the land and city building follow, with chapters on people from the Orient, racial infiltration and the guarded door. Orth writes as a textbook historian of his time, and some of his terms now read as dated. Still, the book gives a clear, early survey of immigration, settlement and the debate over who belonged in the United States.
1487-the-perfect-wagnerite-a-commentary-:
Bernard Shaw's commentary reads Wagner's Ring cycle as a drama of ideas rather than a fairy tale of gods and gold. Wotan, Brunnhilde, and Siegfried become figures of power, law, love, and revolution, and Shaw argues that the cycle's true subject is the modern world and its coming change.

Shaw writes with wit and force, praising Wagner's music drama while quarrelling with its philosophy, especially in the final opera. The book, first written for German readers, helped English audiences take Wagner seriously as a thinker. It remains a bracing, partisan guide to the Ring.
14873-instructions-on-modern-american-br:
G. B. N. Tower, civil and mechanical engineer and former chief engineer of the United States Navy, wrote this 1874 treatise for young engineers learning bridge building. Illustrated with four plates and thirty figures, it gives practical applications, examples, estimates of quantities and valuable tables.

Its preface admits the book is an aid, not a substitute for larger works. A first portion treats the strains to which bridges are subject, then shows how American practice meets them in iron and timber. Tower, late Chandler instructor at Dartmouth, writes for the classroom and the field. The volume now serves as a clear record of nineteenth-century American bridge craft.
14917-the-wings-of-the-morning:
Louis Tracy's 1903 adventure was published by Grosset and Dunlap. It takes its epigraph from Psalm 139, on taking the wings of the morning and dwelling in the uttermost parts of the sea, where God's hand still leads. A frontispiece shows a woman catching a man's arm as he steps half a pace before her to ward off danger.

The wreck of the Sirdar, the survivors, discoveries and Rainbow Island open the tale, with Iris to the rescue following. Tracy, author of A Son of the Immortals and The Stowaways, writes island adventure with romance and suspense. Shipwreck, survival and a strange island drive a story that balances peril with faith in guidance.
15175-a-century-of-wrong:
Issued by F. W. Reitz, state secretary of the South African Republic, with a preface by W. T. Stead, this 1900 book states the Boer case on the eve of war. Chapters trace the Cape, Natal, the Orange Free State, and the Transvaal, then the conventions of 1881 and 1884 and two periods of capitalistic jingoism. Appendices print dispatches.

Reitz argues that Britain wronged the republics for a century, and Stead frames the book as a last message to the world. The argument is partisan, which is its historical value. Students of the Boer War will find it essential reading for the Boer side of a bitter dispute.
1519-much-ado-about-nothing:
Shakespeare's Messina comedy, in this improved text, again pairs Claudio and Hero, whose wedding Don John wrecks with a lie about Hero's honour. Beatrice and Benedick, enemies in wit whom friends trick into confessing love. A night watch of blundering constables overhears the plot and saves Hero's name.

Masked dances, garden eavesdropping, and a wedding turned to accusation give the play its sparkle and its sting. Beatrice's demand that Benedick kill Claudio marks its serious heart. Much Ado is Shakespeare's most balanced comedy, where laughter and honour sit side by side.
1520-much-ado-about-nothing:
Set in Messina after a war, Much Ado follows two pairs of lovers: Claudio and Hero, whose wedding is wrecked by a villain's lie. Beatrice and Benedick, witty enemies tricked into love by their friends. Don John, the bastard prince, plots against Hero's honour, and only a watchman's blundering arrests save the day.

Through masked balls, eavesdropping, and a wedding that ends in accusation, Shakespeare mixes farce with near-tragedy. Beatrice and Benedick's merry war remains the play's delight. It is a sparkling comedy about gossip, honour, and how easily a good name can be lost and won back.
15220-the-life-and-work-of-susan-b-antho:
Ida Husted Harper's first volume on Susan B. Anthony, published in 1899, tells the life and work of the suffrage leader through fifty years, with her speeches, letters, and letters from contemporaries. Portraits and pictures of homes illustrate the book, dedicated to woman, for whose freedom Anthony gave noble endeavor.

Harper, writing during Anthony's lifetime, drew on unpublished records and personal memory to place the reform in history. The volume traces Anthony's growth from early activism to national leadership. Readers interested in women's rights will find it a rich, firsthand biography of a great reformer.
15256-the-young-seigneur-or-nation-makin:
Wilfrid Châteauclair, the pen name of William Douw Lighthall, wrote this 1888 Montreal novel with a bold aim: to map a future for the Canadian nation, drifting without a plan. A lesser aim was to make French Canada's atmosphere clear to English readers, through a lofty French-Canadian hero. The writer calls himself an old Tory and old Liberal.

The book is not, he insists, a party diatribe, though parties are dead to him and he stands in universal opposition. Nation-making runs through its pages as idea and story. Canadian readers will find the novel thoughtful, idealistic, and rooted in its moment.
15363-carving-and-serving:
Mrs. D. A. Lincoln, author of The Boston Cook Book, wrote this 1906 guide to carving and serving, first copyrighted in 1886. Contents run from general directions to sirloin, rump, fillet, round, leg of mutton, saddle of venison, and haunch, then through fowl, fish, salads, soups, pies, and puddings. Utensils close the book.

Lincoln teaches how to cut each joint cleanly, serve each dish well, and slice to the right thickness. Her tone is practical and confident, aimed at hosts and cooks. Kitchen historians will find the guide a detailed record of formal dining in its day.
15460-a-course-in-wood-turning:
Archie S. Milton and Otto K. Wohlers published this course in wood turning in Milwaukee in 1919, with the Bruce Publishing Company. It treats turning as both a commercial craft and a school subject, and it opens with the elements of success in the trade. Plates and chapters guide a pupil from first principles to finished work.

Chapters cover the lathe, its care and speed, pulley sizes, and setting up shafting, then tools: gouge, parting tool, and scrapers, with grinding and whetting. Spindle turning, centering and clamping stock, and spiral turning follow, with methods for fastening stock. A transcriber's note lists small misspellings kept from the original. The course remains a practical manual for shop classes and home workshops alike.
15482-the-primrose-ring:
Ruth Sawyer published this children's fantasy in 1915 with Harper and Brothers, illustrated, and dedicated to the little mother who once wove a primrose ring for her. The storyteller, sitting in the shadow of the market place, asks a question. Would any of it have happened if Trustee Day had not fallen on April 30? That day is May Eve, a bewitched and bewitching time.

Margaret MacLean, in charge of Ward C at Saint Margaret's Free Hospital for Children, buys primroses that morning. She buys them from a flower seller at the street corner. Primroses are gentle flowers, the tale says, used by faeries for thousands of years to work magic. From that purchase, strange and tender happenings follow among sick children, trustees, and a hospital built by charity. The book blends fairy lore with hospital life, warmly and without sentimentality.
15607-family-pride-or-purified-by-suffer:
Mary J. Holmes, author of Dora Deane, The English Orphans, and Lena Rivers, published this long domestic novel, Family Pride, or Purified by Suffering. Chapter one opens at the farmhouse in Silverton, Massachusetts, with Uncle Ephraim Barlow, deacon of the orthodox church. He clings to old-time customs and looks with little toleration on what he calls new-fangled notions.

Born and reared among Bay State rocks and hills, Ephraim grew into manhood with rough points on his character, yet beautiful and grand as a whole, like wild New England scenery. None knew him but to respect him, and few would be missed more at church, where Sunday after Sunday he walked up the middle aisle to his seat before the altar. Later pages follow Katy's sailing, Helen, and Mark Ray's flattery. Holmes writes a sentimental novel of pride, suffering, and purification.
1561-pagan-and-christian-creeds-their-or:
Edward Carpenter's Pagan and Christian Creeds argues that the world's religions are lame attempts to represent one root fact: the central universal life. Creeds, rituals, and ceremonies, he holds, symbolise in rude form the redemption and fulfilment of our most intimate natures, whether pagan or Christian.

Carpenter traces shared myths of dying gods, saviours, and sacred seasons, and asks what Christianity owes to older faiths. His tone is earnest and speculative. The book is a classic of early comparative religion, dated in method but still stimulating for readers interested in myth and faith.
15769-in-the-wars-of-the-roses-a-story-f:
A boys' historical tale by Everett Evelyn-Green, issued in 1901. Evelyn-Green, a popular writer of school and history stories, sets his plot in the Wars of the Roses. A young hero, Paul, meets robbers, shelters, and strange encounters on the road. Notes at the end help young readers with the history.

Paul's kinsman, peril, and a rally of the Red Rose carry the middle chapters. The tragedy of Tewkesbury and the avenging of a prince close the tale. King Henry, his queen, and the little prince appear in the prologue's pageant. The book delights as a gallant introduction to a tangled age: loyalty, danger, and a boy learning to be true.
15796-joy-in-the-morning:
A 1919 novel by Mary Raymond Shipman Andrews, issued by Charles Scribner's Sons in New York. Andrews, author of Bob and the Guides and Crosses of War, writes of war and home. A frontispiece shows a man pinning the thing men die for on the shabby coat of a guide. The title promises joy after sorrow.

Soldiers, guides, and the women who wait for them fill the chapters. War's crosses and a guide's courage test love and duty. Andrews writes with warmth for ordinary heroism, far from grand strategy. The novel endures as a wartime romance of the home front: grief borne bravely, and morning after night.
15820-a-book-for-the-young:
A moral book for children by Sarah French, writing as A Lady, printed in Saint John, New Brunswick, in 1856. French dedicates the little book, by permission, to the Honourable Mrs. Manners Sutton. Her preface calls it a second effort from her pen, offered with deference and respect. J. and A. McMillan printed it at Phoenix House on Prince William Street.

Short tales and lessons teach courtesy, truth, and duty in plain, kind prose. French writes for young readers in a colonial town, where manners mattered. The stories stay short enough for reading aloud. The book gives a glimpse of mid-century Canadian childhood: earnest, polite, and guided by a lady's hand.
15866-humanly-speaking:
A book of essays by Samuel McChord Crothers, issued by Houghton Mifflin in Boston and New York in 1912. Crothers, a Unitarian minister and essayist, writes with gentle wit on human nature. Earlier books like Among Friends and The Gentle Reader made his name. This volume gathers fresh pieces in the same humane manner.

Essays include In the Hands of a Receiver, The Contemporaneousness of Rome, and The American Temperament. Crothers treats business, travel, and books as moral subjects, finding humour in everyday folly. His tone stays kind, never bitter. The book appeals to readers who like essays that think aloud: clear, funny, and quietly wise.
15984-washington-irving:
A life of Washington Irving by Charles Dudley Warner, in the American Men of Letters series. Houghton, Mifflin and Company issued the fifth thousand in Boston in 1884, copyrighted 1881, printed at the Riverside Press, Cambridge. Warner, a friend of letters, treats Irving with affection and clear judgement. The book belongs to a series of brief American biographies.

Chapters run from preliminary and boyhood, through manhood and a first visit to Europe, to society and Salmagundi. The Knickerbocker period follows, then life in Europe again. Warner weighs Irving's humour, his histories, and his place as America's first man of letters. The life still serves as a friendly introduction: Irving, genial and pioneering, in short compass.
16073-wreaths-of-friendship-a-gift-for-t:
T. S. Arthur and F. C. Woodworth published Wreaths of Friendship in New York in 1851 as a gift book for the young. Their preface stops readers at a mock turnpike gate, joking that they want no toll, only a few words before the first story. The authors tease the habit of apologizing for writing at all, then get on with twining their wreaths, tokens of affection in prose and verse.

Stories and poems for children follow, meant to teach kindness, honesty, and good feeling without dull preaching. Illustrations, including Tokens of Affection, decorate the volume in gift-book style. Modern readers can enjoy it as a charming relic of Victorian children's publishing and family values.
1613-count-bunker-being-a-bald-yet-verac:
J. Storer Clouston's Count Bunker continues the adventures of two gentlemen first met in The Lunatic at Large, now chronicled baldly yet veraciously. A supposed count arrives in English society, where polite interest masks sharp curiosity, and imposture, romance, and a run of comic scrapes follow.

Clouston writes with dry, Edwardian wit, letting his rogues talk their way into and out of trouble. The chronicle is light and episodic. Count Bunker is a pleasant sequel for readers who enjoy tales of plausible scoundrels loose among the respectable. Readers who enjoy rogue tales will find it light fun.
16317-the-art-of-public-speaking:
J. Berg Esenwein and Dale Carnagey wrote The Art of Public Speaking for the Home Correspondence School in Springfield, Massachusetts, copyright 1915. Esenwein, author of guides to holding an audience and writing stories, joined Carnagey, a teacher of public speaking in Y.M.C.A. schools and banking classes across the East. The book belongs to the Writer's Library edited by Esenwein and is dedicated to F. Arthur Metcalf.

Its opening chapter tackles acquiring confidence before an audience, the fear every speaker knows first. Later chapters would train voice, gesture, and argument step by step. The book remains a landmark of American self-help, from the teacher who became Dale Carnegie. Speakers today can still learn from its plain, practical counsel.
16579-on-the-art-of-reading:
Sir Arthur Quiller-Couch gathers his Cambridge lectures on reading in this volume, first issued in 1920. Lectures weigh apprehension against comprehension, children's reading, reading for exams, a school of English, the value of Greek and Latin, reading the Bible, selection, and the use of masterpieces. The opening lecture, given in October 1916, starts from Aristotle on pity for acts done in ignorance.

Quiller-Couch writes with wit and warmth, urging readers to read slowly and well. The lectures suit students and teachers of English, but any keen reader will enjoy them. The book stands as a classic defense of reading as an art, not a chore.
16658-piano-and-song:
Friedrich Wieck, father and teacher of Clara Wieck Schumann, wrote this book on how to teach, learn, and judge musical performance, translated in Boston in 1875. Chapters cover elementary piano teaching, an evening at Herr Zach's, many students and few players, the pedal, singing teachers, thoughts on singing, and musical talent. A musical tea-party and secrets fill the lighter chapters.

Wieck died in 1873, and his translator hoped his views would serve America as they had Germany. The book is practical and opinionated, full of studio wisdom. Piano teachers and students will find a charming, stern guide from a master teacher's age.
1675-new-forces-in-old-china-an-inevitab:
Arthur Judson Brown writes on new forces in old China, arguing that an inevitable awakening was under way as reform, missions, trade, and education pressed on the empire. Brown, a missionary secretary, knew China at first hand. Brown, secretary of the Presbyterian Board of Foreign Missions, visited China often.

He describes railways, schools, and new ideas alongside old customs, and he predicts change that few in the West then foresaw. The book captures Western hopes and fears about China at the turn of the century. His awakening theme looked to schools, railways, and a new press to change old China.
16900-the-first-book-of-farming:
Charles L. Goodrich, a farmer and expert in the Bureau of Plant Industry, wrote this 1905 first book of farming, issued by Doubleday, Page in Garden City with pictures. Part one gives the general rules of plant growth: roots, soils, soil water, and how soils were made, with chapters on root uses, soil kinds, texture, and water held in soil. Later parts take up animals, tools, and buildings.

Goodrich writes for beginners in plain, orderly lessons, each with clear heads and short points. He links plant, soil, and water in a system a new farmer can grasp. The book still serves as a friendly first guide to farming science, and as a record of how America taught farming in 1905.
16973-studies-in-song:
Algernon Charles Swinburne wrote this 1880 book of verse, issued by Chatto and Windus in London and dedicated to Mrs. Lynn Linton. Contents run from a song for the centenary of Walter Savage Landor into a grand chorus of birds from Aristophanes. Off shore, after nine years, and a portrait of Felice Orsini follow. Evening on the Broads, the emperor's progress, and the fourteenth of July appear. The launch of the Livadia, six years old, a parting song, and by the North Sea close the set.

Swinburne sings in rich, musical lines, praising Landor, birds, seas, and history with equal fire. His verse is bold, sonorous, and full of classical echoes. Readers who love Victorian lyric poetry will find a varied, high-spirited collection, best read aloud for its sound and its sweep.
16987-craftsmanship-in-teaching:
William Chandler Bagley's 1911 book treats teaching as a craft to be learned with care, not a knack to be left to chance. Twelve chapters cover optimism, skill in the force, tests of good oversight, the link of boss and teacher, and the place of drill, study habits, and clear aims. Science and literature each get a chapter on how they should be taught.

Bagley writes for teachers and heads of schools, in a firm, hopeful voice that prizes hard work and plain goals. His plea for the definite in schooling still sparks debate today. The book is a classic of early US teacher training, and it reads well beside modern talk about what makes a good teacher.
17166-a-life-of-st-john-for-the-young:
George Ludington Weed's 1900 life of St. John for the young gathers only scenes where John is named or plainly present. Gospel tales, Acts, John's letters, and Revelation supply the known events, while old traditions that fit his character fill gaps with care. Weed skips scenes shared by all twelve disciples, so the book stays on John's own path.

The style is simple and warm, made for children and new readers of the Bible. John's youth, his closeness to Jesus, and his later years as a teacher of love stand out. Families and Sunday schools will find a clear, gentle life of the disciple called beloved, told without hard words.
17201-is-life-worth-living:
William Hurrell Mallock's 1879 book, inscribed to John Ruskin, asks whether life is worth living in a new, modern sense. The question, Mallock says, is not whether humans feel happiness, but whether its higher forms rest on a lasting base. Modern thought, he fears, strips away the very parts wise men called needful, and no past age stripped them quite this way.

Mallock writes as a Victorian critic of doubt, in clear, earnest prose with scripture texts at its head. His book suits readers of Victorian faith, philosophy, and pessimism. It asks, with force and care, what remains of life's worth when old beliefs fade, and it still sparks debate today.
17289-the-dance-by-an-antiquary-historic:
An anonymous antiquary's 1911 sketch traces dancing in pictures from 3300 B.C. to 1911 A.D., dedicated to Dr. Eleanor Maxwell. The author calls it a summary of posture, not a full history, since a dance cannot be caught in one picture. Chapters cover Egyptian, Assyrian, Hebrew, and Phoenician dance, Greek dances like the geranos and hormos, and Etruscan, Roman, and later forms.

Pictures from tombs, vases, and museums show costume, pose, and tools of dance through the ages. The text stays elementary by design, pointing readers to larger works on single dances. Dance lovers will find a charming, well pictured primer on how peoples moved, from ritual steps to court minuets.
17307-principles-of-teaching:
Adam S. Bennion's 1921 Principles of Teaching, made for quorum instructors and auxiliary class teachers of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, asks how to teach better. Chapters cover purposes, joys, personality, attainment, native tendencies, individual differences, attention, and interest. Organizing a lesson, illustrating it, aiming it, applying it, and asking good questions each get a turn.

Bennion closes on discipline, class spirit, and conversion as the real test of teaching. His tone is practical and warm, with a bibliography for further study. Teachers in any setting will find plain, useful counsel on planning, holding attention, and helping pupils learn and live what they learn.
17318-public-speaking:
Clarence Stratton, director of English in a Cleveland high school, published this manual with Henry Holt in 1920, with a further printing dated January 1924. He opens with a bold claim: no other means of communication has ever matched the spoken word in value. The book then works through the craft in order, from speech itself, the voice, and words and sentences to openings, closings, and gathering material.

Later chapters cover planning, outlining, explaining, proving and persuading, refuting, debating, and speaking on special occasions, with a chapter on dramatics and appendixes. Readers get a schoolroom guide to standing up and speaking clearly, practical rather than theoretical. It still reads as a sensible handbook for anyone who must plan, shape, and deliver a talk.
17357-the-quickening:
Francis Lynde's 1906 novel, pictured by E. M. Ashe, opens with a revival in Paradise Valley led by the Reverend Silas, in a chapter called Bethesda. Later chapters follow the Dabneys of Deer Trace, blue blood and red, a backslider, a race to the swift, and a trumpet call. Biblical titles like Absalom, my son, the wine-press of wrath, and a soul in shackles mark the hero's road.

Lynde mixes mountain romance with a preacher's tale of awakening, in rich, earnest prose. The frontispiece shows Tom fronting the firebrand Dabney like a man. Readers who like early-1900s novels of faith, family, and mountain life will find a long, colorful story of a soul quickened to new life.
17476-talks-on-talking:
Grenville Kleiser, formerly instructor in public speaking at Yale Divinity School, published this book with Funk and Wagnalls in September 1916. Kleiser, author of guides to speaking in public and to self-confidence in speech, turns here from the platform to daily talk. Chapters cover the art of talking, types of talkers, talkers and talking, phrases for talkers, and the speaking voice.

Later sections teach how to tell a story, talk in salesmanship, handle mannerisms, and speak in public. The advice is plain and practical, aimed at readers who want to be clear, pleasant, and effective in conversation. Readers get an early twentieth-century manual of talk as a social art, still useful for its stress on listening, brevity, and voice.
1753-swan-song:
An old actor named Svetlovidov is left alone in an empty theatre after the audience has gone. He talks to the prompter about the roles he will never play again. Left alone after the audience has gone, Svetlovidov talks to the prompter, remembers his roles, and faces the fact that his art and his life are both nearly over.

The piece runs barely half an hour in performance. It holds Chekhov's whole view of the theatre: glory remembered, youth gone, and a man who can still move an audience of one. It is often paired with The Sea-Gull in collections. It shows the younger Chekhov already writing about age and loss with the restraint that marks his later plays.
17571-piano-tuning:
J. Cree Fischer wrote this guide to piano tuning, subtitled a simple and accurate method for amateurs, published by Dover Publications in New York. Copyright in 1907 belonged to Theo. Presser, and the Dover edition, first published in 1975, republishes the original work. Canadian and British editions followed through Toronto and London publishers.

Readers learn how an amateur can tune a piano step by step, with accuracy rather than guesswork. Fischer writes plainly for the home tuner, not the professional. The book suits piano owners, students, and anyone curious about how a piano is kept in tune.
17608-an-introduction-to-the-study-of-br:
Arthur Symons wrote this introduction to the study of Robert Browning, born May 7, 1812. It is a new edition, revised and enlarged, first issued in 1906 and reprinted in 1916 by Dent in London, Paris, and Toronto. Symons dedicates the little book to George Meredith, novelist and poet, with deep respect and admiration for an illustrious contemporary. A Landor remark praising Browning as a great poet indeed fronts the volume.

Chapters cover the general characteristics of Browning's work and the characteristics of his poems, with an appendix giving a bibliography, reprints of discarded prefaces, and an index to poems. Readers get a critic's guide to a difficult poet, written by a fellow poet. The book still helps newcomers find their way into Browning.
17888-comfort-pease-and-her-gold-ring:
Mary E. Wilkins wrote this 1895 tale of a New England girl named Comfort Pease, who was named for her aunt and given a gold ring and a gold dollar for her name. The ring, too big for a child, was kept in her mother's rosewood work-box with her best brooch and a lock of her dead baby brother's hair.

Comfort longs to wear the ring, and the story follows her small hopes, her pride, and the quiet ways of a thrifty farm home. Wilkins, famed for her plain tales of New England folk, tells it with dry humor and a keen eye for home detail. It is a gentle, short story of childhood want, and of how a small gift can loom large in a child's mind.
18045-rudyard-kipling:
John Palmer wrote this short critical study of Rudyard Kipling, first printed in 1915 by Henry Holt in New York. Palmer takes Kipling's Indian tales in three groups: tales of Simla, Anglo-Indian tales, and tales of native India, with Kim standing above them all.

Chapters move from Simla and the sahib to native India, Soldiers Three, the day's work, the finer grain, and the poems. Palmer reads Kipling as journalist and word-painter, and he treats the politics as much as the art. The book is a brisk, early verdict on a Nobel laureate, useful for readers who want to meet Kipling with a guide.
18093-from-the-valley-of-the-missing:
Grace Miller White wrote From the Valley of the Missing in 1911, printed by Grosset and Dunlap, with scenes from the Fox film version. White, author of Tess of the Storm Country, sets this tale on a canal in late October, where mules haul boats and hard men rule.

A canalman with red hair, a scarred throat, and a brutal temper drives the plot, while Ann Shellington foresees evil and a lost child waits to be found. White writes melodrama with a sure hand, full of pathos and pluck. It is a rousing, old-style tale of the canal country, best read as a period piece of stage and screen.
18095-successful-methods-of-public-speak:
Grenville Kleiser wrote Successful Methods of Public Speaking as a guide for speakers who wished to learn from the best. Kleiser, author of many books on speech, gathers model speeches, a history of speaking, and lessons with extracts for study.

Chapters teach how to build mental power, win confidence, read and declaim, and argue and win, with notes on humor and holding a crowd. Kleiser urges students to profit from great speakers, not to copy them. The book is a plain, earnest manual, still useful for students of rhetoric, and a relic of the age of the lyceum.
18096-the-social-history-of-smoking:
G. L. Apperson wrote The Social History of Smoking, first printed in London in 1914 by Martin Secker. Apperson, author of Bygone London Life, traces tobacco from its first English pipes to its fall from fashion.

Chapters run from the first pipes and tobacco triumphant to Cavalier and Roundhead smokers, the Restoration, and Georgian days when smoking grew unfashionable. Pepys and Evelyn give few hints, yet tobacco held its place in public resorts. Apperson writes with antiquarian charm and wit. It is a delightful social history, best for readers who like manners, smoke, and old London.
18134-sixteen-months-in-four-german-pris:
Henry C. Mahoney narrated Sixteen Months in Four German Prisons, chronicled by Frederick A. Talbot, from page images held by the Toronto library. Mahoney, arrested as a spy, passed through Wesel, Sennelager, Klingelputz, and Ruhleben in the Great War.

Chapters run from arrest and committal to a secret midnight trial, waiting to be shot, and the black hole of Germany. Gaps in the print, marked in the text, hint at words cut by censor or printer. Mahoney writes with plain, bitter force. It is a harrowing prison memoir, and a stark witness to German prison camps in wartime.
18171-the-crucifixion-of-philip-strong:
The Reverend Charles M. Sheldon wrote The Crucifixion of Philip Strong in 1899, printed in New York and London by Street and Smith. Sheldon, author of In His Steps, here gives a minister a hard choice, and lets the cost of faith play out in full.

Philip Strong sits in his study, two letters in hand, unable to decide what is best to do. He calls his wife Sarah upstairs, as he does only in great distress. The tale that follows tests pulpit, home, and conscience. Sheldon writes with earnest, plain force. It is a moving novel of Christian duty, in the style that made Sheldon famous.
18399-the-shipwreck-a-story-for-the-youn:
Rev. Joseph Spillmann, a Jesuit priest, wrote this story for the young, translated from the German by Mary Richards Gray and published in a second edition by B. Herder in St. Louis and Freiburg in 1910, with copyright in 1906. The Shipwreck stands as volume seven of Tales of Foreign Lands, edited by Spillmann.

Chapters follow two young friends, sad tidings, aboard the St. George, the priest of the god of the golden fish, the city, the Chinese New Year, an unexpected departure, and a very real danger. A new plan, a hurricane, being stranded, and at last close the tale. The story opens at the mouth of the great river of Canton, among islands where Hong Kong's fine harbor made it the most important. Young readers get adventure abroad: sea, storm, China, and friendship tested by wreck.
18500-the-complete-works-of-robert-burns:
This Boston edition gathers the complete works of Robert Burns, containing his poems, songs, and correspondence, with a new life of the poet and notices critical and biographical by Allan Cunningham. Phillips, Sampson and Company published it in Boston in 1855, with J. C. Derby in New York, elegantly illustrated.

The volume is dedicated to Archibald Hastie, and its poems, epitaphs, and songs keep the indentations of the original book, as the transcriber notes. Burns, Scotland's national poet, speaks here in full: love songs, satires, and letters together, with Cunningham's life to guide a reader through the man behind the verse.
18751-a-text-book-of-assaying:
C. and J. J. Beringer's text-book of assaying, in its ninth edition of 1904 from Charles Griffin of London, serves those connected with mines. J. J. Beringer, principal of the Camborne Mining School, revised the work, which carries many diagrams and tables.

Its preface warns that assaying means more than silver and gold or furnace work alone, and that the line between assayers and analysts grows harder to draw. The sixth edition had added matter on gold, cyanides, and nickel with a much enlarged index, and the ninth followed little more than a year after its predecessor. The book aims to be a handy, practical guide for daily work at the mine.
18768-the-sky-is-falling:
Lester del Rey's novel, first published by Ace Books in 1973 from Galaxy material of 1954 and 1963, opens with Dave Hanson waking from death. He wakes into a world of sulfur, burned hair, and incense. A shorter version had run in 1954 as 'No More Stars' under the name Charles Satterfield.

Summoned by his true name, Dave finds his breath burning and his tongue tripping over a language that is not English. Around him, voices debate salamanders, succubi, and high-frequency rays, all while the sky itself falls. The tale sets a modern man down among magic workers who must hold a breaking heaven together, with reason as his only weapon.
18900-a-text-book-of-the-history-of-pain:
John C. Van Dyke's text-book of the history of painting, published by Longmans, Green in 1909, offers concise, teachable art history for schools and colleges. Van Dyke, professor of art history at Rutgers, avoids archaeological disputes and aesthetic theories, giving the main facts as settled by the best authorities.

Chapters run from Egyptian, Chaldaeo-Assyrian, Greek, Etruscan, and Roman painting through Italian schools from early Christian times to 1894, then French, Spanish, Flemish, Dutch, German, British, and American painting. Illustrations serve as sight-help to the text, and each chapter lists principal works and where to find them, for students traveling in Europe.
18927-the-uttermost-farthing:
Mrs. Belloc Lowndes published this novel in 1910, in a Leipzig copyright edition for English readers abroad. Its central figures are Laurence Vanderlyn, an unpaid attaché at the American Embassy in Paris, and Margaret Pargeter, an Englishwoman he has loved for seven years. The story opens as the two plan a secret step they had long sworn never to take.

From that Paris railway platform, the novel follows a love held back by duty, reputation, and the rules of their social world. Lowndes watches how a long, unsatisfied attachment strains both people, and what a single rash decision costs them. Readers get a tense story of private feeling against public standing, told with close attention to motive and consequence.
18986-response-in-the-living-and-non-liv:
Jagadis Chunder Bose, a professor at Presidency College in Calcutta, wrote this 1902 science book on how living and non-living things answer a stimulus. He argues that metals, plants, and animal tissue show like patterns of response to touch, light, and electric shock. His case rests on lab tests, not on analogy alone.

Bose reports trials on tin and other metals, on plant tissue, and on the retina, tracking fatigue, recovery, and the effect of poisons and heat. Charts and plates record each test in detail. Readers get an early, bold claim for unity in nature, from a pioneer of plant science in colonial India.
19138-resonance-in-singing-and-speaking:
Thomas Fillebrown, a Harvard professor of dentistry and oral surgery, wrote this third edition on resonance in singing and speaking, published in 1911. He draws on surgery and voice teaching, dedicating the book to his first voice instructor, William Haskell Stockbridge, pupil of Vannuccini. The aim is a focused, ringing tone.

Fillebrown explains the soft palate, hard palate, teeth, and nasal and head cavities as resonating chambers, and claims a passage between face and forehead cavities that shapes tone. Larger openings, he argues, give broader tone. Readers get a clear, scientific voice manual for singers and speakers.
19258-tom-swift-and-the-electronic-hydro:
Victor Appleton the Second wrote this 1961 Tom Swift Junior tale about the electronic hydrolung, a device for breathing under water. Tom and Bud plan a search trip in the Sky Queen, while Tom's father reports computer results pointing to a high plateau of the Atlantic Ridge near St. Paul's Rocks, at depths of one to three hundred feet.

A pirate missile, an undersea survey, an invisible sub, and a porpoise tag fill the chapters, with models, globes, and a private television network in the Swift office. Readers get a brisk science adventure of invention, teamwork, and undersea danger for young readers.
19370-ullr-uprising:
H. Beam Piper wrote this science fiction serial, Ullr Uprising, printed in Space Science Fiction in February and March 1953. On Ullr, a harsh world of silica, charcoal burnings, and nuclear furnaces, Terrans sing of heathen geeks in no breeks, while red and yellow both mean danger and blood. A Company army general surveys the scene.

An armor tender rocks on contragravity over yellow-green skies, while Niflheim's fluorine air would kill any human at once. The Ullr Company brings synthetic fuel and power plants to a planet where nothing fit to eat grows. Readers get a gritty colonial revolt tale of greed, pride, and war on an unforgiving world.
19384-on-christmas-day-in-the-evening:
Grace S. Richmond wrote this 1910 Christmas story, On Christmas Day in the Evening, with pictures by Charles M. Relyea. It follows families gathering to deck an old church at North Estabrook for Christmas, with laurel ropes, reluctant gentlemen, and a sharp-tongued sister-in-law in Russian sables. The front piece praises imagination as the way changes come.

Sam Burnett orders Edson Fernald and Charles Wetmore about as they sweat off coats to hang greens, while Mrs. Oliver doubts that stubborn small-town folk can be won over. Readers get a warm Christmas tale of family, church, and the work of making a holiday.
19474-uller-uprising:
Beam Piper wrote this science fiction novel of revolt on the planet Uller, first published in the early nineteen fifties. This Ace edition adds a new introduction by John Carr. A trading company, its troops, and local peoples collide when lorry hangars fall and panic spreads through the ranks.

Officers such as Colonel Cheng-Li try to calm frightened men while a general warns that the company is finished. Piper's tale of colony, profit, and native resistance is a classic of the field, sharp on how empires talk to themselves when control slips.
19493-the-head-voice-and-other-problems-:
D. A. Clippinger wrote these practical talks on singing, on the head voice and other problems of tone. He explains how the vocal cords answer the thought of pitch, and how the throat and mouth must stay free of strain if tone is to ring pure.

When rigidity grips the throat, he warns, the voice turns throaty and dull; when the vocal cavity vibrates in sympathy with pitch, tone gains beauty. The book's exercises, gathered in the text and in companion files, made it a staple for teachers of voice.
19528-sixty-years-of-california-song:
Margaret Blake-Alverson wrote this memoir of sixty years of song in California, published in Oakland in the early nineteen teens. She recalls parties, birthdays, and deathbeds where singing bound friends together, from a home gathering in nineteen seven to a last song by a dying friend's bed.

Her motto runs through the book: men must work, love, forgive, and sing, then step forth to meet what comes, still singing. The memoir is both a personal record and a social history of music in early California homes. One memory follows a San Francisco music house, Sherman, Clay and Company, until fire wipes out its stock.
19552-the-plattsburg-manual-a-handbook-f:
O. O. Ellis and E. B.
