Sheckley's tag line gives the joke its edge: if easy payment plans were to be truly efficient, patrons' lifetimes had to be extended. The tale satirizes a world where debt outlives desire. Fans of Sheckley will enjoy a sharp, funny story about wealth, worry, and the price of plenty.
29481-the-fifth-string:
John Philip Sousa, better known for marches, wrote this 1902 novel about Diotti, a violinist whose coming to America stirred more than usual interest. The Bowen-Merrill Company of Indianapolis printed it, with pictures by Howard Chandler Christy. On the night before Diotti's debut in New York, he shines at a gathering hosted by Mrs. Llewellyn, a social leader and devoted patron of the art.

Diotti's marvelous success in the leading capitals of Europe, and his brilliant writings on his instrument, precede him across the sea. The novel turns on art, fame, and the price of genius. Readers of musical fiction will find a charming, period tale from the pen of America's march king.
29528-the-camp-fire-girls-in-the-mountai:
Jane L. Stewart's Camp Fire Girls in the Mountains, fourth in the series and printed in 1914 by Saalfield of Chicago, Akron, and New York, tells Bessie King's strange adventure. Under Miss Eleanor Mercer's care, the girls live with no aid but their own, doing all the camp work, even the rough work no previous camp had asked of them. A frontispiece shows a motor boat racing to and fro, ruining any swim.

Chapters move from peaceful days through forebodings of trouble to a new plan. The girls learn self-reliance, teamwork, and courage in the mountains. Young readers and fans of girls' series fiction will find a wholesome, adventurous tale of camp life a century ago.
29532-six-centuries-of-painting:
Randall Davies surveyed six centuries of painting in this volume, printed in London by T. C. and E. C. Jack. Its contents open with the Tuscan schools: Cimabue, Giotto, the earlier and later quattrocentists, Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo, and Raffaello. Venetian schools follow, with the Vivarini and Bellini, Tiziano, Veronese, and Tintoretto, then the Spanish school.

A frontispiece shows Vittore Pisano, called Pisanello, with St. Anthony and St. George from the National Gallery in London. Davies writes for general readers, tracing schools and masters in clear order. Students of art history will find a readable, well-illustrated survey of European painting from its medieval roots to its later glories.
29625-teething-ring:
James Causey's short tale opens with Melinda at home, wearing a new Chinese red housecoat, nails lacquered scarlet, and Harry Junior asleep like an angel. A little man at the door, a man of five feet, bald and gleaming, with a young-old face, beams that he has geegaws for information. He offers portable force-field generators and a neural distorter, and asks if this is a Class IV culture.

Causey's tag line warns that anyone can err, but in a lofty society, an error proves far more disastrous. Melinda, lately engrossed in a soap opera, must judge a peddler from the stars. Fans of comic science fiction will enjoy a sly tale of advanced toys in an ordinary home.
29659-manual-of-american-grape-growing:
U. P. Hedrick wrote this Manual of American Grape-Growing in the Rural Manuals series edited by L. H. Bailey, beside manuals of gardening, farm animals, fruit insects, weeds, and pruning. Its chapters cover training the grape in eastern America, grape pruning on the Pacific coast, European grapes in the East, grapes under glass, and more. The book serves growers who must match vine, soil, and climate.

Hedrick writes with the practical care of an experiment station man, giving methods a grower can follow row by row. The manual belongs to an age when American viticulture was finding its own grapes and ways. Readers of horticulture and farm history will find a thorough, usable guide to growing grapes in America.
29692-when-the-west-was-young:
Frederick R. Bechdolt's When the West Was Young, printed in 1938 by D. Appleton-Century of New York and London with copyright in 1922, gathers true tales of the frontier West. Its contents run from how Death Valley was named and Joaquin Murieta through Tombstone and Tombstone's wild oats. The show-down, the passing of John Ringo, John Slaughter's way, Cochise, and one against many follow.

Bechdolt writes of men who sought sanctuary in arid solitudes, speaking slowly, in words that came hard. A picture shows John Slaughter gathering a great herd. Readers of western history will find a vivid, story-driven account of outlaws, lawmen, and Apaches in the West's young days.
29926-hittel-on-gold-mines-and-mining:
Hittel on Gold Mines and Mining was printed at Quebec in 1864 by G. and G. E. Desbarats. Its opening claim is plain: mining is the chief industry of California, employing more men and paying larger average wages than any other branch of physical labor. Output and profits were already falling, the book admits, yet mining would long remain the largest source of the state's wealth and the base for other work.

California mines then wrought gold, silver, quicksilver, copper, and coal. Tin, lead, antimony, sulphur, alum, asphaltum, borax lakes, and magnesia springs were found but not yet worked. Platinum, iridium, and osmium came with gold in placers, never alone. Gold yielded about forty millions of dollars a year, quicksilver two millions, while silver, copper, and coal, opened within a year, were still of unknown value. Gold mines split into placer and quartz.
29928-why-bewick-succeeded-a-note-in-the:
Jacob Kainen, curator of graphic arts at the Smithsonian's Museum of History and Technology, wrote Why Bewick Succeeded as paper eleven in the museum's Contributions series. Thomas Bewick, who lived from 1753 to 1828, has been acclaimed as the pioneer of modern wood engraving, whose genius brought the popular medium to prominence. Kainen's study argues that certain technological developments prepared Bewick's path and shaped his work.

Four sections order the note: the contemporary view of Bewick, the low status of the woodcut, woodcut and wood engraving, and wood engraving and the stereotype. No other artist, Kainen says, approached Bewick as chronicler of English rustic life. His little engravings record typical scenes with social and moral overtones, though he had no formal training and never took a lesson. The paper is a short, sharp piece of art history.
29987-join-our-gang:
Sterling E. Lanier wrote Join Our Gang for Analog Science Fact and Fiction in May 1961, with pictures by Douglas. Its headnote sets the bargain plainly: they did not exactly hold a gun at anybody's head, and help was all they offered. Of course, they did encourage people to ask for it. From his cabin port, the subleader of Survey Group Sirian Combine, Commander William Powers, looks down at the world below.

The Benefactor, his ship, sits on bedrock of Island Twenty-seven of Mureess, the name its natives give their world. The natives' name for themselves, Falsethsa, stands for the people, or us, or indeed the only race. Powers, fifty years old with eleven in survey work, has mapped 1,386 small islands, rocky or swampy or both. Island Twenty-seven matters because it holds the planet's largest city, ringed by docks and breakwaters.
30066-laboratory-manual-of-glass-blowing:
Francis C. Frary, assistant professor of chemistry at the University of Minnesota, teaches laboratory glass blowing in a compact McGraw-Hill manual from 1914. An opening chapter sorts lead glass from soda glass, weighs defects and annealing, and sets out the blowpipe, bellows, and light. General operations follow, with cutting, bending, constricting, and flanging of tubing, plus methods of rotation and blowing.

Elementary exercises join tubes of like and unlike size and blow bulbs and tee tubes, while advanced work builds a gas-washing tube, a suction pump, and a Kjeldahl trap. A final chapter covers capillary tubing, ground joints, sealing platinum wire, vacuum tubes, and closed tubes for heating under pressure. The manual suits students who need plain, step-by-step bench craft, not theory alone.
30098-the-venetian-school-of-painting:
Evelyn March Phillipps surveys Venetian painting from its primitive roots to its great masters, with illustrations throughout. Early chapters treat Venice and her art, Umbrian and Veronese influences, the school of Murano, and the Paduan influence, before turning to Jacopo Bellini, Carlo Crivelli, and Gentile Bellini. Giorgione's Madonna with Saints Liberale and Francis at Castelfranco fronts the volume as its chosen image.

First published in 1912 and reprinted in 1972 by Books for Libraries Press, the study moves school by school, tracing how Venice shaped a color-rich art of its own. Phillipps writes for general readers as well as students, naming pictures, places, and debts between masters. The book remains a clear, old-style guide to a school prized for light, color, and serene sacred scenes.
30140-gone-fishing:
James H. Schmitz sets a sly science fiction tale on a rickety lake dock, where Barney Chard waits for his latest business prospect to tire of pretend fishing. Chard, thirty-seven, works as financier, entrepreneur, occasional blackmailer, and occasional con man, and he has come for a secret prize. His prospect is Dr. Oliver B. McAllen, a retired physicist who looks like an aging tramp yet may hold a clandestine invention called the McAllen Tube.

Printed in Analog in May 1961, the story turns on the gap between brains and morals, since cleverness alone does not make a man honest or kind. Forced quiet thought, the tale suggests, can teach the difference between ruthless skill and right conduct. Krenkel drew the pictures, and the short piece stays tense and witty as Chard learns that his mark may be sharper than he seems.
30149-trading:
Susan Warner finishes her series with Trading, completing the story of The House in Town as the fourth of four novels. Robert Carter and Brothers published the New York volume in 1873, entering it in 1872, with a gospel text on a man who travels far and entrusts goods to his servants. Christmas day opens grey over city roofs and streets, with no sun all day, and Sarah Staples finds the crossing cold.

Inside Mrs. Lloyd's front door, Matilda finds only sunshine, busy tying parcels in white paper, writing names neatly on each, and passing them to Mrs. Bartholomew for the Christmas tree. Presents for friends follow in the same careful order. Warner closes her domestic saga with gifts, duty, and household love, in the earnest, plain style her readers knew.
30243-abc-of-fox-hunting:
Sir John Dean Paul, baronet, gives an alphabet of fox hunting in twenty-six coloured illustrations, published by J. Mitchell of the Royal Library, Bond Street, London. A stands for Andrews, his man, first class in his art, while B gives buckskins and boots. C brings the cover hack, D a slap-up dog cart, E the earth stopper, early and willing, and F the foxhounds, far famed for killing.

G gives the gorse cover certain for foxes, and H hunters fresh from their boxes. I gives the innkeeper filling glasses, with jumping lots, a keeper, little boys bound for the throw off, and a master giving the view halloa. Later letters run through nobody craning to follow and the old whipper-in. The parson, a queer place, racing pace, stile and ditch, a tumble, upland, and a zany alone in his glory close the set.
30294-the-century-handbook-of-writing:
Garland Greever and Easley S. Jones set out the rules of clear college writing in The Century Handbook of Writing, published by the Century Company in 1927 under a 1918 copyright. Sentence structure opens with completeness of thought: fragments used as sentences, incomplete constructions, necessary words omitted, comparisons left unfinished, cause and reason confused, and is when and is where clauses. Undeveloped thought and transitions close the section, with exercises on each fault.

Unity of thought follows, warning against unrelated ideas in one sentence, excessive detail, stringy sentences to break up, and choppy sentences to combine. Faulty subordination, the and which construction, and the comma splice get special care, before clearness of reference and coherence take up divided reference, weak reference, dangling participles, and general incoherence. Students get rules, examples, and practice in one compact handbook.
30572-silver-and-gold-a-story-of-luck-an:
Dane Coolidge writes Silver and Gold, a story of luck and love in a western mining camp, copyrighted in 1919 by E. P. Dutton. Coolidge, author of The Fighting Fool, opens with a miners' saying: gold is where you find it, and silver in high places.

Contents move from the ground hog and big boy to hobo stuff, cash, Mother Trigedgo, the oraculum, and the eminent buttinsky. Later chapters add the silver treasure, Bible-Back Murray, and signs to come. Coolidge pairs mining luck with romance, using camp talk, claims, and sudden fortune to drive a brisk western tale.
30573-why-i-preach-the-second-coming:
I. M. Haldeman, pastor of the First Baptist Church in New York City, writes Why I Preach the Second Coming, copyrighted in 1919 by Fleming H. Revell. Contents open with a claim that the second coming is the one event most often recorded in Holy Scripture.

Later chapters argue it is bound up with every fundamental doctrine, every sublime promise, and every exhortation to high, holy, and practical Christian living. Only at the coming of the Lord, a third heading begins, does the full promise arrive. Haldeman preaches with conviction, grounding his case in scripture and in the practical life of faith.
30765-news-writing:
M. Lyle Spencer, a professor of English at Lawrence College who also worked on the Milwaukee Journal, wrote this 1917 textbook on gathering, handling, and writing news stories. He dedicates it to Thomas B. Reid, dean of the Wisconsin newspaper men, and dates his own preface at Appleton, Wisconsin, in March 1917. The book grew out of newsroom practice, not just classroom theory.

Its three parts cover the paper's organization first, then the news story itself, then types of stories. Spencer explains the city room, the lead, the body of the story, the sentence, and the word, before turning to interviews, courts, crime, sports, society, and features. A style book, proof marks, and exercises close the volume. It remains a clear window on how American reporters were trained a century ago.
30768-sowing-and-reaping:
D. L. Moody, the well known evangelist, preached this short book from Galatians chapter six, verse seven, and Fleming H. Revell published it in 1896. Its text, quoted at the head of the first chapter, says that whatever a man sows, that he shall also reap. Moody treats that line as a law proved by daily life, not only by scripture, and he says newspapers alone show it at work.

Eight chapters press the point home in plain speech: a man reaps the same kind as he sows, and he reaps more than he sows. Ignorance of the seed makes no difference, Moody says, and forgiveness does not cancel earthly harvest. Stories from his meetings, including a thief arrested at the door, drive the lesson home. It is a direct, earnest piece of revival preaching.
3093-the-eve-of-the-revolution-a-chronic:
Carl Becker wrote The Eve of the Revolution, volume eleven of the Chronicles of America series, published by Yale University Press in 1918. Becker states his aim plainly, to convey not a record of what men did but a sense of how they thought and felt about what they did. The book recreates the intellectual atmosphere of the colonies on the breach with England.

Scenes include Boston courts adjourned for a fortnight at a time through Hutchinson and Oliver, to young John Adams's rising wrath. Adams fears the courts' inactivity will make a large chasm in his affairs, if not reduce him to distress, even as probate courts go on as if no Stamp Act existed. Becker's brief sketch remains a classic of intellectual history.
3101-washington-irving:
Warner wrote this life of Washington Irving for the American Men of Letters series. It came out in December 1881 as the first volume of that series. The book grew from a sketch written for the Geoffrey Crayon edition of Irving's works. That set ran to twenty-seven volumes, issued month by month from April 1880. The study later appeared again in a volume called Studies of Irving.

Warner follows Irving from his early New York sketches to his standing as America's first widely read man of letters. He weighs the life and the writing together. Readers who know Rip Van Winkle and the Sketch Book learn how a genial New York storyteller became a national figure.
3106-as-we-were-saying:
Charles Dudley Warner collected As We Were Saying with other essays in the backlog edition of his complete writings, published in 1904. Contents include Rose and Chrysanthemum, The Red Bonnet, and The Loss in Civilization. Social Screaming, Does Refinement Kill Individuality, The Directoire Gown, The Mystery of the Sex, The Clothes of Fiction, A Chewing Gum, Women in Congress, and Shall Women Propose follow. The essays began as magazine talk. A chewing-gum passage argues the habit is neither narcotic nor stimulant, soothing nor exciting, and differs totally from tobacco chewing or dipping, despite a popular impression that apothecaries sell it as medicine.

Warner's light essays treat manners, dress, and public life with humor. The volume shows the essayist behind the novelist, urbane and amused.
31116-where-i-wasn-t-going:
Walt and Leigh Richmond's science fiction novella, serialized in Analog in October and November 1963, is set aboard U.N. Space Lab One, a two-hundred-thirty-two-foot wheel in a thirty-six-hour orbit. Chief engineer Mike Blackhawk arrives to take over the station, inspect its gold-plated hull, and begin the delicate job of spinning the wheel for his three-month tour.

Radiation rules cap every crew stay at three months, and the station's first scientists are only now arriving after eighteen months of assembly. The story follows engineers and crew as routine work meets an unnamed confusion that strands their plans. It turns a tale of space construction into a tense study of people cut off far from Earth.
31125-the-life-and-work-of-susan-b-antho:
Ida Husted Harper's second volume of The Life and Work of Susan B. Anthony, published by the Bowen-Merrill Company in 1898, carries the story from 1880 onward in chapters thirty through forty-two. It draws on Anthony's public addresses, her own letters, and many letters from contemporaries across fifty years, under the subtitle A Story of the Evolution of the Status of Woman.

Chapters follow political candidates and the writing of the suffrage History, a legacy and the Nebraska campaign, a departure for Europe, and later campaigns, with portraits and pictures of homes. Dedicated to woman, for whose freedom Anthony gave fifty years of endeavor, the volume is a rich primary source for the suffrage movement.
3133-baddeck-and-that-sort-of-thing:
Warner sketches a summer trip to Baddeck on Cape Breton Island in these light pieces. A preface addressed to Joseph H Twichell admits the debt plainly. Twichell taught him to say the name and showed him its place on the map. He also passed on a home missionary's tempting letter about trout and salmon. The usual demand for such sketches gathered them into this little volume.

The humor lies in modest travel: bad roads, plain lodgings, and grand scenery met without grandeur. Warner writes as a tourist who knows his own limits and enjoys them. The country wins in the end, quietly, while the traveler supplies the jokes.
31517-a-week-at-waterloo-in-1815-lady-de:
A Week at Waterloo in 1815, Lady De Lancey's narrative, edited by Major B. R. Ward of the Royal Engineers, was published in London by John Murray in 1906. It tells how Lady De Lancey nursed her husband, Colonel Sir William Howe De Lancey, quartermaster-general of the army, mortally wounded in the great battle. A portrait shows Major William Howe De Lancey of the 45th Regiment around 1800.

The narrative follows one week of waiting, nursing, and loss after Waterloo, in place of a general's account of the battle. Its power lies in the domestic view of war: a wife at a wounded husband's side, with surgeons, friends, and bad news coming and going. Readers of Waterloo literature will find a moving, intimate memoir, valuable precisely because it stays close to one household.
31549-the-battle-of-the-big-hole-a-histo:
G. O. Shields, writing as "Coquina," published The Battle of the Big Hole at Chicago and New York in 1889. It is a history of General Gibbon's engagement with Nez Percé Indians in the Big Hole Valley, Montana, on August 9, 1877. Shields, author of Rustlings in the Rockies and Hunting in the Great West, opens with an introduction from Camp Pilot Butte, Wyoming, dated March 17, 1889. A letter from Captain Chas. A. Coolidge of the Seventh United States Infantry, a participant in the affair, commends the book. He calls it a graphic and truthful account of the fight and the events leading up to it.

His history, endorsed by a man who was there, remains a standard early account of the battle. Readers of western and Native American history will find a detailed narrative, written when many participants were still living.
31596-the-art-and-craft-of-printing:
William Morris's The Art and Craft of Printing gathers a note by Morris on his aims in founding the Kelmscott Press, together with a short description of the press by S. C. Cockerell and an annotated list of the books printed there. Copyright in 1902 by H. M. O'Kane, the volume is illustrated with Psyche borne off by Zephyrus, drawn by Edward Burne-Jones and engraved by Morris himself. Morris opens by saying he began printing books in the hope of producing some with a definite claim to beauty.

Those books, he insists, should also read easily, without straining eye or mind through eccentric form. A great admirer of medieval calligraphy, he found fifteenth-century books beautiful by force of typography alone. Readers of book history will find here the founding statement of the private-press movement, in Morris's own voice.
31681-hand-and-ring:
Anna Katharine Green's mystery novel brings the famous New York detective Mr. Gryce into a household thrown into confusion by a sudden summons. Called from Utica, Gryce arrives at a house of book-lined rooms and a burnt-out grate. The district attorney and a doctor await him there, unsure who he is or why he has come.

The story that follows turns on detection, testimony, and a ring, as Gryce tests what witnesses say against what the house itself shows. Readers get a classic American detective novel from the author of The Leavenworth Case, built on careful observation rather than action.
31914-the-story-of-general-pershing:
Everett T. Tomlinson's Story of General Pershing, published by D. Appleton and Company, opens on a historic morning, June 13, 1917, at Boulogne, France. A detachment of French infantry in battle uniform, middle-aged men made older by hard service in the trenches, waits with eagerness and expectancy for a boat drawing near the landing stage.

Among the throng are French generals and representatives of other nations. Sir George Fowke stands for General Sir Douglas Haig; Captain Boyd serves as military attaché of the American War Department. Readers get a wartime biography for young readers, following Pershing from his arrival in France to command of the American Expeditionary Forces.
31933-landmarks-of-scientific-socialism-:
Frederick Engels's Anti-Dühring, published here as Landmarks of Scientific Socialism, answers Herr Dühring, who three years earlier had set himself up as a scholar and reformer of socialism. Engels says the work is by no means the fruit of some inward compulsion, but a reply forced on him by Dühring's challenge.

Its three parts cover philosophy, political economy, and socialism, from apriorism, time and space, and the dialectic. They move to the force theory, capital and surplus value, ground rent, production, distribution, and the state, family, and education. Readers get a foundational Marxist text, sharp and systematic, that defends scientific socialism against its critics.
32027-banking:
William A. Scott's 1914 book Banking, published in Chicago by A. C. McClurg and Company, comes from the director of the Course in Commerce and professor of political economy at the University of Wisconsin. Its editor's preface contrasts Europe, where the average man looks upon the bank as a benefactor securing capital at low rates. In America, the bank is too often regarded as a necessary evil.

Scott argues that banking plays a most important part in the nation's economy, though American banking laws are obsolete, unsatisfactory, and actually in some respects harmful. Chapters cover the nature, functions, and classification of banking institutions, from the safekeeping of money and valuables through payments, loans, and investments. Readers get a clear textbook of early twentieth-century banking.
32132-long-live-the-king:
Guy Boothby's Long Live the King was published by Ward, Lock and Company in London, Melbourne, and Toronto. It opens as a backward look at a strange childhood. Boothby, author of Dr. Nikola and The Beautiful White Devil, gives his narrator a pen in hand. The narrator's mind's eye holds a child playing happily on the far side of the River of Years. The narrator finds it scarcely believable that the little fellow and the man in the chair can be the same person.

Between the two, the narrator says, looms so vast a difference that no connecting link seems able to unite them. He cannot yet say whether he is better or worse for the change. An illustration shows a farewell to a king: Farewell, your Majesty, he said. Readers get a romance, where a curious child grows into a man whose life has touched royalty.
32259-modest-remarks-upon-the-bishop-of-:
Modest Remarks upon the Bishop of London's Letter Concerning the Late Earthquakes, priced at sixpence and printed in London for T. Howard in 1750, is a Quaker reply to the bishop. Its author signs as one of the people called Quakers, and addresses the bishop as Friend Thomas, having perused his letter to the clergy and inhabitants. A Malachi epigraph warns the priests: if ye will not hear, and will not lay it to heart, to give glory unto my name, I will send a curse upon you.

The pamphlet answers a bishop who read earthquakes as divine warning, with a Quaker's plain-spoken correction. Readers get an eighteenth-century religious controversy in miniature: earthquake, episcopal letter, and dissenting reply, printed cheaply for quick sale. Its modesty is in the title only, for the argument is sharp, scriptural, and direct.
32260-tourcoing:
Hilaire Belloc's Tourcoing, published in London by Stephen Swift and Company in 1912, is a short battle history. Its six parts run from The Political Circumstance and The General Military Situation through The Plan of the Allies and The Preliminaries of the Battle to The Terrain and The Action. Belloc opens by calling Tourcoing one of those actions on which European history is confused, and English history ignorant.

British troops were among the defeated, and the Duke of York led the reverse, but that affords no explanation, Belloc argues. The almost exactly parallel case of Fontenoy is among the most familiar actions in the country. There another young royal duke, son of the reigning king, an excellent officer in command, was defeated. Readers get a study of a neglected defeat.
32414-home-pork-making:
A. W. Fulton's Home Pork Making, published in New York and Chicago in 1900, guides farmers, country butchers, and suburban dwellers through raising and curing pork on the farm. Fulton, commercial editor of the American Agriculturist and Orange Judd Farmer, worked with pork specialists in the United States and England. The book covers hog slaughtering, curing, preserving, and storing pork from scalding vat to kitchen table.

An epigraph from Charles Lamb praises roast pig and its crisp crackling above all delicacies, setting a hearty tone for practical chapters. Readers learn slaughter, scalding, cutting, salting, smoking, and storage in clear, workmanlike detail. The volume remains a useful record of farm food practice at the turn of the century, when home curing was common household work.
32493-witch-burning:
Mary Elizabeth Counselman's poem, printed in Weird Tales in October 1936, tells of a witch burned in Bingham Square on a Friday afternoon. Faggot smoke runs blacker than shadows on the moon, and licking flames burn strangely green like fox-fire on a fen. She who cursed the godly folk, the poem says, will never curse again.

Before the village gate, a huswife lifts a thin hand in a curse, rigid with hatred. A huckster throws a jagged stone that reddens her pallid cheek, yet scorn marks the way she holds her head. A slight, comely maid, no taller than a child, bound fast to the stake, mutters secret words no one dares to hear. Before rain soaks her bones to ash, she sets her mark on the throng, in cries and a face time cannot erase.
32550-rich-living:
Michael Cathal's Rich Living, printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in February 1955, opens with Curtis Delman, a centenarian lawyer, leaving a space liner on Jupiter. Bent with age and leaning on two heavy canes, he locks away a mile of fine wire carrying detailed instructions compiled over four days.

Delman plans a visit to Rejuvenal, a world the story presents as worth a fortune for a brief stay. His wealth, age, and careful plans set up a tale about what money can and cannot buy when a short visit promises renewal.
32678-commodore-barney-s-young-spies-a-b:
James Otis tells a boys' story of the War of 1812, when British forces burned Washington. Young helpers serve Commodore Joshua Barney, spying, carrying word, and dodging patrols along the Chesapeake and the Patuxent.

In twenty-one chapters the boys meet deserters, feed the enemy to learn his plans, hide from searchers, and watch their own vessels burn to keep them from British hands. The tale ends at Bladensburg and in the capital itself, where flight, suspense, and a narrow escape test their nerve. Otis writes for boys, with brisk scenes and plain talk. The boys learn to watch, listen, and keep calm under fire. Their tale gives a young reader's view of a national disaster.
32760-the-first-day-of-spring:
Mari Wolf tells of Trina, a young woman living in a gentle, managed world where the weather tower sets the seasons and the days are lengthened toward summer. On the first day of spring she rides out and meets Max Cramer, a spaceman visiting from beyond her world, months before festival time.

Max finds her world attractive yet confining, and Trina wishes he were one of her people rather than a man of space. Their old argument resumes: whether to stay in a sheltered Earth or leave it. When Max invites her aboard his ship, Trina must choose between home and the wider universe.
32781-blackboard-drawing:
Frederick Whitney of the State Normal School at Salem, Massachusetts, offers this monograph on blackboard drawing. It is a sixth edition, published by Atkinson, Mentzer and Company. Henry Turner Bailey wrote its introduction, dated September 1903. Whitney treats drawing as a language, as natural to teacher and child as speech or writing.

He teaches free chalk strokes, using two-thirds of a stick of soft crayon on its side. That use gives tones from white to gray. He applies the strokes to geography, history, literature, and nature lessons. Animal sketches, Thanksgiving scenes, and holiday subjects show how a few minutes of sketching can make a subject clearer, without turning the board into a labored decoration.
32812-history-of-cuba-or-notes-of-a-trav:
Maturin M. Ballou gives a political, historical, and statistical account of Cuba, from its first discovery to the present time, published in Boston by Phillips, Sampson and Company in 1854. The book joins notes from his journal, kept during a brief residence on the island, to a historical glance at Cuba's political story.

Ballou drew on Ramon de la Sagra and on Spanish books lent by Edward Everett, collating authorities where statistics were concerned. He writes while Cuba stands critically situated, still a dependency of Spain, yet perhaps soon to change hands. Chapters range from early colonists and aborigines to Cortez, the Aztecs, and the island's present trade and government.
32894-in-the-whirl-of-the-rising:
Bertram Mitford opens on a skating mere, where a girl calls Piers Lamont a coward for watching a drowning boy. Lamont, her fiancé, answers with a mask of bronze impassibility and walks away to jeers. The insult costs him her love and sets the novel's question: what kind of courage does he actually possess?

The story moves to a South African frontier, where Lamont's nerve is tested in earnest. At a tent-pegging contest, the Resident Magistrate Orwell praises a ride Lamont seemed to miss. Later Lamont leads a charge to rescue a wagon whose police escort is half killed by attackers. The whirl of the rising gives him the adequate motive he claimed to lack on the ice.
32911-the-white-hand-and-the-black-a-sto:
Bertram Mitford's novel of the Natal rising opens on a mountain top at night, where a man who has just shed a lifelong burden finds himself no longer alone. A stranger has followed him up the dark plateau, and in a flash of lightning the two grapple in silence, each knowing the other cannot be allowed to leave alive. The scene sets a story of pursuit, violence, and divided loyalties.

Mitford builds the tale from the frontier world of Natal, where white settlers and Black peoples lived in uneasy, often hostile nearness. The title points to that divide and to the hands, white and black, that meet in conflict and in uneasy trust. It is a period adventure, written from a colonial viewpoint, and it moves with the pace of a thriller set against a real uprising.
32962-a-handbook-of-laboratory-glass-blo:
Bernard D. Bolas's Handbook of Laboratory Glass-Blowing teaches a craft every chemist once needed: shaping glass by hand for the laboratory. It was published in London in 1921 with diagrams by Naomi Bolas. Early chapters cover general principles, choice of apparatus, tools, and glass itself. They then move to easy examples, cutting and sealing tubes, making thermometer bulbs and pipettes, joining tubes and branches, and blowing bulbs and funnels.

The handbook is practical and precise, guiding a worker through each step and warning where cracks lead and how to control them. In an age of ready-made apparatus, it preserves a skill that let a laboratory make, mend, and adapt its own gear. For historians of science and for glass workers, it remains a clear, well-diagrammed introduction to a demanding hand craft.
33074-the-pig-breeding-rearing-and-marke:
Sanders Spencer's Pig: Breeding, Rearing, and Marketing, published in London in 1919, is a thorough farmer's guide to pigs. A frontispiece shows breeding sows of the large and middle white breeds, including the author's own Holywell Countess Victoria, one of the best ever bred. Early chapters treat non-pedigree pigs and pure breeds with their standards, before the book moves through the practical work of keeping pigs for profit.

Spencer writes for farmers who wanted sound, tested advice on breeding, feeding, housing, and selling, and his book reflects British pig farming at the end of the First World War. Its detail on breeds and markets makes it useful to agricultural historians as well as to smallholders. As a manual it is plain, orderly, and full of the kind of knowledge that came from the yard rather than the lecture room.
33084-practical-angora-goat-raising:
C. P. Bailey and Sons of San Jose, California, published Practical Angora Goat Raising in 1905 after forty years of farming Angoras in America. The preface notes that beginners had long been without textbooks, and that very few practical treatises existed, so the Baileys drew on their own experience and on the personal observations of Dr. W. C. Bailey in the interior of Asia Minor. A brief history of the Angora goat opens the book, with several pages on breeding and kidding.

The aim is a practical textbook for the beginner, selecting only the essential points for successful management of Angora flocks. Mohair, hardiness, and the goat's fit for brush land made the animal attractive to western farmers, and the book shows how a new industry taught itself. For agricultural historians, it is a clear record of an early California livestock venture, written by its founders.
33146-careers-of-danger-and-daring:
Cleveland Moffett's Careers of Danger and Daring collects accounts of risky trades for young readers. It was published by the Century Company in 1903. It is dedicated to his children Anne Eunice and Cleveland Lusk in the hope it may help them form habits of courage and usefulness. Its opening section follows Steeple Bob, a steeple-climber, from first acquaintance through blowing the top off a steeple with dynamite. The lesson is that a climber's greatest danger lies in being startled.

Later sections, illustrated by Jay Hambidge, George Varian, and others, take up divers at work near a wreck and other dangerous callings. It shows how men and women earned a living at heights, depths, and edges. Moffett writes with admiration for skill and nerve, not for recklessness. The book remains a guide to work that thrilled boys of 1903, and a record of trades that modern safety rules have changed.
33191-more-mittens-with-the-doll-s-weddi:
Aunt Fanny's More Mittens, with The Doll's Wedding and Other Stories, the third book of the Mitten Series published in New York in 1863, gathers children's tales for young readers. Its contents include a letter from Aunt Fanny, The Doll's Wedding, What Came of Gipsying, The Child Heroine, Aunt Mary, Little Peter, and The Story Told to Willie. The volume is dedicated to Ilken Annie of Staten Island.

An illustration shows a griffin stalking out smoking his pipe, with fashionable beasts of the neighborhood in tow, giving a flavor of the book's fancy. Fanny Barrow, writing as Aunt Fanny and author of the six Nightcap books, tells moral tales with humor and warmth. The collection remains a charming period children's book, full of dolls, adventures, and the kindly voice of an aunt telling stories to her darlings.
33365-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
This volume of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica covers entries from Cerargyrite to Charing, in alphabetical order. Its articles span minerals, places, history, and science, each set out in the dense, exact style of the great reference work. Readers will find long treatments of major topics, such as Chalcis, beside short entries on smaller terms, all arranged for quick lookup.

As a slice of the famous eleventh edition, the volume shows how knowledge was summed up before the First World War: thorough, confident, and rich in detail. It serves best as a work to dip into, whether for a mineral, a town, or a term in science. Scholars still prize this edition, and this volume gives a full taste of its scope.
33424-instruction-book-on-ring-spinning:
Francis L. Lincoln's Instruction Book on Ring Spinning, published in Warren, Massachusetts, in 1885, gives help to those engaged in that department of mill work. Lincoln writes in his preface that the book imparts knowledge that only long practice can otherwise teach, aimed at spinners who run ring frames day by day. His guide is short, practical, and plain.

The book's value lies in its workshop detail: how frames work, how faults arise, and how a spinner keeps yarn even and strong. Its tone is that of a foreman teaching a hand, not a scholar lecturing. For readers of textile and labor history, it is a clear window on mill work in the 1880s, when ring spinning was still new.
33453-a-traitor-s-wooing:
Headon Hill's Traitor's Wooing, published in London in 1909, is a tale of love and treason. Violet quietly asks a lover whether that is all he has to say to her. Hill, author of Her Splendid Sin and The Hidden Victim, writes with the brisk, romantic verve of the Edwardian thriller. His frontispiece captures Violet's quiet challenge, a scene that sets the book's tone.

The novel blends romance with intrigue, as a traitor's courtship tests loyalty, love, and honor. Its pace is fast, its scenes vivid, and its close aims to satisfy readers who love a good twist. For fans of early thrillers, A Traitor's Wooing offers a lively, old-fashioned story of a heart caught between love and country.
33464-roses-and-rose-growing:
Rose G. Kingsley's Roses and Rose Growing, by the author of Eversley Gardens, is a richly illustrated guide to growing roses well. With twenty-eight full-page colored plates and nine half-tone pictures, it covers kinds, planting, pruning, and care, plus a chapter on growing roses for exhibition by the Reverend F. Page-Roberts of the National Rose Society. Kingsley writes for gardeners who love the rose above all flowers.

The book's charm lies in its practical detail and its beautiful plates, including a single hybrid tea called Irish Elegance. Its tone is clear and encouraging, suited to beginners and exhibitors alike. For rose lovers, it remains a classic manual, full of the lore and labor that make a rose garden thrive.
33736-the-tempering:
Charles Neville Buck writes a Kentucky mountain novel in this 1920 Doubleday book. It opens with a boy perched disconsolately on a rotting fence, lamenting to laurelled mountain silences that nothing ever comes to pass in his pocket of the Kentucky Cumberlands. Behind him a log cabin breathes smokily through a mud-daubed chimney, and a twisting creek bed serves as highway.

From that restless start, the novel follows its hero through mountain life, love, and conflict, toward the tempering of character its title promises. Buck, author of The Call of the Cumberland and The Battle Cry, writes with attention to dialect, landscape, and clan feeling. Readers of Appalachian fiction will enjoy a story of a young man shaped, like steel, by hardship, loyalty, and the evening star over the ridges.
33751-a-treatise-on-etching:
Maxime Lalanne, praised by P. G. Hamerton as the best French landscape etcher of the present day, after Claude among past masters, explains his art in this treatise. The authorized Boston edition of 1880 offers text and plates together, so readers can follow each process and see its results.

Koehler's preface argues that other books load etching with complicated detail that frightens beginners, while Lalanne describes processes in a plain, lucid manner, as simple as a good work of art. Growing English interest in etching made the translation timely. The treatise remains a classic manual for printmakers, combining technical clarity with an artist's sense of what makes an etching live.
33897-the-red-mustang:
William O. Stoddard wrote this boys' adventure tale for Harper's Young People's Series, copyrighted in 1890. Its hero, Cal Evans, rides for help, joins cavalrymen, and faces a band led by Kah-go-mish, while a red mustang runs through the action. The story is set on the frontier, around a garrison town called Santa Lucia.

Short chapters move fast from chase to siege to rescue, with horses, soldiers, and Native fighters at the center. Stoddard writes for young readers, so the peril is sharp but the tone stays brisk and clear. The book offers a lively sample of the frontier tales that filled American boys' shelves in that era.
33934-she-knew-he-was-coming:
Kris Neville wrote this short science tale, illustrated by Ed Emsh. On Mars, under a bluish sun low over green dust, lights flicker on in a city as the Earth liner Azmuth lands in the morning. Anne and Milly watch from a window and talk of Mary, who expects that Earthman, while stevedores unload the sleek hull at the spaceport.

Anne says she does not like Earthmen, though they spend money, and doubts whether her man is even aboard. Neville writes the Martian street in bright, strange detail. The tale turns on waiting, hope, and a meeting that may or may not come.
34068-a-brief-sketch-of-the-work-of-matt:
Richard L. Maury wrote this brief sketch of his father Matthew Fontaine Maury's war work, published at Richmond in 1915. Maury, a Confederate naval captain, brought torpedoes into Confederate service and kept improving them until they changed coast and harbor defense. In 1861 he mined the James River and led the first torpedo attack on the Federal fleet at Hampton Roads.

Eleven young naval officers carried the torpedo war to other southern waters, planting and firing mines with daring and coolness. Maury's sketch credits torpedoes with the loss of fifty-eight ships. The book gives a son's account of a new weapon at war.
34159-the-a-b-c-of-drag-hunting:
Grace Clarke Newton wrote this hunting alphabet, published in New York in 1917 by E. P. Dutton and Company, with pictures from paintings by Richard Newton, Junior. Newton, author of A Small Girl's Stories and Poems in Passing, gives each letter a verse on drag hunting. A stands for Ambition, which leads a rider to buy a qualified hunter. B stands for the Beauty learning to go.

The verses follow riders, hounds in full cry, clubs, and meets, in light, cheerful rhyme. The book serves young riders and hunting folk who like verse with their sport. It remains a charming alphabet of the hunting field.
34358-iolanthe-s-wedding:
Hermann Sudermann wrote four tales Englished by Adele Seltzer and printed at New York in 1918. Sudermann had written The Song of Songs. Iolanthe's Wedding leads, then The Woman Who Was His Friend, The New Year's Eve Confession, and The Gooseherd. I tell you, gentlemen, it is a rotten piece of business to stand beside an old friend's open grave, the first tale opens.

You stand with your feet planted in the upturned earth and twirl your moustache and look stupid, while you feel like crying the soul out of your body. In him was lost the greatest genius for mixing punches, cocktails, grogs, and cobblers. A drinking friend mourned, a wedding ahead, and small town hearts fill Sudermann's warm German tales in a plain dress.
34553-over-the-plum-pudding:
John Kendrick Bangs gathered his comic tales as Over the Plum-Pudding in nineteen hundred and one. Bangs was known for A House-Boat on the Styx and The Idiot. The tales had first run in Harper's magazines, Life, and other papers.

He gave the book to his son, whose love of plum puddings fits the title. Tales include a ghost who fails his test, an unmailed letter, and a band of spooks. Hans Pumpernickel keeps a vigil, and a Baron bears a strange curse. Fritz becomes a wizard, and a poet rises and falls. Light verse and nonsense carry the whole set.
34743-gamblers-and-gambling:
Henry Ward Beecher, the famous Brooklyn preacher, delivered this lecture against gambling. Henry Altemus printed it at Philadelphia under an eighteen ninety six copyright. Beecher opens at the foot of the cross, where the soldiers cast lots for Christ's coat. He calls that scene the pattern of the gambler's character in every age: cool self interest beside suffering.

From there he defines his subject with care. Gambling, he argues, is staking property on mere hazard. It takes gain without giving an honest equivalent in labor, produce, or useful skill. Betting is gambling, and dealings in fancy stocks often are too. He contrasts the gambler with the farmer, the mechanic, the pilot, and the lawyer, whose earnings pay for real services. The lecture then tours the gambling world's haunts and ruin. It is a leading voice against lotteries and cards.
35015-wrinkles-in-electric-lighting:
Vincent Stephen wrote Wrinkles in Electric Lighting, a hand book put out in London and New York in 1888. Stephen aims the book at men who run light plants on board ship. The word wrinkles here means short, wise hints from use. The first pages build the thought of a stream of power from the ground up.

Stephen sets the weak stream of a wet cell next to the flow of blood in the body. Push with no bulk, he says, will not do the work. Bulk with no push fails in the same way. He then deals with drag on the stream, and with heat when a wire is too thin. Copper is the chief stuff for wires that bear the stream. The book suits men who must keep lamps lit far from help.
35093-the-road-to-understanding:
The Road to Understanding is a novel by Eleanor Porter, author of Just David, issued at Boston and New York in 1917. Porter dedicates it to a friend named on the page. A pictured caption shows a doctor leaping forward with a low cry at sight of a woman. The contents open with frosted cakes and shotguns, in one chapter head. An only son and honeymoon days follow.

Nest building, a chapter called the wipe, and the husband fill the early list. Stumbling blocks come next, as the marriage of the tale meets its trials. Porter had won world fame with a tale of a glad girl a few years before. Her readers came to this story for the same medicine: hard lives sweetened by patience and goodwill. The road of the title is the slow road by which two people learn to understand each other.
35115-wine-water-and-song:
Chesterton gathered these songs in Wine, Water, and Song, third edition. Methuen printed the book in London in August 1915. Most songs come from his novel The Flying Inn, the note says. Two more came by leave of The New Witness editor here.

Contents open with The Englishman and the song Wine and Water. The Rolling English Road and The Song of Quoodle follow fast. A Logical Vegetarian, the Saracen's Head, and a Good Rich Man appear. The Song of the Oak and Right and Wrong close the list. Who Goes Home and the Road to Roundabout stand last among the song titles listed.
35326-the-long-lane-s-turning:
The Long Lane's Turning is a novel by Hallie Erminie Rives. Dodd, Mead published the book at New York in 1917, from rights of the two years before. The tale had earlier run under the title The Heart of a Man. Pictures by Frances Rogers dress the volume. Rives had written Satan Sanderson and other novels before this one.

The contents run to fifty chapters of courtroom and camp life. Early titles name counsel for the defence, a prodigal, and a judge in lamplight. A rough sawyer from a logging camp stands accused of stealing a comrade's earnings. The case draws a full courtroom though the facts seem sordid and small. Later chapters bring a jailbird, a governor's hand, and a revelation. A frontispiece shows a woman speaking in a clear, trembling undertone to a listening man.
35722-ontology-or-the-theory-of-being:
Ontology, or the Theory of Being, by Peter Coffey, was published in London and New York in 1918. Coffey taught logic and metaphysics at Maynooth College in Ireland. He gives the book to his past and present students there. In his preface he claims a gap in English text books. Students of philosophy, he says, lacked a general metaphysics from the scholastic view.

Chapters treat being, becoming, existence, and essence. Later parts take up the true, the good, and the beautiful. Substance and accident, nature and person, space and time all get chapters. Cause forms the close, with chapters on kinds of cause and on final causes. Coffey argues that old school questions still live in modern debate, under new names.
364-the-mad-king:
Edgar Rice Burroughs sets this adventure in the small Balkan realm of Lutha, where a mad king has fled his guards. An American named Barney Custer, who looks just like King Leopold, is swept into court plots, escapes, and battles. Part one ends with a coronation; part two brings Barney back to face a firing squad and a traitor king.

Burroughs piles on sword fights, races to the capital, and last-minute rescues, all at a gallop. Barney's nerve and honor carry him where rank alone fails. The tale charms as pure swashbuckling fun, with a hero who must play king to save a land he barely knows.
36475-privateers-and-privateering:
Privateers and Privateering is a naval history by Commander E P Statham of the Royal Navy, published in London in nineteen ten. Eight illustrations appear in the book, with a French privateer as frontispiece. A list of modern authorities opens the scholarly apparatus. Works on American privateers and letters of marque in the War of eighteen twelve head that list.

Privateers were private ships licensed to seize enemy trade in war, and Statham tells their long story. Courts, prizes, and daring captains share the pages with the law that licensed them. Theodore Roosevelt's naval war history is among his sources. The book catches the last age of sail and steam raiding before modern navies ended the practice.
36662-the-palm-tree-blessing:
Evangelist Shepard wrote a discourse on the palm tree, printed at Kansas City in 1913 by the Nazarene Publishing House. Shepard had written Wrested Scriptures Made Plain. The palm tree is noted for its beauty, chapter one begins. It is certainly one of the most beautiful trees in nature, he says, and that is why folk plant them to deck their grounds.

No one plants scrub oaks in gardens, he notes, but nature's beauties. Straightness, lasting freshness, and fruitfulness follow as further chapters. Each trait of the tree is turned into a mark of the sanctified Christian life. The palm stands through storm and drought as the believer should. Holiness preaching of the age loved such nature sermons, and Shepard works his one tree hard and well.
36667-a-discourse-on-the-evils-of-dancin:
The Reverend John F Mesick preached A Discourse on the Evils of Dancing on March 8, 1846. He delivered it to the German Reformed Salem Church of Harrisburg, Pennsylvania. Theo Fenn printed the sermon at Harrisburg that year. The vestry published it at their own request. Twelve of them signed a letter asking for the manuscript. They hoped to circulate it in the Sabbath schools among the votaries of dancing.

Mesick answers that the discourse was a regular duty. His text is Romans, chapter twelve: Be not conformed to this world. The Bible, he holds, is the only rule for all who wish to be saved. The vestry called dancing a custom much practised even by patterns in society. They hoped readers would learn its evil consequences and abstain. Such printed sermons were pamphlet warfare for small-town morals.
36689-the-new-england-cook-book-or-young:
The New England Cook Book, or Young Housekeeper's Guide is a cookbook printed at New Haven in 1836 by Hezekiah Howe and Company with Herrick and Noyes. Its title page promises a collection of the most valuable receipts, covering all branches of cookery in a minute and methodical manner, plus an appendix of miscellaneous receipts on housewifery.

The preface defends adding one more cook book, arguing that most works of the kind mislead beginners until their cake is all dough. The writer claims enough knowledge of the science of gastronomy to guide the unpractised housekeeper plainly. Books like this one carried measured, ordered recipes into ordinary American kitchens at a time when cooking knowledge still passed mainly by word of mouth.
36801-a-logic-of-facts-or-every-day-reas:
A Logic of Facts, or every day reasoning, is a handbook by Holyoake, issued at London in 1866 in its fourth thousand. A motto at the head praises the man whose thoughts and words answer a clear why. An introduction dated 1848 states the book's quarrel plainly. The logic of the schools, however needful in its place, fails half the common want of daily life.

School logic starts with the handling of an argument's premises, Holyoake argues. The more practical lesson starts with the premises themselves. A thousand errors arise from taking premises for granted, he says, for one that comes from misplaced terms. School logic is an elaborate attack on the lesser evil. Popular reason alone can correct popular sophistry, he quotes with approval.
37034-a-revised-and-illustrated-treatise:
A Revised and Illustrated Treatise on Grain Stacking is a farm manual by John N DeLamater of Norwalk, Ohio, printed in 1884. Its full title promises instructions how to properly stack bound grain so as to preserve it, in the best possible manner, for threshing and market. DeLamater's preface says the field was, so far as he knew, untried.

He had the work under consideration for fifteen years, giving close attention to details of building. He made careful observations on results when the stacks were being taken down. The instructions begin with placing the foundation: three rails laid about four and a half feet apart and parallel, covered by rails crossways. Such a foundation serves for ten or twelve large loads. If the stack is flat and as near an ellipse as the eye can judge, keeping it balanced will be easy.
37042-the-coming-of-the-king:
The Coming of the King is a historical novel by Joseph Hocking. Ward Lock published the book at London in 1904, with pictures by Grenville Manton. Hocking had written All Men Are Liars and other tales before this one. The contents run to thirty chapters of intrigue in the days of Charles the Second.

The narrator opens by saying his history will clear his name. He insists he has done nothing he need fear to bring to light. All his acts, he says, were done in good faith with open eyes. Chapters promise a black box, a king's marriage contract, and a midnight meeting. A gaoler, an escape, and the Fleet Prison mark the middle of the tale. The Duke of York and the king himself enter the later chapters, with Charles sitting as judge.
37462-boating:
Walter Woodgate wrote Boating for the Badminton Library of Sports and Pastimes, the famous series edited by the Duke of Beaufort. The frontispiece shows a general view of Henley Regatta. The Badminton volumes taught Victorian gentlemen their sports, each written by an authority. Woodgate, a celebrated Oxford oarsman and coach, was the natural choice for rowing.

The book treats the sport whole: boats and their building, oars and sculls, training, steering, and the great races. Woodgate wrote from a lifetime on the river, and his judgements on style were argued over for decades. The volume also preserves the world of amateur rowing before it professionalised: university crews, the regatta season, and the ethics of the amateur. For historians of sport the Badminton Boating remains a primary source, and Woodgate's voice, opinionated and experienced, is half its value. The series set the pattern for sporting books ever since.
37698-dawn-of-the-morning:
Dawn of the Morning, by Grace Livingston Hill, is dated 1911. Grosset and Dunlap published the novel at New York. Hill had written Marcia Schuyler and Phoebe Deane before. A poem by Gannett, Wings of the Morning, fronts the book. Chapter one opens in the year 1824. A pleasant town between Schenectady and Albany holds the scene. The colonial house of Hamilton Van Rensselaer stands there. Solemn hedges shut in the family pride, and hide its sorrow. A little girl plays in the sombre garden borders. The stately house oppresses her spirit. Her only friend seems a tall clock on the stairs.

It ticks in a hopeless tone, yet winks at her kindly. One morning it ticks awesomely as she descends. Her father has summoned her to his study. She delays her steps all she can.
37781-notwithstanding:
Notwithstanding is a novel by Mary Cholmondeley, author of Red Pottage, published in London in 1913. The first edition of October 1913 sold out and was reprinted within the month.

The story opens in Paris on a bright September day. Annette, aged twenty-one, leans on the parapet of the Pont Neuf and stares at the Seine, swollen and angry after rain, licking at the stone supports of the bridges. She is angry herself, with the deep, still anger that comes once or twice in a life to gentle people. Annette looks younger than her years, loose-limbed and unfinished, like a colt not yet grown into its grace. A German motto at the front asks what chance is but raw stone taking life under the sculptor's hand.
37901-profitable-squab-breeding:
Profitable Squab Breeding is a practical guide by Carl Dare. Dare published it at Des Moines, Iowa, in 1914. The subtitle promises help for the beginner and the experienced breeder alike.

Chapters cover breeds, house plans, nests, feeds, and mating. Later chapters treat banding, market prep, and pigeon diseases. Dare argues that squabs have replaced scarce game birds on many tables. He says demand keeps growing in large and small markets. The book draws on his lifetime in the work. Small farming manuals like this one spread widely in the mail order era.
38026-fridtjof-nansen-a-book-for-the-you:
Jacob Bull wrote this life of Fridtjof Nansen for the young, translated by Mordaunt Barnard and published by Heath in Boston in 1903. Barnard had helped translate Nansen's own Farthest North. Ten chapters carry the explorer from boyhood to fame. A map of his polar route fronts the book, and pictures show his birthplace, his ship, and his meeting with Jackson in Franz Josef Land.

Nansen's boyhood at Store Fröen, near Christiania, opens the story. Youthful adventures and winter climbing follow. Then come the preparations for Greenland and the sledging journey across it, the first crossing ever made. The second half treats the Fram expedition: the ship frozen into the ice, the dash farthest north on foot, and the strange wedding trip and marriage between voyages. Bull wrote for boys who dreamed of the pole, and Nansen, still living and honoured, made a hero whose adventures needed no invention.
38156-a-second-coming:
Richard Marsh wrote a novel of Christ come again to modern London. John Lane, The Bodley Head, issued A Second Coming in New York and London. Rights rest from 1900, with a London form in the Roman year MCMIV. A front talk frames the tale: the Man in the Street asks, the Scribe replies.

Chisholm bursts into a dull dinner crying that Christ has come again. Guests and servants stare as entrees cool on the table. Tales told, a tumult, and a passion of the people sort the parts. Readers gain a bold, earnest fable of faith tested by city life.
38443-the-croxley-master-a-great-tale-of:
The Croxley Master, a tale of the prize ring by Conan Doyle, was printed in New York in 1907. McClure, Phillips and Company held the copyright of that year. A plate shows the fighter in the outdoor ring.

Robert Montgomery, a medical assistant, sits at his desk with his head in his hands. Before him lies the open ledger of his employer's prescriptions, with bottles waiting to be filled. Outside the surgery window, great chimneys rise over a district blighted by smoke and greed. It is Sunday, and the furnace fires are banked, yet the gloom hangs on. Montgomery's real trouble is money: sixty pounds stand between him and his final year at the university. Without that sum his medical degree, and his career, are lost to him.
38570-when-a-cobbler-ruled-the-king:
When a Cobbler Ruled the King is Augusta Husiell Seaman's historical novel for young readers. The Macmillan Company of New York published it in 1919, with drawings by George Wharton Edwards. Its copyright dates to 1911, and Seaman dedicated the book to her husband. The tale runs through the French Revolution, from the Dauphin's garden to the star of Napoleon Bonaparte.

The story opens in May 1792, with a boy of twelve and a girl of seven hurrying hand in hand along the Rue St Honoré in Paris. Chapters set the red cap on the Dauphin and face the terrible tenth of August. Then the cobbler enters and the king exits: Simon the cobbler takes command of his royal charge. Seaman tells the Revolution through children's eyes and the strange guardianship that followed the fall of the Tuileries.
38718-lawrence-clavering:
A E W Mason wrote Lawrence Clavering, issued by Ward, Lock and Company in London and Melbourne. Mason had earlier written The Watchers, Clementina, and The Four Feathers. Twenty three chapters fill the novel. Lawrence tells his own tale in the first person. A picture at his lodgings in Avignon starts the story. The great gallery at Blackladies was meant to hold that picture, but never will.

Chapters take Lawrence on a walk with Lord Bolingbroke, who preaches a sermon as they go. He rides one way while his kinsman rides an other, then crosses to England for a strange adventure. Blackladies, Mr Herbert, and a dispute with grave results fill the middle. A talk with Lord Derwentwater, an escape, and the march to Preston bring high stakes. The tale is set in the Jacobite rising age, with love and honour at risk.
38796-second-string:
Anthony Hope wrote a novel about young men, sport, and love in England. The book first came out in 1910 with Thomas Nelson and Sons. Its title, Second String, hints at men not first in line. Parts bear names like Home Again and A Very Little Hunting. The world of Meriton is one key ground in the tale.

Chapters bring a strong voice, set plans, and a race to join. A shawl by a pane, a stole kiss, and marked cash stir the plot. Love and fear pull the leads in two ways. The close deals with guilt, reform, and an empty place. Hope writes with his known light, deft hand.
388-the-crossing:
Winston Churchill, the American novelist, follows a Kentucky youth from the Blue Ridge to Louisiana in this frontier epic. Born under King George III, the hero crosses the mountains, joins the fight for Kaskaskia, and drifts through Danville, St. Louis, and New Orleans. War, trade, and love mark his long road west.

Churchill writes in three books: borderland war, river drift, and Louisiana life. The hero meets soldiers, French settlers, and proud ladies, each testing his mettle. The novel stands as a broad tale of how the West was won, told with sweep and a fond eye for early American grit.
39129-the-optimist-s-good-morning:
The Optimist's Good Morning is a book of uplifting extracts compiled by Florence Hobart Perin. Little, Brown, and Company of Boston published it in 1911, from copyright of 1907, and Perin dedicates it to her mother and father. A long index names the authors she drew on, page by page.

The company is mixed and mostly hopeful. Emerson appears again and again, with both Brownings, Carlyle, Phillips Brooks, and Henry Ward Beecher. Older voices join them: Confucius, Marcus Aurelius, Epictetus, and George Fox. Poets and preachers share the pages with Alice Cary, Bliss Carman, Paul Laurence Dunbar, and Charlotte Perkins Gilman. Each selection is short, meant to be taken like the greeting of the title. The book is a storehouse of good mornings, gathered from several centuries of writers who looked on the bright side.
39318-practical-bookbinding:
Practical Bookbinding, by Paul Adam, director of the Dusseldorf technical school for artistic and practical bookbinding, was rendered from the German by Maw, librarian of the King's Lynn public library. The book was printed in London in 1903 with 127 pictures. Two parts divide the craft: forwarding, the making of the book block, and finishing, the cover and its decoration.

Early chapters sort materials for sewing and pasting, for covering, and for decorating, then the tools. Sewing, cutting, rounding, backing, edge work, and headbanding follow in order. A metric and British measure table opens the volume for workshop use. Later chapters treat the blocking press, hand finishing, account books, school books, and the mounting of maps and drawings. Adam writes a full bench manual.
39379-collins-illustrated-guide-to-londo:
Collins Illustrated Guide to London and Neighbourhood is a handbook for strangers in the capital, issued in London in 1873. William Collins, Sons and Company published the guide from Paternoster Row. It holds fifty eight illustrations by Sargent and others, and a clue map by Bartholomew. Its preface says the aim is to furnish strangers with a handy and useful guide.

The guide gives a concise description of the chief places of interest in the metropolis. It also gives the best modes of obtaining access to them for a visitor. Information on railways, omnibuses, and steamers is included for the traveller in the city. Its contents run from a general description and a first glance at the city to palaces, mansions, and the Houses of Parliament. Hotel charges are listed at the front for the budgeting stranger, a practical touch for its market.
39398-a-system-of-easy-lettering:
Howard Cromwell made a system of easy lettering for sign writers and draughtsmen, printed in New York in 1897 in its fourth thousand. Rights date from 1887. The preface says a formal preface seems hardly needed for so simple a system. Divide any surface to be lettered into squares or parallelograms in pencil, he tells the reader.

Form the letters in ink or paint in the style chosen, then erase the pencil lines, and the lettering is complete. Plate after plate shows alphabets built on the grid, stroke by stroke. Signs, show cards, and titles can all be drawn by this grid method without free hand skill. Working painters and shop men of the day kept such a book at hand.
39730-the-girl-who-had-nothing:
The Girl Who Had Nothing, a novel by Mrs C N Williamson, was published by Ward, Lock and Company of London in 1905. Pictures by John Cameron go with the text. Mrs Williamson also wrote The Lightning Conductor with her husband. The heroine is Joan Carthew, a child of twelve who has decided that today is her birthday, and has marked it by running away from home.

Joan's home is a Brighton lodging house where she lives as a guest who does not pay, and is often reminded of it. Her mother, an actress whose stage name was Marie Lanchester, left her there with money for one season and never returned or wrote. The chapters bring an old lady in a victoria carriage, her nephew, a steam yacht called Titania, and a journalistic mission. An old enemy and a new love close the tale.
39761-the-knack-of-managing:
The Knack of Managing is a business book by Lewis K Urquhart and Herbert Watson, printed at New York by a McGraw-Hill house. It opens with a saying laid to Mr Schwab: given the right organization, it is no harder to manage the United States Steel Corporation than to run a peanut stand. The authors say that view comes close to their own.

Their stress falls on one point: the basic principles of management apply to every business alike. Managing a steel company is not such a far cry from running a pretzel plant or a furniture factory. Each business differs in its own money, sales, production, and labour problems. But those, the authors say, are only the clothes the business wears. One man's trade may differ from another's as a Paris gown differs from sweatshop wear, yet the body beneath is the same.
39861-life-of-henriette-sontag-countess-:
A cheap life of Henriette Sontag, Countess de Rossi, sold for twenty-five cents. The book came out in New York in 1852. A portrait of the great singer fronts the small book. Stringer and Townsend put it out on Broadway. Ads in it praise tales of high life in the same town.

Sontag's stage fame in Europe and America grounds the tale. Court rooms and grand halls fill her bright road. The book adds odd tales and notes from her path. Such cheap lives let plain folk know a famed name fast. Song fans of that age took them up by the score. Her voice is the star of each page here.
39886-modern-painting-its-tendency-and-m:
Modern Painting: Its Tendency and Meaning is a survey of modern art by Willard Huntington Wright. It was first copyrighted in 1915 and reissued at New York in 1922. A Gauguin picture fronts the book. Chapters run from ancient and modern art through the precursors of the new era.

Wright gives chapters to Manet, the early Impressionists, Renoir, and Cézanne. The Neo-Impressionists, Gauguin, Degas, Matisse, and Picasso follow. Cubism, Futurism, and Synchromism each get a chapter before a conclusion surveys the lesser moderns. Written in Paris in 1915, the book was an early American guide to the art that shocked its age. It explains the new schools with sympathy and order.
39907-wilderness-of-spring:
Wilderness of Spring, a novel by Edgar Pangborn, was first issued in nineteen fifty eight by Rinehart and Company in New York and Toronto. Pangborn sets much of the tale in Deerfield in seventeen oh four. He notes that Pastor John Williams of Deerfield was a real man. Names such as Belding, Stebbins, Hoyt, Wells, and Hawks also come from that town and time.

The tale opens with young Ben Cory by firelight on a winter night. Pangborn warns that speech in the book is a blend, not a strict copy of old speech. He keeps some use of thee and thou and of hath and doth. The note helps readers hear the past without strain.
40320-mr-punch-afloat-the-humours-of-boa:
Mr Punch Afloat is a book of jokes and comic pictures on boating and sailing, drawn from the pages of Punch. It belongs to the Punch Library of Humour, edited by Hammerton. The series set out to give the cream of the magazine's fun, from its start in 1841 to the present day.

The pictures are by the great Punch artists. Sir John Tenniel, George du Maurier, John Leech, and Charles Keene all appear on the title page. Phil May and Raven-Hill stand with them. The humour is that of the river and the yacht: capsizes, sea sickness, proud owners, and green hands at the oar. Each volume of the library is complete in itself, and this one keeps to the water throughout.
40446-red-palmer-a-practical-treatise-on:
A practical treatise on fly fishing named Red Palmer fronts this text. Its opening pages carry trade notices for anglers instead of chapters. R B Lodge offers portraits of anglers at the river side. The photos show men at their own pools and shallows. Happy days come back at the sight, the notice claims. Terms wait on request at Enfield.

W Chalkley lets fishing on the Itchen by day, week, month, or season. He makes tackle at the Square in Winchester. A bayonet-pointed gaff gets a full page of specs. Hooks of tested steel run four to six shillings by size. The year 1887 shows in press notices quoted here. Such front matter preserves the tackle trade that served Victorian fly fishers, prices and all.
4050-mates-at-billabong:
A Billabong story for young readers follows Norah and her mates through station life in Australia. Chapters carry them from Norah's home and a first bath to cutting out cattle, a thunderstorm, the Billabong dance, and Christmas.

A letter home tells of arriving at Cunjee to find no one to meet her, then catching a lift in a dirty, springless buggy out to Billabong. The book mixes bush work, school holidays, and friendship with humor and warmth. Children who like horse and station tales will enjoy this cheerful entry in the Billabong series.
40545-the-splendid-fairing:
Constance Holme opens a Westmorland tale on a blind Martinmas day of mist. Mills and Boon issued the novel at London in 1919. The motto runs: all night long the water is crying to me.

Four names divide the contents: Simon and Sarah, Eliza, May, and Geordie-an'-Jim. The opening weighs the day itself as a lever of fate. A brave, buoyant day might have scattered the clinging obsession in time. A tender day might have healed old sores. This day kept its head among the clouds. Stillness lay on the earth like the hour before dawn. The Simon Thornthwaites go to market simply because they cannot stay away. They look dull and tired, as if finishing a journey rather than starting one. Holme writes her dale folk with slow, exact pity.
40547-the-rival-campers-afloat-or-the-pr:
Ruel Perley Smith sends his rival campers onto the water in a sequel issued at Boston by L C Page and Company in 1906, with pictures by Louis D Gowing.

The boys cruise the Samoset River and its bay in June. The contents promise trouble fast: a collision, a rescue that earns no thanks, and a run out to the fishing grounds near the reefs. Squire Brackett blusters through several chapters. A prize yacht called the Viking is searched and then lost. The crew flees in the night before a timely arrival ends the book. Smith wrote the series for boys who liked boats and camps. This volume trades the woods for sails and squalls. It also hides a man in a cabin who should not be there.
40638-a-history-of-wood-engraving:
A History of Wood-Engraving is a work by George E. Woodberry, printed at London in 1883. In his preface Woodberry says he has gathered the facts that men of cultivation should know about the art of engraving in wood. He has left aside matter that belongs to mere book lists. He treats the art in its main works as a mirror of the life of men.

Woodberry shows the craft as a picture of the stages of civilization in turn. Where ground is disputed, most of all in the early history of the art, he names the writers he relies on and those who hold other views. He thanks the Boston Public Library, the Boston Museum of Fine Arts, and Harvard College for leave to copy cuts. More than half his pictures come from the collection of Professor Charles Eliot Norton of Harvard.
407-the-reporter-who-made-himself-king:
Richard Harding Davis tells of a young reporter who lands in a small island kingdom and, by nerve and press craft, makes himself its ruler. Davis opens with a jest on how reporters are trained, then lets his hero prove that bold news sense beats long training. The tale moves from newsroom talk to palace plots in brisk steps.

The reporter charms chiefs, fools rivals, and turns a coup into copy, all with a newspaperman's eye for a story. Davis writes with humor and dash, poking fun at both kings and papers. The short tale endures as a witty fantasy of the press age, when a bold man might still invent his own crown.
40802-the-behavior-of-the-honey-bee-in-p:
The Behavior of the Honey Bee in Pollen Collecting is a government bulletin. Casteel wrote it for the Bureau of Entomology, issued December 31, 1912. It is bulletin number one hundred twenty one of that bureau series. Howard, chief of bureau, sent it to the Secretary of Agriculture in Washington.

Cross pollination of fruit flowers makes bee pollen work worth exact study. Casteel watched bees at the bureau apiary in the summers of 1911 and 1912. Structures the bee uses to handle pollen are described first in the text. The pollen supply and the bee actions in gathering follow in order. Bee keepers and fruit growers are the readers it aims to serve.
41035-fire-and-sword-in-the-sudan-a-pers:
Fire and Sword in the Sudan, by Rudolf C Slatin Pasha, was published by Edward Arnold in eighteen ninety-six. Major F R Wingate translated the narrative. Slatin was a colonel in the Egyptian army and formerly governor and commandant of the troops in Darfur. His subtitle promises a personal narrative of fighting and serving the dervishes, eighteen seventy-nine to eighteen ninety-five.

Slatin's preface, dated at London in October eighteen ninety-five, explains his haste. He kept no notes or diaries during his captivity, so memory alone supplied the record. He escaped the Mahdi's camp only months before writing. The book is dedicated, by permission, to Queen Victoria, for her sympathy with European prisoners in the Sudan. Slatin's account of the Mahdist state from inside became a standard source.
41133-studies-in-the-art-of-rat-catching:
Studies in the Art of Rat-Catching is a sporting manual by Barkley. Murray published the popular edition in London in 1896. Barkley had written travel books before it. A preface explains the odd subject. The publisher himself asked how such a book came to be.
