Barkley tells the story over a country-house fire. Boys pressed him for more rat-catching tales of old days. One boy wished they taught the art at school. Barkley promised to write his memories from abroad. He shaped them as school exercises on purpose. Head-masters will not adopt the book, he jokes. The contents begin with ferrets and their hutches. Choosing and feeding ferrets come first. Dog language and ratting tools follow.
41135-the-theory-and-practice-of-model-a:
The Theory and Practice of Model Aeroplaning is a technical manual by Johnson, published by Spon in London and New York in 1910. Johnson had already written on airships, soaring flight, and how to build a model aeroplane. His frontispiece calls the balance the most important tool in building model aeroplanes. The introduction divides models into two classes and states the first requisite of a model.

Johnson insists that model aeroplaning is an art in itself, not a toy version of the real thing. Chapter one takes up the question of weight, of primary importance in both rubber-driven and power-driven models. It cites Professor Langley's experiences and asks how to get the most strength with the least weight. Chapter two turns to resistance: the shape of least resistance, the aerofoil surface, and skin friction.
41519-thought-culture-or-practical-menta:
Thought-Culture, or Practical Mental Training, is a book by William Walker Atkinson, printed at Chicago with copyright in 1910. It stands in his New Psychology series, sold at a dollar a volume or ten dollars the set. Fowler issued the London edition. Fourteen chapters run from the power of thought to constructive imagination.

Atkinson treats attention, perception, abstraction, and association of ideas in turn. Judgment and reasoning close the course. The series page names its companions: The Will, Memory, Suggestion and Auto-Suggestion, and The Psychology of Success. One theme, the publisher says, binds the set into a whole. Atkinson opens by asking what thought itself is, a word we use every waking hour yet can hardly define.
41632-the-art-of-entertaining:
The Art of Entertaining is a book of manners and hospitality by Mrs Sherwood, published in New York by Dodd, Mead and Company in 1893. It is dedicated to Chauncey Depew, in praise of his wit and learning. The preface sets America beside England, France, and Italy in the art. The first rule, Sherwood says, is as old as the patriarchs in their tents. The western settler who gave his last meat to a guest had it by heart. That is the hospitality of the heart, the base of the whole art.

From that meal to a Newport dinner is a long stair, she notes. The book hopes to help the reader climb it rung by rung. It joins the poetry and history of entertaining to plain hints on feeding guests. Wit and taste must feed the soul where meat fails.
41784-wyoming:
Wyoming is a tale of the Revolution by Edward Ellis, with copyright in 1888 at Philadelphia. It stands as number one of the Wyoming Series, and Ellis also wrote the Young Pioneer and Log Cabin books. The tale opens on the sultry third of July, 1778, in the Wyoming Valley, where smoke rolls up from a settlement and guns rattle in the distance.

Fred Godfrey, a sturdy youth of eighteen, rides at breakneck speed toward the fight. All who are dear to him live in that valley, and he fears he comes too late. Fred had donned the Continental uniform the day he turned seventeen, just as his father had promised when the war broke out.
41924-renaissance-in-italy-volume-2-of-7:
John Addington Symonds wrote The Revival of Learning as volume two of his seven-volume Renaissance in Italy. It first appeared from Smith, Elder and Company in London. The volume follows The Age of the Despots, published in 1875, and comes before the volume on the fine arts. Symonds opens with lines from Petrarch's Africa, a fitting start for a book about learning reborn.

In his preface Symonds explains his method. He did not aim to rewrite the whole history of learning. Instead he treats each part of his theme as it bears on the general culture of the Italian Renaissance. He chose points and details that show how scholarship, letters, and study shaped the age. Later volumes on the fine arts and on Italian literature complete the design, making this the volume where the recovery of classical learning takes the centre of the story.
41938-principles-and-practice-of-fur-dre:
Principles and Practice of Fur Dressing and Fur Dyeing is a trade book by William Austin. A Van Nostrand house of New York brought it out in nineteen twenty two. Austin works as a chem hand to the fur trade in his own words. Part one treats furs and their marks in the scheme at front. Fur lore is a must, that part holds in its first head words.

Kind gaps, clime, age, wear life, and weight of furs fill its heads. Skin build, hair build, and chem make of furs fill part two ranks. Dress craft past and first steps fill parts three and four in scheme. Tan ways, dry and end work, and water choice fill mid parts. Dye past, dye rules, and fake rich furs on cheap skins close it.
42080-the-voice-in-singing:
The Voice in Singing is a treatise on vocal science by Emma Seiler, translated from the German and published by Lippincott of Philadelphia in 1879 in a revised and enlarged edition. Seiler was a member of the American Philosophical Society. The translator's preface asks recognition for her claims as a lady of rare scientific attainments, lately come to live in America. The contents fall into four parts after an introduction.

Vocal Music comes first, then the Physiological, Physical, and Aesthetic parts, with an appendix. A commendation preserved in the copy comes from Helmholtz himself. In preparing his work on the sensations of tone, he writes, he had the honour of becoming acquainted with Madame Seiler. She assisted him in his essay upon the formation of the vowel tones and the registers of the female voice. He praises the delicacy of her musical ear and her ability.
42157-the-nursery-august-1881-vol-xxx-a-:
The Nursery is a month sheet for the most young readers, put out at Boston. The host print is count two of the thirty year run, of eighteen eighty one. Its rights were put on the rolls that year. The list of parts falls in two heaps. One heap is prose, and one is verse. Plates stand with the tales and songs.

The young fish man heads the prose heap. A small slip, two games, and more of a famed coon fill the first run. A boy and his goats, a maid and her nut beast, and a draw drill come next. A sweep of chim neys, a boy and his dog, and a wish to be a king fill the rest. Ten ticks with a boy, a cat tale, and the fruit of a boy close the prose.
42245-thunder-and-lightning:
Thunder and Lightning is a work of popular science turned from the French of Flammarion. The front pages carry a note on his Popular Astronomy in the English of J. Ellard Gore, with three plates and 288 pictures. That notice calls the larger work a clear and true account of what is known of the bodies of space. It treats their motions and their make-up in six books.

The text at hand takes up the storm: thunder and lightning as its title states. The head as shown is front matter and notices of the author's kindred works. The book stands in the line of Flammarion's works for the plain reader on the sky and its forces. Page pictures from the first print can be had with the text in a linked form, as the note at the head states.
42521-god-and-the-king:
Marjorie Bowen wrote a historical novel published in 1911, dedicated to a Dutch general who ran the military history branch. Part one, The Revolution, begins on June 30, 1688. Chapters follow a messenger from England, the Princess of Orange, and the policy of the Prince. France moves, storms hit, and a second sailing follows.

Part two, The Queen, turns to a dark dawning and a woman's strength. Part three, The King, covers the Bank of England, a breaking friendship, and France challenging again. A French quote in the opening praises a prince skilled at forming leagues. Bowen builds a wide canvas around William of Orange.
42543-sappho-a-new-rendering:
Stacpoole Englished the songs of Sappho in this new rendering for Hutchinson of London. His first chapter sets the Greek poet at a vast remove from us. Sappho lies beyond the fashions and the ages, he writes, almost beyond the wing of thought.

To feel that gap, he says, count not in years but in ages of the world. Rome and the age of Christ lie between us and her. Beyond the cross stands Athens, with the white flower of the Acropolis. In her day Nineveh still stood, and Phoenician sails were setting out for Africa. Draco, Jeremiah, and the Buddha's father were her near kin in time. Such a frame suits her few, bright songs.
42860-the-andes-of-southern-peru-geograp:
The Andes of Southern Peru reports a geographical survey along the seventy-third meridian. Isaiah Bowman wrote the book. He directed the American Geographical Society. Holt published it in 1916 for that society. Photographs came from the Yale Peruvian expeditions.

The book divides into two parts. The first treats human geography. Chapters cover the regions of Peru and the Urubamba canyons. Rubber forests and forest Indians follow. A chapter treats the country of the shepherds. Another asks how geography shapes revolutions and character. The second part treats the land itself. It covers the western and eastern ranges in turn. Coastal terraces and glacial features follow. Seven topographic sheets accompany the text.
42863-bright-ideas-for-entertaining:
Bright Ideas for Entertaining is a party handbook by Mrs Linscott, printed at Philadelphia by George Jacobs in 1905. Its full title promises two hundred forms of amusement for social gatherings of all kinds. Large or small parties, clubs, sociables and church entertainments are all served. Thirty articles in the book first appeared in The Ladies' Home Journal.

The first game is Acting Proverbs, where the company divides into actors and spectators. Each actor performs a proverb in pantomime. One sprinkles and then pours water over flowers: it never rains but it pours. Another rolls a stone about the room for the rolling stone that gathers no moss. Later games include guessing advertisements from cut out pictures pasted on white paper. The book is a hostess's armoury from the parlour game era.
42940-the-battleship-boys-in-foreign-ser:
Frank Gee Patchin wrote this sea tale for boys, issued by the Saalfield Publishing Company of Akron and New York with a 1911 copyright. Sam Hickey and Dan Davis, the battleship boys, open the book in the Bois de Boulogne in Paris, where Sam mocks French names. The chapters promise rescues, a grave charge, and high-priced ice cream.

The voyage runs from Paris society to Gibraltar, the blue Mediterranean, and Egypt, with camels and mummies along the way. Two boys go missing, one takes his first command, and a storm twists around the ship. Patchin wrote for young readers who liked the navy, travel, and brisk talk, and the book gives them all three in full.
43041-double-or-nothing:
Double or Nothing is a science tale by Jack Sharkey, first set in a pulp sheet in the early nineteen sixties. A note at the front tells that a long hunt found no proof its rights were made new in law. A row of dread asks heads the tale in slanted lines.

The mind quails, those lines say, at the thought of no end, or of an end, or of a vast rain of food packs from the sky. The teller then owns he knows not why he heeds his friend Artie at all. The man finds, at all turns, a new device that will change the world. His gift for machines is near past count. Each new plan sucks the teller in once more, and the tale rolls from that trap.
4312-a-life-s-morning:
George Gissing wrote this novel around Wilfrid Athel, an undergraduate sent down invalided soon after the start of Trinity term. The contents follow Beatrice Redwing, a conflict of opinions, the shadow of home, a visitor by express, and a sterner wooing. Later chapters bring Emily's decision, a cutting of the knot, renunciation, and a family conclave.

The title points to a morning of life, when choices still seem open and their costs are only dimly seen. Gissing traces Wilfrid and Emily through courtship, family pressure, and separation. The novel rewards readers who like Victorian stories of love weighed against duty, money, and pride.
4342-organic-gardener-s-composting:
Steve Solomon wrote this practical guide to composting for organic gardeners. He opens by asking what really happens when things rot, and he promises clear meanings for words like humus, compost, and organic matter. Garden books, he says, often confuse readers with vague terms such as stabilized humus.

Solomon explains the compost pile as a fast track for turning crude organic matter into something like soil. He treats the pile as a living process, not a nasty chore, and he gives plain directions for building and keeping it. The book suits gardeners who want rich soil without chemicals, and who want to understand why compost works.
43480-smoking-and-drinking:
James Parton wrote Smoking and Drinking, an essay on two common habits and health. Ticknor and Fields issued the book in Boston in eighteen hundred sixty eight. The front essay turns first to how far the age has come. Schools, free thought, and cheap goods all win praise there.

Parton says no child in the land will soon live far from a school. Free speech on hard themes now draws no real harm, he notes. Steam and mills have cut the cost of cloth and tools. A poor workman can live near as well as his rich neighbor. Health, he argues, is the next great task for the age. Smoke and drink are the foes his short book then takes up in earnest.
43515-visual-signaling:
Visual Signaling is a drill book of the war desk of the United States, made in the desk of the chief call chief. It is count six of the drill books of that corps. It was print at the chief town in nineteen ten. A writ of the war desk stands past its front. That writ bears a date of the spring of that year. It sets the book in force for the host and for the sworn bands of the states.

The book takes the place, that writ says, of all past sheets on the theme. Chiefs and men of the call corps are to make them selves full with its words. The list of parts starts with a lead in. Then comes the kit of sight calls.
43620-doing-and-daring:
Doing and Daring is a New Zealand story for young readers by Eleanor Stredder, printed by Nelson in 1899. Stredder also wrote Lost in the Wilds and Jack and his Ostrich. A verse from Whittier stands at the front, on counting a brother's welfare sacred. A plate shows the old chief.

The chapters open in a mountain gorge and at a whare by the lake. A ride through the bush leads to a new home, then midnight alarms and a rain of mud. A raging sea, a Maori boy, and widespread desolation follow. Edwin makes a discovery, feeds the hungry, and falls into danger. Whero comes to the rescue, and a valley farm closes the tale. The book mixes settler hardship with a warm moral thread, in the Nelson house style for the young.
43797-favorite-fish-and-fishing:
James A Henshall wrote Favorite Fish and Fishing, issued by The Outing Publishing Company in New York in MCMVIII, with a copyright of nineteen oh eight. Henshall had written Book of the Black Bass and Camping and Cruising in Florida. A front plate shows grayling fishing on the West Fork of the Madison River in Montana. Henshall gave the book to the memory of Judge Nicholas Longworth, his friend on many outings.

Five long pieces fill the book. The black bass is called the game fish of the people, and the grayling the flower of fishes. The trout is called the angler pride, with plates of brook, cut throat, steelhead, and rainbow trout. His Majesty the silver king treats tarpon, and a last piece treats Florida fish and fishing. Anglers get lore, tackle talk, and river tales from a master of the sport.
43954-practical-psychomancy-and-crystal-:
William Walker Atkinson wrote a course of drills on mind sight, put out in nineteen eight. The book treats far sense, sight past sight, the read of things held in hand, and gaze into glass balls. Its front list lays out the full course part by part. Each part gives plain steps for the student to try.

First parts treat what the craft is and how to wake the gift. Next come the tube of the stars, the read of a lock of hair or a bloom, and the glass ball. Late parts take up flight of the soul, far sight, and case tales from a famed guild that tests such claims. The tone stays calm and plain, as if the craft were a plain skill to learn.
44230-on-yachts-and-yacht-handling:
Thomas Fleming Day wrote On Yachts and Yacht Handling, published by the Rudder Publishing Company in 1901. Day edited The Rudder, the leading American yachting magazine. He dedicated the book to those who had spent many hours with him round the clubhouse fire. His reason for writing, he says, is simple: the book was wanted, and his excuse is thirty years' experience handling many boats on many waters.

The chapters move through seamanship, boats in general, one-man boats, and sea-going boats. Rigs, reefing, anchors and anchoring, and rigging follow, with stranding last. Day believed a textbook should please as well as instruct, so he wrote in the first person throughout. He argues that the flavour of the individual is lost when a man speaks for another rather than as himself. The book remains a classic of small-boat sailing, plain spoken and practical.
44284-reminiscences-of-glass-making:
Reminiscences of Glass-Making is a history of the glass trade by Deming Jarves. Hurd and Houghton published this second, enlarged edition in New York in 1865. The pieces began as articles in the columns of a village newspaper. A small pamphlet of them had circulated privately in 1854.

Jarves asks little credit for the writing itself in his preface. The work, he says, was done in spare moments stolen from business. His aim was to gather sound information into a short and handy form. Glass-making, he argues, holds a rare place among American manufactures. It ranks high among both the useful and the elegant arts of the country.
44312-the-remarkable-history-of-the-huds:
The Remarkable History of the Hudson's Bay Company is a large history by George Bryce, a professor at Manitoba College in Winnipeg. The hosted text follows the third edition, issued in London by Sampson Low. Maps and full-page plates run through the book.

The frontispiece shows four great governors of the company. Prince Rupert stands first, and Lord Strathcona, the present governor, last. The title promises the French traders of the north-west as well. The North-West, X Y, and Astor fur companies all come into the tale. Bryce writes as a native-born Canadian who knows much of the ground. He brought the book up to date for this edition. He claims to have judged the company men and their foes without fear or favour.
44606-wood-engraving:
Wood Engraving is a craft study by Beedham, with an introduction and appendix by Eric Gill. Faber and Faber of London printed it. Its plates reach back to a wood-cut from the Decameron printed at Venice in 1492, re-engraved by Beedham. Work by Reynolds Stone, Claire Leighton, and Robert Gibbings also appears.

The text argues the art's discipline. One advantage of wood engraving, it says, is that it forces the workman to respect the thing in itself. Mere likeness to nature, easy in drawing, will not serve. Gill's circle held the block to be a moral teacher as much as a tool. The book also speaks plainly of money: there is none in it at the start, though a patient, devoted worker may make part of a living. It is a manifesto of the great revival of the craft.
44720-packing-and-portaging:
Packing and Portaging, by Dillon Wallace, is an Outing handbook published at New York in 1912. Wallace wrote The Lure of the Labrador Wild and The Long Labrador Trail. Packing and the outfit open the contents of the guide at page nine. The canoe and its equipment follow as the second chapter of the book.

Camp equipment for the canoe trip and personal equipment fill the next heads. Food, then the portage itself, form the heart of the canoe half of the guide. Travel with saddle and pack animals opens the horse half of the contents. Saddle gear, adjusting the pack, and practical hitches get chapters of their own. Woodsmen and campers of 1912 got a full kit manual in these pages.
44732-the-library-of-work-and-play-house:
Housekeeping, by Elizabeth Hale Gilman, is a volume in a children library set. Doubleday Page issued the Library of Work and Play volume in nineteen eleven. Sister volumes treat carpentry, gardening, home decoration, and needlecraft for youth. Gilman volume teaches housekeeping as work and play for young helpers.

Part one treats the play house, and part two learning and helping at home. Part three, My Heritage, plans a real house in careful steps. Chapters cover the plan, the accounts, the schedule, and possessions in turn. Care of furniture, upstairs work, and dining room work follow in order. Kitchen, cellar, and fires close the practical course for the home.
44923-slim-evans-and-his-horse-lightning:
Slim Evans and His Horse Lightning, a western novel by Graham Dean, was published at Chicago with a 1934 copyright. It opens on the Sky High Trail among the rugged Cajon peaks, where July sun beats down on dry country. A cowboy on a sorrel horse picks his way through a pass, dust thick on both of them. The rider is Slim Evans, and his horse is Lightning.

Chapter titles promise bushwhackers, a strange letter, and trouble looming. The unknown rider appears, camps vanish, and Slim rides alone as war is declared. Clues, teltale marks, and a night alarm lead through a cloudburst to a trap in the canyons. A confession and a showdown close the tale. Dean wrote for young readers, and the book keeps a fast pace of trail riding, hidden foes, and last minute escapes in the cowboy manner of its time.
45136-he-comes-up-smiling:
He Comes Up Smiling is a comic novel by Charles Sherman, published in Indianapolis by Bobbs-Merrill in 1912, with illustrations by Arthur William Brown. Its title names its hero's habit: knocked down, he comes up smiling. The contents run to twenty-five chapters of road and town adventure.

The first chapter is a beauty contest. Two hoboes talk: the Watermelon tells James, with rare candour, that his face would make a mangy pup unhappy. James sneers back that the Watermelon thinks himself a Venus. A close shave, a Mr. Batchelor, and a plan with a telegram follow. Watermelon yields, a deserted house, and a night's lodging fill the road chapters. Billy appears everywhere, a thief comes in the night, and a broker prince and the seven o'clock express bring the tale to town. Sherman writes the tramp's life as farce, with a warm heart under the jokes.
45372-road-scrapings-coaches-and-coachin:
Road Scrapings, coaches and coaching, by Captain M E Haworth, was published by Tinsley Brothers of London in 1882. Haworth also wrote The Silver Greyhound. Coaching, the driving of four horse coaches for sport, was then enjoying a revival after the railways had killed the old road trade. The book mixes counsel for the coachman with tales of the road.

The introduction owns the plan: advice drawn from long experience, with anecdotes stirred in to cure the dryness of mere instruction. The contents promise the revival and death of coaching, and the death and resurrection of the craft. Young coachmen are told to save their horses and mind their ribbons and whip. Tales follow of how the mail was robbed, of an accident to the Yeovil mail, and of a gallop for their lives. A wild beast attack and roadside burials season the scrapings.
45383-drifting:
Buchanan Read wrote Drifting, a poem, printed by Lippincott at Philadelphia in 1881. Humphrey drew the designs that illustrate the small volume. Its verse opens with the poet's soul far away at sea. My soul to-day is far away, sailing the Vesuvian Bay, it sings. My winged boat, a bird afloat, swims round the purple peaks remote.

Round purple peaks it sails, and seeks blue inlets. High rocks throw a golden glow through the deeps below. Far and dim, the mountains swim in the haze, it runs. On Vesuvius' misty brim the gray smoke stands with outstretched hands. Sorrento swings on sunset wings, where Tasso's spirit soars and sings. I heed not if my skiff floats swift or slow, the poet owns. At peace he lies, blown softly by, a cloud upon a liquid sky. Read gives a dream of the bay of Naples in song.
45584-facts-and-speculations-on-the-orig:
William Andrew Chatto wrote a history of playing cards that John Russell Smith of London published in 1848. His preface takes up the plain man's doubt: what can interest any one in such a subject? Much, he answers.

Chatto treats the grave guesses of the learned with a smile. His own questions are plainer. Where and when were cards invented, and what do their names mean? When did they reach Europe, and how did the game spread? What changes have the figures and suit marks undergone? Last, what have churchmen held on the lawfulness of play? The book works through the old prints and packs to answer.
45700-mr-punch-on-the-continong:
One volume of the Punch Library of Humour, edited by Hammerton and issued by the Amalgamated Press, collects the magazine's jokes and cartoons about travel on the Continent. Its 152 illustrations come from Punch artists such as Phil May, du Maurier, Leech, Keene, Ravenhill, Partridge, Reed, and Cleaver.

The foreword stresses that the humour carries no ill feeling toward other nations. It contrasts this with the French comic press before the Entente Cordiale and with the German press of the day. Punch, it says, laughs hardest at English tourists and their follies abroad. One cartoon has two Londoners in Venice mistake the Bridge of Sighs for Temple Bar. The volume preserves the light, self-mocking tone that made Punch a fixture of British comic life.
45940-reliques-of-ancient-english-poetry:
Thomas Percy, Bishop of Dromore, gathered the old ballads and songs of England in his famed Reliques. Allen and Unwin printed this second volume in London, in a line first set by Swan Sonnenschein in 1885. The book ran through printings to 1927.

Heroic ballads, songs, and pieces of the early poets fill the set, with a few of later date. Richard of Almaigne opens this volume, then a song on the death of Edward the First. A ballad called Chaucer's own, the Turnament of Tottenham, and a song for Agincourt follow. The Not-Browne Mayd, a balet by Earl Rivers, and Cupid's Assault by Lord Vaux fill the first book of this volume alone.
45941-reliques-of-ancient-english-poetry:
Thomas Percy gathered the Reliques of Ancient English Poetry. This file holds the third volume in the edition edited by Henry Wheatley, first published in 1885 and reprinted as late as 1927. Percy's gathering of old heroic ballads, songs, and pieces of the earlier poets first taught England to prize its ballad stock. The third volume opens with poems on King Arthur.

The Boy and the Mantle, The Marriage of Sir Gawaine, and King Arthur's Death stand at its head, some copied from the folio manuscript. A second book takes up the legend of Sir Guy, with Scottish songs, Lord Thomas and Fair Ellinor, and Child Morrice among its ballads. The Reliques shaped how later ages read the old singing past.
46052-a-b-c-of-vegetable-gardening:
Eben Rexford, a famed hand at garden books, wrote this plain guide to growing vegetables. Harper printed it in February 1916 in its A-B-C line, beside guides to speech, building, and housekeeping. Rexford also wrote the line's A-B-C of Gardening.

Getting the garden ready opens the book, then laying out and planting. Seeds that give best results and early garden work follow. Plants in the house, standard kinds of vegetables, and small fruits fill the middle. Hotbeds and cold-frames, small gardens, and left-overs take the late chapters. A last chapter on health in the garden speaks straight to women readers, a sign of its day. Short, clear rules mark the whole.
4607-love-me-little-love-me-long:
Charles Reade tells this mild tale through Lucy Fountain, a young lady of beauty and standing who loses her mother, her sole surviving parent, nearly a quarter century before the main action. Her two trustees, Edward Fountain of Font Abbey and Mr. Bazalgette, a merchant married to her mother's half-sister, agree to share the burden. Lucy spends half the year with each trustee, until marriage takes her off their hands.

The story begins in Bazalgette's house, two years into that arrangement, and Reade lets chit-chat do the work of character. Men and women, he notes, do not come ticketed or with explanations in hand, so readers must judge them by talk. Readers get a gentle Victorian courtship novel, with guardians, suitors, and household talk, and with Reade's usual care for social detail and fair play.
46075-motor-matt-or-the-king-of-the-whee:
Motor Matt, or the King of the Wheel, is the first Motor Stories weekly. Stanley Matthews wrote the tale for the Street and Smith house. The issue is dated February the twenty seventh, nineteen hundred and nine. Five cents bought the first of the long run of Matt tales.

A cover shout bids a price for the man who can stop the boy at speed. Parts name bad blood, a try out, a charm foot, and foul play in turn. A ship named Bluebell and a fast car named Comet crowd the plot. Matt shows his flags and meets a dare in the mid parts of the tale. Road thrills for boys form the whole pull of the new line.
4619-words-of-cheer-for-the-tempted-the-:
T. S. Arthur edited Words of Cheer for the Tempted, the Toiling, and the Sorrowing, published at Philadelphia in 1856. Every life, he says, alternates easy, blossom-strewn ways with hard, rough going, and bright days with storm-blackened ones to follow. On rough roads under a darkened sky, courage falters and trembles, and trusting eyes fail to glimpse the sun shining past the cloud veil.

Yet Arthur insists the rugged path winds steadily upward, and the broad sky still glitters in light. Readers are urged to keep faith in the God who feeds young lions, clothes fields, binds broken hearts, and gives joy to mourners. The volume gathers short pieces meant to be read in trouble, one by one. It suits readers of Victorian devotional writing, and anyone who wants plain, hopeful counsel for hard days.
46237-the-romance-of-book-collecting:
The Romance of Book-Collecting is a book for book hunters by Slater, editor of Book Prices Current, published in New York in 1898. A facsimile of the cover of Poe's Tamerlane stands at the front. The first chapter is a eulogy of catalogues. Old sale catalogues, Slater shows, are the lost maps of the book world. Most go to the rubbish heap or the paper mill. Yet the hunter who keeps them holds the record of where great books have been and what they fetched.

The chapters run on through a comparison of prices and some lucky finds. The hunting grounds of London get a chapter of their own. The vagaries of book hunters, the rules of the chase, and the glamour of bindings fill the rest. The hammer and the end close the book. Slater writes with the joy of a man of the stalls.
4632-the-good-time-coming:
T. S. Arthur published The Good Time Coming at Boston and Philadelphia in 1855. His preface says life is a mystery to all, and the deeper a striving spirit sinks into selfish instincts, the more profound the mystery grows. How earnestly we fix our eyes on the slowly advancing future, impatiently waiting for that good time coming which never comes, while years glide by, beginning in hope and ending in disappointment.

Strange, Arthur says, that we gain so little true wisdom amid sharp disappointments at almost every turn. He too has long been an anxious waiter for the good time coming, which has not yet arrived. Yet hope should not die because of disappointment. There is a good time coming for each of us, if we work and wait patiently, and look in the right direction. Readers get an earnest Victorian moral book about hope, work, and patience.
46416-birds-nests-eggs-and-egg-collectin:
R Kearton wrote on birds' nests, eggs, and egg collecting for young field workers. Cassell and Company issued the book in London and New York in 1913. Twenty-two colored plates show eggs of goldfinch, magpie, raven, and wren. The work first came out in 1890 and was reprinted many times since.

Kearton calls the study of eggs a science worthy of more than schoolboy care. Nest craft, he argues, comes from conditions, not blind instinct alone. He aims to give full, clear facts within a small, plain compass. Bird lovers gain a warm, close guide to nests and the art of finding them.
46519-robert-annys-poor-priest-a-tale-of:
Robert Annys, Poor Priest, a historical tale by Annie Nathan Meyer, was published at New York in 1901. Its subtitle calls it a tale of the great uprising. The priest of the story belongs to the world of John Ball, the famed preacher of the peasants' rising. Meyer tells the reader plainly where her debts lie.

She took Ball's likeness and parts of his sermon from William Morris and his Dream of John Ball. Those bits, she says, were too fine and true to spare in setting the blunt old priest before modern readers. Years of close reading of church historians also fed the book. The tale brings the rising of 1381 to life through one poor priest's eyes. Meyer blends fact, Morris's vision, and her own telling into a short, earnest novel of revolt, faith, and the common people's hopes in a hard age.
46601-gems-for-the-young-folks-fourth-bo:
Gems for the Young Folks is the fourth book of the Faith Promoting Series, printed at Salt Lake City in 1881 by the Juvenile Instructor Office. The set was made to teach and hearten young Latter day Saints. Short true pieces fill the book.

The preface says men of long church service had begun to write down rich bits of their lives for the young. The editor warns that the old elders were fast passing away, and their tales would be lost if not set in print now. Some gems are brief, yet each holds a lesson or a rule of life. A part holds testimonies for the truth. The next book was to tell of Elder Jacob Hamblin, a frontier man and worker among the Indians.
46821-seeing-and-hearing:
Seeing and Hearing is a book of essays by George Russell, author of Collections and Recollections. Grant Richards published the work at London in 1907. Russell dedicates the volume to the memory of a friend who died that year. The contents list fifty three short essays on the life of society.

The topics range from a coronation to Christmas and New Year's Day. Secret societies, wills, pensions, and mourning each receive a chapter. Meals fill a run of essays, from luncheon and tea to dinner and supper. Oxford, the public schools, and Sunday in London show his range. Russell writes as an insider of the world he describes. The essays mix memory, gossip, and judgement on the manners of his age.
46915-a-treatise-on-painting:
Leonardo da Vinci wrote A Treatise on Painting, here turned into English by John Francis Rigaud. J Taylor issued the book in London, in the form first set in eighteen hundred two. Twenty three copper plates and more figures crowd its pages. John Sidney Hawkins wrote a fresh life of the master for it.

Rigaud first sorted the loose notes under fit heads for readers. The Italian text had come down in rich but tangled form. A plate portrait from a Florence museum fronts the work. Light, shade, colour, and the human frame fill its rules. Young painters were its first mark when Leonardo set them down. Hawkins drew his life from stores no man had used before. The book stands as the great shop book of the Renaissance. Each rule points back to a keen eye at close work.
47089-writing-illuminating-lettering:
Edward Johnston's Writing and Illuminating, and Lettering, issued by John Hogg in London in 1906, is a handbook of fine handwriting in the Artistic Crafts Series edited by Lethaby. Johnston supplies the diagrams himself, with Noel Rooke, and the book carries examples in red and black and plates of old work.

The editor's preface sets out the series aim: trustworthy textbooks of workshop practice that treat design as part of good workmanship, not as surface ornament. A frontispiece shows a medieval writing room, copied from a miniature of 1456. The handbook teaches letter forms, tools, and methods step by step. It became a founding text of the modern revival of calligraphy, turning a trade skill back into an art.
47200-oracles-from-the-poets-a-fanciful-:
Caroline Gilman made a fortune-telling game from lines of the poets. John Wiley issued Oracles from the Poets in New York in 1848. Rights were first entered in 1844 by Wiley and Putnam. The book is given to her children at the front, for whose amusement the pages were first arranged.

Gilman built the game after seeing the pull of a plain fortune teller in a young girl's hands. Six months of spare hours went into choosing the verse answers. Shakespeare's Sir Oracle and Macbeth's witches front the title page as apt patrons. Parlor readers gain a genteel game that smuggles fine poetry into play.
47343-little-masterpieces-of-science-hea:
Little Masterpieces of Science: Health and Healing, edited by George Iles, came out in New York in 1902. Doubleday, Page and Company issued the small volume, with a portrait of Louis Pasteur in front. Ten medical writers share the pages.

The first piece, by Paget, tells the escape from pain as the history of a discovery. Davy tried nitrous oxide about 1800 and urged it for surgery, the summary notes. Wells, Long, Morton, and Warren then took up gas and ether in turn. Simpson brought in chloroform to ease the pains of childbirth. The next piece pairs Jenner and Pasteur as the twin heroes of preventive medicine. Jenner's clue came from a countrywoman who said cow-pox kept small-pox away. In 1796 he vaccinated a patient with success.
47578-country-rambles-and-manchester-wal:
Country Rambles is a book of rural wanderings by Leo Grindon, printed at Manchester in 1882. Its full title adds Manchester walks and wild flowers. The rambles cross Cheshire, Lancashire, Derbyshire, and Yorkshire. Grindon also wrote The Manchester Flora and Manchester Banks and Bankers. A Longfellow verse stands at the front, sending the worn and sorrowing to the woods and hills.

His preface explains the book's making. Part reprints his little volume of 1858, Manchester Walks and Wild-Flowers. Part draws on his accounts of Field Naturalists' Society trips from 1860 to 1881, with much new matter added. The old book had long been unprocurable, and Grindon hopes to wake a new generation's taste for country scenes.
47639-hints-on-wolf-and-coyote-trapping:
Hints on Wolf and Coyote Trapping is a government leaflet by Stanley P Young, a senior biologist in charge of predator control. It was issued in July nineteen thirty as a leaflet of the Bureau of Biological Survey. Young opens with the range of coyotes and wolves in the United States of his day. That range lay mainly west of the Mississippi River.

Wolves west of the hundredth meridian had been so reduced that they caused little concern, he states. Drifting animals from Mexico were the main exception in the south. Alaska held the heaviest wolf ground that remained. Sets, baits, and trap craft for stock protection fill the practical hints that follow.
48115-the-king-behind-the-king:
Warwick Deeping wrote this romance of old France, and McBride, Nast printed it at New York in 1914. Forty-one chapters carry the tale. Its title names its theme: the power that stands behind the throne and moves the king.

Fulk of the Forest opens the tale on the road to Witch's Cross. A full moon shines like a silver buckler behind him. He comes to a stand among the yews of the Black Gill. Before him runs a black aisle of huge yews, arched and pillared like a church choir. Deeping's rich, brooding style fills that first page, and his tale of love, faith, and secret rule unfolds from it.
48116-a-guide-to-the-mount-s-bay-and-the:
A Guide to the Mount’s Bay and the Land’s End surveys western Cornwall for guests and sick folk alike. W Phillips printed the second edition in London in eighteen hundred twenty four. A doctor wrote the book but left his name off it. The Royal Geological Society of Cornwall takes the gift page.

Chapters treat the lay of the land, plants, farms, and fish work. Old stones, mines, and rock lore each get a full part. New sea baths at Penzance draw praise in the front notes. A talk at the back weighs the mild air of Penzance. It sets that air beside Devon and the south of Europe. Weak guests chose winter homes by such guides in that age.
48183-glimpses-of-nature-and-objects-of-:
Mrs Loudon wrote these glimpses of nature from a visit to the Isle of Wight. Grant and Griffith printed the second edition in London in 1848. Forty two illustrations aid young persons in forming habits of observation. The tour set out August 21, 1843, from Bayswater with Agnes.

Her husband died less than a month after the first edition. She never looked at the book again till this revision work. A new chapter on shells and sea weed joins the second edition. Southampton Bar in olden time fronts the volume as a plate.
48325-karl-krinken-his-christmas-stockin:
Karl Krinken, His Christmas Stocking, a Christmas book by the authors of The Wide, Wide World and Queechy, was published by James Nisbet and Company of London in 1878. A note signed Amy Lothrop sorts out the sisters' shares in their joint books. Whatever a reader likes best, she jokes, should be thanked to Miss Wetherell; the dull pages are hers.

The frame is the stocking of a poor boy whom Santa Claus has never once remembered. Inside it stand the stories: of the three apples, of the red cent, of the two shoes, of the pine cone, of the hymn book, and of the cork boat. The stocking tells its own story at the end. The book pleads the cause of poor children at Christmas.
48437-the-art-and-practice-of-hawking:
The Art and Practice of Hawking is a manual by Michell, printed at London in 1900. Methuen issued it, with three photogravures by Lodge. Michell dedicates the book to the Earl and Countess of Warwick and to all other lovers of hawking. The contents map the whole sport, from its history to its daily practice.

The first chapter traces hawking from ancient China into Europe, through royal falconers to modern revivals. The second sorts the birds used: long-winged falcons, short-winged goshawks, and eagles. Furniture and fittings follow, jesses, bells, hoods, and the lure. Later chapters treat eyesses, passage hawks, and training. Michell writes for a sport that had nearly died and was coming back.
48711-hints-on-mountain-lion-trapping:
Stanley Young wrote Hints on Mountain-Lion Trapping as leaflet number 94 of the Bureau of Biological Survey, issued in April 1933. Young headed the division of predatory animal and rodent control. His subject is the American mountain lion, also called cougar, panther, puma, and catamount. The animal is among the largest predators in the United States and can weigh more than 200 pounds.

Young explains why control seemed needful. The lion is the greatest natural enemy of deer. When game runs scarce it turns to young stock, taking colts, lambs, and kids, and sometimes full-grown horses and cattle. Its range covers the wilderness west of the hundredth meridian, heaviest in the Rocky Mountain states and the desert ranges of the southwest. The leaflet then gives practical trapping guidance for federal and local hunters. It stands as a plain record of how the government treated predators in the nineteen thirties.
49108-the-amethyst-ring:
Anatole France wrote this novel, Englished by Drillien for the Lane house. John Lane printed it in London and New York in 1919. It forms part of the English set of France works. Chapter one finds Madame Bergeret set to leave her husband home.

She moves to her mother, the widow Pouilly, as the tale opens. She half wished to stay, and would have forgiven the past. Drawing room opinion forced her hand, the tale makes clear at once. Town talk called her common and a burden on all near her.
49228-the-origin-of-the-knowledge-of-rig:
The Origin of the Knowledge of Right and Wrong is a philosophical lecture by Franz Brentano. Cecil Hague translated it into English from the German. Constable published it at Westminster in 1902. A biographical note accompanies the translation. The translator's note explains how the version came to be made. Hague wrote it in leisure intervals while studying at Prague. Professor Marty supervised the work carefully and constantly there. Help came from Manchester and Glasgow scholars as well. Adamson's revision was among his last services to truth, Hague records.

An author's preface brings the lecture before a larger public. Brentano asks how we know right from wrong at all. The essay founds his account of moral knowledge on feeling rightly directed. It became a classic text of value ethics in brief compass.
49275-metal-spinning:
Metal Spinning is a shop manual in Machinery's Reference Series, number fifty seven, second edition. The Industrial Press published it in New York with rights dated nineteen twelve. Two papers make up the number, one on principles and one on tools. Tuells writes the first, and Painter the second, both drawn from Machinery magazine.

Spinning forms sheet metal into round hollow shapes on a lathe with hand tools. Chandeliers, cooking ware, silver hollow ware, and motor lamps are its products. Brass, copper, zinc, aluminium, iron, and soft steel all yield to the spinner. Dies beat spinning for mass output, but dies cost much and break often. Spinning forms are cheap wood, easy to change when styles shift in trade. Small runs, trial pieces, and work dies cannot do are spinning's home ground.
49294-lay-down-your-arms-the-autobiograp:
Lay Down Your Arms, by Bertha von Suttner, is cast as the life story of Martha von Tilling and turned into English by T Holmes. Longmans printed a new impression in New York and London in 1914. The German book, Die Waffen Nieder, was a huge hit in Europe.

In his preface Holmes says a peace group asked him to do the work, and he found it a delight. He notes that a cut, unsanctioned form had run in the United States and gave no just idea of the book. Suttner writes of a Europe under the grim shadow of the sword, taxed for arms and drained of its sons. The tale shows war cost through one woman life. Peace readers get the famed anti war novel in full.
50366-proof-reading:
Proof-Reading is a set of essays by F Horace Teall, published in Chicago in eighteen ninety nine. Teall was a critical proof reader and editor on two great dictionaries, as his title page states. He also ran a proof room notes department in a printers' magazine. The essays speak to readers, their employers, authors, and editors alike.

Teall admits in his preface that the essays were not first written for a book. For that reason the subject is not treated in a steady, complete system. Cases, disputes, and momentary events from proof room life fill the pages instead. The value lies in that workshop view of how print was corrected before it reached the public.
504-the-fifth-string:
John Philip Sousa, famed for marches, writes this short novel of a violinist and a devil's bargain. Diotti, a star player fresh from Europe's courts, comes to America under impresario Henry Perkins. At a New York reception he charms society, but a fifth string on his violin holds a strange power over love and fate.

Sousa mixes concert scenes, social satire, and a touch of the supernatural. Diotti must learn that art bought at a price costs more than fame. The book charms as a light, musical fantasy by a man who knew the concert world from the podium.
5083-the-man-of-feeling:
Henry Mackenzie's short novel, first published in 1771, follows Harley, a young man of tender feeling who travels from the country to London and back. The story survives as a set of fragments, each episode showing Harley moved by the sorrows of strangers: a beggar, a fallen woman, a mad girl, and soldiers returned from war.

Mackenzie made feeling itself the hero, and the book became a landmark of the sentimental novel. Modern readers will find its earnest emotion old-fashioned at times. Its short scenes still show how eighteenth-century writers asked readers to judge character by compassion rather than by wit or wealth.
50834-the-awakening:
A science fiction story by Jack Sharkey. Galaxy Magazine printed it in February 1964. The headnote promises a rich surprise. Sleepers awake after ages of hiding, it says. They emerge into a world richer than they dared dream. Rik, the first to wake, feels a creeping chill instead. Milky light swirls around his slab.

The vault's air pump has failed during the long sleep. Carbon dioxide thickens the air he breathes. His partner Zina lies still as frozen wax nearby. Rows of sleepers fill chamber after chamber, fifty to a room. They had hidden from a war meant to set the surface burning. Rik must fix the pump before he can learn what waits outside. Sharkey builds the tale inside the shelter's waking machinery.
50873-mediaeval-church-vaulting:
Clarence Ward wrote Mediaeval Church Vaulting, the fifth of the Princeton Monographs in Art and Archaeology. Princeton University Press published it in November 1915. Ward taught architecture at Rutgers College and lectured at Princeton. He dedicated the book to A M, with lasting affection. Four chapters divide the subject by place in the church. Nave and aisle vaults come first, then transept and crossing, apse, and ambulatory.

The first chapter opens in the Romanesque period, from the early eleventh century to the mid twelfth. Three chief forms then covered naves and aisles: the dome, the tunnel vault, and groined vaulting. The ribbed vault arose and drove all three out, and the Gothic era began. Domes rest either on spherical pendentives or on squinches and trumpet arches. Ward traces both lines back before Justinian.
51095-book-of-mormon-stories-no-1-adapte:
Book of Mormon tales were told in plain words for the most small young. Book one came out in Salt Lake City in 1892. Cannon and Sons put it out for church schools and homes. It is a mate book to a set of plain Bible tales. Each plate on a wall chart gets its own tale here.

Lehi and his sons lead the book's first tales in full. Lehi's call in Jerusalem and the wild road come first. The sons go back to the town twice at great risk. Nephi's dream and his ship end the long road tale. The new land is won at the close of book one. Young Saints get their faith's tale at knee height.
51109-elocution-simplified-with-an-appen:
Elocution Simplified is a manual of public speaking by Walter Fobes, published at Boston in 1877. Lee and Shepard issued it; Fobes had graduated from Boston University's school of oratory. George Baker, of the Reading Club series, wrote the introduction. An appendix treats lisping, stammering, stuttering, and other speech defects. Fobes dedicates the book to Lewis Monroe, his own teacher of the art.

Why write it, the preface asks, and answers: because it is needed. No cheap digest of elocution was both methodical and practical, Fobes claims. His epitome contains nothing a good reader or speaker does not need. Physical gymnastics open the method: attitude, standing and sitting positions, poise. Chest expansion and arm exercises follow in graded lessons. Study joined to practice, he promises, starts a pupil on the road to oratory.
5116-pragmatism-a-new-name-for-some-old-:
William James delivered these lectures at the Lowell Institute in Boston in late 1906 and at Columbia University in early 1907. In them he presents pragmatism as a way of settling disputes about ideas: judge a belief by the practical difference it makes in life, rather than by abstract argument alone.

James applies that test to questions of truth, belief, religion, and human nature, arguing with philosophers he admired and those he opposed. The lectures read as spoken talks, direct and full of examples, and they remain a clear entry point into a philosophy that measures ideas by their consequences.
5124-henrietta-s-wish-or-domineering:
Charlotte M. Yonge's domestic novel follows Henrietta and the family circle around her, beginning with a summer arrival at Teignmouth on the Devon coast. Its second title, Domineering, points to the book's central tension: strong wills within a household. The harm appears when one person's wishes override the rest.

Yonge traces courtship, friendship, and family duty through small, telling scenes of everyday life. The novel belongs to her long series of moral family stories. It will appeal to readers who enjoy nineteenth-century domestic fiction where character is tested at home rather than on a battlefield.
51358-gutenberg-and-the-art-of-printing:
Emily Pearson wrote this life of Gutenberg and the art of printing. Noyes, Holmes printed it at Boston in 1871 with plates. Pearson gives the book to gifted minds at work in the art. Her preface calls printing the telescope of the soul itself.

Printing brings past and present minds near, she writes with feeling. No great one led the way save Gutenberg, she contends there. Friends urged a memorial tale of the chevalier and artisan. She wove it from the most sound warp and woof she found. A first printed sheet stands at the front as a plate for the reader to study.
51470-narrative-and-critical-history-of-:
Justin Winsor, librarian of Harvard, edited a great history of America in eight volumes. Houghton, Mifflin copyrighted volume five in 1887. Its subject is the English and French in North America from 1689 to 1763. More than two hundred and seventy pictures fill the book, and the medal struck for the fall of Quebec marks the title page.

The first chapter, by Andrew McFarland Davis, treats Canada and Louisiana. It is followed by a critical essay on the sources and by notes from the editor. A study of the maps of Louisiana and the Mississippi basin under French rule stands with them. The second chapter, by Winsor himself, treats New England in the same years. Portraits, autographs, plans of New Orleans, and maps of the great river abound. The plan of the whole work joins plain telling to a weighing of the books and papers the tale rests on.
51473-the-donkey-the-elephant-and-the-go:
Buschlen wrote a rhymed playlet printed at Great Falls, Montana, in 1920 and sold for twenty five cents. By virtue of its simple rime, the playlet may claim a small share of the license granted to poets, the announcement says. It assumes the goat may already be taken as the emblem of the farmers' and workers' political party. Nationally, that is unfortunately not as yet quite a fact, he owns.

The right to present the discussion as a play, for purposes of raising money, may be had only by writing to the author at Box 1625, Great Falls. The right to present it free, by way of assisting the farm and labor movement, is granted to everyone who holds a copy. Donkey and elephant plead their old parties' cases in verse. The goat answers for the farmers. A campaign meeting turns into a small stage piece for grange halls.
51700-gift-card-designing:
Gift Card Designing is a craft book by Pedro Lemos, published at Worcester in 1922. The School Arts Magazine issued it through the Davis Press. Lemos opens with a complaint about card shopping. No gift hunt, he says, is less satisfying than the hunt for greeting cards. Buyers turn the display over and over and settle at last in doubt. Old lace edged cards belong to a vanished age, he notes.

Before the world war, cheap foreign cards flooded America by the million. Sweat shop printing made home shops fall back as competitors. Yet print quality alone never sold a card, Lemos argues. Design and idea are the selling factor. Cards must speak to the local and personal feelings of a community. A card from far away cannot voice what a neighbour means. The book teaches readers to make such cards themselves.
5180-children-s-internet-protection-act-:
This court opinion, issued on May 31, 2002, by a three-judge court in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, decides challenges to the Children's Internet Protection Act. The American Library Association, Multnomah County Public Library, and others sued the United States, arguing that the law's conditions on library funding violated the First Amendment.

Judges Becker, Fullam, and Bartle set out the statutory framework, findings of fact, and their reasoning on filtering in public libraries. The opinion is a primary legal document, useful for readers studying internet freedom, library policy, and how courts weighed free speech against the protection of children online.
52052-the-puzzle-king:
John Scott made a book of puzzles, catches, and tricks with figures and cards. H J Diddams and Company printed The Puzzle King at Brisbane in the Roman year MDCCCXCIX. Scott had written How to Become Quick at Figures and Doctrine of Chance. The motto at the front runs, laugh and grow fat.

Scott calls his book a sugar-coated pill of numbers for home fun. Business blunders, school tales, and odd sums train the mind by play. Answers stand at the back for the numbered questions throughout. The work is fully Australian in author, printer, and artist, the front note boasts.
52074-soldering-brazing-and-welding:
Soldering, Brazing and Welding, edited by Bernard Jones, editor of the weekly journal Work, was published in New York and London in 1917 by Funk and Wagnalls. Seventy-eight pictures show the work. The editor's preface explains that practical men wrote the pieces, first in the columns of Work. The handbook covers processes every metalworker meets early.

Chapters open with the various ways of joining metals, then soft solders and the fluxes used with them. Soft-soldering with the copper bit follows, then work with the blowpipe. Later chapters take up brazing and the newer welding methods, electrical and oxy-acetylene among them. Jones owns that welding alone could fill a book; this one serves as a full guide to soldering and brazing, and an entry to welding.
52101-much-ado-about-something:
C E Lawrence wrote the novel Much Ado About Something. John Murray issued it at London in 1909. Lawrence had written Pilgrimage before this. The book goes to his father and mother. Twenty-two chapters carry the tale. Down Fairyland Way opens the action.

High revel waits in Fairyland at the start. Creatures gather in the Violet Valley from all sides. Oberon and Titania head the coming court. Mab, Puck, and Gloriana join the royal set. Pixies, gnomes, and kelpies crowd the muster. Sprites and brownies own fealty to the Fairy King. The night ranks as the greatest since year One. May Day waits just past midnight in the tale. A whimsical blend of fairy court and London talk, the book moves from elf mounds to Parliament before Oberon's crown closes it.
52107-that-reminds-me-a-collection-of-ta:
That Reminds Me is a collection of tales worth telling, printed at Philadelphia in 1905. Its motto runs: show me a nation's humor, and I will show you its civilization. A foreword argues that if truth is often spoken in jest, there is more than the passing laugh in such a gathering of anecdote, repartee, and pleasantry.

For some years the Public Ledger of Philadelphia had offered premiums for contributions to a column of jests called Tales Worth Telling. The best of these are now collected in permanent form for a wider audience. The foreword finds much Americanism in the tales: they have the flavour of the soil and the relish of nationality. Some are plants of foreign growth that have taken on a new appearance in this atmosphere. Not all are equally laugh-provoking, the editor owns; anecdotes are meant for different minds.
52154-cease-firing:
Cease Firing is a Civil War novel by Mary Johnston, published by Houghton Mifflin of Boston and New York in 1912. Colour illustrations are by N C Wyeth. The book is the second of two dealing with the war between the States, after The Long Roll.

Johnston dedicates it to the memory of two Johnstons in grey. One was a major of artillery, the other a general. Maps show the Mississippi from Memphis to New Orleans, and the road from Chattanooga to Atlanta. The contents march with the war's second half. Vicksburg, Chickasaw Bayou, and Port Gibson open the fighting. The Stonewall chapter marks Jackson's fall. Gettysburg, Chickamauga, and Missionary Ridge follow. The Wilderness, the Bloody Angle, and Cold Harbour grind through 1864. Johnston wrote the Confederacy's war as a vast family tragedy, told from inside the South.
52197-home-arts-for-old-and-young:
Home Arts for Old and Young is a household book by Caroline Smith, known as Aunt Carrie, printed at Boston in 1873. The book is illustrated and opens with Christmas: how to make a Christmas tree, the bran pie, Twelfth Night, and the Christmas bag. Amusements for the holidays follow, from reading clubs and private theatricals to charades and tableaux.

Later sections teach ventriloquism, natural magic, and the garden, from seed planting to the rose, carnations, and bulbs in winter. House arts fill the rest: knitting down to a baby's blanket, plain needlework for young ladies, and fancy work in spangles, feathers, and cork. It is a full Victorian storehouse of home skill and play.
52355-battle-of-new-orleans-its-real-mea:
Reau E Folk, chairman of a Tennessee commission of research on the true value of the victory at New Orleans, published an exposure of untruth being taught young America, dated 1935. The battle, he holds, is the second most important military event in the republic's life. The book is dedicated to the state of Tennessee, which authorized the investigation. The Ladies' Hermitage Association shares the dedication.

So do the descendants of the soldiers who fought, and school teachers everywhere. Folk argues the textbooks underrate Jackson's victory of 1815. His commission's name states the conclusion in advance. The volume is regional piety armed with documents, addressed to the classroom.
52424-cave-hunting-researches-on-the-evi:
Cave Hunting, researches on the evidence of caves respecting the early inhabitants of Europe, is a study by Boyd Dawkins. Macmillan of London published it in 1874, with a coloured plate and woodcuts. Dawkins was curator of the museum and lecturer in geology at Owens College, Manchester.

He dedicates the book to the Baroness Burdett Coutts, founder of Oxford's geology scholarships, whose first scholar he was. Since Buckland's Reliquiae Diluvianae of 1823, no one had gathered the scattered facts into one work. Dawkins attempts that gathering here, in one connected narrative. Since Buckland wrote, human relics had been found with extinct animals in caves. That discovery, he says, revolutionised ideas about the antiquity of man.
52439-an-essay-to-shew-the-cause-of-elec:
An Essay to Shew the Cause of Electricity is a pamphlet by John Freke, surgeon to Saint Bartholomew's Hospital, in its second edition of 1746. Freke addresses the essay, in letter form, to William Watson, and dedicates it to Martin Folkes, president of the Royal Society. It asks why some things are non-electricable.

The full title promises electricity's influence in blasts on human bodies, blights on trees, damps in mines, and its effect on the sensitive plant. In his preface Freke says he first wrote his thoughts only for friends more likely to carry the subject further. They assured him the piece was intelligible and full of new ideas, and pressed him to print it. The pamphlet belongs to the first decade of electrical science, when the cause of the phenomenon was still open to a surgeon's speculation at a shilling a copy.
52454-eben-holden-s-last-day-a-fishing:
Eben Holden's Last Day A-Fishing is a short tale by Irving Bacheller. Harper published it in New York in 1907. Bacheller had made Uncle Eb famous in an earlier novel. He dedicated this volume to a friend who loved the North Country. Three short parts make up the whole.

The narrator opens on a city street in early June. A caged cock in a freight wagon crows defiance. The sound recalls his own imprisonment in the rock-bound city. That evening he travels to Hillsborough. Uncle Eb, a likely boy of eighty-six, still lives in the old home. A white handkerchief flickers welcome from the trees. The narrator plans a holiday full of surprise for the old folk.
53040-the-art-of-living:
Robert Grant wrote The Art of Living, held in 1895 and 1899 by Charles Scribner's Sons at New York. Ten themes fill the book, each in two parts. Income leads the set. The dwelling, house furnishing, and food follow. Education, work, and the use of time get parts in turn.

The summer problem, the case of man, and the case of woman come next. The conduct of life closes the book. Grant opens with Rogers, a book keeper of twenty two years for a banker friend. Rogers raised five children on two thousand two hundred dollars a year. He sent sons to college and to a mining school on that pay. Grant tells the tale with warm praise for plain thrift.
53420-frank-nelson-in-the-forecastle-or-:
Frank Nelson in the Forecastle is a boys' sea tale by Harry Castlemon, one of the Frank Nelson series. Its sub-title sends the Sportsman's Club among the whalers. A frontispiece shows Archie, Fred, and Eugene in the main cross-trees of the Stranger. The publisher's list at the front shows the scale of Castlemon's world for boys. The Sportsman's Club books, the Gunboat series, the Go-Ahead series, and more fill the page. All are in cloth, black and gold, made for the Christmas trade.

Frank and his club mates ship before the mast on a whaler. The forecastle, the rough bunk room of the common sailor, is their school. Whale hunts, storms, and shipboard pranks fill such a tale. Castlemon was a chief maker of the American boys' adventure book. His tales taught sea craft and grit in the same breath.
5351-if-i-were-king:
Justin Huntly McCarthy's If I Were King, published in 1901. It is dedicated to the loveliest lady this side of heaven, and opens with its famous refrain: if I were king, what tributary nations would I bring to stoop before your sceptre? Beneath your feet the poet would fling treasures, stars as pearls upon a string, and the world as a ruby for a finger ring.

McCarthy, a playwright and novelist, turns the romantic boast into a historical romance of Francois Villon and the Paris of Louis XI. Readers get a swashbuckling tale of a poet made king for a day, in which love, wit, and danger carry the story to its gallant end.
53696-baden-powell-of-mafeking:
J S Fletcher wrote Baden-Powell of Mafeking, a life of the famed scout and soldier. Methuen and Company issued the book in London. Sketches by Fletcher show camps, fights, and the man at work. Kin and friends gave him facts for the tale.

Part one asks what sort of man Baden-Powell was. Boyhood, school, and sport shape the young scout. Part two follows the Ashanti trek of eighteen hundred ninety five. The Matabele war of the next year comes after. Part three tells the siege of Mafeking in full. Town folk sat tight as shells fell round them. Horse beef and thin rations mark the hard last days. Relief at last brought joy through the whole empire.
53729-in-partnership-studies-in-story-te:
In Partnership holds tales by Brander Matthews and H C Bunner, some written by both men together. The joint byline gives the book its title. It came out in New York in 1884.

The Documents in the Case, a joint tale, opens the set. It starts with a mock obituary of a Sir William Beauvoir from a London paper. Venetian Glass and The Rival Ghosts are Matthews' solo work. The Red Silk Handkerchief and Love in Old Cloathes are Bunner's. Seven Conversations of Dear Jones and Baby Van Rensselaer joins both hands again. The set shows two friends at play with the short tale. Playing a Part adds one more Matthews tale to the set.
53919-sister-gertrude-a-tale-of-the-west:
D F E Sykes wrote a tale of the West Riding drawn from his own life. The Worker Press issued Sister Gertrude at Huddersfield in its sixth thousand. Sykes had written histories of Huddersfield and the Colne Valley. A front life traces his fall and return in plain words.

Edward Beaumont in the tale stands for Sykes himself, the note owns. Law practice, politics, a weavers' dispute, and drink mark his ruin. Bankruptcy in 1885 drove him from practice and from the district. Yorkshire readers gain a frank tale of pride, loss, and self-respect won back.
54330-how-women-may-earn-a-living:
How Women May Earn a Living is a guide book of its age for women who must work for pay. It came out from a great house with shops in London, Paris, and New York. Bound at its front are the house ads of the day, a strong part of its first form.

Those ads praise a vast home doctor book, by the best hands of the great London sick houses. That book, a news sheet is quoted to say, will be of great and sure use. It not just tells how to cure some ills by plain rules. More to the point, it tells how to shun them. Sense and clear words mark it through. The guide then takes up its own theme: the trades and posts a woman of the age could take.
54476-the-art-practice-of-typography-a-m:
The Art and Practice of Typography is a manual of American printing by Edmund Gress, editor of The American Printer. This second edition was published in New York in 1917. It gives a brief history of printing up to the twentieth century. Reproductions show the work of early masters of the craft.

A facsimile of the first printed Declaration of Independence fronts the book. Gress then treats the modern use of type faces and methods of arrangement at length. The manual served working printers who wanted both the history and the practice of their trade. It belongs to the years when American printing was raising its design standards.
54568-a-handbook-of-invalid-cooking:
Mary A Boland wrote A Handbook of Invalid Cooking. The Century Company issued it at New York in 1893. Boland taught cooking at Johns Hopkins Hospital. Its training school for nurses used her lessons. Private nurses form a second mark for the book. Home carers of the sick form the third.

Lessons on food's properties fill Part One. Chemistry remarks open those lessons in general. Classes of foods get their own studies there. Air and water earn special articles too. Recipes for the sick fill the rest. The Johns Hopkins need bred the book, her preface says. Other schools were taking food teaching up then, she notes. A nurse's cookbook joined diet science to the tray, so broth and gruel could heal as well as feed.
54570-an-old-man-s-darling:
An Old Man's Darling, a novel by Mrs Alex McVeigh Miller, was published by Street and Smith of New York, under copyrights of 1883 and 1900. It is a story paper novel in thirty nine chapters. Mrs Miller was among the most popular writers of such tales, which sold in cheap editions to readers across the country. The title hints at the storm at its centre: a young girl bound to an old man.

The opening is set at Cape May. On the shore sits a beautiful girl, fair as a poet's dream, singing a gay little song. An old crone, a fortune teller by trade, hobbles up and asks to tell her fortune for a silver piece. Whether the fortune will be good or ill hangs over the chapters to come. Love, money, and an old man's claim drive the plot.
5500-the-advancement-of-learning:
Francis Bacon wrote The Advancement of Learning as a survey of human knowledge, addressed to the king in two books covering divine and human learning. This edition, transcribed from the 1893 Cassell publication, presents Bacon's argument that learning had been neglected and misused, and that a true account of its branches would serve both church and state.

Bacon maps the fields of knowledge, praises their uses, and criticizes empty disputes that produce heat without light. Readers get a founding text of modern thought about science and education, written in rich early modern prose. It remains a landmark for anyone tracing how knowledge came to be organized.
55226-superior-fishing:
Superior Fishing, or the striped bass, trout, and black bass of the northern states, by Robert Barnwell Roosevelt, was published by Carleton of New York in 1865. Roosevelt was a sportsman of the first rank and a brother of Theodore Roosevelt's father. The book promises full directions for dressing artificial flies, with the feathers of American birds, for the angler's own use.

An account of a sporting visit to Lake Superior opens the matter, under the name of the Western World. The index ranges over fly making, casting, trolling, and the dressing of salmon, trout, and bass flies. Camp cookery, tents, canoes, and the choice of rods and reels all have their entries. Trout ponds, whitefish, and the pickerel of the northern lakes fill out a sportsman's handbook of the Civil War years.
55414-grand-teton-a-guide-to-grand-teton:
Grand Teton is the National Park Service handbook for Grand Teton National Park in Wyoming, Handbook 122, produced by the Service's Division of Publications and issued in 1984. The guide opens with the abrupt grandeur of the Teton Range and the valley called Jackson Hole, with the Snake River, Jackson Lake, and chances to see elk, moose and pronghorn.

Part one is a welcome essay by Mardy Murie, the Jackson Hole conservationist, beginning at the Maude Noble Cabin where a 1923 meeting is marked by a bronze plaque. Part two covers the natural history, geology and history of the mountains, valley and river, including wildlife and wildflowers. Part three is the practical guide: approaches, visitor centres, ranger activities, camping, hiking, backcountry rules, mountaineering, boating, fishing and winter use. The Grand Teton itself, the caption notes, rises to 13,770 feet.
55472-ski-running:
Ski-Running is a handbook of the sport by D M M Chrichton Somerville, W R Rickmers, and E C Richardson, who also edited it. Horace Cox of London published this second edition in 1905, dedicated to the Ski Club of Great Britain. Numerous photographs and diagrams fill the book, and Halstrom's picture Paa Skare fronts it.

The preface says the first edition came two years earlier and the sport has since grown by leaps and bounds. A history of the ski opens the volume, with a new chapter on Continental ski-running added. The technical part is remodelled and enlarged: the ground and the snow, outfit, and the elements of the running itself. Norwegian experts supplied hints throughout, and Herr Zdarsky gave a practical demonstration of his teaching methods. The authors own their earlier errors frankly and aim to serve beginners and experts alike.
55750-ground-tumbling:
Spalding put out a small guide to ground tumbling in its sport book line. Spalding sold sport goods from shops in many towns in the United States and England. The front pages list those shops town by town. The guide's own text teaches rolls and ground feats. Such small books were cheap and fit a coat pocket.

Gym hands learn how to fall, roll, and rise with grace and no hurt. Clear steps build from plain rolls to hard feats. Ground work forms the base for mat and bar work. Coaches and boys in gym class were the key readers. The plain form made self-teach at home a real path.
55887-manual-of-library-cataloguing:
Manual of Library Cataloguing is a professional handbook by Henry Quinn, librarian of the Chelsea Public Libraries in London. The Library Supply Company published it in 1899. Quinn had been principal cataloguing assistant at the Liverpool Free Libraries. The chapters treat the principal entry, then subject, title, and series entries in turn.

Later chapters cover title entries, indexing contents, and the classified catalogue. Alphabetization, arrangement, and printing follow. Appendixes list abbreviations met in books, sizes of books, and modern pseudonyms with their real names. A list of subject headings for a dictionary catalogue closes the book. It served the new trained librarians of the public library movement.
56158-the-story-of-go-sta-berling:
The Story of Gösta Berling is a novel by Selma Lagerlöf, translated from the Swedish by Pauline Bancroft Flach. Little, Brown of Boston published this English edition in 1898. The translator's preface sets the scene for English readers.

The tales, she explains, are founded on actual occurrences in Värmland. That lonely province of southern Sweden kept its old customs long. Mining was the chief industry of its sparse people among the forests. Long, narrow lakes, joined by rivers, shape the country of the story. Lagerlöf grew up amid the wild legends of that countryside. The Crown Prince of Sweden himself encouraged her early efforts. An introduction called The Priest, and one called The Beggar, open the novel. Christmas Eve at Ekeby and a great ball follow in the first part.
56394-sailing: Sailing, by Knight, stands in the All-England Series of handbooks. Knight had written The Cruise of the Falcon before this volume. The series sold its small cloth books at one shilling each; Sailing, a double volume, cost two. Yachting suppliers' pages front this copy: compasses, boats, and charts are offered there. The series list names cricket, lawn tennis, rowing, golf, and swimming as sister volumes.
56584-daily-training:
Benson and Miles wrote Daily Training, a book of health rules put out by Dutton at New York in 1903. Benson and Miles wrote from notes they had kept for years. Their preface says the rules are simple and can be kept at small cost in time and self-denial. They aim at folk who feel, as a rule, not very well. The two men lived very different lives, yet agreed on broad rules of health.

One ate flesh foods each day, while the other had scarcely touched meat for years. One played an outdoor game most days, while the other took no such exercise for days and still felt fit for hard tests. Both held that diet and movement could be traded, in a sense, with care. The book gives plain, cheap ways to gain and keep good health.
56784-the-theory-and-practice-of-brewing:
Michael Combrune, a brewer, wrote The Theory and Practice of Brewing, in a new and enlarged edition of eighteen hundred and four. The book first came out with leave of the Worshipful Company of Brewers. Combrune gave the work to Doctor Peter Shaw, physician to the king.

Brewing, Combrune says, had long run on vague rules handed down by word of mouth. He aims to set the craft on truer, fixed grounds. A word list explains the trade's terms, and sections treat fire, air, and water. Later parts work through malt, hops, and the making of malt liquors. Shaw's counsel, he says, shaped the book from start to end.
56796-1000-things-worth-knowing:
Nathaniel Fowler, a tireless maker of self-help books, packed a thousand useful facts in this volume. Sully and Kleinteich printed 1000 Things Worth Knowing at New York in 1913. Its motto is its promise: that all who read may know.

Abbreviations in common use open the store. Bachelor of Arts, agent, barrel, Bachelor of Divinity: the short forms of a paper age stand in a row. Fowler wrote on citizenship, letter writing, and starting in life, and his hand shows throughout. Weights, laws, customs, and plain questions get plain answers. A desk book for the clerk, the student, and the curious, in the great age of the fact almanac.
56816-hints-on-driving:
