Hints on Driving is a handbook by Captain C Morley Knight of the Royal Artillery. George Bell and Sons published it in London, first in 1894. This printing is the revised second edition, reprinted in 1902.

Knight teaches the art of driving horse drawn carriages. The book is illustrated by G H A White. A letter from General Albert Williams praises it for beginners and coachmen alike. Knight added material drawn from service in India. The first edition sold out in just over three months. Handbooks like this one kept carriage skills alive as motor cars began to appear.
56914-the-book-of-elves-and-fairies-for-:
The Book of Elves and Fairies, by Frances Jenkins Olcott and published in 1918, gathers fairy lore for young readers. Houghton Mifflin issued the book with colour pictures by Milo Winter. Its subtitle states its twin aims in plain words. It serves for story telling and reading aloud, and for the children own reading as well.

Olcott had already made books of Persian genii tales, Bible stories, and holiday tales for the young. A colour plate of Mab, the mistress fairy, fronts one tale in this volume. Such a book was made for the family circle and the schoolroom alike in its era. Parents and teachers could pick a tale for an evening and read it aloud with ease. Elves, fairies, and kindred folk of old tale fill its pages from start to end.
56948-an-autumn-sowing:
An Autumn Sowing is a novel by Benson, first issued in November 1917 and twice reprinted within two years. Its first chapter opens in a church, where a leading character settles in for an edifying half hour. The preacher's text promises wailing and gnashing of teeth. As the sermon proceeds, the hearer feels his hopes amply justified, the narrator says with dry wit.

The doctrine of eternal damnation wears a safe and solid look from that pew, buttressed by other stalwart sayings. It is the justice of it that appeals to the man, whose name is Keeling. Mankind had been fairly warned, he holds, and rules were made to be obeyed. A second principle, mercy, enters only for those truly sorry. Benson sets his satire of smug religion in the first pages.
57116-illustrated-horse-breaking:
Captain M Horace Hayes, late of the Buffs, wrote Illustrated Horse Breaking. W Thacker and Company published it at London in 1889, with houses at Calcutta and Bombay. J H Oswald Brown drew its fifty-two illustrations. The front pages list Hayes's earlier books: Riding on the Flat and Across Country, Veterinary Notes for Horse Owners, and Training and Horse Management in India. The Standard called him a master of his subject.

Soundness and Age of Horses and Indian Racing Reminiscences stand in the same list. The Veterinary Journal praised his Indian training book as a guide for amateur horseman and surgeon alike. Hayes had served in India and wrote from the saddle and the stable. A breaking manual with pictures served officers, dealers, and country riders. His name sold the book before a page was turned.
57291-keys-to-fungi-on-dung:
Keys to Fungi on Dung is an identification manual by Richardson and Watling, published by the British Mycological Society in 1997. The keys cover the coprophilous fungi, the ascomycetes and other moulds that fruit on animal dung. Watling was of the Royal Botanic Garden at Edinburgh, and the keys had grown through editions since 1968.

The preface traces the work's life from the society's bulletin of 1968 to this updated edition. The long reference list that opens the book maps the science: revisions of Sporormiella, Gymnoascus, Chaetomium and their kin, paper by paper. It is a specialist's tool for an unglamorous corner of mycology, kept current for thirty years by its authors.
57569-hints-on-child-training:
H Clay Trumbull, editor of the Sunday-School Times, wrote this book of counsel for parents, printed by John D Wattles of Philadelphia in 1891, with an 1890 copyright. His preface grants that hints may help where a formal treatise would bewilder. A parent can meet one need at a time more easily than hold a whole system in view.

Trumbull tells how a friend once asked his theory of child-training. He answered that he had no theory: he had plenty before he had children. Now he does, with fear and trembling, what seems the better thing for the hour. The hints grew from thirty years of practice with his own children, and from the papers' wide welcome, and he sends them out for young parents.
57602-my-german-prisons-being-the-experi:
My German Prisons tells what two and a half years as a prisoner of war felt like, in the words of Captain Gilliland of the Loyal North Lancashire Regiment. The book was issued at London in 1918, while the war still ran. Gilliland dedicates it to James Gerard, the late American ambassador at Berlin. Every British prisoner, he says, owes Gerard a debt of thanks.

A portrait of the captain in uniform fronts the volume. His tale covers capture, camps, and the long wait for exchange or peace. Such books fed a home public hungry for word of the men in Germany. Gilliland writes as an officer who kept his eyes open in the wire. His record stands as a first hand source on prison camps of the Great War. It mixes hardship with notes on guards and fellow prisoners.
57681-cotton-manufacturing:
Cotton Manufacturing is a practical textbook by Brooks. The author published the third edition at Blackburn in 1892. Spon sold it in London and New York. Over eighty illustrations support the text. Brooks lectured on cotton spinning and weaving at Blackburn. He held top honours in the subject from 1887.

A preface explains the book's purpose. Few works, Brooks writes, treat the whole range of cotton processes. Fewer still sit within an artisan's purse. The City and Guilds syllabuses are included in full. Chapters treat weaving and the fabrics woven in cotton. The preparatory processes get special space. Sizing receives its own treatment. A chapter on mill calculations is added. A glossary of terms closes the volume.
57737-a-dead-reckoning:
A Dead Reckoning is a story in nineteen chapters by T W Speight, printed in Chambers's Journal in 1889. Speight was the author of The Mysteries of Heron Dyke and By Devious Ways. The tale opens in talk between a young wife and her Aunt Jane. Six months ago to the day, the wife says, she and Gerald were married.

She tells her aunt that she has been so happy since Gerald whispered to her in the summer-house that all her life before seems as unreal as a dream. Aunt Jane holds that such short courtships are dreadful, and begins once more on her old tale of Captain Singleton. A third lady on the sofa, pretending to read a novel, sneezes and sits up at the name. The scene sets a domestic comedy of marriage and meddling kin. Speight's serial ran in a popular journal of literature, science, and art.
5774-they-call-me-carpenter-a-tale-of-th:
Upton Sinclair imagines a second coming in modern America in They Call Me Carpenter, published in New York in 1922. The narrator's strange adventure begins with a motion picture made in Germany, seen three years after the end of the First World War. From that screen, a carpenter figure steps into contemporary life, and Sinclair uses him to judge wealth, churches, studios, and politics.

The volume offers a provocative fable, earnest and satirical by turns, in which ancient teachings meet modern headlines. Sinclair writes plainly, letting the carpenter's simple questions expose greed and hypocrisy. The novel suits readers of social satire and religious fiction, and it remains a bold example of a novelist using fantasy to preach reform.
57786-french-ways-and-their-meaning:
French Ways and Their Meaning, by Edith Wharton, was published by Appleton in New York in 1919. Wharton, long resident in France and fresh from war work there, explains the French to American readers at the moment the two peoples had fought side by side. Chapters treat first impressions, reverence, taste, intellectual honesty, continuity, and the new Frenchwoman.

Wharton argues that French habits, often misread by visitors, rest on deep principles: respect for form, for reason, and for the past. She opens by mocking a French journalist's book on America, in which Boston's fine cemetery is made to prove that all Americans worship money. The essays are among her finest nonfiction, a defense of France written with love and precision.
57924-fort-laramie-national-monument-wyo:
Fort Laramie National Monument, Wyoming is a historical handbook by David Hieb. It is number twenty in the National Park Service historical handbook series. The Government Printing Office printed it at Washington in 1954. A reprint followed in 1961, the title page notes. It sold for twenty five cents from the Superintendent of Documents. The series describes historical and archaeological areas in the park system. A dedication states the system's purpose in the front pages. It conserves the scenic, scientific, and historic heritage of the nation.

The contents begin with the early fur trade on the Platte. That trade ran in the years from 1812 onward. Fort Laramie's story grew from that fur trade start. The handbook serves visitors to the monument in Wyoming. A cavalry hat and gloves illustrate the title page.
58015-the-speedy-appearance-of-christ-de:
The Speedy Appearance of Christ Desired by the Church was printed in 1815. Thomas of Southwark issued the sermon that year. Church, minister of the Surrey Tabernacle, preached it on the death of a friend. The date was August 27, 1815. Isaiah's promise and the cry, Even so come, Lord Jesus, stand at the head. The sermon's own text is the last verse of Solomon's Song. Make haste, my Beloved, it runs, and be thou like to a roe upon the mountains of spices.

Church expounds the Song as a picture of Christ and his church. Their union, he argues, is eternal, unbreakable, and perfect. It is set forth by the foundation and the building, he says. Head and body, vine and branches, give the same figure. All salvation, in his frame, depends on that union.
58319-the-story-of-paper-making:
The Story of Paper-Making is a plain account of the craft for readers who are not paper makers. It was published at Chicago by the Butler Paper Company in 1901. The firm says the lack of a non-technical book on the subject led it to issue one for the layman.

The chapters move in time. First come the things paper pushed aside. Then come papyrus and parchment, and the birth and early spread of paper itself. Old ways of making paper give place to the modern mill. A chapter treats watermarks and the kinds of paper on sale. The book ends with the size of the trade in the United States. Pictures run through the text, starting with a modern paper mill.
58392-the-babees-book-medieval-manners-f:
Edith Rickert turned these medieval guides to manners into modern English from Furnivall's texts. The Babees' Book came out as a private printing at New York at Christmas 1913. Its first title is in the old spelling: the book for the young ones.

Old verse guides taught a child how to sit at table, carve, speak, and serve in a great house. Rickert keeps their charm while making them plain to a new age. Elizabeth Tingle Fairbanks stands in a plate at the front, in the book's gift style. A child of 1913 could read how a child of 1450 was taught to wash, bow, and hold his tongue. Mirth and good form mix in these short rules.
58560-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
An index gathers the Project Gutenberg texts of the writer Ernest William Hornung. David Widger drew up the list and set out each work it holds. Hornung is best known for his tales of a gent thief. The thief's name, Raffles, heads more than one book in the list.

The first books named are the two sets of the Raffles tales. Dead Men Tell No Tales and A Thief in the Night stand near them. A tale of a crime doctor and a tale of a rope's shade are listed. Far-off tales of bush life in the south lands are in the run. War verse and a book on the young guard close the list in part. Full lists of what each book holds are given for each text.
58592-milch-cows-and-dairy-farming-compr:
Charles L Flint, secretary of the Massachusetts State Board of Agriculture, wrote a manual on milch cows and dairy farming, printed at Boston in 1859 with many illustrations. Its long title promises the breeds, breeding, and management of dairy stock in health and disease. The selection of milch cows is treated fully. Guenon's method gets a full explanation.

Forage plant culture and the making of milk, butter, and cheese follow. A treatise on the dairy husbandry of Holland is included. Horsfall's system of dairy management is added at the end. Flint adapts recent improvements to farming in the United States and British provinces. Grass lists in the contents run from timothy to red clover.
58594-white-lightning:
White Lightning is a novel by Edwin Herbert Lewis, issued at Chicago in 1923. Covici-McGee published the book. A verse from The Ballad of Ryerson serves as motto. It speaks of thunderbolts locked in ore and shore. The first chapter is titled Hydrogen. An auburn-haired boy of twelve stands at a smithy door. Two girls hang on his arms, forgotten for the moment. He watches the smith sprinkle water on the fire.

The boy concludes that water will burn. Most lads would miss that point, the narrator says. The scene is set in Chicago in 1905. The boy is Marvin Mahan, son of a mining engineer. His father is oftener away than at home. Lewis builds his tale on a boy's bent for science. Wonder at the forge opens a life of inquiry. The novel joins a city childhood to big industry.
58838-the-king-s-ring:
The King's Ring, a romance of the days of Gustavus Adolphus and the Thirty Years' War, by Zacharias Topelius, was turned from the Swedish by Sophie Ohrwall and Herbert Arnold. The London edition carries a portrait of Topelius. Three linked tales make up the book: The King's Ring, The Sword and the Plough, and Fire and Water.

An opening sketch treats a surgeon born in East Bothnia on August 15, 1769, the same day as Napoleon. Chapters move through the battles of Breitenfeld and Lutzen, Lady Regina and her oath, Finns at Lech, and the siege of Korsholm. Peasants, burghers, and soldiers cross paths as love and war test the North. Topelius, Finland's great storyteller, blends saga with history.
59016-post-exchange-methods-a-manual-for:
Post Exchange Methods is a manual for army post shops by Captain Bunker. Its full title adds that the guide serves stewards, chiefs, and councils. The post shops sell goods and fare to troops on army grounds. Rights date the work to the year nineteen fifteen.

The front note says most post shops rest in hands new to book work. Aides are plain troops, not trained clerks, in the run of the posts. No one set rule for the books stood in force in that day, he notes. Parts of the old rules had gone stale with new trade ways in shops. A clear count scheme for big and small shops fills the whole guide.
59080-the-earth-s-beginning:
The Earths Beginning is a science book for lay readers by Robert Ball. The author was a famed star scholar who wrote a shelf of such books. Colour plates and many prints crowd the text of this one. No year is shown in the front pages of the hosted text.

Ball tells how the Earth may have formed from fire and cloud in deep time. A front print shows a sunset dyed by the great Krakatoa blast. Talks on the sun, the stars, and the sky fill his past list. Plain speech and fine plates aim the book at keen home readers. The work forms part of a set that taught the age its new star lore.
59206-the-story-of-spanish-painting:
The Story of Spanish Painting is an art history by Charles Caffin, printed at London by Fisher Unwin in 1910. Caffin also wrote How to Study Pictures and The Story of Dutch Painting. El Greco's Saint Jerome, from the collection of the Marqués de Castro Serna, is the frontispiece. Twelve chapters and a postscript make the book.

The story of the nation comes first, as it must for Spain. In 1492 the Catholic sovereigns Ferdinand and Isabella entered Granada in triumph. The great names then take their chapters: El Greco under his own name Domenico Theotocopuli, Velasquez, Mazo and Carreño. Ribera, called Lo Spagnoletto, Murillo, Cano and Zurbarán follow. Goya closes the history. Caffin writes for the traveller and the gallery goer, tying the painters to the nation that made them.
59281-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
The Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Henry Wadsworth Longfellow is a list book. David Widger made the list of works held in that free store. The Song of Hiawatha heads the list with two full part schemes. Peace pipe, four winds, and child days open that verse tale scheme. Fast, friends, sail, and fish parts fill its first ranks in order.

Woo, feast, corn bless, and glyph writ stand mid scheme in that tale. Ghost, famine, white man foot, and part day close its part scheme. Dante Hell, Purgatory, and Paradise in Longfellow turn stand next in list. Full verse works, Hyperion, and Tales of a Wayside Inn fill more ranks. Slave verse and Miles Standish court tale stand in that list too.
59526-the-englishwoman-in-egypt-letters-:
The Englishwoman in Egypt holds letters from Cairo by Mrs Poole, printed at Philadelphia in 1845 in the Home and Traveller Library. Poole lived in Cairo through 1842, 1843, and 1844. Her kin was E W Lane, author of The Modern Egyptians.

Poole says a strong wish to see Egypt grew in her, fed most of all by Lane own books. He was about to visit the land for a third time as she wrote. Her letters tell what a Western woman could see in Cairo homes that men could not reach. She writes on dress, visits, baths, and family life behind closed doors. Travel readers get a rare woman view of Egypt in the 1840s, told by an eyewitness at home there.
59873-the-sword-of-the-king:
Ronald MacDonald wrote The Sword of the King, a tale put out by the Century Company at New York in 1900. The tale is told by Philippa Drayton, who first met her love when she was a child of five. Her nurse, weary from a long walk in heat, dragged the small girl up the elm avenue to Drayton Hall. Philippa sat down in the road and cried out in pain. Then came the thud of hooves, and a young rider reined in his horse by her side.

The rider, Edward Royston of Royston Chase, scolded the nurse with a frown that suited a grown man. MacDonald notes Philippa may owe the sharp memory to later talks with her lover. From that first meeting, a warm tale of love and sword play grows.
60065-wings-and-stings-a-tale-for-the-yo:
Wings and Stings, a tale for the young, is a story by the writer known as ALOE, issued in London in 1879. Nelson and Sons published the book from Paternoster Row in that year. The author is named as writer of The Silver Casket and The Robbers Cave. A hymn verse by Watts on the little busy bee stands as its motto.

The preface jokes that most young readers treat a preface as a stile before a field of haymaking. The author makes the stile as small as possible and is not offended if some skip it at one bound. The tale itself uses bees and their stings as its machinery of moral teaching. It follows the manner of Victorian books for the young. In those books, nature study and conduct lessons were bound in one small volume.
60121-the-glory-of-clementina-wing:
The Glory of Clementina Wing, by William Locke, is a novel printed at the Bodley Head in 1911. Lane issued it in London and New York that year. Locke had a shelf of novels behind him, from Idols to The Beloved Vagabond.

The first chapter paints its street before its people. Romney Place, Chelsea, might pass for a street in a sleeping cathedral city. Yet five minutes' walk brings any clashing thoroughfare of London. It is the quietest, primmest street imaginable. Organ-grinders and German bands are barred, and coal men find no custom. Little dogs on leads and lazy Persian cats rule the pavements. Early Victorian houses stand in a double row, with railed basements and prim steps. Some houses hide studios at the garden level, lit by sloping skylights for the north light.
60171-vahram-s-chronicle-of-the-armenian:
Charles Fried Neumann translated Vahram's chronicle of the Armenian kingdom in Cilicia, printed in London in 1831. Vahram was a priest from Edessa and secretary to King Leon III. Neumann admits in his preface that the chronicle is brief and bare. He also notes that Vahram often reads the passions of men as the hand of God.

Even so, Neumann holds that a writer of the time is worth having. The kingdom fought the emperors of Constantinople and stayed a friend and ally of the Franks. Its coast had long been a seat of trade. Neumann adds notes and background to help readers follow the sparse text.
60262-where-are-we-going:
Where Are We Going, by David Lloyd George, was printed in New York by George H Doran Company under a 1923 copyright. Lloyd George was British prime minister from 1916 to 1922. The book asks where Europe stands after the Great War.

The first chapter, The Great Peril, treats post war Europe, poverty and taxation, and race hatreds unchanged. It asks how war is begun and treats the churches and the League of Nations. The second chapter holds that Europe is still arming, more militant than ever. The third treats trouble in the Mediterranean and hot cinders dropped in the Balkans. Later chapters weigh the League record, the Treaty of Versailles and its critics, and what France is after on the Rhine. History readers get a war leader frank fears in print.
60396-spring-morning:
Frances Cornford wrote Spring Morning, a slim book of poems issued by the Poetry Bookshop in London. This copy is a new edition of 1923, the third thousand, with woodcuts by G Raverat. The poems bear short names: A Recollection, Youth and Age, A Child's Dream, and To a Fat Lady Seen from the Train. Others are The Old Witch in the Copse, In Dorset, The Watch, Dawn, and Mountains.

The title poem sings of moist woods, primrose leaves, daisies on the open hills, and a yellow butterfly dropping like a blossom from the sky. In A Recollection, a child hears that a kind pink-faced guest has died and feels a strange pride at knowing a person who has died. Cornford's verse is plain, brief, and close to common sights, with a child's clear eye held in grown-up form.
60415-when-william-iv-was-king:
John Ashton wrote When William IV Was King, with forty-seven illustrations. Chapman and Hall published it at London in 1896. Ashton was the author of Social Life in the Reign of Queen Anne. In his preface he reverses the usual plan of such books. Earlier lives of the king held much Life and very little Times, he says. His book treats the chief topics of talk in the seven years of the reign.

Then began the reign of steam, Ashton writes, and the first passenger railway was opened. Steam navigation grew general, and science and art woke up. The contents for 1830 cover the death of George IV and the sale of his clothes. The proclamation of William, the Beer Act, and the burial of the old king follow. Ashton preserves the talk and texture of the 1830s.
60446-norah-of-billabong:
Norah of Billabong is a novel for young readers by Mary Grant Bruce, published by Ward, Lock and Company. It belongs to her Billabong series, set on an Australian cattle station. The front pages quote reviews of the earlier books, praising their healthy picture of up-country life and their grip on the reader.

Norah and her brother Jim grow up among horses, cattle, and the bush. The stories mix station work, mishaps, and festivity with a quiet pathos. Bruce knew the life she wrote about, and reviewers said so at the time. Her Billabong books became loved schoolroom reading in Australia, and this volume carries the family story forward.
60515-homecoming:
Homecoming is a short tale by Miguel Hidalgo, first put out in a sheet of tales of the far worlds in the fourth month of nineteen fifty eight. A few lines of verse stand at its head. Those lines ask what lasts for all time, love or death, and give the hard word back: not even for all time lasts for all time. The tale then turns to sand, horse, and a lone ride.

A great horse plods slow past shift sand at the start. Its ride man is of mid size, with huge strong hands and eyes that seem void. Strange eyes, alive and with flame in them, those eyes are. They have no place in his dust caked, worn frame, yet there they are, in search, in search at all times, on the clear sky line.
608-areopagitica-a-speech-for-the-libert:
John Milton pleads for free printing in this 1644 speech to Parliament, unlicensed itself by design. Milton argues that complaints freely heard, deeply weighed, and swiftly reformed mark the utmost bound of civil liberty. He warns that licensing books before print strangles truth more than any heresy.

Milton writes in grand, rolling prose, full of classical allusion and moral fire. His image of truth as a wounded body, scattered yet living, ranks among English prose's finest. The tract endures as a founding text of free speech, where a poet defends the press against its own Parliament.
60808-war-flying:
War Flying holds the letters of a pilot who signs as Theta, printed at Boston in 1917. The letters went to his home folk, from training through war service. A line from Campbell on the sentinel stars heads the book.

Book one treats training, from theory to practice, a first flying lesson, and going solo. A crash stands among the episodes. Book two treats active service, with an alphabet of air slang at its head. Letters name map study, a forced landing, and archies, the anti aircraft guns. Theta writes on night flying, photos, hide and seek in the air, and men listed as missing. One letter is headed aged nineteen. Readers get the Royal Flying Corps war as a young pilot lived it, week by week.
60814-bohemian-cech-bibliography-a-findi:
Thomas Capek and Anna Vostrovsky Capek made a finding list of writings in English about Bohemia, printed in New York and Chicago in 1918. Adverts at the front praise a companion book on Bohemia under Hapsburg rule. That book argues the Bohemian and Slovak peoples deserve freedom. The list itself is a tool for readers who want to study the land and its people.

Entries point to books and pieces on Bohemian history, arts, and national hopes. One entry notes an old history of Bohemia kept in the British Museum as the earliest tale of the nation in English. In a war year when Bohemia sought a new place in Europe, such a list helped English readers find their way.
610-idylls-of-the-king:
Alfred, Lord Tennyson retells Arthur's rise and fall in twelve linked poems in this Victorian epic. The Coming of Arthur opens the cycle; Gareth, Geraint, Balin, Merlin, Lancelot, and the Holy Grail follow; Guinevere and The Passing of Arthur close it. A dedication mourns Prince Albert as an ideal knight.

Tennyson writes in rich, musical blank verse, keen on honor, love, and betrayal. Camelot's glory fades as vows break and trust dies. The poems endures as the great Victorian Arthurian work, where a king's dream of order meets human frailty.
61076-on-everything:
Belloc filled this book with short essays on all sorts of things, true to its title On Everything. Methuen of London first printed it on November 4, 1909, and a second edition followed in 1910. Belloc had by then written Paris, Hills and the Sea, and On Nothing, among other books.

Near forty pieces range from song and an empty house to the rights of wealth and a talk in Carthage. Some are place pieces, on the Weald, old towns, streams, and the road into the west of England. Others sketch men: the statesman, the barber, a rich man made sad, and a man at peace. Short tales like The Dream and The Strange Companion sit among the essays.
61136-e-being:
E Being is a science fiction story by James Stamers, from Worlds of If of March 1962. Its blurb says an E being can cause earthquakes, eat power lines, and beat light speed. The narrator claims to be the first man to reach the speed of light itself. Einstein, he says, only hinted at the effects in neat squared terms.

For fifty years men chased matter turned to energy for big bright bangs, he writes. No one asked what energy divided by light speed would make of a man. He is that answer, speaking through the motor of an electric typescripter in the tale. The voice and premise hook the reader from the first page of the story.
6118-the-rose-in-the-ring:
George Barr McCutcheon sets The Rose in the Ring amid circus folk, opening with a fugitive, a dressing tent, and David entering the sawdust ring. A stranger appears, something is learned about the Braddocks, and David Jenison's story unfolds beside the brothers Cronk.

An invitation to supper, a thief in the night, love winging a timid dart, and artful Dick going visiting lead to a sale. The second book gives the daughter of Colonel Grand, a stranger at the hall, a man who served his time, and a telegram delivered. McCutcheon mixes circus color with romance and debt.
61246-the-prisoners-of-hartling:
The Prisoners of Hartling is a novel by JD Beresford, published in New York in 1922. The catalog title is garbled, but the title page and opening pages name the book plainly. A line from Ecclesiastes about riches kept to their owner's hurt stands at the front.

The story opens with Arthur Woodroffe, a doctor's paid assistant in a poor district of London, restless after the war and hungry for space and purpose. His employer Somers teases him for craving the thrill of saving the wounded under fire. Somers urges him to find the same meaning in saving the sick at home. The talk sets up the novel's concern with men held fast by money, habit, and the lives they have settled into.
61340-the-art-of-story-telling:
The Art of Story-Telling is a practical treatise by Marie Shedlock. John Murray published it in London in 1915. John Adams, a professor of education, wrote the preface. Adams ranks Shedlock in the very first class of story-tellers. The gift of Scheherazade, he writes, is hers by birthright.

The chapters teach the craft step by step. Early ones treat the difficulties of libraries and clubs. The essentials and artifices of the art follow. Elements to avoid and elements to seek each earn a chapter. A chapter on questions and answers gives platform advice. Stories told in full fill a long section. A list of story titles and collections closes the book. An index completes the apparatus.
61504-forever-is-not-so-long:
Forever Is Not So Long is a science fiction story by Anton Reeds. The Project Gutenberg text was taken from Astounding Science-Fiction for May 1942. Its headnote asks how many, if told the future, would dare to enjoy the life that waits for them.

The story opens in September 1931. At Ploving Manor in England, young people dance on the lawn to new music from America. Their parents, the lost generation of the last war, watch from the terrace. Stephen Darville stands in the shadow of the shrubs, watching for Jean. He wants the dance and the girl. He also wants the thing that waits for him in Professor Ploving's workshop. The tale turns on what that workshop holds.
61985-harrods-for-everything:
Harrods for Everything is a large price list and guide for the Harrods store on Brompton Road in London. The cover calls Harrods the supply centre for the Empire and the house of quality. Phone lines and a wire word are given for orders. Country buyers could order by post with the same care as in the store. Harrods paid the post cost on cloth and fashion goods to any part of the kingdom.

A full index lists goods by trade and by shop floor. Heads run from farm tools and art goods to books, boys clothes, china, clocks, and coal. Page numbers point to each class of goods in the main list. The book shows the vast range of a great London store of that age. It is a rich source for dress, home, and trade of the time.
62191-hong-kong:
Hong Kong is a report on the British colony by Gene Gleason, published by the John Day Company in 1963. Gleason calls Hong Kong the last Western outpost on the mainland of China, next to Portugal's Macao. He names it the Berlin of East Asia, held in a risky balance between two ways of thought and two cultures.

The ten chapters move from British rule's rough start to crowds fleeing south from China. Gleason treats the colony's stance toward the two Chinas, its factory growth and growing pains, and its high land and low water. Farms, fisheries, crime, and graft follow, with a ramble around the colony and a chapter on shopping before dinner.
62257-practical-organ-building:
Practical Organ-Building is a workshop manual by Dickson, precentor of Ely Cathedral, in its second revised edition of 1882. Dickson argues in his preface that no short, practical treatise on organ construction exists for all classes of readers. The great work of Hopkins and Rimbault, he says, never enters the details essential to the workman.

His authorities are French: Hamel's Facteur d'Orgues of 1849, founded on the folios of Dom Bedos. Dickson praises a forty-page tract on organ voicing and tuning by a practical operator as an introduction to the art's highest branch. His own little book aims at the bench: how the most elaborate of musical instruments is actually put together, for the dwellers in workshops rather than the organ loft.
62638-buffalo-bill-the-border-king:
Buffalo Bill, the Border King, or Redskin and Cowboy, is a dime novel by Colonel Prentiss Ingraham, copyrighted by Street and Smith in 1907. Ingraham was one of the intimate friends who, with Ned Buntline and Josh Billings, used to gather in the dingy Rose Street office of the New York Weekly. Out of those talks came the Buffalo Bill stories. This volume opens with an appreciation of William Cody himself.

Cody was born in Scott County, Iowa, on February 26, 1846. Before his teens the family migrated to Kansas, then little more than a wilderness, and his father Isaac was killed. A passage preserved with the text tells a famous episode from the Civil War. Riding through St Louis, Cody rescued a frightened schoolgirl, Louisa Federci, from a band of tormentors. In true romantic style, the two were married on March 6, 1866.
63572-the-gold-thread-and-wee-davie-two-:
Norman Macleod wrote two tales for the young, The Gold Thread and Wee Davie, in one small volume. Thomas Nelson printed it in London, Edinburgh, and New York. The first tale opens with Eric, the son of good King Magnus, lost in a vast forest. His blue velvet dress is torn by briars and his fair hair is in curls.

Eric hunts all day for his lost gold thread and calls for his father. The wood around him grows sad and still, with ravens, hawks, and dark ravines. At last the sun sinks and the trees shine gold at the top while dark fills the ground. The tale is a moral story in fairy tale dress. It uses a lost child and a lost thread to teach care, courage, and trust.
63724-death-disarmed-of-its-sting:
Death Disarmed of Its Sting is a funeral discourse by Lyman Atwater, printed at New Haven in 1845. Atwater pastored the First Congregational Church in Fairfield. He preached the sermon at the funeral of Roger Minott Sherman on January 2, 1845. Hamlen printed the tribute the same year. Its text is Paul's cry: O death, where is thy sting?

The discourse asks how death, the natural conqueror, can itself be made to die. The answer lies in Christ, who brought life and immortality to light. Atwater then considers in what way, to what extent, and for what persons death loses its sting. The sting of death is sin, he argues from the next verse. The sermon turns doctrine into comfort for mourners.
63784-lead-smelting-and-refining-with-so:
Lead Smelting and Refining is a technical work edited by Walter Renton Ingalls. The Engineering and Mining Journal issued it in New York in 1906. Part one gives notes on lead mining in the United States. Ingalls writes on sources of lead production across the whole country. Wheeler adds notes on the source of the southeast Missouri lead.

Later parts treat the smelting and refining of lead in works practice. Tables, plant notes, and district reports serve engineers and managers in trade. Southeast Missouri anchors much of the mining matter in the volume. Height is spelled both height and hight in the old text, a note warns. Workers in the lead trade of 1906 got a full desk reference.
6382-bat-wing:
Sax Rohmer opens toward six on a hot summer evening, with Paul Harley of Chancery Lane seated in his private office reading. Harley, detective hero of the tale, is summoned to Cray's Folly. There a shadow on a blind, cast by a woman raising her arms in a peculiar fashion, looks remarkably like a bat. The contents promise a voodoo swamp, a vampire bat, Val Beverley, a barrier, the Lavender Arms, and the call of M'Kombo.

Obeah, a night walker, morning mists, Ysola Camber, unrest, and a night of full moon follow, with Inspector Aylesbury of Market Hilton, a Spanish cigarette, and the wing of a bat. Colin Camber's secret, a Lee Enfield rifle, and a seventh yew tree lead to confession and experiment. Rohmer writes a thriller of West Indian magic and English country houses, where fear of Camber puzzles even Harley's specialised mind.
64093-christmas-offering:
Elizabeth Dimond of Bristol, Rhode Island, published her Christmas Offering at Providence in 1847, printed by Knowles and Vose. A letter to her friend Mrs Smith, dated December 18, 1847, fronts the poems. In it Dimond says she wrote the chief poem in her eighty-fourth year, while musing on God's mercy and wisdom. The opening piece, Thoughts on Creation, retells the making of the world in rhymed verse. A watchman asks what of the night, and the poem moves from chaos to the sun, the moon, and the garden of Eden.

Adam walks the garden in the verses, surveys his form, and hears the one command about the hallowed tree. Other poems follow the title piece in the small volume. The whole is a work of old age offered as a Christmas gift to a friend. Its verse keeps the plain rhyming manner of early American religious poetry.
64140-soup-and-soup-making:
Soup and Soup Making is a cook book by Emma Ewing. She was the head of a school of the cook craft in a great lake town. Her books in the works stand past the front: a book on bread in the works, one on greens, and one on small rich dishes. This book is the first of a set of cook craft drill books. It was put out in eighteen eighty two.

Its index is a roll of the soups in short form. A gold soup heads the roll. A green stalk soup, beef tea, and a bird soup come next. A sweet grain soup, a cut soup in the French form, and a spiced soup of the east stand past them.
6476-himalayan-journals-volume-1-or-note:
Joseph Dalton Hooker's Himalayan Journals, volume one, first published in 1854 and dedicated to Charles Darwin, opens in the Sunderbunds and Calcutta Botanic Garden. Hooker, fresh from Antarctic voyaging with Sir James Ross, where botany was his chief pursuit, desired to add to his knowledge of natural history in India. The volume's first chapter runs through Burdwan, a rajah's gardens and menagerie, coal beds, lac insects, camels, and effloresced soda on soil.

Mahowa oil, Jains, and the ascent of Paras nath follow, with Doomree table land, hot springs, wild peacock, poppy fields, and the geography of Behar and Central India. A mid passage climbs to Kursiong bungalow, superbly placed on a narrow ridge, west window over the Balasun valley, east over the Mahanuddee. Hooker writes a naturalist's journal, plant by plant, valley by valley.
6477-himalayan-journals-volume-2-or-note:
Joseph Dalton Hooker's Himalayan Journals, volume two, first published in 1854, opens at chapter eighteen with arrangements for a second journey into Sikkim. Opposition of the Dewan, Lassoo Kajee, Tendong, a legend of flood, the Lama of Silok foke, Namtchi, and the Tchebu Lama fill the early pages. A gigantic oak, Teesta valley, commencement of rains, and ascent to Lathiang follow. Bad roads, orchids, and opposition of lamas slow the party.

Lepchas swim the Teesta, moxa treats sprains, and Singtam offers a grand view of Kinchinjunga, with wild men, landslips, bees' nests, and honey seekers. Choongtam brings rhododendrons, yew, venomous snakes, and hornets, with a temple and Tibetan salute. A mid passage tabulates thermometer readings and elevations across July and October, mean temperature falling from fifty to forty one degrees. Hooker writes high Himalaya as measurement and wonder.
6478-himalayan-journals-complete-or-note:
J. D. Hooker's complete Himalayan Journals, in the 1891 edition, gathers his notes as a naturalist in Bengal, the Sikkim and Nepal Himalayas, and the Khasia mountains. The opening chapters run as before. Sunderbunds vegetation, Calcutta Botanic Garden, Burdwan, a rajah's gardens and menagerie, coal beds, lac insects, camels, and effloresced soda on soil come first. Then come Mahowa oil, Jains, and the ascent of Paras nath. Doomree, hot springs, wild peacock, and poppy fields follow.

A mid passage measures air at a high pass, comparing vapour and humidity with Calcutta at the same hour. It then waits for coolies among rocks identical in natural history and geology to Kambachen pass. Hooker bids adieu to the sublime and majestic peak of Junnoo and continues four miles at nearly the same level. The complete edition lets a reader follow the whole journey, plant, rock, and weather together.
64922-pyrotechnics-the-history-and-art-o:
Brock wrote Pyrotechnics, the History and Art of Firework Making, at London in 1922. Daniel O'Connor put out the book, with many plates in color. It is given to the memory of the author's brother, Frank Arthur Brock, who fell at Zeebrugge on April 23, 1918. A verse by Thomas Hood praises a firework maker of Vauxhall. A front plate shows a vast show at Quebec in 1908, called the largest ever fired in the Western Hemisphere.

Part one traces firework art from its roots, through the East and Europe, to London pleasure grounds. Later parts take up making, new making, and accidents. Part two sorts simple fireworks by kind: rockets, shells, mines, Saxons, and lances. The book serves both makers and fans who love the bright sky craft.
65020-the-complete-distiller-containing-:
A complete distiller gathers the whole art of distillation into one old handbook. Its maker says he read most past treatises and took from each what he thought most needed. Part one gives the method for each process, the instruments used, and the whole doctrine of fermentation. Spirits drawn from malt, raisins, molasses, and sugar are covered.

Rectifying spirits and copying the color and flavor of French brandies follow. Part two tells how to distill simple waters from plants and flowers. Part three gives compound waters and rich cordials once imported from France and Italy, plus those made in Great Britain. Distillers of a past age could run shop and still room from these pages alone.
6522-fruit-gathering:
Rabindranath Tagore, writing in his own English from Bengali, offers short poems that treat a life like fruit ripening on a branch. Early verses speak of youth as a flower that drops a petal or two without loss, while later ones speak of age as fruit that holds nothing back. The garden, the river, and the evening wind run through the whole set.

Each poem is brief, yet it carries a full turn of feeling, from longing and loss to quiet surrender and joy. Tagore keeps the images plain and close to hand, so the sense lands at once rather than through hard thought. Fruit-Gathering reads as a small book of songs for the late season of a life.
655-life-and-letters-of-robert-browning:
Mrs. Sutherland Orr writes Robert Browning's life and letters in this second edition, prefaced in April 1891. Letters given by their recipients or copied by Browning's sister fill the volume, tracing the poet from family origins and boyhood through marriage and fame. Miss Browning's memory, Orr notes, was the only record of his youth.

Orr writes with careful, devoted prose, letting Browning's own words carry much of the tale. Chapters follow his grandfather, his father, and his early verse. The book serves as a key early biography, where a friend's care preserves a poet's voice for later readers.
65533-secret-of-the-painting:
Robert Moore Williams wrote a tale of a painting men would kill to own. Secret of the Painting ran in Imagination in April 1957. Tom Calhoun knew the canvas held a key to world-shaking knowledge, the blurb states. Luke Shaw, the narrator, meets a smooth foe in a bar at the start.

The stranger's fine, unpressed clothes and a bulge under his left arm spell trouble. His jaw juts like a perfect target for a left jab, Shaw thinks. A whining tone hides a growl of command in the man's voice. Pulp fans get a fast tale of greed, art, and hidden science.
656-life-of-robert-browning:
William Sharp writes a concise life of Robert Browning, the poet of dramatic monologues, from his London youth to his marriage with Elizabeth Barrett and his long Italian years. Sharp keeps the story clear and brief. Sharp, a Scottish critic, wrote short lives of poets for a wide audience.

Browning's poems, from early experiments to the great monologues, are set beside the life that shaped them. The book suits readers who want a first biography of Browning without the bulk of a full scholarly life. Browning's marriage to Elizabeth Barrett, and their life in Florence, gives the life its romance.
65767-ride-the-crepe-ring:
Ride the Crepe Ring is Milton Lesser's science fiction story from Imagination magazine of March 1952. Socrates Smith, called Smitty, runs a resort on Mimas, a small moon of Saturn. A glassite dome holds off the cold while the rings shine overhead. Inspector Farquhart has come to check the place, and Smith sweats through the interview.

Smith's last venture, a palace above Jupiter's Red Spot, drew asthma suits and ruin. Now he has something different: twenty war-surplus two-man cruisers. His guests will ride the rings themselves. The story's lure, set out at the head, is Norma's wish to dodge meteors in Saturn's forbidden ring. A thrill, yes, but the question is whether she will live to enjoy it.
65884-newspaper-writing-and-editing:
Willard Grosvenor Bleyer wrote a textbook on newspaper writing and editing. Houghton Mifflin Company issued the work in 1913, printed at the Riverside Press. Bleyer led the journalism course at the University of Wisconsin. Fourteen chapters run from how a paper is made to its public function.

A big-city daily holds 60,000 to 80,000 words, as much as a novel, Bleyer notes. Such papers print up to 900,000 copies a day, all within hours. News values, story shape, headlines, and proof-reading each get full teaching. Students gain a founding text of American journalism training.
66273-stories-and-story-telling:
Angela Keyes wrote a guide to tales and how to tell them with art. She led English work at Brooklyn's school for new class heads. Her book came out in New York and London in 1916. Its rights date to 1911 in her name in this copy. Kinds of tales to tell leads her list of guide parts.

The rules of the art and how to get a tale fill the front. How to tell it and the child's own share come next in line. Then a store of tales stands ready for class use in full. Her own Fairy Horseshoe and Andersen's Thumbelina shine there. Folk tales from France and the East share that store. Class heads get both rule and tale.
66331-a-treatise-on-bread-and-bread-maki:
A Treatise on Bread and Bread Making, by Sylvester Graham, was printed at Boston in 1837. Graham was a famed voice for plain food and clean living. A line of holy writ heads the book, that bread strengthens man heart.

Early parts trace the past of bread, from the bruising of grain to the finding of leaven. Parts on diet laws argue that food in its natural state is best. Graham treats the stuff of bread, and holds that sifting out the bran harms the loaf. He warns of bad flour, cheats, and poison used to hide them. Later parts treat yeast and ferment in full. Health readers get the case for whole, honest bread, made plain.
66399-virgil-lucretius-passages-translat:
William Stebbing translated passages of Virgil and Lucretius, for Longmans in 1917. Stebbing was a fellow of Worcester College at Oxford. He had written a biography of Sir Walter Ralegh before this book. The Virgil half opens with Orpheus and Eurydice from the Georgics. Happy husbandmen and a Tarentine garden follow in the contents.

A golden age, limbo and Tartarus, and Elysium take their turns. The ghosts, Euryalus and Pallas, and the gates close the Virgil set. Lucretius follows with his hymn to Venus from the nature of things. Philosophy, the fear of death, and primeval man stand in his list. Iphigenia, maternal love, echo, and the seasons round it out. The Orpheus rendering opens with old Proteus telling the tale by the sea. Virgil overheard and resang it, if not word by word, Stebbing writes.
66546-the-ivory-king:
The Ivory King, a popular history of the elephant and its allies, was written by Charles Frederick Holder. Scribner issued it at New York in the Marvels of Animal Life series, with copyrights of 1886 and 1888. A tiger's attack fronts the book as its first picture. Holder dedicates the volume to his mother.

The elephant, he begins, is the true king of beasts, the largest and strongest of living land animals. In ages past its kin roamed every zone, from the Arctic shores to the Gulf of Mexico. Where great cities now hum, the trumpeting of mastodons once broke the stillness of the primeval forest. Holder mourns their passing and warns of the living elephant's fate. Nearly seventy five thousand elephants, he writes, were destroyed each year for ivory. His book joins natural history with a plea, early for its time, against that slaughter.
66562-mission-work-among-the-negroes-and:
Mission Work Among the Negroes and the Indians is a Catholic report on what the annual collection for the missions was accomplishing. Foley Brothers printed it at Baltimore in eighteen ninety three. A commission charged with dividing the fund heads the report. James Cardinal Gibbons, Archbishop of Baltimore, leads it.

The report opens with a financial statement. It covers the year from the first of January eighteen ninety two to the first of January eighteen ninety three. Page after page lists the collections sent in by the archdioceses and dioceses of the country. Smaller dioceses follow in a long roll, Albany among the first named. The statement shows a national church gathering money diocese by diocese for mission work. Church history readers get the fund's own account of its reach across the country.
66768-a-town-is-drowning:
A Town Is Drowning, a novel by Frederik Pohl and Kornbluth, was published in 1955. Ballantine Books issued it at New York as an original novel, not a reprint. The pair also wrote The Space Merchants and Search the Sky, the front list notes. A note at the front ties the tale to fresh headlines of its day.

The novel takes the reader into the new flood country of the Northeast, it states. That region had long been free of hurricanes and their floods before those years. Now disaster had struck more than once, terrible and grim, the note goes on. Torn from today headlines is the tag the publishers gave their disaster tale. Ordinary folk under rising water give the book its human centre.
6689-fielding:
Austin Dobson writes the life of Henry Fielding for the English Men of Letters series, with a focus on fact over criticism. He notes that Fielding's works have already been well judged by many writers. Leslie Stephen is latest among them. So Dobson turns to biography instead. He checks tales about Fielding, corrects slips in older lives, and adds new details.

The memoir that follows traces Fielding from youth to novelist and magistrate, with care for dates and sources. Dobson's tone is modest, learned, and clear. Fielding is a solid, readable life of the Tom Jones author, useful to any reader who wants the man behind the novels.
66988-motor-camping:
Motor Camping is a practical guide by Long and Long, published in New York by Dodd, Mead and Company in 1923. Diagrams and illustrations support the text. The book belongs to the first years when families toured and slept by the road in their cars.

Chapters treat the growth of motor camping, its economy, and the weekend camper. One chapter is given to camping with a Ford, including folding beds made for the car. Another gives a home-made outfit that stood an eight-thousand-mile trip. Equipment chapters cover tents, trailers, motor bungalows, food, and medical kits. Camp sites near the great cities are listed, and later chapters take up autumn and winter camping. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
67187-the-gates-of-morning:
H De Vere Stacpoole wrote a South Seas novel copyrighted in 1924, by the author of The Blue Lagoon. Book one opens with the canoe builder. The revolt of the old men and the little ships follow. Civilization peeps in by chapter five. The men of the Kermadec, a pearl, and the mind of Sru fill the middle chapters.

A tragedy closes book one as the party makes south. Book two brings the maid of Aioma and war. Stacpoole set many romances on Pacific islands. His lagoon books sold the South Seas to landlocked readers. Dodd, Mead published this one at New York in 1925. Kanoa's mind gets a chapter in book two.
67246-in-the-morning:
Willis Boyd Allen wrote In the Morning, a book of verse put out in New York in 1890. A line from Luther heads the book, on tears that last the night and joy that comes with dawn. A line from Emerson bids the reader hear what the morning says, and trust it. Allen gives the book to his mother.

Verse on the feast of the birth of Christ leads the list of poems. New life, a calm that is not in the storm, and a scale of tones in tune follow. Poems bear the names of blooms, of months, and of days of the year. Marigold, pansy, and gold rod stand for the warm months in bloom. A tale of Carlo at the feast, a cross, and a vale of joy fill the midst.
67284-bee-keeping:
A bee man who wrote for The Times made a plain guide to bee-keeping. The book came out in London in 1864. He signs no name but his post at the paper. Drawn plates show hives and tools. His aim, he says, is use, not high thought on bees.

Parts deal with gain, joy, and how to start a yard. He shows where to set the bee house and which hive to buy. The folk of the hive, foes of bees, and care through the year fill the mid part. His own Times letters and notes from fans close the book. New bee men get sound, tried rules.
67288-the-right-thing:
Ray Cummings wrote a tale set in a lone mountain cabin on a frosty night. Beth waits alone as moonlight fills the pass below Sugar Loaf. A wolf howls up the mountain while coffee steams on the wood stove. Her table is set for one, and a phone hangs by the fireplace.

A knock sends her hand to a small revolver hid in her apron. Tom stands hurt at the door, pale and lame, leaning on the frame. He knew she was alone and stopped though he should have pressed on. Love, pain, and duty meet in a quiet, tense night tale.
6737-the-social-cancer-a-complete-englis:
Charles Derbyshire gives a complete English version of José Rizal's Noli Me Tangere, called here The Social Cancer, issued in Manila and New York in 1912. A companion volume, The Reign of Greed, renders the sequel, El Filibusterismo. The translator's introduction opens with a train image: readers fly through centuries in minutes, while those who live them feel each day drag.

Rizal's novel shows Philippine life under Spanish rule, with priests, officials, lovers, and rebels caught in a rotting social order. Its power helped stir a nation toward freedom. The Social Cancer is a landmark novel of colonial protest, still fierce and moving today.
67446-modern-whaling-bear-hunting-a-reco:
Burn Murdoch wrote Modern Whaling and Bear-Hunting, published in London by Seeley, Service and Company in 1917. The book holds 110 pictures, most of them his own drawings and photographs. Murdoch had sailed as artist and historian on a Dundee whaling voyage to the Antarctic. That trip shaped his knowledge of the trade.

The title promises a record of present-day whaling with modern gear in many parts of the world. It also covers bear and seal hunting in the Arctic. An opening scene shows a whale being lanced from a boat. The spear goes in five feet and twists free as the whale rolls. A publisher's note recalls the 1892 Dundee voyage. Three stout whaling ships spent three months among pack ice and bergs near Graham's Land.
67494-blackboard-sketching:
Frederick Whitney, director of art at the State Normal School in Salem, Massachusetts, made a book of blackboard sketches, printed in Springfield in 1909. Teachers and pupils had asked him for lessons they could use without personal instruction. Each plate shows the chalk strokes that make the effect, with directions on the facing page.

Early lessons teach the strokes on the simplest objects, so the teacher learns the medium itself. Later plates serve history, primary numbers, and arithmetic. Problems of commission and measurement get their own sketches. Whitney aims to give any teacher a quick, clear way to picture a lesson on the board while the class watches it grow.
67907-robinson-crusoe-told-to-the-childr:
Robinson Crusoe Told to the Children is a short form of the great cast away tale, made by John Lang. It stands in a set of tales told to the young, run by a named hand. Plates by Robinson stand in the book. It was put out at London and New York. A note to a boy named Alec heads the work.

When Defoe wrote the tale, that note says, near two years of a great age had not yet run. Boys of that day had more time on their hands than boys of this. They had less books and less games as well. They, and their sires, read the tale and loved it. When the sire of Alec and the hand were boys, they read it oft as well.
68052-address-of-president-roosevelt-on-:
Roosevelt gave it at Provincetown, Massachusetts, on the 20th of August 1907. It was printed at Washington by the Government Printing Office in the same year. The monument marked the landing of the Pilgrims near three centuries before.

The coming of the Pilgrim, followed in far larger numbers by the Puritan, shaped the destinies of the continent, he says. He asks for deep thanks that the Puritan stamped his mark so deeply on American life. The Puritan's faults were plain, he grants, as strong natures show their failings in bold relief. But men must be judged by the age they lived in and the work they had to do. The speech is a set piece of Roosevelt's creed of national character.
68148-tea-and-the-effects-of-tea-drinkin:
Tea and the Effects of Tea Drinking, by Tebb, public analyst to the borough of Southwark, reports an inquiry made in 1904. The borough council, at the request of Sir William Collins, let him test the make up of tea and look for ingredients that harm the drinker. The book opens with a short history of the tea plant.

Tebb traces the word from the Chinese tcha to Pepys sipping tee and Pope rhyming tay, then describes the shrub, its picking, and its spread. His tea tests follow. The work is Edwardian food science aimed at a drink England treated as a daily need.
68750-through-the-school-the-experiences:
Al Priddy tells how a mill boy fought his way through college in a memoir issued by the Pilgrim Press at Boston in 1912. Luther H Cary holds the copyright. Priddy had written Through the Mill before it.

His preface calls the forty chapters absolutely real autobiography. They aim to give the reader faith in American education. They also rebuild the struggles and tests of character that attend a poor lad's progress. Chapter one prices his start: fifteen dollars and sixty-five cents' worth of international travel. An inspiring reception waits in front of Chief Pungo Memorial Hall. He helps a real poet sing his hymn. Thropper's puff tie and lost pious reputation season the fun. Scriptural quotations help him keep the good side of the young women. Priddy writes in the plain voice of the parson's study.
68778-elements-of-show-card-writing:
John DeWild wrote this course of instruction on making business-building show cards for the educational department of the Associated Advertising Clubs of the World, copyrighted in 1923. The text opens by insisting on proper materials from the start, since improper materials handicap the beginner.

The outfit lists five sizes of round speedball pens, model C pens or broad-pointed pens, and black drawing ink. It adds two red sable rigger showcard brushes, bottles of black and light red showcard color, and a T square. A drawing board at least twenty-two by twenty-eight inches, squared up on two sides for rapid lining, completes the kit. Cardboard sizes follow: full sheets at twenty-two by twenty-eight, halves, quarters, and eighths, with weight told in plies of pulp. Practice runs on large instruction sheets and charts supplied by the clubs, on heavy paper enameled on one side.
68779-personal-reminiscences-of-henry-ir:
Personal Reminiscences of Henry Irving is a memoir by Bram Stoker, first printed in 1906. Heinemann issued the revised one-volume edition in 1907. Stoker managed Irving's theatre and knew him for decades. The book is dedicated to the memory of Toole. Toole was Irving's loving comrade and true friend. A pastel portrait of Irving in his last years fronts it. The contents begin with Stoker's earliest recollections.

He first saw Irving at Dublin in 1867. Captain Absolute was the part that struck him then. Two Roses at Dublin in 1871 follows in the tale. The old school of acting is set against the new. Stoker weighs Irving's place in that change. He wrote Dracula while in Irving's service. This memoir is his other monument to those years. It gives the actor's daily life from inside his circle.
68912-education-and-living:
Randolph Bourne, author of Youth and Life and The Gary Schools, collected these essays on schooling, published by the Century Company at New York in 1917. Many had first appeared in the Republic during 1915 and 1916. The opening essay asks what the broadening of the public school means, with its gymnasiums, pools, shops, gardens, and organized play.

Bourne argues that Americans are growing restless at how much schools resemble penitentiaries and orphan asylums rather than free communities for children. Twenty-eight essays follow, on wasted years, learning out of school, taste, vocational education, continuation schools, and the colleges. His problem throughout is how to turn schooling from a mechanical institution into a life fitted to each child's needs.
69050-the-coming:
The Coming, a novel by Snaith, was issued at New York by Appleton in 1917. Snaith had written The Sailor and Anne Feversham before it. The opening line is a grave scriptural echo: he came to his own and his own knew him not. A parish vicar sits at the heart of the first scene.

The vicar sat at his study table, pen in hand, on a Saturday morning. His weekly sermon was not yet begun, though the hour pressed. On Sunday mornings he read an old discourse to his flock. In the evening, forty years of practice required a new and original sermon. His rustic flock was not in the least critical, the tale smiles. A quiet parish meets an unquiet coming in Snaith’s fable.
69062-a-bacteriological-study-of-ham-sou:
A Bacteriological Study of Ham Souring is a bulletin by McBryde, a Department of Agriculture bacteriologist, issued in 1911. The bureau calls ham souring a heavy loss to the packing industry and credits the study with finding its cause.

The contents map a full laboratory investigation. After chapters on curing and on detecting souring, the paper sets out its own experiments. These cover the examination of sour and sound hams and inoculation tests. Later sections ask how the bacillus enters the ham, whether infection can begin before slaughter or come from the pickling fluids, and close with prevention and the disposal of soured hams.
6912-school-and-home-cooking:
Carlotta Greer, head of foods and household management at East Technical High School in Cleveland, wrote this text for pupils to use both at school and at home. Its use ends note taking, which Greer calls dictation in disguise, and so saves much time. Lessons follow a psychological method, starting from what lies within a beginner's own life and building outward to new needs.

Foods rich in each foodstuff are grouped in a logical order, while each lesson approaches its dish in the order a learner can grasp. The book gives enough dishes and hand processes to train a pupil well, and an illustration shows a corner of Washington's kitchen at Mount Vernon. It is a plain, practical school book for the kitchen.
69139-nothing:
Nothing, a war tale by Martin Pearson, ran in Astonishing Stories in October 1942. The little man with the grey beard stared at the narrator, who stared back. This is getting us nowhere, the narrator remarks, nowhere at all, in the opening. He nodded and sat down on the hard stone of their trap.

They are trapped under a building that came down when a bomb landed in the street. The rest of the tenants were probably away or dead in that raid. Only the old man from the second floor rear and he reached the cellar in time. Tons of brick, rubbish, and beams block every way out for the pair. They must wait until rescuers dig them out from the street above. Blitz dread in a buried cellar fills this short war tale.
69167-body-snatching:
Body-Snatching is a pamphlet on the theft of corpses for the dissecting room. Baldwin, Cradock, and Joy published the piece at London in 1824. The text first ran in the third number of the Westminster Review. Its owners allowed the reprint so the knowledge might spread widely.

The writer opens on the value every person sets on life and health. Skilled doctors, he argues, do more plain good than any other class of men. Ignorant doctors are worse than the plague, killing in silence while trusted as saviours. Yet the public knows almost nothing of how the body works. Surgeons need dead bodies to learn their art, and the law starved the supply. The tract presses the case for legal anatomy. It helped prepare the ground for reform of the anatomy laws.
69488-practical-forging-and-art-smithing:
Practical Forging and Art Smithing is a manual by Thomas Googerty, published in Milwaukee in 1915. Bruce Publishing issued the book for school and shop use. Its first chapter treats the forge, its tools, and the anvil. Making and cleaning the fire come next, then welding and flux. Later chapters take up electric and gas welding. Fagot, lap, jump, and butt welds each get their method.

The middle chapters work through small shop jobs in order. Staples, links, chain lines, bolts, and hooks are made step by step. Tongs, cold chisels, and punches follow, with steel and its tempering explained. The Bessemer and open hearth processes are described for the student. The art smithing half turns to leaves, scrolls, and grilles. Door latches, hinges, candle sticks, and lanterns end the course.
69493-lessons-in-chalk-modeling-the-new-:
Lessons in Chalk Modeling, the new method of map drawing, is a teaching book by Ida Cassa Heffron. Heffron had taught at a normal school in Chicago and lectured in the art of teaching. Her book carries one hundred illustrations and an introduction with advice on the use of the map. It was copyrighted in 1900.

The first part argues for the study of land forms before any drawing of maps begins. Field lessons matter, she holds, along with the habit of modelling and drawing what pupils see. Learning to read pictures also helps children picture a whole continent. The second part gives fifteen lessons in chalk modelling. They start with surfaces sloping away from the viewer, light and shade, and the marking of distances.
69600-a-christmas-greeting:
A Christmas Greeting is a book by Marie Corelli, published by Dodd, Mead of New York in 1901. Its essay takes the old greeting of a merry Christmas as its theme. Corelli asks why a once merry England now hates the sound of the words.

She sees tired, nervous faces in the crowds, and hears endless complaints. The halfpenny press serves up suicide, murder, and mania as literature. Against this she sets the old songs, Yule games, and country dances of Merrie England. Its yeomen and squires kept open doors, so England was merry once, she argues. A pessimist answers that the wish is a farce for him, since he has no cause to be merry. Corelli replies that the world does not wag in his particular way.
69752-a-year-of-prophesying:
Wells wrote a book of forward looks at the world in his own sharp way. Its front lists name his tales, from Kipps to The Dream. Dream tales like The Time Machine stand in one proud row. Books on the world and its ways stand in the next. A Year of Prophesying takes its place in that line of thought.

Wells was famed for tales that saw the next age first. Here the same gaze turns to fact in short, bold pieces. Wars, tools, and new ways of life fill his sights. He writes as if the future can be read with care. Readers of 1920s thought get his voice at full force.
69793-caught-napping:
An anonymous church satire, Caught Napping reached a third edition with Palmer of Little Queen Street, London, in 1866, and its whole text runs to only three chapters. The narrator calls himself an Anglican of the Anglicans, a perfect man whose four angles impinge upon his neighbours and produce many a sore wherever he goes.

Sitting in his study with his feet on the mantelpiece, reading the Guardian newspaper over letters on the ritual question, he nods off despite himself. He insists the vision that follows cannot be a dream, since dreams require imaginative faculties, which are entirely deficient in Anglican skulls. In the vision he finds himself in the catacombs after losing the thread of time for ages. Churchmen of old, Sancroft, Andrews, Bull, and Cosin, seem to caper in a reel before his scandalized eyes.
69844-a-history-of-italian-painting:
A History of Italian Painting is a survey by Frank Jewett Mather, professor of art and archaeology at Princeton. Stanley Paul of London published it in 1923. A Giotto, the Dormition of the Virgin at Berlin, serves as frontispiece.

Nine chapters run from Giotto, founder of a new Florentine humanism, to the realists and eclectics, with notes and hints for reading. Siena continues the mediaeval style, and Masaccio brings a new realism. Fra Filippo Lippi follows, with Botticelli and Leonardo opening the golden age. Raphael and Michelangelo crown it. Venetian painting before Titian, then Titian himself, fill two chapters. Mather opens with Leonardo's test of a picture: movements fit for the figure's mind.
69954-the-cameron-pride-or-purified-by-s:
The Cameron Pride, or Purified by Suffering, is a novel by Mary Holmes. Hurst and Company issued the book in New York as part of her uniform series. Holmes gives the volume to her brother Kirke Hawes, in memory of an October day on the Silverton hills.

Those hills, her note from Brown Cottage in February 1867 says, are where Morris and Kitty lived. The tale opens at the farm-house at Silverton and moves to Linwood. Wilford Cameron visits, returns in spring, and heads toward marriage at Saint John's. Extracts from Bell Cameron's diary fill the middle chapters. Katy's first evening in New York, Saratoga and Newport, and trouble in the household follow. Aunt Betsy consults a lawyer before the close.
70021-edna-browning:
Edna Browning, or The Leighton Homestead is a tale by Mary Holmes. It came out at New York in eighteen seventy-two. A front list shows it as the last of a row of past twelve tales by the same hand, each at the same price. Past thirty heads fill it, from the hero of its first head to the croquet party and past.

Heads tell of the home stead, of a girls wire note, of a brave small wife, and of the days past a crash. Ednas first weeks at a house, an aunts wrath at the news, and a north room take heads. A debt paid, a year past, a yes given, and a hid thing of a next girl fill the late rows. A press note calls Holmes a sweet and keen hand whose books hold their hands fast.
70330-the-essentials-of-bandaging:
The Essentials of Bandaging is a surgical manual by Berkeley Hill, instructor in bandaging at University College, London. This second edition, revised and enlarged, appeared in 1869. It covers the management of fractures and dislocations, with directions for using other surgical apparatus. The book is illustrated by 122 engravings on wood.

Hill states plainly what the book is for. It grew from his teaching on bandaging and surgical apparatus at University College Hospital. It does not try to include every good method of treating surgical injuries. Instead it gives the student or practitioner instructions by which he may refresh his memory before acting. The second edition adds lists as an appendix: what the sick room and operating room need before ordinary operations, and the instruments for forty-nine different operations. It is a pocket-sized memory aid for the working surgeon.
70440-the-awakening:
Henry Bordeaux wrote The Awakening, rendered into English by Ruth Helen Davis. E P Dutton and Company in New York issued the book with a copyright of nineteen fourteen. Bordeaux had earlier written The Fear of Living. Davis gave the rendering to her dear aunt Virginia. Four parts fill the novel. Elizabeth is the heroine whose awakening gives the book its name.

Part one opens with the first act of procedure in a suit for divorce or separation. A petition to the presiding judge states grievances and asks for an attempt at reconciliation. In the provinces, Bordeaux notes, clerks in solicitors offices rush to peek at the draft for scandal. Later parts bring Albert diary, Anne de Sèzery, and Elizabeth day by day. Paris, a chartreuse, and opened eyes close the tale. Readers get a French tale of marriage, law, and renewal.
70467-the-attache-at-peking:
A B Freeman-Mitford wrote letters from his years as an attache at Peking. Macmillan issued the book in London and New York in 1900. He had written Tales of Old Japan and The Bamboo Garden. The letters were set down long before, as his preface grants.

Freeman-Mitford holds that old ways changed slowly in Peking, so the record still stands. Life within the walls, trips through the land, and Chinese manners fill the pages. He warns that calm could break, as unrest in Shantung once threatened the capital. Readers gain a near view of court and street life in a tense age.
7047-back-to-billabong:
Mary Grant Bruce brings her folk back to Billabong in 1921, opening with a Mackellar verse on a brown land of open spaces, gaunt forest, and treeless plain. If once loved, the verse says, that land must draw its lovers back again. Contents run from Lancaster Gate in London through the Rainhams, playing truant, coming home, and the turn of fortune's wheel, to sailing orders and watch dogs.

Tommy boards a strange taxi, Australia welcomes the travelers, and Billabong itself appears, with colonial experiences, influenza and furniture, and the home on the creek. The Cunjee races, Wally's race ride, and building up again close the tale. A schoolroom row over a map opens the book, with red haired, snub nosed Wilfred defiant at his table.
70485-the-things-which-belong:
Constance Holme wrote The Things Which Belong, taking its title from the words, the things which belong unto thy peace. Mills and Boon in London issued the novel in nineteen twenty five. Holme had earlier written Crump Folk, Going Home, The Lonely Plough, and The Trumpet in the Dust. An author note grants the local colour but calls the situation between the folk purely imaginary. A prologue, then three parts, His, Hers, and Theirs, structure the book.

The prologue opens as a pen drops from a writer fingers, as if weighted. He felt he would never use a pen again. Mattie face flushed, but she said nothing, though he had expected joyful speech. It was the second time that evening her silence surprised him. Folk often fall silent at the late fulfilment of a long desire, he recalls. A quiet Cumbrian tale of marriage and longing follows.
7058-mankind-in-the-making:
H G Wells presents Mankind in the Making as a companion to Anticipations and the pamphlet The Discovery of the Future. Read alongside those earlier works, it sets out a broad account of how societies grow and how people should act within public life. Wells takes up questions of society and government from a fresh vantage, treating the entire social and political order as parts of a single unfolding pattern.

All social and political activities, he argues, stand in a defined relation to that scheme, and to this method and trend he directs the reader's attention. The preface asks to save misunderstanding by stating aim and scope at the outset. The book is Wells the prophet at work, planning how a species might consciously shape its own future.
70674-the-glamour-of-prospecting:
Cornell's The Glamour of Prospecting, first published by Fisher Unwin of London in 1920, recounts the wanderings of a South African prospector in search of copper, gold, emeralds, and diamonds. A map and illustrations follow him through desert country.

The opening chapters chase diamond rumours in German South-West Africa, around the new port of Luderitzbucht, and sail up the coast on a sealing cutter to Walfish Bay. Later chapters cross the Namib desert to Cape Cross, Swakopmund, and Windhuk, then prospect by motor car into the southern Kalahari. Namaqualand and the Richtersfeldt bring copper prospects, the mouth of the Orange River, a mountain of copper, and the Great Fish River. Cornell writes as a working prospector, and the glamour of his title is mostly dust, rumour, and hope.
70760-corpus-earthling:
Corpus Earthling is a science fiction novel by Louis Charbonneau, a Zenith original published at New York in 1960. The tale opens with the narrator studying a redhead asleep on his couch. Even she, Laurie Hendricks, might be one of them, he thinks: one of the things from outer space. She wakes, smiles, and draws him into a kiss that blots out thought.

The first chapter plunges into a dream within a dream, an alien mind inside a sick mind. The narrator fights toward waking and firm reality. Charbonneau builds a tale of hidden invaders who wear human flesh. It works the paranoia vein of cold-war science fiction, where any lover or neighbour may be the enemy.
70920-whilst-father-was-fighting:
Whilst Father Was Fighting, by Eleanora H Stooke, is a children's story of a family holding together while the father is away at war. The Religious Tract Society published it in London. Stooke had written Little Maid Marigold.

The tale opens in an attic bedroom. Bob Middleton comforts his five-year-old brother Jackie, who is afraid of the dark and dreads another whipping from Aunt Martha. Chapters bring a new lodger, a dog named Stray, and an enemy made by Bob and the dog. A ruby brooch, an earl's daughter, and news of Tom Smith carry the plot. Stray comes to the rescue before the conclusion. Pictures show big boys stealing apples in the street. The book teaches courage and kindness to small readers in wartime homes.
71042-poster-advertising:
Poster Advertising, by Hawkins, advertising manager of the Fairbank Company of Chicago, makers of Gold Dust washing powder and Fairy soap, was published in 1910.
