Subtitled a talk on posting as an advertising medium, the book offers hints and suggestions to poster advertisers, with thirty-two pages of full-color reproductions of posters used by national advertisers.

Hawkins explains why bill-posting works: the display is large, unavoidable, and builds a maker's name until the name itself becomes a reputation. Chapters cover poster sizes, costs, and the practice of the trade. Written by a working manager of famous brands, the book is a primary record of American outdoor advertising in its lithographed golden age, before radio and the automobile remade the roadside.
71197-the-haunter-of-the-ring:
The Haunter of the Ring is a tale of horror by Robert Howard, first printed in Weird Tales in June 1934. Its blurb calls it a strange story of dark powers and occult evil. The narrator visits the study of John Kirowan, a student of dark lore. A big young friend, Gordon, sits there haggard and worn. The narrator bursts in with a prize in his hand. He has bought it dear from Ahmed Mektub, a robber of antiquities. It is a ring, and he means to make them stare.

At the sight of a knife drawn in jest, Gordon starts like a hunted man. He gulps brandy like a man half famished. He owns it was no thought but blind instinct: the fear of one against whom any hand may be turned. Kirowan takes the tale in hand. The ring's past is the door to the horror.
71829-the-law-relating-to-betting-time-b:
The Law Relating to Betting, Time-Bargains and Gaming is a legal handbook by Stutfield, a barrister and former Vinerian scholar at Oxford. The Project Gutenberg text follows the third edition, revised with Cautley, and published in London in 1892. The book is dedicated to a judge of the High Court.

The preface notes that the courts have been kept busy by new forms of gambling. Judges must rule on the legal shape of each fresh device. Parliament has done less. One act stopped agents from dodging the gaming law of 1845, but left a gap the author points out. Another act guards boys at the universities and schools from betting and loans. The text then works through the case law, down to fights over bucket shops in the Scots courts.
72009-scaffolding:
Thatcher, a building surveyor, wrote Scaffolding, a treatise on the design and erection of scaffolds, gantries, and stagings. Batsford published the second, revised edition in London in 1907. The book carries 146 diagrams and six full-page plates, the first showing derrick staging photographed in a London street. It is written for contractors, builders, and clerks of works.

A note explains the new edition. Changes in the law affecting scaffolding and the men who erect it forced a revision. Thatcher also folded in the safety suggestions of the Chief Inspector of Factories, whose annual report had urged practices meant to cut the number of fatal accidents at building works. The chapters define the northern and south country systems, working platforms, and travelling gantries, and a legal chapter treats liability. The book is a working manual from the years when scaffolding was still poles, ropes, and the scaffolder's craft.
72069-go-to-sleep-my-darling:
Winston Marks wrote this tale of Bertrand Baxter, a man lost among women. The tale ran in Infinity in November 1958. Baxter, age 46, sells sporting goods and was a star tackle. Coaches and school men love his sixth sense for their needs.

Women buyers baffle him, though they find him good looking and strong. He wed Rolanda but never learned to read her mind at home. Fate gave him four daughters, to his deep confusion each day. Only baby Annie, two months old, now makes sense to him at all. Abernathy and Crisp employ Baxter as their sporting goods man.
72226-the-first-american-king:
The First American King is a novel by George Gordon Hastings, published by the Smart Set Publishing Company in nineteen oh five. A new edition appeared in February of that year, from a nineteen oh four copyright. The contents divide the tale into three books, from a cave of whispers to a new era.

Book one opens at Dr Belden's establishment on the southern shore of Long Island. The place is a cross between a sanatorium and a physical culture resort. Belden examines each arrival, prescribes diet and exercise, and refits human wrecks at a hundred a week. Book two moves onto the broad highway, with cocked hats, revelations, and a great court ball. A mystery of the palace, a counterplot, and the last stand of the guards fill book three. Hastings builds a Ruritanian intrigue out of an American rest cure.
72290-pneumatic-conveying:
Pneumatic Conveying is a short engineering primer by Phillips on moving materials by air. Pitman published it in London in a series of technical primers. Neale edited that series. Each volume cost half a crown net. The series treats the principles of one branch of engineering at a time. Its manner is practical throughout.

A series preface states the shared aim. Each book gives the student a handy survey of his branch. Companion volumes treat the steam locomotive, water power, and the electric furnace. Phillips writes for students of conveying machinery. Experiments reported in the text found the discharger a weak link. Wet, sticky materials packed tight at high speed. Work with a collaborator overcame the fault. The primer turns such workshop findings into rules.
72542-behind-the-scenes-in-peking:
Behind the Scenes in Peking is Mary Hooker's account of the siege of the legations during the Boxer rising of 1900, published in London in 1911 with many photographs. Hooker writes as a resident writing home: the book opens with a letter dated the twenty-sixth of May 1900, before the storm broke, describing the foreign colony's summer habits.

The letter explains the hills fifteen miles from the imperial city, where diplomats escaped the sizzling summer in leased Buddhist temples, and the British minister's great house in its compound. The illustrations carry the siege: barricades, the International gun, and the French legation in ruins. Portraits of Sir Robert Hart, Sir Claude MacDonald and the murdered Baron von Ketteler frame an eyewitness record of the fifty-five days.
72661-playwrights-on-playmaking:
Playwrights on Playmaking is a set of studies of the stage by Brander Matthews, professor of dramatic literature at Columbia University. It was published by Scribner's Sons in 1923. Matthews had written lives of Shakspere and Molière, and many books on the drama.

The prefatory note is a farewell. At seventy, and going down into the dim valley beyond, Matthews calls this sheaf of essays probably his last. Half a century of playgoing lies behind it. He sets down the theories of the theatre that he has made his own. They are few, he says, and can be declared briefly. To him they seem so plain that he is ever surprised to see them challenged. The title essay gathers what great makers of plays have said about their craft.
72827-nonsense-for-old-and-young:
Nonsense for Old and Young, by Eugene Field, was published in Boston in 1901, with drawings by John Frohn. A motto from Oliver Wendell Holmes heads the book: a little nonsense now and then is relished by the best of men. A foreword says the editors tried to add pictures to the fun of Field's conceits.

Most pieces first ran in the Denver Tribune in the fall of 1881 as The Tribune Primer. About one hundred and sixty-two quips appeared, styled like a child's first reading lessons, with short sentences and a liberal spread of capital letters. Ninety-four came out in book form in 1881; the rest, less five too local to keep their sting, appear here with pictures for the first time. Field's wit stays light and sly.
72950-the-bunnikins-bunnies-and-the-moon:
The Bunnikins Bunnies and the Moon King, by Edith B Davidson, was printed at Boston in 1912, with plates by Clara E Atwood. Davidson had also written The Bunnikins Bunnies in Camp. The book is given to a child named Barbara, with kind words from Mr Bunnikins Bunny.

The tale opens with Mr Bunnikins Bunny home sick, with a headache, a toothache, and the shivery shivers all over. Mrs Bunny gives him hot pepper tea and tucks him in with a hot water bottle at his toes. His friend Mr Gray Squirrel calls and says what he needs is a change of air. Talk turns to a trip by air ship, which scares Mrs Bunny half to tears. Young readers get a soft, funny animal tale with bright plates.
73031-the-fear-of-living:
Henry Bordeaux wrote the Fear of Living, a French novel. Davis made the authorized English version for Dutton in 1913. Marcel's Homecoming opens the contents of the first part. Brother and Sister and the Battle of Flowers follow there. A sister's secret comes next in the list.

A proposal and a farewell fill part one. Marcel's departure closes that part of the family tale. Thirteen at table opens the second part of the contents. A policeman's message and a mother of sorrows follow in it. The pageantry of death and two more secrets stand later. The fear of living is a disease, the opening chapter states. It extends its ravages to old civilisations like our own. Dante branded one kind of that fear long ago in hell. Sad souls there lived without blame and without praise, it quotes.
73075-willow-the-king:
J C Snaith wrote a novel about a cricket match, drawn by Lucien Davis and dedicated to his colleagues at a Nottingham amateur cricket club. The eve of Little Clumpton versus Hickory opens the book. The narrator jokes that local folk rate the match above Waterloo and Omdurman. Half the team sit in his billiard room weighing the morrow.

Opinion is unanimous for once: Little Clumpton must not lose. Chapters follow the match, a cricket lunch, and record breaking play. Cupid puts his pads on in one chapter. A telegram from Stoddart shakes things later. Snaith treats village cricket as high drama, with love and heredity in play.
73495-the-man-who-knew-everything:
The Man Who Knew Everything is a spy tale of the cold war by Randall Garrett. It first ran in a fiction magazine in October of nineteen fifty six. A cheeky head note claims the Reds have no secrets left at all. The joke rests on a man who can know each fact he seeks.

The tale opens in a hid lab in Arlington, in the state of Virginia. A doctor twists dials to shape a green wave line on a screen. His aim is a beam for talk that beats plain radio for speed and hush. A throb in his head is the one sure thing in the art at the start. From that lab bench the plot spins out to state craft and spies.
7354-on-something:
H. Belloc's On Something, dedicated to somebody, gathers essays on a plea for the simpler drama, a notebook, and unknown people. A Van Tromp, threepenny bits, the hotel at Palma and a proposed guide-book, and the death of wandering Peter follow. The tree of knowledge, a Norfolk man, the odd people, and a letter of advice and apology to a young burglar follow. The monkey question, the empire builder, Caedwalla, a unit of England, the relic, and the ironmonger complete the set.

A force in Gaul, bridges, a blue book, Perigueux of the Perigord, the position, home, the way to fairyland, and a portrait of a child close a book that wanders by design. Belloc writes on whatever catches his eye, with wit, learning, and strong opinion. The essays reward readers who enjoy a companionable, combative mind.
73671-camping-and-camp-cooking:
Camping and Camp Cooking is an outdoors manual by Frank Bates, writing as Matasisso, first copyrighted in 1909 and issued in a new revised edition in 1914. Bates had written on game birds and on lake, field, and forest stories. Part of the book first appeared in a sportsman's magazine. A chapter on cleaning fish was written for this volume by Leslie Bosworth.

Chapter one treats camp outfits. An outfit should be light and compact, with needless articles left out and needful ones included. That reads a little funny, Bates admits, yet it is the gist of the whole question. A man learns it while hauling a hundred-pound outfit over a swampy carry in the rain. Bates contrasts his practical trip with the hard model of Nessmuk, the famous woodsman. A city clerk patterning his holiday on Nessmuk, he argues, would simply not take the trip at all.
73706-mysteries-of-the-missing:
Mysteries of the Missing, by Edward Smith, was first under copyright in 1924 and reissued by the Dial Press in 1927. Smith had written Famous Poison Mysteries before this book. The frontispiece shows the Ross house at Germantown, where the tale of Charlie Ross begins.

A note on disappearing opens the case list, and then the chapters take up one lost soul at a time. A vanished archduke, the Tichborne heir, and the kidnappers of Central Park all appear. Dorothy Arnold, Eddie Cudahy, and the Whitla boy get chapters of their own. Later parts treat Ambrose Bierce, a lost millionaire, and ghost ships at sea. A book list at the end points readers to more sources.
73742-the-house-of-the-missing:
The House of the Missing is a mystery novel by Sinclair Gluck, published in New York in nineteen twenty two. A contents list of more than twenty chapters maps a search in brisk steps. It opens with the narrator acquiring a friend, then a chapter called The Shadow of the Web. That's All We Know and Roving Commissions follow in pulp order.

A girl in gray, a famous tea, and amateur burglary mark the middle chapters. A second burglary, a darkest hour, and a room of voices raise the stakes toward the end. Walk into My Parlor promises a trap sprung in spider style. Missing persons, webs, and clues drive a snappy period detective tale.
741-thomas-hart-benton-s-remarks-to-the-:
Thomas Hart Benton rose in the Senate on 12 January 1837 to move that a censure of President Jackson be expunged from the journal. Three years earlier, he notes, the Senate had passed the resolve, and at once he gave notice that he would seek its erasure. He argues that the resolve was unjust, and that time has proven his case.

Benton's speech is a long, dogged defence of Jackson and of the Senate's right to correct its own record. He speaks with the bluntness of a western senator sure of his ground. The text is a key document of the Bank War era, showing how party feeling, pride, and procedure shaped one of the fiercest fights of the age.
74149-a-hat-in-the-radio-ring:
A Hat in the Radio Ring is a story by Garret Smith about politics in the age of radio. It opens at a keynote dinner, where Boss Quaid glares at the microphone opposite the toastmaster's seat. The radio, he growls, is playing hell with politics. Barney Fogarty, his secretary, explains the change to a guest.

In the old days, Barney says, a keynote dinner could be kept bottled up. The newspaper boys were fixed, and a wrong turn could be kept out of the papers or toned down. Now everybody has a radio and gets the gas hot from the cylinder. Folk do not even go to meetings any more, unless the meetings are hand-picked, like this one. The bosses fear a dark horse popping up on the state power question. Smith's tale catches the moment when broadcasting broke the party machine's control of the news.
74154-the-reaction-between-manganese-dio:
Arthur Hopkins wrote this doctoral thesis for Johns Hopkins University in 1893. He thanks Professor Morse, who suggested the work and guided it. Thanks also go to Remson for teaching and Ames for physics. Contents start with an introduction and a note on apparatus used.

Hopkins tests how manganese dioxide acts on potassium permanganate in acid. A black oxide of manganese gets the same test in acid too. He counts how much nitric acid the reaction neutralizes in trials. Later parts test stability and the effect of varied amounts used. Arthur John Hopkins offered the work at Johns Hopkins in 1893.
74199-the-nobles-are-coming:
Gene Cross wrote The Nobles Are Coming, a tale printed in Fantastic Universe in October nineteen fifty-four. The scene is Mars, a world of rust-red hills and a port town. An editor's note praises Cross for hinting more than he tells.

A lone traveller rests in a cave after his ground car breaks down. In the dark, a stir and a whisper break the silence. A voice names its owner as Mister J J Abrogado, a Serbo-Croat prospector. He had walked all day and most of the night toward Marsport. The two men talk of the Nobles, and then raw terror strikes.
74229-jack-henderson-on-tipping:
Cobb wrote this merry book on tipping, told in letters from a man named Jack Henderson. Hurst and Company of New York printed it in 1905, with drawings by Marshall Smith. The front plate asks, in big type, how much you have got.

Jack writes to Billy from Detroit and owns that he has not roamed far. Still, he holds that tipping is one of the up-to-date skills a man needs. There is an art in tipping, he says, but the lost art is getting by with none. He backs the anti-tipping club with a wink: let most men join it, and his own tips will shine the more. Slang and jokes fill his case.
74447-discourses-of-brigham-young:
John Widtsoe picked and set in order talks by Brigham Young for this book. Young led the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints as its second head. The talks came from the long Journal of Discourses set. Widtsoe groups them by theme for ease of use.

Early parts define the gospel, the Godhead, and how God speaks to man. Later parts treat free will, sin, growth, and the fate of man. Young speaks in plain, firm terms on work, faith, and daily life. The book gives a clear map of his thought in one place.
74538-vegetarian-supplement-to-scientifi:
Mrs Dora C C L Roper wrote a Vegetarian Supplement to Scientific Feeding, printed at Oakland, California, by the Buckner Printing Company in nineteen fifteen. Roper, a doctor of osteopathy, gave the pages to all who read them. Her earnest desire is to maintain health and prevent diseases made by wrong and intemperate eating and drinking, she says. A Franklin line heads the book, Eat not to dullness, Drink not to elevation.

Part one treats classes and functions of food, recipes of cooked and raw foods, and one hundred simple and fancy menus. Sandwiches, right and wrong food mixtures, hygiene, economy, and sanitation follow. Part two treats the brain and nervous system, circulation, and care of the body. Stimulants, constipation, obesity, and psychotherapy share the pages. A table of food caloric values closes the book. Health seekers get an early meatless diet guide.
74930-memoirs-and-resolutions-of-adam-gr:
Memoirs and Resolutions of Adam Graeme of Mossgray is a novel by Margaret Oliphant, published in eighteen fifty nine. Oliphant hides her name behind her earlier books on the title page. Those books include Passages in the Life of Mrs Margaret Maitland and Lilliesleaf. Hurst and Blackett issued the work in London in three parts.

Book one tells the history of Adam Graeme in his own first person voice. The tale opens with wonder at the bare fact of being born at all. Graeme calls birth a greater marvel than death, which is only a change of dress. His mother died in the hour that gave him life, he records. That sad start clouds the course of his whole long life story. Chronicles of the borough of Fendie fill out the later books.
75063-hospital-housekeeping:
Hospital Housekeeping is a manual by Charlotte A Aikens, printed at Detroit in a second edition of 1910. Aikens had directed the Sibley Memorial Hospital at Washington and superintended hospitals at Des Moines and Pittsburg. The first chapter treats the hospital housekeeper and her province, with bookkeeping and the hospital inventory.

Later chapters cover the main entrance and porter, the private rooms, and the daily cleaning. The hospital ward chapter treats bed making, ward lockers, and the care of patients' clothing. The linen room and the laundry have chapters of their own. Aikens writes that hospital housekeeping is intensely practical business. It demands a housekeeper of no inferior or uncertain attainments. All the elements that make for success in home housekeeping, and many more, are needed in a hospital. The manual is a guide to running the domestic side of a modern hospital.
75177-marine-bayonet-training:
Marine Bayonet Training is a Fleet Marine Force manual, numbered one dash one, dated nineteen sixty five. Headquarters of the Marine Corps at Washington issued it for the operating forces. General Chapman approved it as chief of staff on March twenty fifth. It replaces a bayonet fighting manual of March nineteen fifty seven.

The manual states three aims in its opening letter to the reader. It sets out the Marine way of bayonet fighting, old and new in brief. It describes stances and moves for the fighter alone and in a group. Both attack and defence are treated for each case in the text. A training program, pugil stick work, and assault course building are included. Sections then take up the guard position, foot movements, and the thrust in order.
75179-her-majesty-the-king:
Her Majesty the King, a romance of the harem done into American from the Arabic by James Jeffrey Roche, was copyrighted in 1898. A New York edition with pictures by Oliver Herford followed in 1902. Roche dedicates the book to a descendant of the lady who told him the tale. He marvels at her wit as he writes the dedication.

Since Scheherazade, he says, none has matched his teller in wit and wisdom. The frame thus promises a tale in the manner of the Arabian Nights. A woman rules as king in the story, by the riddle of the title. Harem intrigue and eastern colour fill the romance. Roche gives the tale an American voice while keeping its eastern dress. The book is a light, ornate fancy of its decade.
75302-dyes-and-dyeing:
Dyes and Dyeing, by Charles Pellew, is a practical survey of colour for cloth, issued at New York in a new and enlarged edition of 1918. Pellew had been a professor of chemistry at Columbia University. A plate of indigo dyed batik from Madras fronts the book. The first chapter is an introduction to the whole subject.

That chapter takes up the dyes of the ancients and of our ancestors. Animal, vegetable, and mineral colours stand in their old order there. The book then works through modern dyes and their use. Copyright pages show a first form in 1913, much grown by 1918. Pellew writes for students, craftsmen, and the curious reader. Batik, indigo, and the new coal tar colours share his pages. The work joins lab science to the dyer’s vat.
75442-camp-fires-and-camp-cooking:
Captain Sanderson, commissary of subsistence of volunteers, wrote culinary hints for the soldier, printed at Washington in 1862 for distribution to the troops. The book came from headquarters of the Army of the Potomac in January 1862. A receipt for making bread in the portable field oven furnished by the subsistence department is a headline part. The author has personally helped cook the dishes he treats of, he says.

He used only camp fires, camp kettles, and soldiers' rations, and knows that a little attention from any sensible man will produce the most savory results. The utensils furnished by government are of the most primitive character, he notes. Camp kettles of iron, varying from four to seven gallons, should be made so as to slide one into the other. In clayey soil, the salt boilers' plan for an oven is the neatest, he adds. Union cooks get real help here.
75503-knitting:
Marie Louise Kerzman gathered and edited a hand book called Knitting: How to Knit and What to Knit, put out in Brooklyn in 1884. Many art cuts show each move of the hands. The book starts with the stuffs of the craft: cotton, worsted, silk, or thread, and the needles to work them.

Stockings and all work in rounds, she notes, call for four needles, three to hold the work and one to knit with. Five ways to cast on stitches are taught step by step, with the loose end held just so across thumb and first finger. From those first loops the book builds to full goods a home knitter could make and use.
75757-baths-and-bathing:
Baths and Bathing is a health primer on the uses of water for the body. Hardwicke and Bogue issued it at London in 1879 in the Health Primers set. Editors of the series were doctors Down, Power, Granville, and Tweedy of London. Its chapters move from the action of baths to a visit to a bath.

Skin structure comes first, since baths work through the skin on deeper parts. Pores number some twenty eight hundred to the square inch, it calculates. Papillae, the touch organs, crowd the ridges of the skin as well. Varieties of baths and famous bathing localities fill the middle chapters in full. Plain medical counsel for home bathing is the primer plain aim.
75832-first-lessons-in-the-principles-of:
Lady Barker wrote First Lessons in the Principles of Cooking, in three parts. Macmillan and Company published it at London in 1886. Twelve lessons fill the contents. The first part treats the chemical makeup of food and its effect on the body. Bread and beef, fish, and vegetables have their lessons there. The second part turns to practice: the preparations of flour, potatoes, and broth from beef.

Fuel and fire close the second part. The third treats boiling and stewing, then baking, roasting, and frying. Bacon gets a lesson of its own, and the gist of the whole matter ends the book. Barker's introduction lays a duty on every head of a household, large or small, rich or poor. No waste may be permitted in the preparation of food.
75865-mind-reading:
Mind Reading is a five cent pamphlet by W E Skinner, printed at Boston in April 1896 in the Multum in Parvo Library. Skinner promises a correct account of how to read people thoughts. The monthly cost fifty cents a year by subscription.

Skinner says long essays on mind reading bore most readers and teach them nothing they can use. True thought transfer, if it comes at all, is rare and will not work in a mixed crowd. The method he gives is the one used by Stuart Cumberland and Washington Bishop, famed stage readers. It rests on muscle reading, not on magic. One game has a guest hide a pin while the reader is out, then lead him to it by the hand. Stage fans get the trick laid bare.
76079-a-child-s-guide-to-reading:
A Child's Guide to Reading is a handbook for young readers by John Macy, published in New York in 1909. Two quotes stand at its door. Hazlitt calls reading while young the greatest pleasure in life. Bagehot adds that much in great books can be caught only when first met in childhood. The chapters run from guides and rules to the purpose of reading. Fiction gets two chapters and a list of books. Poetry gets a chapter and a string of poets, Tennyson, Longfellow, and Wordsworth among them.

Macy opens with the Maine woods guide as his model. A good guide does more than the paid work, he says. He is friend and philosopher to the green hunter. So should a reading guide be to a child. The book steers the young to the great shelf with a light, fond hand.
76205-the-spring-song:
The Spring Song, a novel by Forrest Reid, was printed in London in 1916. Reid had earlier written The Bracknels and Following Darkness. A line from Donne stands at the front as a motto. Chapter heads name Grif, Pouncer, and Inspector Dorset. Later heads speak of danger, fire, and a glittering net.

The story opens on a train in June heat and bright sun. Griffith Weston rides with Barbara, Ann, and Jim, plus Miss Johnson. Pouncer hides under the seat. Grif is a quiet, keen boy with a grave, sweet face. The sisters and brother glow by contrast. From this bright start, the tale moves through music, questions, and dark turns at home.
76358-they-return-at-evening:
They Return at Evening is a book of ghost tales by Wakefield, first out in nineteen twenty-eight. Past ten tales fill it, from That Dieth Not to An Echo. One tale is set past a golf hole of a town of the north. One treats a red lodge and one a third coach. A plate heads the book.

Its first tale opens past a man glad that a dread hour is past. He had looked for a trial of soul and found near a farce. As a town man of mark he won soft words and the best of care past the law man at the death probe of his wife. She was found dead at the foot of the steps to the plot. He turns, past that close, to the thought that he is a slay man him self, safe past a sharp chain of chance.
76400-evelyn-manwaring:
Evelyn Manwaring, a tale of Hampton Court Palace by Greville Chester and published in 1883, follows a young woman into palace life. Chester had won praise for tales of Norfolk lad life and of a cathedral close. Chapter one brings Evelyn to the palace on her arrival. A good Samaritan, a manor called Holmcastle, and its squire enter in quick order.

The Manwaring family tree stands at the heart of the plot in the heads. A fall, a blasted life, and a branch lopped from that tree darken the tale. Exile for Wilfred, a duke letter, and a tree re grafted promise turns of fate. Chapters set at Hampton Court bring in its aunts, its mock court, and a duchess in full state. Family pride, disgrace, and repair drive the story to its close.
76449-professor-tim-paul-twyning:
George Shiels wrote two Irish comedies in three acts, Professor Tim and Paul Twyning, issued by Macmillan in London in 1927. Professor Tim first ran at the Abbey Theatre in Dublin on September 14, 1925. Sara Allgood and Barry Fitzgerald were in that first cast, in parts they would make their own.

The play is set in farmer John Scally's kitchen and in a rival farmer's dining room, all in one day. Scally's wife's brother is the glib Professor Tim, and a rural councillor named Kilroy and his son cross the Scallys at each turn. An auctioneer, a groom, and a housekeeper round out the cast. Farm pride, land hunger, and match making drive the laughs.
76632-a-vocabulary-of-criminal-slang:
A Vocabulary of Criminal Slang, by Louis Jackson, defines underworld speech for officers. Jackson held the rights in 1914 at Portland, Oregon, priced one dollar fifty. Hellyer of the city detective department helped him compile the word list. The book is dedicated to the sheriff of Multnomah County, Oregon, in honor.

Publicity, Jackson argues, is the fastest solvent of criminal cant and guile. Slang of twenty five years back is nearly dead today, he notes. When judges, press, and police know the terms, crooks lose their cover tongue. Dope, now meaning news, began as a clipped form of opium, he shows. Plain officers and lawyers are the readers the glossary serves.
76688-fundamentals-of-fiction-writing:
Fundamentals of Fiction Writing is a craft book by Arthur Sullivant Hoffman, an editor by trade. Bobbs Merrill published it at Indianapolis with rights dated nineteen twenty two. Sixteen chapters and an appendix on manuscripts and editors make up the volume. Hoffman dedicates it to James Gannon, whose teamwork let him test his rules.

The first chapter argues that sound work rests on simple, first step thinking. Men slight the basics as beneath them, he says, and so build unsound work. Chapters then treat the illusion of fiction, readers, clearness, and overstrain of effect. Convincingness, holding the reader, and pleasing the reader follow in the scheme. Plot and structure, character, and the place of action close the main course. Style must fit its matter, the last chapter insists to the learner.
76703-sing-song:
Sing-Song is a book of cradle rhymes by Christina Rossetti. It was put out at London and New York in eighteen ninety three. One mint and twenty plates by Arthur Hughes stand in the book. Two kin hands cut those plates in wood. The list of parts is a long roll of short first lines.

Those lines give the span of the book at a glance. A babe's bed with no babe in it starts the roll. A town plum that is not a plum, a gem or a coal, and a brisk lamb come next. A house of cards, a small bird in a gilt cage, and all the bells in ring fill the first page of the list.
76785-cro-knitting:
Bernhard Ulmann and Company of New York published a pattern book on cro knitting, copyrighted in 1914 and priced at twenty five cents. The front pages advertise materials for crochet and macramé work. Bucilla crochet cotton is praised as smooth, highly mercerized, and fit for laces, center pieces, belts, and bed spreads. It came in white and ecru in fifteen sizes.

Bear macramé cord, heavier and hard twisted, serves for bags, portieres, and lamp shades. Glossilla thread imitates silk, and Klondyke thread is a soft metal thread in gold and silver tones. The book itself presents original designs for cro knitting and crocheted lattice work, with full working directions.
76801-an-atlas-of-gas-poisoning:
An Atlas of Gas Poisoning was issued by the Medical Research Committee in London in 1918, for official use only. The atlas reproduces drawings of the effects of poison gas on the body, prepared for doctors treating gassed soldiers. It was printed in a size uniform with the reports of the Chemical Warfare Medical Committee.

Those reports, listed here, treat the pathology and treatment of lung irritant gases month by month through 1918. Later numbers cover the blood, the heart, and fatal cases. The American Red Cross helped provide part of this issue for the American Army Medical Service. The atlas belongs to the grim medical literature of the First World War, when gas forced armies to learn a new kind of casualty care.
77242-the-way-the-world-is-going:
A book of forecasts by H G Wells, published at Garden City in 1929. Doubleday, Doran issued the first edition. Its subtitle promises guesses and forecasts of the years ahead. The articles first ran in great weekly newspapers. Wells complains, in a prefatory note, about their mutilation. Editors cut paragraphs at the eleventh hour to fit space.

America treated the text better than London did, he allows. One magnificent cut removed his whole Sacco and Vanzetti article there. He restores his original wording here, cross-heads removed. Shouting across an intervener, he calls the method. The flavour of shouting in these pieces is deliberate. Wells surveys war, money, machines, and world order for Sunday readers.
77248-fan-s-silken-string:
Fan Silken String is a tale by Annette Lyster for Christian readers. The Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge issued it in London. Seven chapters carry the story from Ben Fairfax walking tour onward. Ben carries off his sister, wanders, and meets Pearl in the early parts.

How Ben sin found him out forms the turn of the short tale. Fan spins a second silken thread in the last chapter of the book. Chapter one opens on a fine summer haymaking day in the Midlands. Men and maidens with forks and rakes cross a sunny farm field. Haymaking machines were rare then, so the old style sight still held.
77284-the-scrubtown-sewing-circle-s-than:
Maude L Hall wrote The Scrubtown Sewing Circle's Thanksgiving, subtitled An Old Ladies' Sociable. Dick and Fitzgerald published the short play in New York, with copyright in nineteen ten. The whole piece runs about thirty five minutes. The scene is a quiet country parlor in the village of Scrubtown, New Hampshire.

Six women carry the cast. Mrs Tattle, a widow, heads the society as president. Mary Ann Green, an old maid, serves as secretary. Granny Noddle is a deaf old lady, and Betsey Noddle is her granddaughter. Mrs Gossip hosts the meeting, and Percilla Primp is a new member. A costume list tells how each woman should dress, down to caps, mittens, spectacles, and a cane. Granny knits through the scene. Church and school groups get a brief comic sociable built for a small all female cast.
77319-the-sunlight-book-of-knitting-and-:
The Sunlight Book of Knitting and Crocheting is a pattern book edited by Adelaide Gray, copyrighted in Chicago in 1913. Its preface promises the latest novelties beside new ideas for articles of lasting style. Every step is made clear for beginners, it says, because the directions were written from actual work on each article.

The patterns cover a wide household list. There are bootees, afghans, hoods, and sacques for the baby. For girls come skirts and tasseled caps, for boys sweaters and sturdy mittens. Men get skating caps and sweaters, grandmothers shawls and slippers. Opera capes and motor jackets fill out the fancy work. Pictures and directions go together throughout.
77357-testing:
Testing, a science fiction story by Jacques Jean Ferrat, looks ahead to a war of starships and planet busting bombs. Echelon Leader Hannibal Pryor is its unwilling hero. His sponsor, Star Marshal Stefan Lopez, backed the losing side in a recent vote on Sirius Nine. Pryor pays for that defeat with a dull posting.

Instead of dropping the planet buster from the great battleship Erebus, Pryor must check Rigel Four, the planet picked for the test. His flying laboratory will circle it twice while machines do the work, then return to where half the inhabited worlds are gathering to watch. The head note adds that only the wisdom of the very old can stop a terrible war. Pryor chafes at the milk run and grows fat with nothing to do.
77396-hints-on-news-reporting:
Hints on News Reporting is a handbook by Murray Sheehan, printed at Girard, Kansas, in 1922 in the Ten Cent Pocket Series. It opens with the question: what is news? Sheehan quotes the ideal Daniel Defoe set down for his news-writing more than two hundred years earlier: to be explicit, easy, free, and very plain.

Despite its age, the advice could hardly be bettered for a newspaper man of today. What the modern reader wants is a detailed account of some happening, in a style that can be read rapidly and understood throughout. Defoe's own Robinson Crusoe shows the style: a child of seven can follow it, and grown-ups delight in it. News for one buyer may be dress-goods prices, while another wants columns of society names and the clothes they wore. The hints teach the reporter to find and write the news plainly.
77410-a-dictionary-of-the-art-of-printin:
A Dictionary of the Art of Printing is a reference book on the printer's craft, set out word by word. It explains the terms, tools, and processes of the printing house of its day. The hosted text keeps the old long letter s exactly as printed. Old ligatures and letters from many alphabets appear in its tables, as a printing dictionary must show them.

Entries run from the parts of the press to the kinds of type, paper, and ink. Tables of alphabets and marks help the reader know each character by sight. Such dictionaries served apprentices and masters when printing was a hand trade of wood, metal, and muscle. This one preserves the language of the composing room before machines remade it. It stands as both a word book and a museum of the craft, fixing in print the printer's own terms for his art.
77554-coffee-merchandising:
William H Ukers, editor of The Tea and Coffee Trade Journal, wrote this handbook to the coffee business, printed by his journal's company at New York in 1924. Ukers had written All About Coffee and A Trip to Brazil. He gives the book to his co-workers on the journal. A near view of the berries of Coffea arabica fronts the plates.

A short history of coffee opens the book: early legends, persecutions, and the first printed notices. Coffee houses of London and Paris and the spread of planting round the world follow. Cultivation, preparation, and marketing fill the handbook's core, as the title promises. A late chapter sums up new science on coffee as a wholesome drink for most people, the servant, not the destroyer, of civilization.
77794-a-picture-of-stirling:
A Picture of Stirling is a small view book of the Scots town, issued in 1830. Eight views were drawn by Masson and cut in copper by John Gellatly. The words that go with them are by Robert Chambers, the author of The Picture of Scotland.

The first plate shows Stirling from the river Forth. The town stands on a rise near the river, thirty-five miles north-west of Edinburgh. About nine thousand people live there. Its trades are carpets, tartans, and cotton goods, and small ships can reach it by the Forth. Chambers says the place is prized less for trade than for its old stones. Its castle rock and its place in Scots history draw the tourist, and the views set both before him.
77925-booklet-making:
Booklet Making, by Henry Turner Bailey, is a school craft manual that treats the making of a small book as a problem in art teaching. Bailey edited The School Arts Book. The Prang Company published the manual in 1912.

Bailey argues that making a good booklet joins several school subjects and skills in one project. No other school work, he claims, gives pupils more pleasure or more solid training of hand and eye. Success, he warns, rests on forethought: the teacher must think the problem through to the end. The book sets out ten well-worn steps, from choosing the kind of booklet to the finished binding. In the primary grades a pamphlet of six or eight pages, sewn with a single thread, may be all that should be tried. A motto from De Vinne heads the work.
78013-arrian-on-coursing:
Arrian on Coursing renders the Cynegeticus from the Greek. Its author was the younger Xenophon, the title page states. A graduate of medicine translated it for Bohn in 1831. Annotations, classical and practical, stand with it. A sketch of the author's life is added.

An appendix treats the hunting dogs of antiquity. Two hundred fifty copies were printed, it notes. Literary amateurs of the leash get its dedication. The version does not aim at pleasing the mere literary man, it owns. No general welcome was hoped for it, it adds. The coursing public alone is its addressed audience throughout. The original was written for those same amateurs long ago, it says. One reader will shrug at it, the preface allows. Coursing is a sport not to his taste, it grants. Arrian gives greyhound men their classical charter in English.
78905-model-yachts-and-model-yacht-saili:
Model Yachts and Model Yacht Sailing, by James Walton, tells how to build and sail self acting models. Walton belonged to a Victoria model yacht club, named in his initials. Griffith and Farran published the book in London in eighteen eighty. Fifty eight engravings show hulls, sails, and gear in its pages.

Six chapters run from first principles to sailing and steering the finished yacht. Hull making, deck fittings, and rudders come before masts and standing gear. Sails and their setting get a chapter, then the art of the race itself. Tables list the waters in London where model yachts may be sailed. Results of real contests and regattas are printed at the end of the book. Walton argues a self acting yacht is as much under command as a crewed one.
78972-figure-piping:
Figure Piping: Its Methods and Its Uses, by F Russell, was published in London in nineteen oh three by Baker and Confectioner Limited. Russell was known as one of the most skilful and artistic pipers in the trade. His specimens at the Food and Cookery Exhibition had won judges' applause. The editor's preface commends his instructions as clear as his work is artistic.

The chapters proceed from outlines of birds to outlines of animals. Bas relief work, menus, and miscellaneous subjects follow. Russell explains that piping artists asked him for new subjects. He adds that figure piping had proved itself for two seasons against every rival form of decorative sugar work. The little book is a trade manual for confectioners who signed cakes with birds and beasts in icing.
78974-whalers-and-whaling:
Whalers and Whaling, by E Keble Chatterton, stands as number sixteen in the Nautilus Library of sea books. Philip Allan printed it in London, first in 1925 and again in the library dress in 1930. Twin library titles treat mysteries of the sea, sea wolves of the Mediterranean, and the loss of the Titanic.

Chatterton opens on the hunt for the North East and North West Passages. That desire drew the sailors of northern Europe toward the Arctic seas in all sorts of ships, though with long lulls. Whaling grew out of those ice voyages, as men learned the wealth of the great fish. The book then traces the whale fishery ports, ships, and crews across the centuries. Sea fans get the whale trade told by a famed sea writer.
79191-groping:
Groping is a short story by Helen Hull from The Seven Arts magazine. The tale ran in volume one, February 1917, across some nineteen pages. Cynthia and Mary share a small dormitory room late at night here. Mary braids her dark hair before the mirror in a scarlet robe. Cynthia leans by the wall in a gray kimono, watching her friend.

Mary asks whether Cynthia spoke truth about never kissing any man. Cynthia owns she thought kissing waited on being engaged to a man. Mary laughs and asks how a man would know she wished it. The room takes on the air of a midnight confessional between friends. Other girls had talked of love, then drifted off to their beds. Left alone, Cynthia opens by slow degrees from her shy reserve. She hopes Mary will tell more of love once in bed.
79249-memoir-of-the-life-of-thomas-young:
A Memoir of the Life of Thomas Young, with a catalogue of his works and essays, was issued in London by John and Arthur Arch in MDCCCXXXI. The memoir was drawn from short memoranda in Young own writing, by a friend of long acquaintance. The writer feels incompetent to give more than an imperfect sketch, he grants. Young was born at Milverton in Somersetshire on June thirteenth, seventeen seventy three.

He was the eldest of ten children of Mr Thomas Young, the memoir says. Young was distinguished in more departments of literature and science than any other individual of his age and country, it holds. He read the Rosetta Stone toward decipherment, proved the wave theory of light, and mastered many tongues. The catalogue of works fills the back. Science readers get a near contemporary life of a giant mind.
79250-waiting:
Helen R Hull wrote a story of a woman looking back over her life. Waiting ran in The Touchstone, Volume Eight, in February 1921. Anne Stephens, in her early forties, scans the path her life has climbed. Half a dozen scenes stand clear while the rest sinks from view.

A still winter day in her father's workshop leads the memories. Her mother bursts in, sharp as the cold air, to scold his idle making. Joy in making things is the only good joy, her father murmurs. Readers gain a quiet, deep tale of family love and its wounds.
79445-the-pentateuch-of-printing:
The Pentateuch of Printing is a history of printing by William Blades, issued at Chicago in 1891. McClurg published it with a memoir of Blades by Talbot Reed. Its five parts borrow the names of the Bible's first five books. Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy structure the craft's story. A chapter on Judges is added at the end. The frontispiece shows the earliest dated woodcut, of 1423.

Illustrations crowd the volume: clay tablets, stamped lamps, and playing cards. A facsimile from a block book and a scriptorium monk follow. Caxton portraits and specimens of his first type appear. Punch, matrix, and type case diagrams explain the printer's tools. Blades was himself a printer and the great historian of Caxton. The playful Bible frame carries a serious technical history.
79483-blunder-enlightening:
Blunder Enlightening is a novelette of tomorrow's frontier by Dave Dryfoos. Sam Sarno and his wife land on a world in the Altair system. A teaser says the beings there simply and flatly ignore man. Humans were braced for alien life that might be hostile or fearful. Flat disregard was the one stance no one had dreamed of at all.

Sarno trudges home over the rolling prairie of Altair 3 at sunset. He is tall, blond, and husky, yet he walks like an old man. A day spent ranging a native garden and a granite cliff has worn him. Strange, virgin ground hides unknown dangers behind each bush and stone. The tale asks what men do when aliens will not even notice them.
8114-personal-recollections-abridged-chi:
Charlotte Elizabeth, the evangelical writer, wrote Personal Recollections, here abridged chiefly in parts pertaining to political and other controversies prevalent in Great Britain at the time. Her letters trace childhood, youth, and early days: martyrs' prison and palace gardens, music and study, politics and Protestantism. Private journals and romance, loss of hearing, rural life, and ruinous customs such as tight-lacing. The abridgement keeps the controversial heart of the book.

Charlotte Elizabeth writes as a convert and campaigner, frank about her convictions and her quarrels. Her recollections give a vivid view of evangelical and political life in early Victorian Britain. For readers of women's autobiography and religious history, the volume offers a strong, opinionated, and very personal witness.
8131-the-misses-mallett-the-bridge-divid:
E. H. Young divided this novel into three books: Rose, Henrietta, and Rose and Henrietta, following two sisters whose lives a bridge divides. The opening paints a spring day on high land above a distant channel, with gorse, larch tassels, celandines, sheep and lambs, and hills veiled in blue. From that landscape, the story turns to the sisters' choices, marriages, and the distance that grows between them.

Young writes with lyrical attention to place and to women's inner lives, in the tradition of the English domestic novel. The bridge of the title stands for the separations, of temperament, marriage, and fate, that part even close sisters. For readers of early twentieth-century women's fiction, it is a beautifully observed and quietly moving book.
8147-the-man-who-would-be-king:
Rudyard Kipling's tale follows two British adventurers, Daniel Dravot and Peachey Carnehan, who set out to make themselves kings in Kafiristan, a remote land beyond Afghanistan. The narrator, a journalist, first meets them as vagabonds with a grand scheme, and later hears the end of it from a broken, half-mad survivor. The epigraph quotes the Law of their brotherhood: brother to a prince and fellow to a beggar, if he be found worthy.

Dravot does become a king, with army, law-courts, revenue, and policy complete, until pride and a forbidden marriage undo him. Kipling's story is a parable of empire and ambition, told with grim humour. It remains one of his most famous works, and a warning about the dream of ruling others.
8162-modern-painting:
George Moore wrote Modern Painting from chapters first published in The Speaker, gathered in the sequence originally intended. And dedicated the book to Sir William Eden, saying its subject had been the subject of nearly all their conversations. His contents cover Whistler, Chavannes, Millet, and Manet, the failure of the nineteenth century, and artistic education, among other topics. Moore writes as a novelist turned critic, with strong likes and dislikes.

The book argues for modern French painting against academic convention, in prose that is itself a performance. Moore's judgments can be fierce, but they are never dull. For readers of art criticism, it remains a vivid document of the moment when Impressionism and its successors were still fighting for acceptance.
8444-c-sar-or-nothing:
Pío Baroja's novel Cæsar or Nothing, translated from Spanish by Louis How, opens with a prologue and a first part set in Rome. Contents follow the Paris-Ventimiglia express, an extraordinary family, and Cæsar Moncada. They move on to people who pass close by, the Abbé Preciozi, and the little interests of people in a Roman hotel, before old palaces, old salons, and old ladies.

Baroja, a leading Spanish novelist of the Generation of 1898, writes of ambition and will, with a hero who would be Caesar or nothing. Readers get a novel of Rome and Spanish life, ironic and restless, in a translation that brought Baroja to English readers. It suits those tracing modern Spanish fiction beyond its better-known names.
8581-the-art-of-money-getting:
P. T. Barnum wrote The Art of Money Getting, or Golden Rules for Making Money. He opens with a claim about American opportunity. With land plentiful, he argues, a healthy person ready to take respectable work can earn a living. Because so many trades remain uncrowded, willingness alone can open a paying line of work.

Barnum, the showman, gives rules for getting and keeping money, with anecdotes from his own career. Readers get a classic of American self-help, shrewd and readable, from the age of the self-made man. The book's advice, work hard, advertise well, and avoid debt, still circulates in business writing today.
8866-wild-flowers-worth-knowing:
Asa Don Dickinson adapts Wild Flowers Worth Knowing from Neltje Blanchan's Nature's Garden, in a 1917 volume arranged by plant family. Water-plantain opens with broad-leaved arrow-head, arum follows with jack-in-the-pulpit and skunk cabbage, spiderwort with Virginia day-flower, and pickerel-weed with its namesake. The lily family runs long: American white hellebore, wild yellow, meadow, field, and Canada lilies, red, wood, flame, and Philadelphia lilies, yellow adder's tongue, Clintonia, and Solomon's seal in several forms.

Early wake-robin, purple trillium, and birth-root continue the catalogue, each flower described for recognition in the field. Dickinson's adaptation keeps Blanchan's friendly, non-technical voice, so beginners can name what they find on a walk. Nature lovers still use such books for their clear descriptions and seasonal guidance, and this volume preserves early twentieth-century wildflower knowledge in a compact, field-ready form.
8868-botchan-master-darling:
Kin-nosuke Natsume, known in English as Soseki, writes Botchan, translated here as Master Darling by Yasotaro Morri and revised by J. R. Kennedy in 1919. The translator's note admits no translation can equal, much less excel, the original. Judges excellence by how far it reproduces tone, colours, style, delicacy of sentiment, force of inert strength, and expressions native to Japanese. The ablest translator, Morri says, can do no more, and wanting more demands too much.

Botchan himself, a brash young Tokyo teacher sent to a provincial school, narrates eleven chapters of pranks, rivalries, and moral blundering with comic energy. The novel satirizes Meiji schooling and small-town pretension, and it became one of Japan's best-loved books. English readers get a lively, funny classic, and a first taste of Soseki's voice before his later, darker novels.
8877-geoffrey-strong:
Laura E. Richards writes Geoffrey Strong, author of Captain January, Melody, and Marie, dedicating the story affectionately to Richard Sullivan, kindest of uncles, friends, and critics. Contents move from the temple of Vesta and the young doctor, through garden fancies, mostly professional matters, letter-writing and hysterics, and information, to festivity, revelation, side lights, and over the way. Broken bones, convalescence, and recovery close the arc, with illustrations of a silent paddle, a young doctor glancing around, and a hand still on a hammock rope.

The young doctor hero, his patients, and the women around him carry a light, wholesome romance of professional life and country society. Richards writes with humour and warmth for young readers and their families. Geoffrey Strong is a pleasant, old-fashioned novel of medicine, manners, and growing up, and a good sample of an American children's author writing for a wider audience.
8886-a-rough-shaking:
George MacDonald tells A Rough Shaking through Clare Skymer, a boy first met in the opening chapter. How I Came to Know Clare Skymer, then seen with his parents, without his parents. In a new family and new home. What drew out his first smile, Clare and his brothers, Clare the defender, the black aunt. Clare on the farm follow, before he becomes a guardian of the poor, a vagabond, and a tramp with helpers and hosts along the way.

Baker's cart, beating the town, blacksmith and forge, Tommy reconnoitring and found out, treasure trove, and justifiable burglary carry Clare through a rough, picaresque youth. MacDonald uses the boy's shaking, by loss, poverty, and kindness, to teach endurance and faith without preaching at every turn. Readers who enjoy Victorian boys' stories with a moral heart will find Clare a memorable, stubbornly good hero.
897-the-rose-and-the-ring:
William Makepeace Thackeray wrote this fairy tale for children, opening with a prelude about a Christmas party abroad where no magic lantern could be found. The tale follows Prince Giglio and Princess Angelica, each given a magic gift, a rose and a ring, that makes its bearer beloved by all who see it.

Thackeray spins the gifts into a comedy of love, mistaken heirs, and court intrigue, with fairies, usurpers, and a touch of satire on royalty. His humour is warm and knowing, aimed at children and their parents alike. The book remains a beloved Victorian fairy tale, witty, tender, and gently moral.
9091-ester-ried-yet-speaking:
Pansy, the pen name of Isabella Alden, wrote this sequel to Ester Ried, her popular tale of a Christian home. The book asks what Ester's life and death still say to those left behind, and it follows her family and friends as they try to live by her example. Chapter titles ask plain questions about duty, fashion, and the home.

Scenes of parlors, schemes, and small trials carry a steady moral: faith should show in daily acts, not just in words. Pansy wrote for young readers and their mothers, in a warm, direct style. The book remains a sample of the Sunday-school novel that shaped many American homes in its day.
9096-weighed-and-wanting:
George MacDonald wrote this novel around Hester, a young woman shown at her piano in the frontispiece. Chapters follow bad weather, father, mother, and son, a magic lantern, and songs and singers. Hester and Amy, Vavasor, and Major Marvel move through concerts, failures, and a journey that tests them all.

The title points to a soul weighed and found wanting, then remade by love and truth. MacDonald blends domestic realism with moral depth, and his characters grow through small acts of courage. The novel rewards readers who enjoy Victorian tales where character grows through trial and grace.
9328-cleveland-past-and-present-its-repr:
Published in 1869, this history of Cleveland joins biographies of pioneer settlers and prominent citizens to a history of the city. Commerce, manufactures, ship building, railroads, telegraphy, schools, and churches all get historical sketches, with photographic views and portraits by E. Decker. The preface notes how often Cleveland's founding has been told.

Colonel Charles Whittlesey's early history closes with the War of 1812, and this volume carries the story forward. Pioneer gatherings, newspapers, and directories had kept the tale alive. The book remains a rich source for Ohio history, and for the growth of a lake city.
9508-stories-worth-rereading:
Stories Worth Rereading, printed in 1913, gathers short tales and true sketches chosen for young readers and home reading. The pieces stress honor, pluck, kindness, and faith, in plain, earnest prose. Titles include Their Word of Honor, The Strength of Clinton, Jack's Fidelity, and Honor Thy Father and Thy Mother. True tales sit beside fiction, from David Livingstone to a San Francisco quake scene.

Other pieces warn against drink, praise a mother's ring, and tell of mission work from India to China. A boy without a reference, a mite box drive, and a sleigh ride all teach the same code: keep your word and stand by others. A reader gets a wholesome, old-style story book, rich in moral tales meant to be read aloud and kept in mind.
9608-the-cords-of-vanity-a-comedy-of-shi:
James Branch Cabell wrote The Cords of Vanity, a comedy of shirking, in a revised and expanded edition with an introduction by Wilson Follett. Follett calls the book an act of reclamation and fresh creation, and jokes that he may be its only known buyer. Cabell, famed for ornate fantasy, here turns to a hero who dodges duty with wit. The subtitle names the game: vanity's cords bind a man who will not face life.

Chapters follow confidences, loves, and evasions, as the hero talks his way past each call to act. Cabell's prose stays rich and ironic, half jest and half moral tale. A reader gets an early Cabell comedy, clever and bittersweet, on the art of getting by without growing up.
973-howard-pyle-s-book-of-pirates-fictio:
Howard Pyle wrote and drew these tales of buccaneers and marooners of the Spanish Main, compiled by Merle Johnson with a foreword by the compiler. The Ghost of Captain Brand, With the Buccaneers, and other pieces mix fact, fiction, and fancy, as Pyle imagined the pirate world of the seventeenth century.

Pyle's pirates are bold, cruel, and romantic by turns, and his pictures fixed the pirate image for generations: striped shirts, cutlasses, and treasure maps. The book gathers his best pirate work in one volume, with Johnson's notes to guide the reader. It remains a classic for lovers of sea adventure and of Pyle's art.
a-book-for-the-young: Sarah French offers a small book of poems and pieces for young readers. Its contents range from an address to the young and a dying horse to a ghost story, an embarkation scene, and the execution of Montrose. The verses treat courage, loss, and moral choice in plain and earnest language. French presents the collection as a modest gift meant to guide and entertain its youthful audience.
a-century-of-wrong: Jan Christiaan Smuts presents the Boer case in this account of a century of wrong. Its chapters run from the Cape of Good Hope through the founding of Natal, the Orange Free State, and the South African Republic. Smuts then treats the conventions of 1881 and 1884 and what he calls capitalistic jingoism. With a preface by Stead, the book asks readers to hear the other side.
a-course-in-wood-turning: Archie Seldon Milton teaches wood turning in a practical course for students. The book covers lathe speed, methods of fastening stock, spiral turning, and the making of plates and bowls. Illustrations and plates guide the learner through each process step by step. Milton's course serves schools and workshops where turning is taught by hand.
a-final-reckoning:
A Final Reckoning is an 1887 adventure novel by G A Henty. Its hero is a young English lad who, after a rather stormy boyhood, emigrates to Australia to start again. There he finds employment as an officer in the mounted police, a job that puts him on the colony's rough frontier.

A few years of active work bring him many brushes with both Aboriginal people and bushrangers, and promotion to a captaincy. In the end he settles down to the peaceful life of a squatter, a sheep or cattle farmer on his own land. The novel is classic Henty: a boy's colonial career told as a chain of frontier tests, ending in earned respectability.
a-king-and-no-king: Francis Beaumont writes a king and no king, a Jacobean tragicomedy of love and power. Its cast includes Mardonius and Bessus, two captains, the queen mother Arane, her daughter Panthea, and Spaconia. The first scene opens with the captains discussing the king. Beaumont's play mixes court intrigue, passion, and wit.
a-life-of-st-john-for-the-young: George Ludington Weed writes a life of St. John for the young. The incidents of John's life come chiefly from the Gospels, Acts, Epistles, and Revelation. Weed notes that some traditions about John are in harmony with scripture and some are not. The book gives young readers a clear life of the beloved disciple.
a-life-s-morning:
George Gissing's novel A Life's Morning follows a brilliant young scholar whose strength fails under his own ambition. Wilfrid Athel wins a scholarship to Balliol College at Oxford and drives himself without rest. A breakdown sends him home before he turns twenty-three. His father hopes quiet country life will restore him.

At home Wilfrid meets Emily, a young woman of strong mind and small means, and their attachment grows. Beatrice Redwing, wealthy and assured, offers a very different future. Family pressure, pride, and money pull the lovers apart. Chapters move through renunciation, parted paths, and a final reckoning at mid-day. Gissing writes a sober love story about talent, class, and the cost of surrendering one's own judgment.
a-rough-shaking: George MacDonald follows Clare Skymer in this story, from how the narrator came to know him, through his parents, a new family, and a new home. The chapter titles trace Clare as defender, farm boy, guardian of the poor, vagabond, and tramp, past a baker's cart, a blacksmith's forge, treasure trove, and justifiable burglary. Workhouse, magistrate, and policeman await a boy whose rough shaking comes from a world harder than himself.
a-text-book-of-assaying: Cornelius Beringer, with J. J. Beringer, writes this textbook of assaying for the use of those connected with mines, revised in a ninth edition with diagrams and tables. The first part treats the object and sampling of assaying, dry and wet gravimetric methods, volumetric assays, weighing and measuring, reagents, formulae, and specific gravity. The second part turns to metals in turn, beginning with silver, gold, platinum, cyanides, and mercury.
a-text-book-of-the-history-of-painting: John Van Dyke writes this textbook of the history of painting as one of a series of concise, teachable histories of art for classroom use in schools and colleges. Limited time for art study dictates a condensed style and a scope held to the general features of art history. Archaeological disputes and aesthetic theories are left aside. The main facts, as the best authorities have settled them, are given, with a bibliography at the head of each chapter for readers who want particulars.
a-young-girl-s-wooing: Edward Payson Roe tells a young girl's wooing in this illustrated volume of 1884, opening with a crescent of a girl and Graydon Muir. The contents follow a parting, effort, achievement, the secret of beauty, rival girls, a meeting, and old ties broken. Promptings of Miss Wildmere's heart, strategy, perplexity, and a declaration of independence carry the story on. An illustration asks whether Graydon is so bent upon winning her, in a courtship of gossamer threads and enemies' plans.
actions-and-reactions-by-rudyard-kipling:
Actions and Reactions is Rudyard Kipling's 1909 collection of short stories, presented here in an edition under his full byline. By 1909 Kipling was among the most famous living English writers, the author of The Jungle Book, Just So Stories, and Kim. This collection belongs to his later work, when his stories grew denser and more oblique.

The tales range across the worlds Kipling made his own: England at home, the empire abroad, and machines and men under strain. As in the companion edition, each story's action carries its reaction with it, often in a following verse. The book preserves Kipling's mature storytelling at the point where his fame rested as much on these crafted tales as on his early successes.
an-essay-on-medi-val-economic-teaching: George O'Brien writes an essay on mediaeval economic teaching, dedicated to Michael Cronin and issued from University College, Dublin. The study traces how medieval thinkers treated wealth, trade, and just price. O'Brien's clear survey joins economic history to the moral thought of the Middle Ages. The past here still speaks to how we judge wealth.
an-introduction-to-the-study-of-browning: Arthur Symons guides new readers into the study of Browning, in a short book on a great poet of his own time, given to George Meredith, novelist and poet. Symons walks through Browning's voice poems, his hard style, and his force, in plain terms. The study helped a new set of readers find their way into a hard but rich poet, and it still reads well today.
ancient-town-planning: Francis Haverfield writes on ancient town-planning, published by Oxford University Press, with plans and illustrations. The study shows how Greek and Roman towns were laid out, with streets, walls, and public squares following order and purpose. Haverfield's book founded the modern study of ancient urban design. Plans and views help the reader see each town whole.
anthony-wilding:
Anthony Wilding is a 1910 historical romance by Rafael Sabatini, set during Monmouth's Rebellion in the West Country of seventeenth-century England. The Duke of Monmouth, the ill-fated claimant called King Monmouth in the story, tries to rally troops who will not obey him. Against that failing rising, the hero Anthony Wilding pursues a private quest of his own.

Wilding sets out to woo a bride who does not want him, and his courtship becomes tangled with the rebellion around it. Sabatini weaves the political and personal plots together until each changes the other. Wilding emerges from the adventure wiser than he began, in a romance that mixes battle, intrigue, and love in Sabatini's swashbuckling manner.
areopagitica-a-speech-for-the-liberty-of:
John Milton addressed this speech to the Parliament of England against the licensing of books. Parliament had ordered that nothing be printed without official approval first, and Milton answers that free printing is the condition of a free commonwealth. The epigraph from Euripides sets the claim: true liberty is when free-born men may speak freely to advise the public.

Milton argues that licensing came from the very machinery of censorship England had thrown off. It cannot stop falsehood without also stopping truth. A virtuous reader, he says, is made by grappling with books of all kinds, not by being kept from them. He asks what it profits a nation to kill the thought in the book as well as the man. The speech failed in its moment and became the classic defense of a free press.
as-we-were-saying:
Charles Dudley Warner collected these short essays from his newspaper column, the Drawer, and this text comes from the Backlog Edition of his complete writings of 1904. The contents list twenty-six pieces, beginning with a defence of the rose against the fashionable chrysanthemum. Warner's persona is the fireside talker, and the first essay sets the tone of genial combat.

The subjects are the small change of civilized life. Fashion gets several essays: the red bonnet, the Directoire gown, frocks and the stage, and the clothes of fiction. Women in Congress and shall women propose treat the woman question with period caution. Chew on the list and you find chewing gum, dinner-table talk, altruism, and the burden of Christmas. It is journalism written to be re-read, in paragraphs of a column's length.
back-to-billabong:
Mary Grant Bruce's Back to Billabong returns her young Australians from London school to the station life they love. The book opens at Lancaster Gate in London, where red-haired Wilfred refuses to draw a beastly old map again, to his teacher's exasperation.

Chapters follow playing truant, coming home, sailing orders, watch dogs, a strange taxi, and the welcome of Australia itself. At Billabong come colonial experiences, the home on the creek, the Cungee races, and Wally riding a race. Bruce writes with the affection for open spaces that Dorothea Mackellar's epigraph celebrates. Young readers who love Australian station stories will find Billabong waiting, brown and dear, as ever.
baddeck-and-that-sort-of-thing:
Charles Dudley Warner gathered these light sketches of a summer trip to Baddeck, on Cape Breton Island, and addressed the preface to his travelling companion, Joseph H. Twichell. Twichell taught him the name, showed him the map, and produced a missionary's letter promising trout and salmon in the Bras d'Or lakes. The missionary, Warner reports, was never found.

The journey the two men actually made was mostly imposed on them by the arrangements of provincial travel. They crossed Nova Scotia by coach, rail, and steamer toward a week's fishing that kept receding. Warner's preface lays down his rule: the book contains only what they saw, no library compilation. The comedy is in the gap between the expedition planned and the one fate delivered, told in his gentlest manner.
bat-wing:
Sax Rohmer published this detective novel in 1920, sending his sleuth Paul Harley of Chancery Lane into a country-house mystery steeped in obeah. A frontispiece shows a woman raising her arms so her shadow on the blind resembles a bat. Chapters promise a voodoo swamp, a vampire bat, the call of M'Kombo, and a night walker at Cray's Folly.

Colin Camber, a recluse with a secret, stands at the case's centre while Inspector Aylesbury of Market Hilton cross-examines and theorises. Madame, lately widowed, apologises for the absent Colonel at dinner and arranges cigars with him after. A Spanish cigarette, a Lee-Enfield, and the wing of a bat serve as clues. Rohmer mixes West Indian terror with the classic English murder puzzle, narrated by Harley's friend Knox.
botchan-master-darling:
Yasotaro Morri translated Botchan, a Japanese novel by Kin-nosuke Natsume, and J R Kennedy revised the English text in 1919. Natsume, who wrote as Soseki, made the hero a brash Tokyo youth sent to teach in a country school. The translator's note warns that much tone must be lost.

Botchan clashes at once with Red Shirt, Badger, and Clown, the staff room rogues he names on sight. A grasshopper row and a whoop-la affair stir the school against him. Plain speech and quick fists are his only tools. Kiyo, the old servant who adores him, frames the tale with love. Kennedy's text keeps the comedy brisk. English readers met modern Japan through a school satire still read there today.
britannica-1911-agriculture-crops-and-cr:
Crops and Cropping reports a loosening of old rotation rules. Early twentieth-century farmers crop more freely than their fathers. Formal rotation systems bind them less closely now. Science underlies that new freedom, the section argues. Experiment stations have taught plant-life's real requirements. Rothamsted is the greatest and oldest such station. Lawes founded it at Harpenden in 1843. He and Gilbert published about one hundred and thirty reports. Their plots grew single crops for decades running.

Findings fill the long technical section. Wheat grew fifty-seven years in succession on one plot. Manured and unmanured plots ran side by side. Legumes like clover leave soil richer in nitrogen. Hellriegel and Wilfarth explained that mystery in 1886. Grass plots under different manures vary kaleidoscopically, it says.
britannica-1911-aidan-king:
Aidan, king of the Scottish kingdom of Dalriada, who died in 606, receives a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of Gabran, an earlier king of Dalriada. When his kinsman King Conall died, Aidan succeeded him. St Columba himself crowned him at Iona, a sign of the island monastery's weight in his world.

Aidan refused to let his kingdom stay dependent on the Irish Dalriada across the sea. Independence at home did not bring safety abroad. He came into collision with his southern neighbours and led a large force against Aethelfrith, king of the Northumbrians. The Scots were defeated at a place called Daegsanstane, probably in Liddesdale. The entry points readers to Bede and to Adamnan's life of St Columba for the record of his reign.
britannica-1911-albert-i-german-king:
Albert I, German king and duke of Austria, who lived from about 1250 to 1308, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Eldest son of Rudolph I, founder of Habsburg greatness, he was invested with Austria and Styria in 1282. A year later his father left him their sole government, which he ran with marked success.

Rudolph could not secure the German throne for his son, and the princes chose Adolph of Nassau in 1291, fearing Albert's power. Albert recognised his rival, then took the field when princes turned against Adolph. Adolph fell at Gollheim near Worms in 1298, and Albert was elected at Frankfort. He secured Bohemia's crown for his son Rudolph in 1306, pressed claims on Thuringia, and was defeated at Lucka in 1307.
britannica-1911-albert-ii-german-king:
Albert II packed three crowns into a reign cut short by war. Born in August 1397 to Albert IV of Habsburg, he followed his father in Austria in 1404 and took up rule in 1411. Good counsel helped him clear out ills that had grown while he was a child. He was king of Hungary and of Bohemia, German king, and, as Albert V, duke of Austria.

Albert fought beside the German king Sigismund against the Hussites, then wed Sigismund's daughter and heiress Elizabeth in 1422. Sigismund named him as his heir. Hungary crowned him in January 1438; Bohemia's crown came six months later, though the land itself never fell into his hands. Frankfort picked him as German king that March, an honour he had not chased. He died at Langendorf in October 1439, defending Hungary from the Turks, a keen, warlike prince whose brief reign held much promise.
britannica-1911-alcinous-king:
Alcinous, a king in Greek legend, is noticed in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He ruled the fabulous Phaeacians on the island of Scheria, and he was the son of Nausithous and grandson of Poseidon, the sea god. His place in literature is fixed by one great act of hospitality. A storm cast Odysseus onto his island's shore.

The king's daughter Nausicaa relieved the shipwrecked hero, and Alcinous received and entertained him at court. Homer tells that story across books six to thirteen of the Odyssey. The gardens and palace of Alcinous were famous in antiquity, as were the wonderful ships of the Phaeacian sailors. Scheria was identified very early with Corcyra, where Alcinous was honoured as a hero. In the Argonaut legend his island home is called Drepane instead.
britannica-1911-amuck-running:
Despair, not madness, is the cause argued for running amuck. Jealousy at home or losses at play can leave a man weary of life, and the frenzy works, in effect, as the Malay form of suicide. Older opinion had blamed sudden insanity. The Malay term, more properly amok, names the fit itself: a man rushes out with a kris or other weapon and cuts at all he meets until he is killed.

In British lands the custom has died out, a quoted authority notes, since offenders dislike capture and a cold-blooded trial. The word may be Indian in origin, and Indian cases follow: a Rajput prince fell on Shah Jahan's court in 1634 and killed five officials. At Hyderabad, two envoys stabbed a prince and twenty-six attendants. Malabar's hired assassins end the survey.
britannica-1911-annealing-hardening-and-:
Annealing, Hardening and Tempering is a craft entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It explains heat work used to set the traits of a metal or a mix. Heat can make a stock soft and easy to bend or stretch. Heat can also fix a set grade of hardness in the piece.

The entry notes that some heat work shifts the stuff in a plain way. Crystals or fibres in the metal seem to sort into a new lay. Other heat work brings a true change in the stuff itself. Trapped gases in the grain drive that second kind of shift. The piece calls the shop worth of these steps past all doubt.
britannica-1911-anointing:
Anointing is set out in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica as the rub of oil, fat, or warm butter on a man or a thing. The rite is in use in all faiths and among all stocks of men. It serves two ends in the main. It can free a man from foul force and from sick force.

It can as well bring into a man a holy force from on high. The two ends are near kin, for to drive out the ill is oft to bring in the good. So the text starts with the use of the rite to make a thing holy. One stock is said to rub the fat of a slain man on the kin who live. Men of east Africa rub on the fat of a lion to gain heart.
britannica-1911-art-teaching:
