Art teaching is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry opens with a broad claim: each branch of the mind tends to outgrow its first limits. Teaching habits live long, above all in art, and new ideas push out the old only slowly. So art teaching as a whole is seldom level with the thought and work of the most advanced artists of the day.

The article then sets out the old school system as used in the chief art schools of Britain. Pupils drew from casts of old statues, first in outline and then in light and shade. They also made studies of the body's structure, learned perspective, and drew and painted from the living model. The entry links this training to the study of old sculpture more than to painting itself.
britannica-1911-ashburton-alexander-bari:
Alexander Baring, 1st Baron Ashburton (1774–1848), was an English politician and banker. He was the second son of Sir Francis Baring, founder of the house of Baring Brothers. Raised in his father's firm, he was sent to the United States on business. There he wed Anne, daughter of William Bingham of Philadelphia, and built wide links with American houses. On his father's death in 1810 he became head of the firm.

Baring sat in Parliament for Taunton, Callington, Thetford, and North Essex between 1806 and 1835. He judged politics as a man of business would. He fought the orders in council and the trade limits placed on the United States in 1812. He also spoke against the 1826 act to end small bank notes, and he was a firm foe of Reform.
britannica-1911-assaying:
Assaying is a trade article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the testing of ores for their worth. In its strict sense the word names the finding of how much gold or silver an ore or mixed metal holds. The article uses the term in a wider sense as well.

The piece sets out the main steps of the dry way of testing. Gold and silver ores are almost always tested by fire. First the prized metal is drawn into a button of lead, while the waste melts off as slag. Then the lead is burned away in a shallow dish, leaving a small button of pure metal to be weighed. The text also sets out a set weight, the assay ton. With that weight, each small grain found stands for one ounce to the ton.
britannica-1911-automatic-writing:
Automatic writing is writing performed without the agent's volition. Psychical researchers gave it that name. The writer may not know the words written. Some automatists know the word being written. Two or three words on either side register too. Clear perception of whole meaning is rare. Trance states can produce such writing. Hystero-epilepsy and morbid states can too. Normal wakefulness sometimes suffices, surprisingly.

Modern spiritualism made the phenomenon important historically. It appeared on a large scale about 1850. America was its first great stage. Numerous long writings purported spirit guidance then. Some were written in unknown tongues. Andrew Jackson Davis's Great Harmonia is notable. Charles Linton's Healing of the Nations followed. England's spiritualist newspapers filled with similar reports. Myers and Janet anchor the closing references. Podmore signs this psychical research survey.
britannica-1911-backnang:
Backnang is a German town in the kingdom of Württemberg, nineteen miles by rail north-east of Stuttgart, with 7,650 people in 1900. Its church dates from the 12th century and rewards a look, the entry says. History touched the town in 1325, when it was ceded to Württemberg by Baden.

Work defines the modern place: notable tanneries and leather factories, with woollen and cloth mills beside them. Nearby stands the Wilhelmsheim sanatorium for consumptives, patients with lung disease, set in the country outside town. Church, leather, cloth, and the sanatorium are the four facts this short entry gathers about Backnang.
britannica-1911-bagging:
Bagging is the cloth stuff used for making bags, and a textile entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces its fibres. The entry sends readers also to the heads of sacking and tarpaulin. The stuff was first made from Baltic hemp. In the early nineteenth century, Sunn hemp from India was used as well.

Modern needs call for many types of bagging, the entry notes. All kinds of fibres now serve the purpose. Most bagging is made today from yarns of the jute fibre. The cloth is woven in general with the plain weave. Its warp threads run in pairs in the common form. Large amounts of bag cloth are also made with single warp threads. A figure in the entry shows the weave used for both kinds.
britannica-1911-baking:
Baking is the action of the verb to bake. Forms of the word run through Teutonic languages. German backen is one such cousin form. Old English and Norse carry related forms too. Baking means cooking by dry heat. Bread making is its primary application. Loaves and cakes take their texture from it.

The term also covers firing by heat. Pottery hardens by that dry process. Earthenware takes the same name in workshops. Bricks are baked in kilns likewise. Moisture leaves the clay as heat rises. Hardness and lasting shape come from that change. The short entry points elsewhere for detail. Bread, ceramics, and brick articles carry fuller accounts. Dry heat is the single thread through all uses.
britannica-1911-baring:
Baring is the name of a family of English financiers and bankers. The firm of Baring Brothers was founded by Francis Baring (1740–1810). His father John, son of a Lutheran minister at Bremen, came from Germany to England. He set up a cloth manufactory near Exeter. Francis was born there and trained in a London commercial house.

In 1770 Francis and his brother John opened a London banking house. By his death in 1810 Francis was counted the first merchant in Europe. He directed the East India Company for years, chaired it in 1792–1793, and sat in Parliament as a Whig. The 1911 Britannica entry traces the firm's passing to his sons, above all Alexander, Lord Ashburton, who spread its work across America.
britannica-1911-barking:
Barking is a market town in Essex, England, on the river Roding near its junction with the Thames, eight miles east of the City of London by rail. Its urban district grew from 14,301 people in 1891 to 21,547 in 1901. The church of St Margaret is Norman with later perpendicular additions and holds many monuments.

Barking was famed for its nunnery, one of the oldest and richest in England. Erkenwald, bishop of London, founded it about 670. The Danes wrecked it, and King Edgar restored it in 970. Its abbess ranked as a baroness, and a turreted gateway survives. The 1911 Britannica entry adds the modern town: gas works at Beckton, rubber and chemical works, sewage works at Barking Creek, and a shipping trade.
britannica-1911-basilica-building:
Basilica, a word of Greek origin, is the subject of a very long architectural article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Strictly, a basilica was a large covered building near a city's business centre, arranged for merchants, litigants, and public business. In a looser sense the word covered audience halls, covered walks, riding schools, markets, and, in the age of Constantine, the great new buildings raised for Christian worship.

Form and history occupy most of the article. Drawing on Vitruvius and surviving remains, it sets out a normal plan: a columned hall with nave and aisles and clerestory lighting, the high windows above the aisle roofs. Rome's first basilica, the Porcia, dates from 184 BC, and the Basilica Julia and Trajan's Ulpia followed around the forum. Vaulted examples such as the Basilica of Maxentius close the Roman story, while provincial cities across the empire built basilicas of their own.
britannica-1911-battambang:
Battambang, also called Battambong and locally Phratabong, is the chief town of the north-western part of Cambodia, in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands in a rich plain on the river Sang Ke, which flows east into the Tonle Sap, the great lake of Cambodia. The town is a group of bamboo houses, but it has a walled ring of some past interest. Its people are about 5000, two-thirds Cambodian and the rest Chinese and Siamese.

Hands changed over the town by treaty. Siam took it when it overran Cambodia in the late 1700s, and France let Siam keep it when the frontier was fixed in 1867–1872. A treaty in 1893 barred Siamese armed forces there beyond police. In 1904 that deal was set aside. By a further treaty in March 1907 the district was at last ceded to the French, within whose protectorate of Cambodia it then lay.
britannica-1911-beheading:
Beheading, in the 1911 Britannica, is an execution entry on death by the axe or sword. Greeks and Romans both used it, and Xenophon says the Greeks held it a most honourable death. The Romans laid the head on a block in a pit, outside the walls for civil cases. Before death the man was tied to a stake and whipped with rods.

An axe served at first, then a sword, held the more honourable tool. William the Conqueror is said to have brought the custom to England, and Waltheof was its first victim in 1076. It was kept for offenders of high rank. The roll of the fallen runs from Archbishop Scrope in 1405 through Lady Jane Grey and Mary queen of Scots to Charles the First and, last of all, Lord Lovat in 1747.
britannica-1911-belvedere-building:
Belvedere, also written Belvidere, is Italian for “fair-view.” In building it names any structure placed high, in the top of a house or on raised ground, so as to command a fine prospect. The form changes with the builder’s fancy and the site.

A belvedere may be an angle turret, a cupola, or a loggia, an open gallery made for sitting and looking out. Sometimes the name covers the whole building that holds such a feature. The best-known case is the Belvedere gallery in the Vatican at Rome, home of the Apollo Belvidere, and the entry sends readers from this short note to the article on Greek art.
britannica-1911-bet-and-betting:
Bet and betting names the staking of money on a future event. The word may come from the French abeter, to instigate, kin to the English abet. The 1911 Britannica article says betting is as old as gambling itself. It began, it claims, with royal and noble gamblers in the East. It spread west and down through all classes. By the 19th century Britain needed laws to curb it.

Most betting, the article says, gathers around horse racing. Early backers often could not find anyone to take the other side. That gap created the professional bookmaker. He lays money against many horses and profits if he prices with care. The article then surveys turf practice, gaming law, and foreign systems. The French pari-mutuel pool, paying winners from a shared fund, closes the piece.
britannica-1911-billeting:
Billeting is the practice of lodging soldiers in private homes, with board provided. Troops on the march have always used village shelter and supplies, the 1911 Britannica article says. In England its history turns on protests against abuse of the system. Petitions under Elizabeth, James I, and Charles I led to the Petition of Right. That measure of 1628 declared forced billeting illegal. An act of 1679 repeated the ban.

James II still issued billeting orders in defiance of the law. The Bill of Rights listed such quartering among the kingdom's grievances. Once a standing army existed, legal rules for billeting had to be made. Later acts set rates, duties, and magistrates' roles in close detail. By 1911 barracks covered most needs, and billeting had shrunk to an emergency tool. The Army Act of 1909 kept it for Territorial forces in a national crisis.
britannica-1911-biltong: Biltong is a South African Dutch word for sun-dried strips of meat. The 1911 Britannica entry is a single line. It unpacks the word itself in a short bracket. Bil means buttock, and tong means tongue. The meat named is that of the antelope or the buffalo. It is cut into strips and dried in the sun. No curing method is given. No place or use is described beyond the word's roots.
britannica-1911-binturong:
Binturong, also called the bear-cat, is a mammal of southern Asia, with the scientific name Arctictis binturong. It is the single species of its genus in the civet family, the Viverridae. It ranges from Nepal through the Malay Peninsula to Sumatra and Java. Tufted ears set it apart from the rest of its family. So does its long, bushy tail, which can grip branches. That tail nearly equals the head and body in length, some 28 to 33 inches.

Its fur is long and coarse, dull black with a grey wash on the head and front legs. The 1911 Britannica entry calls it a night animal that lives in trees in the forest. It eats small vertebrates, worms, insects, and fruits. By nature it is said to be fierce in the wild. Taken young, though, it tames easily and turns gentle and playful. It is allied to the palm-civets, or paradoxures.
britannica-1911-birdsnesting:
Birdsnesting is the pursuit of collecting and preserving birds' eggs, with or without the nests. The 1911 Britannica article notes that wild birds' nests and eggs are now protected by law almost everywhere. Britain and the United States both guard them under local laws. Taking is allowed for science only, under special licence. Custom limits a collector to one egg from a nest. A nest itself should wait until the young have flown.

The article then gives the craft in practical detail. Each egg, unless hard-set, should be blown as soon as it is taken. A small drilled hole and a curved blow-pipe replace the old two-hole method. Cabinets keep eggs from light, which fades their delicate colours. A taken nest should be disinfected with hyposulphite of soda or insect powder. Handbooks by Newman, Kearton, and others close the how-to survey.
britannica-1911-bitterling:
Bitterling, in Latin Rhodeus amarus, is a little carp-like fish of central Europe. It belongs to the Cyprinid family. The 1911 Britannica entry presents it as a remarkable case of symbiosis, two species living to each other's gain. In the breeding season the female's genital papilla grows into a long tube, nearly as long as the fish itself. That tube works as an egg-laying organ, an ovipositor, for a special task.

Through it the fish lays her few, large eggs inside pond mussels, between the mussel's gaping valves. There, once fertilized, they develop in safety for about a month. The fry then leave their host and swim free. The mussel repays the favour in its own way. It casts its embryos onto the parent fish, where they stay encysted in the skin a while. Both species breed at the same season, the entry notes.
britannica-1911-blasting:
Blasting is the breaking of rock by an explosive charge set in or against it, and the entry is a long technical account of the craft. The blast works by gas formed all at once at great heat and pressure, which splits the mass apart. Before explosives, rock was won by hammer and chisel or by fire-setting, heating the face and cooling it so it flaked.

Modern digging cannot do without blasting, in open cuts, quarries, tunnels, shafts, and mines. A hole is drilled for the charge, and its depth, width, and load all vary with the rock, the explosive, the shape of the mass, and any cracks present. Later sections work through charges, tamping, firing, and safety in detail for engineers and miners.
britannica-1911-bleaching:
Bleaching is the whitening of cloth and other goods. The entry is a very long industrial history and handbook. Sun, air, and damp do the same work slowly in nature. Washed linen left outdoors shows the change plainly. The trade art speeds that change up. It serves chiefly cotton, linen, silk, and wool. It also whitens paper pulp, beeswax, and some oils.

Almost nothing sure is known of ancient practice. Egypt was famed early for white linens all the same. English bleachers were called whitsters down to the late 1700s. The pages that follow trace old grassing and souring methods. They cover the coming of chemical agents. They set out the plant and steps used for each fibre. Dyers and mill men get a full working account.
britannica-1911-blood-letting:
Blood letting is the taking of blood to ease certain states of disease, as a 1911 Britannica medical entry explains. From three or four ounces up to thirty may be drawn in extreme need. The means are opening a vein, applying leeches, or the rarer use of cupping. In such states it can bring relief and save life when nothing else acts fast.

Past excess in its use for near every ill turned public feeling hard against it. The entry argues that swing of opinion has gone too far the other way. Vein opening needs a medical hand, and friends of the sick often resist it. Leeches meet far less prejudice from the public, the entry observes.
britannica-1911-body-snatching:
Body-Snatching is an article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It names the secret digging up of dead bodies from churchyards. The corpses were sold to anatomy schools for dissection. Those who did the work were often called resurrectionists or resurrection-men.

Before the Anatomy Act of 1832, no licence was needed to open an anatomy school. Yet no lawful supply of bodies existed for the students who needed them. Snatching a body was only a misdemeanour, fined or briefly punished. The trade paid well enough to draw many into the risk. The entry tells how common the crime became. Families watched fresh graves for days to guard them from the spade. Iron coffins were often used to keep the dead safe in the ground. Readers meet one of the grimmest trades of the age of surgery.
britannica-1911-book-collecting:
Book-collecting is defined as gathering books that hold lasting interest in their matter, their make, or the story of the single copy, and that are hard to get. Rarity matters, the entry insists, only when interest comes first. A rare book nobody wants is no prize, and a book anyone can buy at any moment gives no reason to collect.

That ease of buying often proves a false hope, so horn-books ended far rarer than First Folio Shakespeares. The long essay then ranges over the kinds of collecting, fine bindings, first editions, illustrated books, and famous sales. It weighs condition, completeness, and provenance, and warns the new collector where money and taste are most often wasted.
britannica-1911-book-keeping:
Book-keeping is the orderly written record of business dealings, kept so a firm can find, with the least trouble, both the details of each dealing and its total effect on standing. The entry calls it part science and part art, a thing grown rather than invented, still changing as trade changes.

The ideal system joins the fullest record with the least labour. Yet honesty must be guarded, so no system passes unless its record can be checked as true and complete. That check is an audit, done for big concerns by professional accountants. The huge article that follows sets out single and double entry, ledgers, journals, and day books, with the rules by which merchants of the time kept their accounts straight.
britannica-1911-bookbinding:
Bookbinding is the craft of covers that guard written or printed matter, and the entry follows those covers from the earliest writing materials. Assyrian clay tablets of about the 700s B.C., recording slave sales and loans, were often sealed inside an outer shell of the same shape with a short title impressed on it.

Egyptian papyrus rolls were tied with papyrus tape, sealed with Nile mud, and stored in hollowed wooden cases. Bark books folded like a concertina, and waxed wooden diptychs found at Pompeii, carry the story forward. The long technical history then runs through parchment codices, monastic binding, leather and gold tooling, cloth cases, and the machine binding of the modern book trade.
britannica-1911-bookselling:
Bookselling is traced here from the ancient world, where the trade began with poets reading their work aloud to sell copies. Hearers' words were taken down on the spot, and scribes supplied written copies to those rich enough to pay. The prophet Jeremiah dictating to Baruch is given as an early picture of the method.

Plato is said to have paid one hundred minae for three small treatises of Philolaus. The great Alexandrian library, founded about 300 B.C., spurred Athenian booksellers to hunt down stock. In late republican Rome a library became standard household furniture, and the librarii ran a flourishing trade. The history continues through manuscripts, the printing press, and the modern shop and catalogue trade.
britannica-1911-breeds-and-breeding:
Breeds are lasting kinds of farm animals and crop plants that people have shaped and kept going. Breeding covers every push people apply to a wild stock to fix such a kind. Charles Darwin and his 1868 book on variation under domestic life mark the start of exact study here, giving both the best store of facts and the first sound theory.

Early ties between people and tame stock grew from chance picking of wild kinds that bore life near humans and proved useful or pleasing. Over time the picking turned planned: each new crop or litter kept the animals or plants best fitted to human wants. Whether a breed holds depends on natural variation, on change under tame life, on traits lasting across births, and on human care in picking mates.
britannica-1911-bronzing:
Bronzing is a process that gives objects of metal, plaster, wood and other stuffs a surface like bronze. On metals a green bronze colour can be raised by the action of vinegar, dilute nitric acid and sal-ammoniac. New bronze pieces can be made to look antique by brushing the clean bright metal with a mix of sal-ammoniac and salt of sorrel in vinegar. Rubbing it dry, again and again as needed.

Other recipes follow: one with sal-ammoniac, cream of tartar, common salt and silver nitrate, and platinic chloride solution. Which can produce almost any colour on copper, iron, brass or new bronze according to dilution and the number of coats. Plaster and wood pieces are sized, then covered with bronze powder such as Dutch metal beaten to fine leaves and powdered.
britannica-1911-buck-carl-darling:
Carl Darling Buck (1866–) was an American philologist. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his career and books. He was born at Bucksport, Maine, on 2 October 1866. He graduated at Yale in 1886. He stayed there three years as a graduate student. He also studied at Athens and at Leipzig. In 1892 he joined the University of Chicago. He became professor of Sanskrit there. His chair also covered Indo-European comparative philology.

Buck's main work lay in a narrower field. He studied the Italic dialects of ancient Italy. His books treat the Oscan language in depth. They cover its vowels and its verb system. His Grammar of Oscan and Umbrian appeared in 1904. He also wrote a short account of the Italic languages. With W. G. Hale he prepared A Latin Grammar, in 1903. His journal work took up sound changes in language. One noted paper discussed Brugmann's Law.
britannica-1911-bull-fighting:
Bull fighting is the national sport of Spain, called tauromaquia there. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces the sport from ancient games. Bull combats were known in old Thessaly and in Roman arenas. Moors likely brought their own form into Andalusia long ago.

Moorish chiefs held fights in ruined Roman amphitheatres for sport. Christian knights took up the rivalry with keen pride. Kings of Castile joined the game on horseback with lances. Court custom kept the fight at every great feast for ages. Under the Bourbons the nobles slowly left the ring. Paid fighters on foot took their place by 1700. The first great sword killer came from Ronda in Andalusia. He set the sword still used for the kill today.
britannica-1911-cane-fencing:
Fighting with a walking stick is taught in a sport entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The French call the art canne, from their word for a cane. It works like single-stick fencing, but with no guard for the hand. The thrust counts as much as the cut in this art. That mix brings it close to sabre play in its moves.

Cuts match those of the single-stick, the entry sets out. Fast whirls of the light stick come before most cuts. Those whirls, called moulinets, aim to throw off a foe. Thrusts copy foil play but may use both hands for force. Two-hand thrusts let the cane strike home at close range. Masks, gloves, and padded gear guard the fencers in the schools.
britannica-1911-capito-wolfgang:
Wolfgang Capito (1478–1541) was a German reformer. His other names were Köpfel and Fabricius. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his career. He was born of humble parents at Hagenau in Alsace. He studied medicine, law and theology in turn. He took a doctorate in theology as well. He joined the Benedictines and taught at Freiburg. In 1515 he went to the cathedral church of Basel.

At Basel Capito met Zwingli and wrote to Luther. In 1519 he moved to Mainz, as chancellor to its archbishop. In 1523 he settled at Strassburg for good. From 1524 he led the reformed faith there. He attended the conferences of Zurich and Marburg. With Bucer he drafted the Confessio Tetrapolitana. He cared more for unity of spirit than for formulas. His work to bridge Lutherans and Zwinglians drew suspicion. He died at Strassburg in November 1541.
britannica-1911-carding:
Carding is the combing of textile fibres before spinning. The word comes from the Latin carduus, a thistle. This 1911 Britannica article describes the process and its tools. The practice is so ancient that its origin cannot be traced. Fibres are brushed until they lie straight and parallel. Imperfect fibres are separated from the perfect ones. All impurities are removed in the working. The sound fibres are then fit for further treatment.

Teasels were the first tools of the carding trade. Hand cards replaced them in time. The article describes the early “stock cards” in detail. They were wire brushes, 4 inches broad by 12 long. Their teeth were bent at a uniform angle. One card was nailed to a bench for the work. The other rode on a two-handled bar above it. The article follows the process into the age of machines.
britannica-1911-cards-playing:
Playing-cards are the subject of this long 1911 Britannica article. Their origin is obscure, as with all ancient pastimes. Many nations have been credited with the invention. The generally accepted view is that cards come from Asia. A Chinese dictionary of 1678 is cited in the article. It says cards were invented in the reign of Seun-ho, in 1120.

An Indian tradition claims cards from time immemorial. Very ancient round cards survive in museums there. Their invention is assigned to the Brahmans by that tradition. Egyptians and Arabs have also been given the credit. One ingenious theory links cards to the game of chess. It rests on many singular resemblances between the two. Sir William Jones argued that case in print. The article then asks how cards reached Europe. Even that time and manner are matters of dispute. A council canon of 1240 is often quoted.
britannica-1911-carving:
Carving is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a word that means, at root, to cut. The English verb comes from the Anglo-Saxon ceorfan. It links to a Greek word for writing or scratching. Apart from the kitchen sense of carving meat, the entry ties the word to sculpture. It explains how common speech divides the honour between two names in this field.

The name of sculptor is kept for the great masters of the art. It applies above all to work in stone and marble. The name of carver goes to those who cut the lesser decorations of architecture. The word also applies in a special way to work in ivory. Its substitutes count as well. So do wood and other soft materials. Cross references send readers to the articles on Sculpture, Ivory, and Wood Carving.
britannica-1911-carving-and-gilding:
Carving and Gilding is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on two allied operations in frame making. The craftsmen of the trade were known as “carvers and gilders.” That name stuck as the trade name for frame making. It holds even though little frame ornament is still carved by hand. Much so called gilt work now uses no gold at all.

The trade deals mainly with frames for pictures, engravings, and mirrors. It also handles light decorative fittings for houses. These are finished in “composition” and gilt work. Mouldings in standard sizes come from special factories in ready lengths. Much of the cheaper stock is made in Germany. A “German” moulding is a cheap copy of gilt work. It is made by lacquering white metallic foil. Costlier mouldings are made in oak or mahogany, or in veneers. The entry surveys a trade caught between hand craft and factory supply.
britannica-1911-castle-rising:
Castle Rising, a village in Norfolk, England, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies four miles by road north east of King's Lynn. The Norman castle that gives it fame stands on high ground above the marshy coast of the Wash. Earth banks and a dyke ring the site, crossed by an old bridge.

The keep is square, massive, and fairly whole, so its rooms can still be traced. Rich Norman carving marks the entrance, and a small chapel once stood outside the walls. The village church of Saint Laurence is late Norman with fine ornament. The entry then traces the manor from Archbishop Stigand and Odo of Bayeux to the Albini family, whose son built the castle.
britannica-1911-ceiling:
Ceiling is a term entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It explains the top cover of a church, a hall, or a room. Most ceilings of the day were made of plaster spread flat. Older ones were boarded, or showed bare beams and joists in view.

The entry notes carved beams in England and painted beams in France and Italy. Some ceilings lie flat, some slant on two sides, and some curve like a vault. Ribs laid on boards can split the field, with carved knobs at each cross. Rich plaster work with lace like trim marks the age of Queen Elizabeth. Named great houses are listed as homes of fine work of that kind.
britannica-1911-ch-ungk-ing:
Ch’ungk’ing is a city in the province of Szech’uen, China, and a gazetteer entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica stresses its trade. The city stands on the left bank of the Yangtsze river. It sits where the Kialing joins that great river. A crenelated stone wall, five miles round, surrounds it.

Nine gates pierce that wall of the city. Ch’ungk’ing is the trading centre not only of Szech’uen but of all south western China. The one highway into the province from the east is the Yangtsze route. Mountains make land travel between the regions near impossible. Large junks bring imports up the river from Ich’ang. Those goods are cotton cloth, yarn, metals, and foreign made wares. Smaller boats then spread the goods up the side rivers.
britannica-1911-chasing:
Chasing is the subject of a craft article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Chasing is the art of making figures and patterns on metal with steel tools and punches. The marks can be raised or sunk into the surface. Gold and silver work, plated goods, and like objects use it much. It can form bold grooves and bumps, or copy the look of engraving.

The article walks through the work step by step. The chaser first draws the pattern on the surface. Bold raised parts are blocked out from inside with a long iron tool held in a vise. A blow to the tool's end drives its tip against the metal. The piece is then filled with melted pitch and fixed on a sand bag. With hammer and many small punches, the worker brings out each detail of the design.
britannica-1911-cheating:
Cheating is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a criminal offence in English law. It quotes Stephen's Digest: cheating is the fraudulently obtaining of another's property by a deceitful practice not amounting to felony, where the practice may directly affect the public at large. The offence can rest on the common law or on statute. It is punishable as a misdemeanour. Indictments at common law are rare, since the statutory form usually appears as obtaining money by false pretences.

The entry then follows the word itself. “Cheat” is a variant of “escheat,” the reversion of land to a lord when a tenant's line failed. “Cheater” was first the shortened form of “escheator,” the officer of that process. By the sixteenth century the word had entered thieves' slang. Gamesters called themselves cheaters, borrowing the term, one writer says, from the lawyers.
britannica-1911-cheering:
Cheering is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on the making of sounds that encourage, stir, or welcome. The word “cheer” meant at first face or countenance. It came through Old French from the late Latin cara, head. From expression the sense moved to hospitality and entertainment, and so to food and drink: good cheer. The shout of encouragement came late. Defoe called it a sailor's word, and Johnson's dictionary lacks the sense.

The entry then sorts the cries themselves. “Hurrah,” the typical British cheer, has forms in German, Scandinavian, Russian, and French, and is likely an imitative sound. It was preceded in English by “huzza,” a sailor's cry tied to hoisting. The German hoch and the French vive are cries of acclamation rather than encouragement. The entry ends with American college yells, led by chosen students at athletic contests. It prints set cheers, down to the rhythm of stamping feet.
britannica-1911-cheh-kiang:
Cheh-Kiang is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an eastern province of China. Kiang su bounds it in the north, the sea in the east, and Fu kien in the south. Its area is about 36,000 square miles. Its people number 11,800,000. Apart from a slice of the great delta plain, the province is hilly throughout. The Nan shan ranges run through its centre.

The ranges divide the province into a northern part drained by the Tsien t'ang kiang and a southern part in the Ta chi basin. The valleys between them are numerous, fertile, and often of great beauty. The hills yield large supplies of tea. The coastal plain north of Ning po produces much silk. The province is poor in minerals, since its coal and iron are too scant to pay for mining. Cotton, rice, ground nuts, and wheat grow in abundance.
britannica-1911-chinkiang:
Chinkiang is a port article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Chinkiang, also called Chen-Kiang-fu, was a treaty port of China. It stood in the province of Kiang-su, on the Yangtze River above Shanghai. Rail lines tied it to both Shanghai and Nanking.

The entry explains why the place mattered for trade. The Grand Canal, running north and south, crossed the Yangtze at Chinkiang. That crossing made the town a natural hub for goods moving across China. The article gives the trade value for 1904 and a population estimate. A short war record follows: the town yielded to the British in 1842 after hard fighting. Taiping rebels laid it waste in 1853, and imperial forces retook it in 1858. The piece is brief but covers place, trade, and troubles in a few lines.
britannica-1911-clouting: Clouting is the technical name given to a light plain cloth used for covering butter and farmers' baskets, and for dish and pudding cloths. The same term is often given to light cloths of the nursery diaper pattern, the entry adds. Kitchen, dairy and nursery uses are all the short definition gives for the word. No weave, fibre, maker or place of manufacture is named for the cloth in this brief notice.
britannica-1911-cock-fighting:
Cock-fighting, also called cocking, is the sport of setting game-cocks to fight. Birds were bred and trained for that one end. The game-fowl stood close to the Indian jungle-fowl, the wild stock of all tame fowls. The sport was old in India, China and Persia. Greece took it up in the time of Themistocles.

The entry follows the sport across the Greek world and into Rome and Britain. It describes the chief forms of match. In the battle royal many birds fought until one lived. In the Welsh main, pairs fought in rounds until a last pair met. London pits stood at Westminster, Drury Lane and other spots. A king's cockmaster ran the royal pit at Whitehall. The entry also lists the sport's own books.
britannica-1911-conveyancing:
Conveyancing is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a branch of English law. It is the art of transferring property by written documents. It also covers changes to interests held in property. In early legal systems, transfer rested on possession itself. A public ceremony often marked that change of hands. Documents, where used, served merely to preserve evidence. They formed no essential part of the transfer itself.

In feudal Britain, freehold passed by feoffment with livery of seisin. The new holder was publicly invested with possession of the land. A symbolic act was performed on the land itself. Witnesses stood by to watch that act take place. A deed or charter of feoffment was usually drawn up too. That deed served by way of record of the act. The entry moves from that old practice toward modern law. It shows how writing slowly took over the transfer.
britannica-1911-coping:
Coping, in architecture, is the cap or cover that tops a wall. Stone, brick, tile, slate, metal, wood or thatch can all serve for it. In each case the top should be weathered, shaped to throw off the wet. Romanesque work kept it plain and flat. It jutted past the wall face, with a groove cut beneath to form a drip.

Later work gave the slope a steeper pitch, mainly on the outer side. An astragal bead marked the top in that style. The Decorated style used two or three steps of set-off. In late Perpendicular work the section turned wavy in form. Mouldings then ran round the sides as well as top and bottom. The cheapest kind caps a plain nine-inch brick wall. Brick on edge over two rows of tile, all set in cement, does that job well.
britannica-1911-corning:
Corning is a city in Steuben County, New York, on the Chemung river. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica places it in the south of the state, west of Elmira. Its people grew to near fourteen thousand by 1910. Three rail lines and a fine set of public buildings served the city.

Tobacco from farms around it made Corning a chief market in the state. Glass making led its factory work by far in that era. The Corning Glass Works ranked among the largest plants of its kind. Brick, tile, lumber, and rail car shops added other output. Settlers came in 1789, and city status came in 1890.
britannica-1911-crossing: Crossing is an architectural term for the intersection of the nave and the transept in a church. That crossing, the hosted entry states in its single sentence, is frequently crowned by a tower. Where no tower stands, a dome on pendentives may surmount it instead. The entry gives no examples, dates, or further detail. Its whole content is that one definition, naming the place, its two usual crowns, and nothing more.
britannica-1911-crystal-gazing:
Crystal-gazing, or scrying, is the winning of vision-like pictures by fixing the gaze on a clear deep surface, such as a crystal ball. Some gazers need no such aid and read the palm of the hand. Objects used across the world include ink pooled in the hand, water in a vessel, mirrors, quartz, and polished black stone. The entry lists users from Egypt and Polynesia to the Zulus and the Incas.

The practice served divination everywhere, to catch thieves, report far-off events, or foretell the future. A child was often chosen as the gazer. The early church condemned mirror-gazers, yet the art survived through the middle ages and past the Reformation. Dr Dee is its famous English case. Later pages weigh the psychology of the visions, citing Janet and Myers. The entry closes with an Arabian passage on the art from Ibn Khaldun.
britannica-1911-cupping: Cupping was an operation used by surgeons to draw blood from an inflamed part and so relieve it, described in a short entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The skin is washed and dried, and a glass cup is pressed on after the air inside it has been heated. As the air cools, a partial vacuum forms and blood is drawn to the skin under the cup. In moist cupping, small wounds are first made in the skin; in dry cupping it stays unbroken.
britannica-1911-curling:
Curling, a game played by throwing large rounded stones on ice toward a mark called the tee, is the subject of this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Where the game began is not precisely known. It has been popular in Scotland for at least three centuries. Some writers trace its name and terms to the Netherlands. Others link the word curl to a German word for a game.

The article weighs the Flemish theory with care. Flemish merchants settled in Scotland in the late sixteenth century and may have brought the game. Yet no early mention of it appears in the writing of the continent. Camden, describing the Orkney Islands in 1607, gives early British evidence. In parts of Lanarkshire and Ayrshire the game is called kuting. It much resembles quoits played on ice. Readers get a history of the game's names, terms, and disputed roots.
britannica-1911-custer-george-armstrong:
George Armstrong Custer, an American cavalry soldier who lived from 1839 to 1876, is sketched at length in the 1911 Britannica. Born in New Rumley, Ohio, he left West Point in 1861 and went at once to the war in Virginia. He served on the staffs of Kearny and McClellan, and his bold scouting won quick notice. In June 1863 he rose to brigadier general of volunteers.

Custer led the Michigan cavalry brigade at Gettysburg and served under Sheridan in 1864. He fought in the Wilderness and Shenandoah drives, at Cedar Creek, and in the last drive that ended the war. In 1866 he became lieutenant colonel of the Seventh Cavalry. He beat the Cheyenne at the Washita river in 1868. Sent to Dakota in 1873 against the Sioux, he ends the entry near the Little Big Horn in 1876.
britannica-1911-darjeeling:
Darjeeling is a hill station and district of British India in Bengal, 367 miles by rail north of Calcutta. The sanatorium held 16,924 people in 1901 and serves as the Bengal government's summer quarters. Its climate stays between 30 and 80 degrees, and its glory is the view of Kinchinjunga's white wall of snow. An earthquake in 1897 and landslips in 1899, which wrecked houses and the hill railway, mark its disasters.

The district covers 1164 square miles of lower Himalayas and plains, with Everest and Kinchinjunga both visible from the town. Its history runs from a sanatorium grant through the 1850 expedition against Sikkim to the 1866 addition of hill lands east of the Tista. Rivers, peaks and game fill out the gazetteer detail.
britannica-1911-darrang:
Darrang is a district of British India in Eastern Bengal and Assam, lying between the Bhutan and Daphla Hills and the Brahmaputra. Its headquarters are at Tezpur, and its area is 3418 square miles of mostly level plain. The district held 337,313 people in 1901, and rice is its principal grain crop. Tea has made the Tezpur side prosper, while Mangaldai's rice land filled up between 1880 and 1890 and its people now stand still or decline.

Tradition makes Darrang part of the realm of Bana Raja, beaten by Krishna near Tezpur. Koch kings held it in the sixteenth century, the Ahoms dominated after 1637, and a British expedition defeated its rajas in 1792. The district passed under British control with the rest of Assam in 1826.
britannica-1911-decolourizing:
Decolourizing is a chemistry article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In practical chemistry, decolourizing means stripping coloured impurities out of a substance. Makers of sugar and wine faced this problem every day. The entry names the agents that do the work and shows them in use.

The agent used most often is charcoal, best when prepared from blood. Shaken into a coloured liquid, it often drags the colour down with it. What is left behind runs clear. Filtering wine through charcoal can take out its red colour. The dark impurities that arise in sugar making yield to the same trick. Other decolourizers are named as well: sulphurous acid, permanganates, and manganates. All of them found work in the sugar industry. The piece is a short, useful note from the factory chemistry of its day.
britannica-1911-electrotyping:
Electrotyping is a technical article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It applies the art of electroplating to printing. In copying engraved plates for the press, copper can be laid down upon the first plate. That plate is first made slightly dirty with a weak wax mix, so the new shell will not stick fast.

The reversed plate so made is stripped off and used in its turn as the working face. Even the finest lines of the first work are faithfully brought back, the entry says. A bath of copper salts and acid is used, worked at a set strength of current. Tough copper of high quality is vital, it warns. Moulds for plates or art work are often taken in plaster or beeswax first.
britannica-1911-embalming:
Embalming is the art of preparing dead bodies, chiefly with drugs and spices, to keep them from rotting and from insect attack. The ancient Egyptians carried the art to great perfection. The entry rejects the idea that the practice grew from a lack of fuel for burning or from flooded burial soil.

The entry holds that embalming began in the wish to keep the body for a future life, a belief it compares with Peru and with Greek and Roman funeral rites. Set classes in Egypt were charged with the work. Herodotus is quoted for three Egyptian methods, the dearest costing a talent of silver. In that method the brain was drawn in part through the nostrils with a bent iron tool. The abdomen was then cleaned with palm wine and filled with myrrh, cassia, and other materials before the cut was sewn up.
britannica-1911-encaustic-painting:
Encaustic painting takes its name from the Greek for “burnt in,” and covers paintings made with vehicles in which wax is the chief ingredient. Ancient methods needed heat, which earned the term. Wax can be used without heat, yet the old name is kept for all wax painting.

Pliny's three kinds of encaustic are set out in turn. In the first, a stylus painted on ivory or polished wood soaked in a ground colour. In the second, ready wax colours in small sticks were spread with a spatula, a brazier standing by to heat the tools; the house painters of Herculaneum and Pompeii likely worked so. In the third, a brush laid on wax melted by heat, and the colours hardened fast. The entry adds that modern wax painting, such as Schnorr's work in the Munich Residenz, sits between oil and fresco in range and effect.
britannica-1911-epping:
Epping is a town article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Epping is a market town in Essex, England, north-east of London. It lies high, at the northern edge of Epping Forest. The entry gives its population and names its church and chief trades.

Much of the article belongs to the forest itself. Epping Forest is part of the ancient Waltham Forest, which once covered most of the county. The forest served as a royal hunting ground, and it was threatened with total clearing. An act of 1871 set up a board to guard what remained. The city of London then bought the freehold interest in the land. Back in the town, the article notes a brisk trade in butter, cheese, and sausages. The piece joins a small town's facts with the rescue of its famous woods.
britannica-1911-etching:
Etching, from the Dutch etsen, to eat, is a form of engraving in which acid eats the copper plate. In line engraving the burin ploughs the furrow instead. A plate is first coated with etching-ground, a mix that resists acid. The ground must cling to the copper yet yield cleanly to the etching point.

Abraham Bosse's ground melted 2 ounces of white wax with an ounce each of powdered gum-mastic and bitumen. Three ways of laying it are described. A heated plate can be rubbed with a silk-wrapped ball and evened with a dabber. A paste thinned with oil of lavender can be spread cold with a leather roller. A third way applies the ground in solution, as photographers apply collodion. The coated plate is then smoked black over a torch of twisted wax dips.
britannica-1911-fairy-ring:
Fairy Ring is a nature article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the dark green circles found on old grassland. Popular belief held that fairies danced in them at midnight. The article gives the plain cause: a fungus growing outward from a centre. Each year's crop of fungi rises from the new growth at the edge. The deep green comes from the decaying fungi, rich in nitrogen.

The article adds measured detail. The most even rings are made by the fairy ring champignon, though other fungi form rings too. One ring in a pine wood was watched for nine years and grew about eight inches a year. The fungus was never found inside the circle, because its food there was used up. The piece is a neat example of the edition explaining a folk marvel by patient observation.
britannica-1911-fang:
Fang is the name of a strong people of Africa, and the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out their land and look. They hold the Gabun district north of a great river in French Congo. Their name means men in their own tongue. They call themselves by more than one form of that name.

The entry draws them as a fine made stock of a deep warm hue. A few are far more dark, and those are said to be of slave stock. Their faces are bright and keen, of an oval form with high cheek bones. More than one of them files the teeth to points. The hair of the women is worn long, past the nape of the neck. The men shape theirs in more than one form, at times built up on a wood base. Cloth is scant. A chief wears a leopard skin.
britannica-1911-felling: Felling, an urban district in Durham, England, is the subject of a brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It forms an eastern suburb of Gateshead, in the Jarrow division. The entry gives it 22,467 people in 1901. Its large working population is employed in the coal mines nearby and in the various trades that serve them.
britannica-1911-fencing:
Fencing is the subject of a long article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The article takes fencing in its modern sense, not all sword use. It means skilled single combat under set rules and limits. Those limits, the text says, are part of what makes the play fine and exact.

The history is tied to the history of the private duel. The account starts near the mid fifteen hundreds. At that time the old trial by battle fell out of use. Armour also fell out of use, in war and in private fights. New skill in fence grew up to meet the needs of men bound by a code of honour. The first masters of the art often came from low ranks. Readers get both the roots and the rules of the sport.
britannica-1911-finishing:
Finishing, in the textile trades, names the last set of treatments given to cloth, and a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry explains the term in full. The entry covers bleached, dyed, or printed fabrics of every kind. Each treatment aims to give the cloth a set look on its surface. The treatment can also change how the cloth feels in the hand.

Some steps done before bleaching or dyeing sit outside the finisher trade, and the entry leaves those to other headings. It stresses how strong the change can be. One fabric can be made to look like a wholly different class of cloth. The same base cloth can yield quite different goods by the choice of finish alone.
britannica-1911-fitch-sir-joshua-girling:
Sir Joshua Girling Fitch, a school reformer, is followed in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Southwark in 1824, he came of a poor but bookish home. He began as a helper master in a Borough Road school. Night study and classes kept his own learning moving all the while. By 1850 he held a London degree, then a master's two years on.

Fitch rose to head a training college in the Borough Road. In 1863 the state made him an inspector for the York district. Set tasks on school boards took him across the whole field. In 1877 he moved to East Lambeth as inspector there. Chief inspector posts crowned his work till he retired in 1894. Few men knew English schooling so wide or so deep.
britannica-1911-flight-and-flying:
Flight and flying form the theme of a long 1911 Britannica entry on how living things take to the air. The urge to fly has drawn men for ages, the entry states at the start. Birds and beasts that fly enjoy a freedom that ground bound kinds lack. Yet the feat looks at first sight like a wild dream for man.

All flying creatures, however varied, fly by one and the same rule, the text argues. That shared rule means the air must be met in a set way to win lift. So the entry starts by close study of the shape of wings and bodies. It builds its case from nature before it turns to machines.
britannica-1911-foil-fencing:
Foil-fencing is the art of attack and defence with the fencing-foil. The word appears in several spellings in English writers of the later sixteenth century. At first it meant an imitation of a real weapon more than a weapon itself. Blunt practice swords have been used in all ages. Most were wooden and flat in form. When, late in the seventeenth century, cutting action with the small-sword was given up, foil blades were usually made of steel, round, three-cornered or four-sided in section.

The long article treats the foil as a school of arms in full. It works through grip, guard, footwork, thrusts and parries. Readers learn how the light practice weapon taught the moves of the real duel sword while blunting its danger. It is a practical manual as much as an encyclopedia entry.
britannica-1911-gaming-and-wagering:
Gaming and wagering are terms of close kin sense that are hard to part with care. The 1911 Britannica entry sets out the shades of each word in turn. A game may be any pastime or sport, lawful or not. Gaming now at all times means the stake of coin or its worth on the result of a game of pure chance, or of chance mixed with skill.

Gambling bears the same sense, with a hint that the stakes are too high or the habit base. A wager is coin risked on any chance event in which the man who lays it has no stake at risk but the sum laid down. Betting is kept for wagers on sport, and lottery for a draw of prizes by lot. At old common law, no games were banned as such.
britannica-1911-garretting: Garretting, more rightly galletting, is a term in architecture defined in a very brief 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. It names a process used in coarse masonry work. Small splinters of stone, called gallets, are inserted into the joints of the work. Their purpose is to protect the mortar joints. They are stuck in while the mortar is still wet. That single process, with its spelling note, is the whole substance of the entry as hosted.
britannica-1911-geelong:
Geelong is a seaport of Grant county in Victoria in Australia, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. It is situated on an extensive land locked arm of Port Phillip known as Corio Bay. It lies 45 miles by rail south west of Melbourne, the capital. Its count in 1901 was 12,399 for the city proper, and 23,311 with its adjacent boroughs.

Geelong slopes to the bay on the north and to the Barwon river on the south. Its position, and the shelter it obtains from the Bellarine hills, render it one of the healthiest towns in Victoria. As a manufacturing centre it is of considerable importance in the colony. The first woollen mill in the colony was established here in its early days. The tweeds, cloths, and other woollen fabrics of the town are noted throughout Australia.
britannica-1911-gilding:
Gilding, the art of laying gold over a surface for ornament, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Gold may be spread by hand work or by the use of chemicals. The art was known in the old world long ago. Herodotus tells that the Egyptians gilded both wood and metals.

Gold leaf work is also named more than once in the Old Testament. Pliny says the first gilding seen at Rome came after the fall of Carthage. The Romans then gilded the roofs of shrines and halls, the Capitol first of all. Soon the taste spread so fast that even poor and plain homes showed gilt work. The piece thus traces the craft from Egypt to Rome.
britannica-1911-ginseng:
Ginseng is the root of a plant kind, and the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out its source and its fame. The true root is a son of Manchuria and Korea. It is used in China as a drug of high rank. More than one root is sold in its stead by trade. The root of an American kin plant is the chief of those stand ins.

At one time the root from Manchuria was held the most fine of all. In the wake of that fame it grew so scarce that a ban from the throne said no man could dig it. The root made in Korea is now the most prized kind. The root of the wild plant is set past the root of the farm plant in worth. The old plant is held the best of all.
britannica-1911-godalming:
Godalming is a market town and borough in Surrey in England, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. It lies 34 miles south west of London by the London and South Western railway. Its count in 1901 was 8,748 souls in the town. It is beautifully situated on the right bank of the Wey. That river is navigable from there to the Thames for boats.

Steep hills, finely wooded, enclose the valley at Godalming on all sides. The chief public buildings are the church of Saints Peter and Paul, the town hall, and a technical institute. Charterhouse School, one of the principal public schools of England, stands half a mile north of the town. It was founded in 1611 in London and was transferred to Godalming in 1872. Its grounds cover 92 acres, with a chapel, library, and hall in Gothic style among its buildings.
britannica-1911-goldbeating:
Goldbeating is the art of hammering gold into leaf, and the 1911 Britannica entry stresses its great age. Homer refers to it, and Pliny states that one ounce of gold was beaten into 750 leaves, each about three inches square. Even those leaves, the entry notes, were three times as thick as the ordinary leaf gold of 1911.

The art probably began among the eastern nations, where gold working and gold ornaments are ancient marks of the culture. Egyptian mummy cases still carry original leaf. The article then follows the craft in detail: the tools, the skins the gold is beaten between, and the stages of thinning. It is a workshop account as much as a history. Note: this record's hosted file is a shared page chunk; the goldbeating entry stands complete within it.
britannica-1911-gong:
A gong is a sounding instrument of Chinese make, also called a tam-tam. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica shapes it as a broad thin disk with a deep rim. Gongs run from about 20 to 40 inches across. They are cast from bronze rich in tin. That mix, cooled slowly, turns out very brittle. Chinese craft turns that flaw to gain. They quench the hot casting in water to soften it.

Soft, the metal can be hammered and turned on a lathe. Heat and slow cooling then harden the finished gong. The alloy thus acts just opposite to steel. A hard pad of leather on a short stick beats the gong. The sound swells in waves of tone, now shrill, now deep. The craft stayed a Chinese secret for ages. A French chemist first cracked it in Europe.
britannica-1911-great-awakening:
Great Awakening names a marked revival of religion that centred in New England in 1740 to 1743. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it a history entry. The movement in fact covered all the American colonies in the decade to 1750. The word awakening in this sense was used by Jonathan Edwards at a revival at Northampton a few years before.

George Whitefield was the great driver of the wider movement. He, Gilbert Tennent, other clergy and many untrained laymen shared a style of preaching that was full of feeling and drama. They roused hearers to a pitch of excitement that often rose to frenzy. They laid great stress on bodily effects as proofs of conversion, and attacked clergy who would not join them as dead men. Edwards and others pushed back.
britannica-1911-hai-phong:
Hai Phong is a place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes a sea port in French Indochina, on a branch of the Red River delta. The town lies inland from the gulf and links by rail and river to Hanoi. It ranks as the second trade port of the French lands there.

The entry breaks its count of souls into local, Chinese, and European shares. Rice trade draws many of the Chinese to the port. Ship yards, a naval base, and courts and a bank mark its rank. River boats run from the town far up the river to hill towns. Cotton spinning and cement making are the chief works in town.
britannica-1911-hayne-robert-young:
Robert Young Hayne (1791–1839) was an American political leader. He was born in Colleton district, South Carolina, on 10 November 1791. Langdon Cheves' Charleston office trained him in law. He was admitted to the bar in 1812. The state legislature took him from 1814 to 1818. He spoke for the lower house in his last year. Attorney-general of the state followed until 1822.

The United States Senate received him in 1823. Free trade and states' rights were his twin causes. He fought the tariff bills of 1824 and 1828. Slavery, he insisted, was a domestic institution for states alone. His January 1830 debate with Daniel Webster made him immortal. Nullification was his doctrine in that debate. The constitution, he argued, was a compact between states. He later governed South Carolina and ran a railway. He died at Asheville in 1839.
britannica-1911-hearing:
Hearing, in physiology, is the function of the ear. It is the special sensation caused by sonorous vibrations. Those vibrations excite the auditory nerves. The article sets anatomy aside to the ear article itself. Sound's physics likewise sits in its own article. What remains is transmission and sensation. How do vibrations travel from outer ear to nerve? What are the characters of auditory sensation itself?

The external ear comes first in the analysis. The pinna collects waves and reflects them into the canal. Filling its hollows with wax weakens and misdirects sound. Canal and drum transmit the vibrations onward. Middle-ear ossicles and inner-ear fluids follow in sequence. Pitch, loudness and timbre are analysed as sensations. Direction judgement gets careful experimental treatment. McKendrick's very long survey ends with binaural direction of complex tones. Silvanus Thompson's similar view closes the discussion.
britannica-1911-herring:
Herring, in the 1911 Britannica, is a fish entry on the most prized food fish of its genus. The herring belongs to Clupea, a genus of more than sixty species round the globe. Sprat, pilchard, and shad are its kin. No sea fish genus matches Clupea for sheer counts, and no species matches the herring for worth in trade.

The herring teems in the North Sea and the north Atlantic. Old belief held that it came down each year from Arctic seas to spawn. That view is now held wrong: the fish lives by the coasts all year, in deeper water till spawning time. Marks that tell it from its kin are fine teeth on the palate and smooth gill covers. Its spawn sticks fast to gravel in shallow water, and spring and autumn races are set apart.
britannica-1911-hibbing:
Hibbing is a village of St Louis county, Minnesota, U.S.A., 75 m. N.W. of Duluth. Its people numbered 2,481 in 1900, 6,566 by the state census of 1905, and 8,832 in 1910. Of the 1905 count, 3,537 were foreign-born, Finns the largest group at 1,169, then Swedes, Canadians, Austrians and Norwegians. The Great Northern and the Duluth, Missabe and Northern railways serve it.

The village lies amid the great Mesabi iron-ore deposits of the state. In 1907 forty iron mines were at work within 10 m. of it. Lumbering and farming are also important trades. Hibbing owns and runs its own water-works and electric-lighting plant. It was settled in 1892 and incorporated in 1893, so its growth from camp to mining village took less than twenty years.
britannica-1911-hsuan-tsang:
Hsüan Tsang was the most eminent of the Chinese Buddhist pilgrims who travelled to India while their faith flourished there. They went to visit the sites hallowed by the life of Sakya Muni, to study in the great convents, and to gather books and relics. Their narratives throw great light on the geography and history of India in a dark period,

A longing to study Buddhist philosophy at its source grew irresistible in Hsüan Tsang. In August 629 he set out alone, slipping past the strict ban on crossing the frontier. He travelled through central Asia to India, studied in its monasteries for years, and turned home laden with books, images and relics. In April 645 he was received with public and imperial enthusiasm. The emperor T'ai-Tsung pressed him to write his journey down, the record that made his name immortal in the East.
britannica-1911-inverkeithing:
Inverkeithing is a royal town in Fifeshire in Scotland. Its count of folk in nineteen one was past one thousand six hundred. It sits on an in bay of the firth shore, north west of Edinburgh by rail past the great span. Its trades run to skin work, ship build, mills, paper, rope, and bricks.

With four near towns it sends one man to the law house. Its grant came from a king of old. Its church dates to the twelve hundreds but was built new past a fire, with its old tower kept. A fight near by in the past age saw a famed chief win.
britannica-1911-keel-moulding: Keel moulding, in architecture, is a round moulding that carries a small fillet along it, in a form somewhat like the keel of a ship. It is common in the Early English and Decorated styles of Gothic building. The entry is a single short notice, giving the name, the shape that earns the name, and the two styles in which the moulding is most often found. Nothing more is said of its placing, its making, or its history, and the record rests on those few facts alone.
britannica-1911-keng-tung:
Kēng Tūng is the largest of the Shan States in Burma. It lies almost wholly east of the Salween river and covers rather over 12,000 square miles. The Mekong river bounds it on the east and the Siamese Shan States on the south.

The Chinese know it as Mêng Kêng, and the Burmese called it the 32 cities of the Gôn. Its people were counted for the first time in 1901, giving 190,698. The Shans make up the bulk of that count, in several named branches, with hill tribes such as the Kaw beside them. Named Buddhists count 133,400 of the whole, and the rest are classed as animists, though spirit worship runs strong through all classes alike.
britannica-1911-kidnapping:
Kidnapping is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a crime in English law. The word joins a slang term for a child with a verb for to steal. At first it meant the theft of folk to work as forced hands in the American colonies. Blackstone is cited for a wider sense of the act.

The entry sets kidnapping next to false arrest and kindred crimes. In England the term was most used for the theft of a child from its parents. The Act of 1861 is quoted at length. It made the act a grave crime for a child under age fourteen. The term of penal servitude could run to seven years.
britannica-1911-kilwinning:
Kilwinning, a burgh in Ayrshire in Scotland, is described in a place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the Garnock river, south west of Glasgow, with two rail links. About four thousand people lived there at the count in the entry. Its chief sites are a library, a Masonic hall, and a district hospital.

Real fame rests on the ruined abbey at its heart. The abbey was founded about 1140 for monks of the Benedictine order. It was one of the richest houses in Scotland before its fall in 1561. Kilwinning is held to be the birthplace of Scottish freemasonry. Its lodge is called the mother lodge of Scotland. Work in the town came from iron, coal, and clay pits nearby. Eglinton Castle, seat of the earls of Eglinton, stands a mile away.
britannica-1911-kurseong: Kurseong, or Karsiang, is a health resort of northern India, in the Darjeeling district of Bengal. It stands 20 miles S. of Darjeeling, 4860 feet above sea-level, and held 4469 people in 1901. It has a station on the mountain railway and is a centre of the tea trade. It also holds boys' and girls' schools for Europeans and Eurasians.
britannica-1911-lai-yang:
Lai-yang is a city in the Chinese province of Shan-tung, at 37° N., 120° 55′ E., near the middle of the eastern peninsula. It stands on the highway running south from Chi-fu to Ting-tsu harbour. Well-kept walls of great antiquity surround it, and large pailous, or monumental arches, span its main streets. Some date from the time of the emperor Tai-ting-ti of the Yuan dynasty, in 1324.

There are extensive suburbs to the north and south, and the whole population is estimated at 50,000. The Ailanthus silk produced by the moth Saturnia cynthia is woven at Lai-yang into a strong fabric. The making of a peculiar wax, got from the insect of the la-shu or wax-tree, is also carried on widely in the neighbourhood.
britannica-1911-lansing:
Lansing, capital of Michigan, stands in Ingham county where the Grand and Cedar rivers meet, about 85 miles west-north-west of Detroit. Growth was fast in the count years: 16,485 people in 1900, then 31,229 by the 1910 census. Four rail lines and electric interurban cars serve the city.

On a plateau inside a bend of the Grand stands the State Capitol, built from 1873 to 1878 on a square of ten acres, with the state library inside. Factory districts lie across the river, and factory output more than doubled in worth between 1900 and 1904. East Lansing holds the State Agricultural College, opened in 1857 and described as the oldest of its kind in the country. The capital site was picked in 1847, when woods still covered it.
britannica-1911-lead-poisoning:
Lead poisoning, or plumbism, is called here a disease of trades. It can itself cause deep disease, above all of the nerves and the water system. The workers hit are chiefly those in potteries where lead glaze is used. Other trades at risk include file-making, house painting, glass-making, copper work, coach-making, plumbing, printing, and cutlery. In short, any trade that works with lead may harm its people.

The signs of chronic lead poisoning range very wide. They run from colic and blocked bowels up to loss of sight, loss of power, fits, and death. The article quotes Dr J. T. Arlidge on how the poison spreads. It creeps into the whole mass of the blood. Its force falls mainly on the nerves, and it dulls nerve force and muscle power with it. Those hit take on a pale, waxy hue, and their stomach and bowels fail.
britannica-1911-lighting:
Lighting, as held here, is a long trade account of how rooms and streets were lit by gas and by early electric plant. The hosted text opens mid-course, on petrol-air systems that keep vapour near two per cent. Gas work then takes the lead. England's light gauge was the sperm candle, six to the pound.

William Murdoch first burned coal gas at Redruth in 1779. Holes bored in a stopped tube gave the cockspur flame. By 1807 his gear lit a Manchester works. Burners, mantles, and measures fill the middle pages. Rules for safe electric work close the piece. London, American, German, and French codes all get a note. Fire risk, not brightness alone, drives those last pages.
britannica-1911-lightning: Lightning is the flash that goes with a burst of electric force in the sky. Drops merge inside a cloud. Each large drop holds its charge on a smaller skin. Charge thus climbs through the cloud. Near a hilltop, a tower, or a tree, the burst breaks out as a flash. The burst can run from earth to cloud. Rain drains charge to earth in quiet flow, and flashes often stop when rain sets in.
britannica-1911-line-engraving:
Line engraving, work on copper or steel plates, is explained in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In this method the line itself is cut hollow into the plate. A woodcut works the other way, leaving the black line raised. Only the white spaces of a woodcut are hollowed out.

The article holds that the art is as old as skilled craft itself. An Aztec hatchet shown to Humboldt counts as true engraving, if rude. The great step was learning how to print a cut line, a thing found by chance. In Europe the art grew from the chasing of goldsmiths at Florence. They filled their cut lines with a black enamel of silver, lead, and sulphur, called niello. To check a niello in progress, a smith took a cast of it in sulphur.
britannica-1911-ling:
Per Henrik Ling, a Swedish medical gymnastic practitioner who lived from 1776 to 1839, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Ljunga in the south of Sweden in 1776, he was the son of a minister. He studied divinity and took his degree in 1797 at university. He then went abroad for some years, first to Copenhagen, where he taught modern languages.

Pecuniary straits injured the health of Ling, and he suffered much from rheumatism abroad. He had acquired meanwhile considerable proficiency in gymnastics and fencing in those years. In 1804 he returned to Sweden and established himself as a teacher in these arts at Lund. In 1805 he was appointed fencing master to the university there. He found that his daily exercises had completely restored his bodily health by that time. His thoughts now turned toward applying this experience for the benefit of others.
britannica-1911-lung:
Lung is a body entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It names each of the pair of breath organs in man and in beasts that breathe air. The word comes from old tongues where the root meant light in weight. That old sense lives on in a trade word for the lungs of farm beasts.

Much of the entry deals with wounds and ills of the lung and its sack. A crushed chest can drive rib ends in and let air trap the lung. The entry tells what signs to watch for and what first aid can do. Pus trapped by the chest wall is named and its cause is given. The piece serves readers who need plain facts on grave chest harm.
britannica-1911-macleod-henry-dunning:
Henry Dunning Macleod, a Scottish economist who lived from 1821 to 1902, is profiled in a short life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Edinburgh, he studied at Eton, Edinburgh University, and Trinity College, Cambridge. He graduated in 1843, travelled in Europe, and was called to the English bar in 1849.

Macleod worked on poor law reform in Scotland and gave his life to the study of economics. His first big book, on the theory and practice of banking, came out in 1856. Works on political economy and a dictionary of the field followed in quick order. From 1868 to 1870 the state set him to sort and codify the law on bills of exchange. His chief gift to the field, the entry says, was his work on credit. He was the first to give credit its due weight.
britannica-1911-mafeking:
Mafeking, a town in the Cape in South Africa, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the open veld by the banks of the Upper Molopo river. In 1904 it held a little over two thousand seven hundred people. It serves as a trade and supply hub for Bechuanaland and the west Transvaal.

The town began as the chief station of the Barolong tribe. Its fame rests on the siege of the Anglo-Boer War. Baden-Powell held the town for two hundred and seventeen days till help came in May 1900. Word of the relief set off wild joy in London. That joy gave English a new word, mafficking, for the wild mirth of crowds. Gold fields lie a short way south of the town.
britannica-1911-manures-and-manuring:
Manures and Manuring is a farming article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about feeding the soil. The word first meant what was worked by hand, and slowly came to mean any soil improvement. Chief among these was spreading dung, the waste of farm animals mixed with litter. In time the term spread to other materials as well.

The opening shown here sets up the article's plan. Some manures come from the farm, some are imported, and some are made by industry. From this the article draws its two great classes: natural manures on one side and artificial manures on the other. The introduction fixes terms before the detailed treatment begins. For a farming reader of 1911 it marked the shift from dung alone to a whole trade in soil foods.
britannica-1911-mason-john-young:
John Young Mason is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Mason was an American political leader and diplomat, born in Virginia in 1799. He graduated from the university of North Carolina in 1816. He studied law at the famous Litchfield law school in Connecticut.

Admitted to practise in 1819, he rose fast in Virginia public life. He sat in the state house of delegates through the 1820s. He served in the state constitutional convention of 1829 and 1830. From 1831 to 1837 he sat in the national House of Representatives. There he chaired the committee on foreign affairs for a year. Under President Tyler he became secretary of the navy in 1844. He then served as attorney-general before returning to the navy post. The entry traces a Virginian who held two cabinet offices under two presidents.
britannica-1911-meeting:
Meeting is a plain word for folk who come together to talk or do business. The 1911 Britannica entry first traces the word to its old roots. It comes from an old English verb for to meet and join. Kindred words in Dutch, Swedish, and Gothic share that same root. The old noun moot meant an assembly of the people.

Public meetings fall into two broad kinds in law and use. Some are set by statute, with by laws that fix a quorum. A firm needs at least two folk for a valid meeting, one court held. Loose public meetings for social or public aims need no quorum. They may meet at any hour if the aim is lawful.
britannica-1911-mekong:
Mekong is the great river of Indo China, mapped in a 1911 Britannica entry on its long course. It ranks among the longest rivers in Asia and in the whole world. Its full length is about two thousand eight hundred miles. Much of it flows through China and Tibet, and the rest through French held land.

The source lies high in the Tibetan hills, though its exact spot was not fixed. Up high the stream runs south east past caravan roads at great height. Lower down it cuts through wild gorges with bare rock walls and few villages. Trade from north to south is near nil on that stretch, the entry notes.
britannica-1911-model-yachting:
Model-yachting is the sport of building and racing model yachts. Ship-builders have long made small copies of the ships they build. Each copy matches the great ship in each part, down to ropes, pulleys, and bits of the engine. A fine set of such models is kept in the Victoria and Albert Museum in London. In the case of sailing yachts, these models were often raced on small sheets of water. From that use the modern sport grew.

Men soon found that rich fittings and a complex rig slowed the handling of a model. Models also met winds that were strong for their size, so they needed a deeper draught. Modern racing models thus draw 15 to 20 per cent more water than full-size yachts. They most often have fin keels, and their rigging is cut to the bare needs of speed.
britannica-1911-monro-david-binning:
David Binning Monro, who lived from 1836 to 1905, was an English scholar of Homer. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his birth in Edinburgh.
