Three forebears in a row had held the anatomy chair there. Monro chose letters instead, at Glasgow and then at Oxford. In 1859 he won a fellowship. In 1882 he became provost of Oriel, and held it till his death.

Homer was his favourite study all his life. His Grammar of the Homeric Dialect made his name as an authority. He edited the last twelve books of the Odyssey with rich appendices. Those essays treat the poem's making and its ties to the Iliad. A critical text of the poems and fragments came in 1896. He also wrote on the modes of ancient Greek music. Wide gifts marked the man: tongues, music, painting, and building all drew him.
britannica-1911-morning:
Morning is a short 1911 Britannica article on the history of a common word. Morning means, strictly, the dawn of day or sunrise. In wider use it covers the early part of the day, from dawn up to midday. The word was formed on the same pattern as evening.

The text traces morning back through Middle English forms such as morwening and morwen. The old word morgen is the shared Teutonic word for the dawn. Its root may link to words for dark and murk. A more likely root means to twinkle or shine. The article also shows how morwen lost its last letter sound and became morrow. Word lovers get a neat case of how a daily term grew and changed shape over time.
britannica-1911-mourning: Mourning is a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica on the outward signs of grief for the dead. The word comes from an Old English verb meaning to be sorrowful. Across races and ages the signs have ranged from shaving the head and loud wailing to letting the hair grow. Among Western peoples the marks are now mostly black clothes and black-edged cards and note paper. The entry points readers to the article on funeral rites for more.
britannica-1911-mozley-james-bowling:
Mozley, James Bowling is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an English church scholar. He was born at Gainsborough in Lincolnshire on the fifteenth of September 1813 and died in 1878. He was schooled at Oriel College, Oxford, and won a fellowship at Magdalen in 1840. He took an active part in the Oxford movement.

Yet he could no more follow Newman into the Roman church, the article says, than fly. He helped edit the Christian Remembrancer, then left that post over his broad agreement with the Gorham decision. In 1856 he became vicar of Shoreham, in 1869 canon of Worcester, and in 1871 professor of divinity at Oxford. His books deal with predestination, with baptism, and with miracles. The last set began as the Bampton Lectures for 1865.
britannica-1911-multiplepoinding: Multiplepoinding is a short law entry in the 1911 Britannica. The word is a Scots law term for one kind of suit. That suit settles rival claims to one fund or good. The holder of the fund may bring the suit. A claimant may also bring it in the holder name. All who claim a share are called to appear in court. The court then ranks the claims by their rights. Once the holder pays as ruled, he is freed of claims.
britannica-1911-mustang: Mustang is the wild or half-wild horse of the American prairies, covered in a short entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. These horses descend from stock brought in by the Spaniards after the conquest in the sixteenth century. The word itself seems to come from two Spanish words, mestrenco or mostrenco, defined in 1599 as a strayer. The entry links the term to the mesta, a graziers' body that claimed wild cattle found among the herds, and gives the word's sense as wild, having no master.
britannica-1911-nanking:
Nanking, called the southern capital, is the chief city of Kiangsu province in China. A 1911 Britannica entry gives its people as about one hundred and forty thousand. It stands on the south bank of the Yangtsze river, midway between Canton and Peking. The city in its Ming form dates only from 1368, the entry stresses.

Yet a city stood on the site for more than two thousand years before that date. It bore the name Kin ling first, then Tan yang under the Han house. Tang emperors called it Kiang nan and Sheng Chow in their turn. The first Ming ruler made it his southern capital with a new proud name.
britannica-1911-nipissing:
Nipissing is a lake in Ontario, Canada, between Lake Huron and the Ottawa. Its lake entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It sits near midway on that route, with bold shores and many isles. The Sturgeon river feeds it from the north with its waters.

The lake runs fifty miles long and twenty miles broad at its widest. It drains by the French river into Lake Huron to the west. A low divide splits it from the Mattawa river and Ottawa flow. Planners eyed it as the top level of a canal to Georgian Bay. Rapids on both rivers made that canal plan hard to build. With near rivers it formed the old voyageur route to the lakes.
britannica-1911-norrkoping:
Norrkoping is a place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes a town and port in Sweden, on both banks of a swift river. The town lies where the river meets an inlet of the Baltic sea. Falls in the river give power to its mills and works.

The entry gives town counts for two census years and notes wide streets and new buildings. Fires and war left the town with a fresh, planned look. Cloth and cotton mills lead its trades, with paper, sugar, and ship work as well. A short history runs from a papal note of the town to fire and plague in hard years. German craft workers are named as the seed of its mill trade.
britannica-1911-nykjobing:
Nykjobing is a seaport of Denmark noted in a brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies in the county of Maribo, on the west shore of the island of Falster, ninety-four miles by rail south-west of Copenhagen. Its people numbered 7,345 in 1901.

Its church holds a family tree of the dukes of Mecklenburg, with portraits, of 1627 or earlier. The town keeps the house where Peter the Great of Russia lodged in 1716, restored in 1898. A rail line runs south to the ferry for Germany, on the fastest route from Copenhagen to Berlin. Two smaller Danish towns bear the same name.
britannica-1911-nykoping:
Nykoeping is a seaport of Sweden and chief town of the district of Soedermanland, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes the town and its castle. It lies at the head of the Byfjord, ninety-eight miles south-west of Stockholm, with 7,375 people in 1900. Its port exports iron and zinc ore, timber, wood-pulp, and oats.

The entry notes the ruins of its once famous castle, the town hall of 1662, and the governor's residence. The castle was the seat of the kings of Soedermanland and, after Stockholm and Kalmar, the strongest in Sweden. Kings died within its walls, and a future king was born there in 1622. Fire struck the town in 1665 and again in 1719.
britannica-1911-padding: Padding is a short trade entry in the 1911 Britannica. The term names the stiff fill used in garments. Hair cloth is the best and most supple stuff for it. That cloth costs too much for cheap dress use. Many kinds of fibre serve in its place instead. Hair, cotton, flax, tow, jute, and paper are all used. They are used alone or mixed with each other. The stuffs are first woven into fabrics as cloth. Starch is then laid on to give stiffness with bend.
britannica-1911-peking:
Peking is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on the capital of the Chinese Empire. It stands at the north end of a great river delta plain. For nine centuries it has been an imperial city in the main. Names and ruling houses changed, but its rank held firm.

Its spot near the north frontier suited Tatar invaders as a power base. In 986 Khitan Tatars took it and named it Nanking. Chinese forces won it back in the twelfth century and cut its rank. In 1151 the Kin Tatars made it a royal seat again. A century later it fell to Genghis Khan and his Mongols. Kublai Khan later rebuilt the town and named it Yenking.
britannica-1911-penang:
Penang is an island and town of the Straits Settlements crown colony. The 1911 Britannica entry gives its Malay name as Pulau Pinang. That name means Areca Nut Island in the tongue of the Malays. The isle lies a short way off the west coast of the Malay Peninsula. It runs some fifteen miles long and ten miles wide at most.

Its area is a bit more than 107 square miles in all. The town stands on a point of land nearest the mainland shore. Chinese and Tamil folk fill much of the town, with Malays too. Behind it Penang Hill rises to some 2,700 feet in height. Bungalows of state and of private folk crown that green height.
britannica-1911-pickering:
Pickering, a market town in Yorkshire, England, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica article. It lies north-east of York and is served by the North Eastern railway. Branch lines meet there. The town's urban district held just under three and a half thousand people in the census of 1901.

The church of St Peter is Norman in style, with later work added. Inside are wall paintings from the fifteenth century, called remarkable in the text. North of the town, a castle stands in ruin on a hill. Parts of the keep and towers still stand. Some of the work is Norman, but most is from the fourteenth century. One tower is linked in name and tale with Fair Rosamond. The piece also notes the castle was held by Earl Morcar before the Conquest.
britannica-1911-picketing:
Picketing is a practice used by workers in trade disputes, and this 1911 Britannica entry explains the term and the law around it in England. It means placing one or more men near an employer's works during a dispute. The aim is to draw off his hands or to gain news useful to their side. The entry then sets out the Act of 1875, which made it an offence to watch or beset a home or workplace to force a person to act against his rights.

That Act still left room for attending a place merely to get or give information. The Trades Disputes Act of 1906 then rewrote the rule. It declared such attendance lawful when done in peace. The aim had to be gaining or sharing news, or persuading others in peace to work or to stop work.
britannica-1911-pig-sticking:
Pig-sticking, or hog-hunting, is the chase of the wild boar on horseback with a spear. The chase on foot was common among old peoples. In central Europe it lasts to this day, though guns have made the spear a last-stroke tool. The modern sport grew out of bear-spearing in Bengal. When bears grew scarce early in the nineteenth century, wild pigs took their place as game.

British officers brought in the spear or lance as the weapon in India. Two kinds are used. The long underhand spear has a bamboo shaft of seven to eight feet and a small steel head. The short jobbing spear is heavier and gripped near the butt. It is easier in thick bush but lets the boar come near, at risk to man and horse. The season in north India runs from February to July.
britannica-1911-pigeon-flying:
Pigeon flying is the sport of racing homing pigeons bred and trained for speed. A 1911 Britannica entry calls it a new sport built on a very old art. Birds had carried messages since ancient times, yet racing for sport came late. Belgium is named as the true home of the race game.

Long distance racing began in 1818 with a match of one hundred miles. Races from Paris and London to Belgian lofts followed within a few years. Each Belgian village had its own pigeon club in the years described. The great national race flew some five hundred miles from Toulouse to Brussels each year.
britannica-1911-pigeon-shooting:
Pigeon-shooting is a sport in which men shoot at live pigeons set free from traps. The traps are six-sided boxes that fall flat open when a spring is let go. Five traps are the norm, set five yards apart on the arc of a circle. The shooter stands at the centre of that circle. The full distance is 31 yards, and a man's mark is set by a cut in that distance.

Wires link the five traps to a case called the puller. One string, pulled by a man at the shooter's side, works springs and wheels in the case. It lets one trap fall, and no one can know in advance which trap will spring. A line at a set distance marks the ground in which hit birds must fall to count.
britannica-1911-pinero-sir-arthur-wing:
Arthur Wing Pinero was an English writer of plays who was born in London in eighteen fifty-five. His father was a lawyer of a line long set in London. The son began as an actor at Edinburgh in eighteen seventy-four. He moved to London stages and stayed five years with one famed troupe.

His first hit play came in eighteen eighty. Gay farces then made his name in the mid part of that span, one run past a year. In time he turned to grave plays on love and fault. One such play drew wide talk and put him in the front rank. It was turned into three more tongues.
britannica-1911-pleading:
Pleading is the stating of facts in a court case. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica defines the term and traces Roman practice. In English law it covers papers made by each side in a suit. The word plea most often names the answer of an accused person.

All law systems ask claims and defenses to take a set form. In early Roman law the parties spoke their pleas aloud in court. A slip in the set words could lose the whole case. Later Roman practice used a written formula drawn by a judge. That paper summed up the facts in dispute for the decider. Claims, blocks, and replies each had their own named place. The entry shows form ruling law from its first ages.
britannica-1911-preaching:
Preaching is a long article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It defines preaching as the act of proclaiming a divine message. The message goes both to those who have not heard it and to believers who need teaching. The article treats preaching as a marked feature of the Christian faith.

Inside, the entry traces the history of Christian preaching through the ages. It roots the practice in the Hebrew prophets and in the work of Jesus and his apostles. A first main section covers the early church up to the death of Augustine. Names such as Tertullian, Cyprian, and Origen mark the growth of the sermon. Readers get a clear map of how spoken teaching shaped the church.
britannica-1911-profit-sharing:
Profit sharing is a method of paying labour that is defined with care here. Its concept entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Under the method, workers get a share of business profit plus base wages. The term is often used loosely for other forms of extra pay.

The entry draws sharp lines between profit sharing and close terms. Bonus on output, gain sharing, and pay by product do not count here. In those plans, worker pay does not turn on net business results. A free gift from an owner out of profit is also ruled out. A true plan must rest on a firm agreement, not on whim.
britannica-1911-ptomaine-poisoning: Ptomaine poisoning is a very short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The phrase had come into wide use for one class of food poisoning. The word ptomaine stems from a Greek term for a corpse. An Italian chemist, Selmi, coined it for the base stuffs that form as flesh rots. Those stuffs fall into more than one class of compounds. The entry gives no more of the tale, and sends the reader to the article on medical jurisprudence.
britannica-1911-reporting:
Reporting, the craft of putting speeches and events into readable form, is treated in a 1911 Britannica article. Its chief field is newspapers, with law and parliament reports as kin work. The craft is quite modern as a set trade, the piece stresses. Mere quoting and tale telling are as old as writing itself.

No true system of reporting stood before the start of the 1800s, the text shows. Reports of parliament at first just hinted at what was said. A magazine in Queen Anne's time made a start, and later the Gentleman's Magazine printed debate reports. Its men took notes in secret, since public reporting was banned. Doctor Johnson wrote up speeches for some years, with a bent to one party.
britannica-1911-riding:
Riding, the art of travel on the back of a beast, opens a long craft entry in the 1911 Britannica. The verb to ride first meant to travel or to go, the text says. Road comes from that same root as a word for a way. With no cart named, the word points to horse back travel. Men have used the horse for travel since the first ages of man.

Old finds in India, Persia, Assyria, and Egypt show tame horses in stone age days. Greeks and Romans rode with bridle and bit but with no stirrup at all. Poor roads once made horse back the chief way to travel for all. Steam and good roads have since made it more sport than need. Styles shift by use, from road work to hunt and race.
britannica-1911-rigging:
Rigging names the full gear by which wind drives a sailing ship. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica warns the word means far more than cordage alone. Spars, sails, and ropes all count as part of a ship clothing. Even davits that hold the boats fall under the term, it says.

Ships take their class names from their rig, like cutter or brig. A mast rig or yard rig names one part set by itself. Standing rigging holds the mast firm and is not hauled in use. Back stays and stays work as near fixtures in that scheme. Yards, gaffs, and stays each carry their own sails aloft.
britannica-1911-robert-the-strong:
Robert the Strong, who died in 866, was a count of Anjou and of Blois. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica says his birth and youth are a blank. One late writer names his father as Witichin. Robert rose fast among the Frankish nobles. By 852 he ran the abbey of Marmoutier. Soon he joined a revolt against Charles the Bald. That revolt called in the king's half brother.

Peace in 860 brought Robert back to favour. Charles made him count and set him to guard the land between Seine and Loire. That district had been ravaged by Normans and Bretons. Robert's hard fighting against them won his name and the king's trust. More counties, Nevers and Auxerre, came to him. He fell in battle at Brissarthe in October 866. His two sons both later wore the Frankish crown. That line leads on to the Capetian kings of France.
britannica-1911-rope-walking: Rope walking, the art of walking, dancing, and doing tricks on a rope or wire, is the subject of a brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The rope or wire is stretched between two supports, high or low. The art has been known and liked by most peoples of Asia and Europe since early times. A long pole or a Chinese umbrella often helps the walker keep balance.
britannica-1911-rowing:
Rowing is the act of driving a boat through water with oars. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica takes the word from the Old English rowan. The oldest records show oars at war and on voyages. Friendly trials of speed must have occurred in those days. Virgil paints one in the Aeneid. Yet no record shows rowing as sport in classic or medieval times. Boats and oars thus changed little for ages.

British tales are full of the oar. The old Britons paddled skin covered coracles on their rivers. Saxon and Norse invaders were expert oarsmen. King Edgar was once rowed in state on the Dee by eight kings. Bad roads made rivers the highways of the realm for centuries. Lords kept grand barges at their water gates on the Thames.
britannica-1911-sabre-fencing:
Sabre-fencing is a sport article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It defines its subject as the art of attack and defence with the sabre. The entry first sorts the blades used in the sport. Each kind has its own weight, shape, and circle of users.

Two main forms are described in detail. The military sword is broad and heavy, close in size to the regulation army sabre. Military teachers preferred it for that reason. The light sabre is nearly the same in shape but much lighter in the hand. Both have a slightly curved blade about 34 inches long. A guard on the handle shields the fencer's hand. The article serves readers who want the basic terms and tools of the fencing room set out plainly.
britannica-1911-shaft-sinking:
Shaft sinking is the subject of a mining article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Shaft sinking is a key task in mining for reaching mineral deposits deep below the surface. It serves where the ground shape does not allow tunnels or level drives. Shafts are also sunk for works such as railway tunnels. Varied forms of the task serve for deep bases of heavy buildings and bridge piers.

The article says sinking in solid rock with little water is fairly simple. Where much water or loose wet strata appear, special linings are needed. The work then turns slow and costly. Mine shafts are often very deep in rich districts abroad. Many upright shafts pass four thousand feet in depth. The deepest named was about fifty two hundred feet in 1907, then the deepest in the world.
britannica-1911-shoring:
Shoring is the craft of propping up buildings with short term supports. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica takes the word from shore, a prop. Crews shore a house before digging out a cellar beside it. They also shore when a wall sags or lower floors are rebuilt. Each job calls for its own form of shore. Most shores are heavy rough sawn timbers, braced hard. Steel parts serve for the heaviest loads.

The raking shore is the form in most wide use. Timbers slope from the wall face down to the ground. A stout sole plate spreads their feet so the soil is not cut. A wall plate fixed to the wall spreads the push at the top. Where room allows, a slope of sixty degrees is best. In tight town streets the slope must fit the room at hand.
britannica-1911-sigebert-king:
Sigebert is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a king of the Franks who died in 575. When his father Clotaire died in 561, the Frankish realm was split among four sons. Sigebert's share took in the Rhine and Meuse lands and much of the south.

The article tells of his royal marriage to Brunhilda, a princess of the Visigoths. Their wedding at Metz was marked by a poem from the Italian poet Fortunatus. War with his brother Chilperic broke out in 573 over a slain princess. Sigebert won the field and chased his brother to Tournai. At the height of his triumph, two hired killers struck him down at Vitry.
britannica-1911-simpson-sir-james-young:
Sir James Young Simpson, a Scots doctor who lived from 1811 to 1870, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Bathgate, he was the youngest of seven sons of a baker. He entered Edinburgh university at age fourteen to study arts. Two years later he turned to medicine and won his licence at nineteen. His thesis on death from inflammation so struck his teacher that he was made an assistant at once.

Simpson became a chair holder in medicine and midwifery at Edinburgh in 1840. Late in 1846 he saw a patient made senseless by ether for an operation in London. He put ether to use in childbirth at once, then sought a better agent. In March 1847 he read a paper on chloroform, the drug that made his name, to a medical society in Edinburgh.
britannica-1911-skating:
Skating is set out in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica as a way to move on ice with the aid of skates. A skate is bound to the sole of the shoe by straps, clamps, or screws. The word comes from a Dutch term for the tool. The first skates we know are bone runners kept in store houses.

Those bone runners were worn by the first men of the north and bound with thongs. The old tales of the north speak with pride of skill on ice. Growth of the art is owed in the main to the folk of the north and to the Dutch. In Britain the sport was wide by the twelve hundreds. An old tale of London from eleven eighty tells of young men at play on a frozen fen by the city walls.
britannica-1911-slang:
Slang is the name for words and senses that live outside the standard word stock of a tongue. A 1911 Britannica entry defines it as speech more or less made up or strained in use. Such words gain wide currency in one set of folk but lack full standing. They serve to hide secrets or to swap prim phrases for blunt, low ones.

Each trade and class keeps its own stock of such terms in daily use. The type that fits the sense best is the patter of vagrants and thieves. That jargon is part riddle and part joke, built to baffle outsiders who hear it. The entry notes the name slang now seldom points to that root stock.
britannica-1911-sling:
Sling is an old tool for casting stones, treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word also names a hanging loop that bears a hurt limb, from its like shape. As a weapon it may be the first device by which man stretched the force and range of his arm. Stones for slings have been found from the stone age.

The true sling is a strap or socket of hide with two cords. The slinger whirls it round his head and lets one cord fly, which sends the stone off. A staff sling, fixed to a short pole, threw heavier stones in sieges. The Bible praises the left-handed slingers of Benjamin. Assyrian carvings show slingers at work, and the men of the Balearic isles were famed for the art. Rome used such troops as hired aids in war.
britannica-1911-smuggling:
Smuggling is a breach of the revenue laws, and this 1911 Britannica entry defines it and reviews its history in England. The word comes from an old English verb meaning to creep, with a hint of secrecy. The offence covers bringing banned goods into or out of a country, and dodging customs duties on goods that owe them. English lawmaking on the subject ran steadily from the fourteenth century down.

Under Edward the Third, fake coin brought in from abroad was made treason under the Statute of Treasons of 1351. In the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries smuggling of wine, spirits, tobacco, and bullion was so common as to seem a national habit. As duties fell, the offence shrank in Britain and by 1911 clung mostly to tobacco.
britannica-1911-song:
Song means, first, an act of singing, and, in letters, a short poem made for singing. In that second sense it must in strict use be lyrical in nature. Musicians and others often use the word more widely for any short poem set to music. A song as a poem turns on one single thought or feeling. That thought is voiced in a set of stanzas by the singer.

Almost every nation holds a vast store of old, plain ballads, the entry says. Those folk songs spring from the people and show their tastes and hopes. Beside them stand the more finished works of the trained poet's art. A song in pure letters can stand with no music at all. With Elizabeth's reign, English poets turned at once to this branch of lyric work.
britannica-1911-sounding:
Sounding, the measuring of the depth of water, is explained in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The craft is old, long used for safe sailing at sea. It gained new weight once undersea telegraph cables made a full map of the ocean floor worth having. The word can also be used in a loose sense for testing the depth of anything.

In shallow water a weight on a marked cord, called a lead, does the job. The hollow base of the weight is filled with tallow to bring up a sample of the bottom. For deep water the article turns to sounding machines that use wire. Wire, brought in by Sir William Thomson, lets the weight drop fast and be hauled back at near the same speed. Such gear made deep soundings far more exact than before.
britannica-1911-spalding:
Spalding, a market town in Lincolnshire in England, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It sits on the river Welland and on two rail lines, 93 miles north of London. The count for the urban district in 1901 was 9385 people. The town served as the hub of a rich farm district.

Its parish church of St Mary and St Nicholas dates from 1284 and has four aisles to the nave. A grammar school was endowed in 1568 and a new one built in 1881. Trade rested chiefly on farm goods, with much traffic by water on the Welland. The account also traces the manor back past Domesday Book to Saxon times.
britannica-1911-speke-john-hanning:
John Hanning Speke, who lived from 1827 to 1864, was an English explorer known as the finder of the source of the Nile. The 1911 Britannica article says he was born on the fourth of May 1827 in Somersetshire. Through his mother he gained a post in the Indian Army in 1844. He served in the Punjab wars and won a name as a soldier, a sportsman, and a student of nature.

On leave, Speke roamed the Himalayas and crossed into Tibet to map its south-west parts. Africa drew him early. In 1854 he joined Richard Burton on a trek into Somaliland. Somalis attacked the party near Berbera, and Speke was badly wounded. After service in the Crimea, he sailed with Burton again in 1856. Their goal was the great lakes said to lie in east central Africa.
britannica-1911-spinning:
Spinning is the making of thread by drawing out and twisting fibres. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica takes the word from the Old English spinnan. The art is of great age and near universal spread. It must come before weaving wherever short fibres are used. For ages the tools of the craft barely changed. That stillness makes it the least progressive of old arts.

From the mid 1700s the story flips. Machines for spinning grew in variety and fineness past all rivals. The first tool was a simple wooden spindle, nine to fifteen inches long. A notch near its top caught the yarn while it twisted. A whorl of clay, stone, or wood gave it weight and steadiness. Long fibres were held on a distaff under the left arm. The entry works outward from that humble kit.
britannica-1911-stammering:
Stammering, or stuttering, is the subject of a medical entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is a spasmodic fault of the organs of speech, in which the forming of words is suddenly checked. A pause follows, often with a rapid repeat of the sound where the stop came. The entry notes grades from a slight hitch on some letters to severe attacks.

In the worst form, spasms grip the muscles of tongue, throat, and face, and even those of breath and body. To grasp the cause, the entry turns to how speech is made. Speech results from many muscle movements that shape air as it leaves the throat. If the vocal cords act, the sound is voiced speech. If the glottis is open, the same shaping makes a whisper. Both need a long chain of nerve and muscle acts in exact accord.
britannica-1911-starling:
Starling, a well known bird about the size of a thrush, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. At a distance it looks plain black in its plumage. Up close its feathers shine with shot tints of purple, green, and steel blue. Fresh grown feathers are tipped with buff at their ends.

Those markings wear off in the course of the winter months. In the breeding season the bird stands almost spotless in its gloss. Its Latin name in science is given as Sturnus vulgaris in the entry. A full account of its habits is held needless in this place, the text says. Few birds are more winning in their ways, it holds. Its closeness to man for months of the year lets folk watch its habits with ease. Varied song and glossy dress add to its charm.
britannica-1911-stevenson-adlai-ewing:
Adlai Ewing Stevenson (1835-), an American political leader, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in Kentucky in October 1835 and moved with his family to Bloomington in Illinois in 1852. He was schooled at two colleges and admitted to the Illinois bar in 1857. He held local legal posts in the years that followed.

The article tracks his national career. He sat in Congress as a Democrat in two spells, in the eighteen-seventies and after. As first assistant postmaster-general from 1885 to 1889 he drew sharp blame for sweeping out Republican postmasters in bulk. In 1892 he was elected vice-president of the United States on the ticket with Cleveland, and served from 1893 to 1897. He later sat on a commission sent abroad by President McKinley.
britannica-1911-steyning:
Steyning is a small market town in Sussex, England, covered in this 1911 Britannica article. It lay west-north-west of Brighton on the London, Brighton and South Coast line, and had 1,705 people in 1901. The church of St Andrew keeps a fine set of Norman arches in its nave, and some old houses still stand in the town.

The article then traces the town's past from an early church linked with St Cuthman, whose shrine drew pilgrims. Edward the Confessor gave Steyning to the abbey of Fécamp, and by 1086 it was a busy port with a market, a mint, and two churches. Its decline began in the 1300s as the sea drew back. It sent two members to parliament from 1298 until it lost that right in 1832.
britannica-1911-stirling:
Stirling is the subject of a town article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Stirling is a royal burgh, river port, and county town in Scotland. It stands on the right bank of the Forth, northwest of Edinburgh. Two railways serve the town. Its people numbered near nineteen thousand at the census given. The old town climbs the slopes of a rock hill that ends in a sheer cliff.

The article describes the old bridge over the Forth, a high arched work of four spans. It dates from the late thirteen hundreds and was once called the key to the Highlands. The castle crowns the hill above the town. From the death of a Scottish king within its walls in 1124 to the union of the crowns, the castle was bound up with the Scottish kings.
britannica-1911-swimming:
Swimming is set out in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica as the act of a man to hold himself up and drive himself on in the water. The word comes from an old tongue root shared by the north tongues. A Latin peer word names the same art. The art is held as one of the most good skills of the body for a man to gain.

Some new hands show a knack for the art at their first dip in deep water. In the main it is an art that must be learned by drill. For years Britain held the top place in this form of sport. That claim can no longer be kept, the text says.
britannica-1911-tattooing:
Tattooing is the craft of marks on the skin, made by cuts or pricks with dye set in them. The word comes from a far isle tongue, yet the craft was once near world wide. It tends to fade as town life spreads. A law of the Jews of old is held to ban such marks, yet the craft is still rife in the east.

Its root is in doubt, but fair looks to draw mates is one guess. Stones in old caves hint that the first men dyed their skin. Paint served as guard from cold, bites, and sun, and to look fierce in war. In time the marks took faith and rank worth, as signs of manhood, tribe, or grief.
britannica-1911-ticking:
Ticking, a strong linen or cotton cloth, is explained in a craft entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is most often woven in stripes of colour, with blue or pink on white the most common. The name comes from a word for a case or sheath found in many tongues. People use the cloth for mattresses, awnings, and tents.

Detail follows on how good ticking is made. Warp threads are most often flax, while coloured threads may be cotton. The weft is flax or tow, and cheap grades use cotton or jute. A feather tick should use fine flax yarn set close, with many weft threads per inch. Wax on the inside can stop feathers from working out. The weave is a twill, and the entry shows four kinds with drawings.
britannica-1911-tongking:
Tongking, a province and French protectorate in French Indo-China, is mapped in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies between twenty and twenty three and a half degrees north. Chinese provinces bound it on the north, Laos on the west, and Annam on the south. The Gulf of Tongking washes its east shore.

Its area runs to about 46000 square miles. The people are put at six million, with 33000 Chinese and about 4000 Europeans among them. The land falls into three parts. First comes the delta of the Song-Koi, or Red river, a low and fertile plain that holds the chief cities. Two mountain tracts stand north and west of that delta. A region of plateaus forms the third part of the province.
britannica-1911-tourcoing:
Tourcoing, a manufacturing town of northern France, is described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It lies in the department of Nord, less than a mile from the Belgian frontier. The town stands eight miles north east of Lille, on the railway to Ghent. Its population in 1906 was 62,694, and about a third of its people were Belgian born.

Tourcoing is in effect one town with Roubaix to the south, the entry says. A tramway and a canal branch join the two. With Roubaix it ranks as one of the chief cloth centres of France. Its main work is the combing, spinning, and twisting of wool, in some eighty factories. Cotton work matters too, and the weaving sheds turn out mixed cloth, silk drapery, and fancy goods. Carpet making is a special trade of the town.
britannica-1911-weaving:
Weaving is set out at length in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, starting from a clear first line. The craft works by crossing two or more sets of soft threads at right angles, the lengthwise set called warp and the crosswise set called weft. That one test sets woven cloth apart from all its kin.

The entry is strict about what weaving is not. Felt locks loose fibres with heat, damp and rubbing, while plaited work uses one set of threads at a slant. Nets hold by knots, hosiery by loops, and lace by threads passed round small groups. Even with those bounds, woven cloth runs to a vast range of weights and uses. The account then looks back to early man, whose needs for dress and shelter were few, and who laced strips of fibre and grass by hand.
britannica-1911-weight-throwing:
Hurling great weights for distance or height is set out in a sport entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Such throwing has long drawn crowds in Scotland and Ireland. It thrives too in Germany, Switzerland, and Austria-Hungary, the entry adds. No weight throw holds a place in the British title programme. Shot put and hammer throw do hold that place in Britain.

America puts the fifty-six pound weight in its title meets. The old British weight was a half hundredweight with a ring on top. That ring gripped poorly, so a three-sided handle took its place. The American weight is an iron or lead ball with a grip. Since 1888 men throw it from a seven-foot ring. The throw starts with a swing past the leg and over the head.
britannica-1911-whipping:
Whipping, or flogging, is a form of corporal punishment, and a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry surveys its long history. The entry notes that the lash has been used in all ages and all lands. It points readers to kindred topics such as the bastinado and the cat o’ nine tails. In ancient Rome a citizen could not be scourged.

Scourging was held to be a shameful penalty in Rome, fit for slaves. Slaves there were beaten with rods. In early medieval England the whip was kept for the villein, not the freeman. The Anglo Saxons whipped prisoners with a three corded knotted lash. The entry adds grim household cases. Mistresses might have servants whipped to death, and one tale tells of the young King Æthelred flogged by his mother with candles.
britannica-1911-wollongong: Wollongong is a seaport of New South Wales in Australia, south of Sydney by rail, and the chief harbour on the south coast. Its people numbered three thousand five hundred forty five in nineteen o one. Its harbour, called Belmont Basin, is cut out of solid rock, covers three acres, and is eighteen feet deep at low water. A breakwater guards its mouth, and a fort on Signal Hill defends it. Wollongong is the port for two collieries linked by rail.
britannica-1911-worthing:
Worthing is a town article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a seaside resort in Sussex, England. It stands sixty-one miles south of London, on the London, Brighton and South Coast railway. The count of 1901 gave it 20,015 people. It has a fine sea front and a pleasure pier, with a long range of firm sands.

A public park of twenty-one acres opened in 1881. The chief buildings are modern churches, the town hall of 1834, a free library, and rest homes. The mother parish is Broadwater, a mile north, whose church is a fine cross-shaped work of the Norman age in change. Digs in the town have found a Roman villa and signs of pottery works. Worthing was set up as a borough in 1890, under a mayor, eight aldermen, and twenty-four councillors. Its area is 1,439 acres.
britannica-1911-wrestling:
Wrestling is a sport where two men strive to throw each to the ground. It is one of the most old and most wide of sports. Walls of tomb shrines by the Nile show scores of scenes from bouts. Those scenes show near all the holds and falls known now.

Such proof shows the sport was full grown three thousand years past the dawn of the faith. Greek tales of a bout of two heroes match those wall scenes. Oil and fine sand were used by Greek men to give grip. All holds were let, and grace of move was prized as much as strength.
britannica-1911-wuchang:
Wuchang is the capital of the joined provinces of Hupeh and Hunan in China, one of three cities standing together at the mouth of the Han river. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets it on the right bank of the Yangtsze, facing the foreign settlement of Hankow. It is the seat of a viceroy and ranks among the greatest vice-royalties of the empire.

The native population is put at 800,000, counting the cities on both banks. Wuchang holds an arsenal and a mint, and its official ironworks were set up to make rails and railway gear. When the works lost money under state hands, they passed to the director-general of railways. The city is not open to foreign trade, though many missionaries live inside its walls. It is a junction on the trunk line from Peking to Canton.
britannica-1911-yatung: Yatung is a short entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Yatung was a trade market of Tibet, set at the mouth of the Chumbi valley near the Indian frontier. Under conventions made in the early 1890s, the market was opened to trade with India. The entry records one sharp incident: the Tibetans built a wall across the road between Yatung and Tibet. That act helped lead to the British mission of 1904. By the treaty of that year, a British trade agent was to be kept at Yatung.
c-sar-or-nothing:
Pío Baroja wrote a novel of Rome and Spain, turned from Spanish by Louis How. Cæsar Moncada, its lead, takes his name from Borgia's motto: aut Cæsar, aut nihil — Cæsar or nothing. A prologue and a Rome part open the frame. The Paris to Ventimiglia train starts the run.

An odd family, folk who pass close by, and Abbé Preciozi fill the early heads. Roman hotel small talk and the abbé's trusts come next. Old palaces, old salons, and old ladies set the scene. A ball, a probe of the dark world, and a meet on the Pincio turn the tale. Art, crowd rule, and new rambles mark the mid-run. A pope's portrait, bad days, and Cæsar's own thoughts lead to Don Calixto at St Peter's and in the tombs. A second part moves to Catro in the heads.
carving-and-serving:
Mrs. D. A. Lincoln, author of the Boston Cook Book, published her manual on carving at Boston in 1906. Pupils had kept asking her for a lecture on the subject. General directions come first: printed rules, she argues, beat watching a carver a few times, because the art needs study and daily practice.

Special directions then work through beef roasts, sirloin, fillet, mutton, venison, ham, tongue, and roast pig, joint by joint. Poultry, game, and fish get the same treatment, down to cutting up a chicken for a stew. Later sections cover salads, soups, pies, puddings, and ices, plus the thickness of slices and the tools a carver needs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alms-and-alms:
Alms and almsgiving, from the Greek eleemosyne, pity or mercy, means any gift to help the needy, prompted by charity. Almsgiving means much more than handing goods to the poor. The duty of almsgiving complements the right of property, which Leo XIII called not only lawful but necessary. Once ownership is admitted, rich and poor must both exist in society, and property lets its owner relieve the needy.

Scripture abounds in passages urging gifts for the needy's welfare, and the early Christians fully realized the duty. The Fathers frequently urged almsgiving, St. Cyprian devoting a whole treatise to it, and St. Thomas Aquinas summarized the teaching in the medieval period. As a rule, the poor of every class, saint or sinner, countryman or foreigner, friend or foe, have claims on the charity of those able to give. The entry then treats fruitful almsgiving, its phases, transitory almsgiving, and organized almsgiving.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolic-ble:
The Apostolic Blessing is the solemn blessing, urbi et orbi, which the pope himself gave before 1870 from the loggias, or open galleries, of St. Peter's on Maundy Thursday plus Easter, the Lateran on Ascension Day, and St. Mary Major on the Assumption. Popes often delegated the power to give it on petition and at mission closes. Clement XIII in 1762 restricted that delegated power to patriarchs, primates, archbishops, and bishops petitioning Rome for it.

Those prelates may give the blessing on Easter Sunday and some other feasts. Prelates with pontifical dress and territory of their own may give it only once a year, by a set formula. Superiors of certain orders, above all Franciscans, may give it twice a year in their own churches. Particular priests may also receive the faculty on return from Rome or at the close of missions and retreats.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-augustine-red:
Augustine Reding was Prince-Abbot of Einsiedeln in Switzerland and a theological writer, born at Lichtensteig in 1625, who died at Einsiedeln in 1692. He joined the Benedictines at Einsiedeln in 1641 and taught philosophy at twenty-four. He was ordained and made master of novices in 1649, and took doctorates in philosophy and theology at Freiburg in 1654. After teaching theology at Salzburg, he became prior at Einsiedeln in 1658 and Prince-Abbot in 1670.

As abbot he built the choir, the confession church, and St Magdalene's chapel between 1674 and 1684. His monastery took over the Bellinzona college in 1675 and ran it until 1852. He guarded monastic discipline, pressed thorough training for his monks, and saw their number grow from fifty-three to one hundred. As a temporal ruler his people loved him, and the poor revered him as a father. His chief work, a thirteen-volume scholastic theology, rests on the Summa of St Thomas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benedictine-a:
Kilwinning, a Benedictine abbey in Ayrshire, Scotland, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. A church stood on the site centuries before the Benedictine house, linked in tradition to St. Winning, whom some scholars identify with the Irish St. Finnian. Others call him a Welshman named Vynnyn, while an early Scottish breviary makes him a Scot.

The Benedictine foundation itself came from Hugh de Morville, Constable of Scotland, between 1140 and 1162, on ground already home to a community of Culdees, early Celtic monks. The entry weighs these rival origins, then follows the abbey's medieval life. It is a short study in how uncertain a saint's story can remain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-betting:
Betting, the backing of a claim by staking money or value on its outcome, receives a moral and legal entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. A bet pits one person's forecast against another's, each forfeiting the stake if wrong. No federal statute in the United States governs it, but many states punish bets on horse races, elections, or games of chance, and often void betting contracts.

In Britain, street betting and betting houses are forbidden, and wagering contracts are null. The moral judgment turns on stakes, skill, and harm: small friendly wagers differ from ruinous gambling. The entry joins moral theology to a comparative note on the law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-richa:
Richard Whiting, the last Abbot of Glastonbury, was executed in 1539 as Henry VIII dissolved the monasteries. Schooled at Glastonbury and a Cambridge graduate, he became chamberlain of his abbey. He was chosen abbot in 1525 through Cardinal Wolsey's choice, and ruled in peace for a decade.

A 1535 visit found all in order, yet his rule over the town was taken away and strict orders were laid on him. Still, he was assured the abbey would stand. In September 1539 royal agents seized him at Sharpham and carried him to the Tower for Cromwell to question. He was executed on 15 November 1539 on a treason charge that stays unclear, Glastonbury then being the last monastery left in Somerset.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessing:
Blessing, in its strict liturgical sense, is the Church's rite of setting persons and things apart for sacred service. It calls down God's favor on them. The entry first separates this narrow meaning from the wider biblical uses of the word. Those wider uses can mean praise, a wish for good fortune, dedication, or simply a gift.

Its five sections trace the practice from creation and the patriarchs through Christ and the apostles. They then set out who may confer blessings and what may receive them. They also cover what effect blessings have and the ceremony used. Readers find a compact guide to a rite the Church counts among her sacramentals, grounded at each step in Scripture and early custom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-boycotting:
Boycotting, named for Captain Boycott of Connemara, began as the Land League's bloodless weapon against land-grabbers in Ireland. When tenants were evicted for unpaid rent, landlords needed new takers for empty farms, and a few grabbers could wreck the whole agitation. Violence tempted many, but Parnell offered a sharper tool at a public meeting in 1880.

Asked what to do with a tenant who bid for an evicted neighbor's farm, Parnell had an answer. He urged that the man be left severely alone, put in a moral Coventry, and shunned as a leper of old. The isolation struck not only the offender but anyone who dealt with him. First used against Boycott, Lord Erne's agent, it spread beyond land disputes and beyond Ireland into many other quarrels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cistercian-ab:
Wilhering stands in the Linz diocese, Austria, on the Danube's right bank. Ulric of Willeheringen's castle housed regular canons at first, but when they failed his conditions he replaced them with Cistercians in 1146. Under its first abbot, Geraldus of Runa in Styria, the house was richly endowed and protected by Eberhard, Bishop of Bamberg. Ulric's brother Colo completed the work.

The foundation languished until Henry, the third abbot, with only two subjects, handed it to Burkhard, Abbot of Ebrach, in 1185. Burkhard sent Henry back with twelve monks, and from then the abbey prospered, founding Hohenfurth, Engelszell, and Sausenstein. Reformation losses cut it to three monks and two novices by 1568, but Abbot Alexander's reform from 1587 restored property and observance. Fire destroyed the monastery in 1733, and it was rebuilt under Abbot Bonus Pomerl.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clemens-augus:
Clemens August von Droste-Vishering, Archbishop of Cologne, was born on 21 January 1773 at Münster and died there on 19 October 1845. Besides Münster University, Katerkamp tutored him privately. Young, he joined the learned circle around Baron von Fürstenberg and Princess Amelia von Gallitzin. 

In June 1796 he began an educational tour of Germany, Switzerland, and Italy under Katerkamp, returning in August 1797. Ordained priest on 14 May 1798 by his brother Caspar Maximilian, he was elected coadjutor to the aged Baron von Fürstenberg on 18 January 1807. He succeeded him six months later. As administrator he founded an independent congregation of Sisters of Mercy in 1808, the Klemens-Schwestern. Confined practically to Münster, it still numbered eighty-one houses and 1,126 members in 1904. When Napoleon made Münster part of his monarchy in 1813, he appointed Baron von Spiegel bishop without papal knowledge. After Napoleon's fall, Clemens August was restored by the pope in March 1815.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-comte-d-estai:
Louis Delamarre's entry follows Jean-Baptiste-Charles-Henri-Hector, Comte d'Estaing, a French admiral born at Ravel, Auvergne, on 28 November 1729. He died at Paris on 28 April 1794. First an infantry colonel, he became brigadier-general and sailed to the East Indies with Lally-Tollendal in 1757. Prisoner at Madras in 1759, he won parole, joined the French East India Company, and wrecked British factories in Sumatra and the Gulf. Caught again in 1760, he reached Plymouth, then freedom, rising to lieutenant-general of the navy in 1763.

Vice-admiral in 1777, he sailed from Toulon the next year with twelve battleships and fourteen frigates for the American colonies. Winds spared Howe's fleet, but he took Newport, then storm scattered both fleets. He seized Saint Vincent and Grenada in 1779 and mauled Byron's fleet, but failed, wounded, at Savannah. He backed the king in the Revolution, spoke for Marie Antoinette at her trial, and died on the scaffold.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregationa:
Hugh Henry's entry treats congregational singing through Pius X's Instruction on sacred music, the Motu Proprio of 22 November 1903. Its third point urges special efforts to restore Gregorian chant among the people. The faithful may again take a more active part in ecclesiastical offices, as in ancient times. From that charge the entry frames four heads: ancient use, prohibition and decay, present-day revival, and the revival's character.

Ancient use rests on Ephesians 5:19, speaking in psalms, hymns, and spiritual canticles. Cardinal Bona reads this as witness that psalms and hymns sounded in assemblies from the Church's beginnings. A fourth-century Laodicea decree then marks prohibition's turn, and Baltimore's Second Plenary Council in 1866 voices the later American position. The quoted councils and pope point one way: restoration through instruction in Gregorian chant. Vernacular singing stays within stated limits, with training methods set out in the cited manuals.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cursing:
A moral theology entry sorts out the many senses of cursing. In popular speech it blends with coarse and insulting words. In canon law it can mean the ban of excommunication. In its common biblical sense it is the opposite of blessing: a threat of God's wrath, its actual visitation, or its prophetic announcement.

Instances run from God cursing the serpent, the earth, and Cain, through Noah cursing Canaan, to Christ cursing the barren fig tree and foretelling doom for the damned. In moral theology, cursing means wishing evil upon God or creatures. Saint Thomas treats it as maledictio, and the entry weighs when such speech is grave sin and when it is mere petition for justice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dancing:
This entry traces dancing from natural gesture to art, and weighs its place in Scripture and church discipline. Strong feeling, it argues, lifts the body into rhythmic movement, and as speech grew into poetry and song, so movement grew into dance. Hebrew has eight verbs for dancing, and biblical dances were often women's joyful leaping and circling, from Miriam at the Red Sea to David before the Ark.

Later opinion held dancing unbecoming for men, a view shared by Rome, and the entry follows church cautions through the centuries. Yet it distinguishes spontaneous joy from formal art, and notes dances of many peoples. Readers get both the anthropology of movement and the moral questions it raised for clergy, parents, and pastors guiding their flocks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dates-and-dat:
A chronological entry explains how documents came to be dated, from Roman letter formulas to the Christian era. In classical Latin, writers noted when and where they wrote, as in dabam Romae, I gave this at Rome, and from data, given, came our word date. Constantine's age made dating a condition of validity for imperial decrees, and by the twelfth century a Cologne instrument was challenged for lacking a date.

Yet practice lagged behind theory, and charters still went out undated into the twelfth century, Italian chanceries proving most careful. Sections then cover the Christian era, introduced by Dionysius Exiguus about 527. They cover the reckoning of years by indictions and other cycles. They also cover the reckoning of days by kalends, nones, ides, and saints' feasts, a system always apt to grow complicated and inexact.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-bockin:
Edward Bocking was an English Benedictine whose zeal helped bring down Elizabeth Barton, the Holy Maid of Kent. Born of East Anglian parents near the end of the fifteenth century, he took degrees at Oxford in 1513 and 1518. He served as warden of Canterbury College. He became a monk at Canterbury in 1526. Sent with another monk to test Barton's claimed visions, he urged her on instead.

The entry calls him her chief instigator, moving her to Saint Sepulchre's convent at Canterbury and shaping her claim to speak against Henry VIII's divorce. After the king married Anne Boleyn, Cromwell arrested Barton, Bocking, and others. Bocking confessed the fraud, did public penance at Paul's Cross, and was hanged at Tyburn with six companions in 1534.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-egbert-king:
Egbert, also spelled Ecgberht, was King of the West Saxons, dead in 839, and is often wrongly called the first King of England. Of royal descent from Ine of Wessex, he was exiled by Beorhtric and Offa of Mercia, then chosen king on his return in 802. In 815 he ravaged Cornwall and beat the West Welsh there, and in 825 he turned back a Mercian invasion at Ellandune.

Kent, Surrey, Sussex, and Essex then accepted him, East Anglia bowed to his overlordship, and Mercia submitted after he drove out Wiglaf. In 829 Northumbria met him at Dore and owned him overlord, so that for the first time one man held sway over all the English peoples, though under-kings still ruled beneath him. At home he shaped the shire system, organised the fyrd militia, and befriended the Church at Kingston in 838.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ernricus-pirh:
Ernricus Pirhing was born at Sigarthin, near Passau, in 1606, and his death fell between 1678 and 1681. Twelve years at Dillingen went to teaching canon law and Scripture, and he was still living there in 1675. His Jus canonicum in V libros Decretalium distributum, five volumes from Dillingen dated 1674 to 1677, marks a step forward for canonical science in Germany.

He kept the Corpus Juris's classical divisions while explaining his subjects' canonical legislation completely and synthetically. Seven pamphlets on the titles of the first book of the Decretals, cast as theses, also came from him and were resumed in his Jus Canonicum. An Apologia against two sermons of the Protestant Balduinus followed, at Ingolstadt in 1652 and Munich in 1653. After his death a colleague issued a Synopsis Pirhingana, a résumé of his Jus Canonicum, at Dillingen in 1695 and Venice in 1711.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-bour:
Francois Bourgoing, born at Paris in 1585 and dead in 1662, was the third Superior General of the French Oratory and an early companion of its founder, Cardinal de Berulle. From a family of magistrates, he served as cure of Clichy and resigned that post in favour of St. Vincent de Paul, also a disciple and friend of Berulle. Joining the Oratorians, he founded and directed new houses wherever bishops of France and Flanders called him.

In 1631 he became assistant to Superior General Pere de Condren. On Condren's death in 1641 he took the vacant office, organising and developing the congregation with unceasing zeal and opposing Jansenism energetically. His chief book, Truths and Excellences of Jesus Christ our Saviour, passed thirty editions, including one in 1906, and was translated into several languages, alongside four series of retreat exercises.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-christo:
Franz Christoph Ignaz Moufang, born at Mainz on 17 February 1817 and dead there on 27 February 1890, was a German theologian and leader of the Mainz Catholic revival. He studied at Mainz, went to Bonn in 1834, first for medicine, soon turning to theology under Klee, Windischmann, and Walter, then to Munich. He took his theological examinations at Giessen, entered Mainz seminary, and was ordained on 19 December 1839. His uncle Adam Franz Lennig, pastor at Seligenstadt, stirred his broad interest in religious questions of the day.

After curacies at Seligenstadt, Bensheim, and Saint-Quentin in Mainz, he became religious instructor at the Mainz gymnasium in 1845. When Bishop von Ketteler restored the philosophical and theological school at Mainz seminary in 1851, Moufang became regent and professor of moral and pastoral theology. He became canon in 1854 and spiritual adviser to the diocesan court.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-friedrich-hei:
Friedrich Vering, a German canonist born at Liesborn in 1833, stood among the leading church lawyers of the nineteenth century. He studied law at Bonn and Heidelberg, taught Roman and canon law at Heidelberg, then held the canon law chair at Czernowitz from 1875. In 1879 he moved to the German University of Prague, where he taught until his death in 1896.

Though a layman, Vering staunchly defended Church rights against state encroachment. His best-known work is a broad textbook of Catholic, Eastern, and Protestant church law, first issued at Freiburg in 1876 and thrice revised. He also wrote on Roman private law and inheritance, finished a volume of Philipps on church law, and long edited the Archive for Catholic Church Law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gambling:
Gambling, the staking of money or value on a game of chance, belongs to the family of aleatory contracts, where gain turns on an unknown event. Bets on pure skill, like billiards, fall outside the term, while whist mixes skill with chance. Small stakes for zest hardly count as gambling at all, which connotes high play. The entry judges the practice by moral theology.

Theologians allow gaming only on four terms. The stake must be the player's own and free, play must be unforced, fraud is barred though bluffing is not, and the sides must stand roughly equal. Break any term and gaming turns wrong. Beyond that, excess breeds passion, lost time and money, idle company, and scandal. Betting on races, matches, or future prices stands under the same moral rule.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-geoffrey-keat:
Geoffrey Keating, an Irish theologian, historian, and poet born in Tipperary about 1569, kept Irish learning alive under persecution. Schooled in Munster and Leinster, he was ordained at twenty-four and sailed with forty students to Bordeaux's new Irish College in November 1603. There he took his doctorate in divinity, mourning Ireland in verse when the Earls fled in 1607.

Back in Ireland about 1610, Keating served Knockraffan parish and ended the abuse of delaying Mass for late gentry. Spies tracked him, a lady's anger drove him to a Galtee cave, and he spent six disguised years gathering history across Ireland. His history's preface came in 1629, its parts in 1631 and 1632, beside the Three Shafts of Death and his Key-Shield of the Mass.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hans-baldung:
Swabian painter Hans Baldung, called Grien for his love of brilliant green in dress and pictures, was born at Gmünd about 1476 and died at Strasbourg in 1545. A lifelong friend of Dürer, who left him a lock of hair at death, he worked with Dürer at Nuremberg. His unsigned portraits have sometimes passed as his master's.

An exceptional draughtsman and good colourist with a fertile imagination, he spent seven years at Freiburg. There his great altarpiece shows the Coronation of the Virgin with Apostles inside the wings and scenes of Our Lady outside. Works fill galleries from Berlin and Vienna to Munich and Frankfurt, and he became a Strasbourg citizen in 1509 and a senator in the year he died.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hans-memling:
Bruges painter Hans Memling, born about 1430 and dead in 1494, was long wrapped in a romantic legend of a wounded soldier of Charles the Bold nursed by Hospitallers. The entry dismisses that tale as sacristans' fancy from the eighteenth century. Records instead show a prosperous burgher, owner of three houses in 1480 and among the city's highest taxed citizens, married with three sons.

His certain works run from a 1467 portrait of Spinelli through the Donne triptych, the St. John hospital altarpieces, and the shrine of St. Ursula to the Lübeck polyptych of 1491, some twenty exquisite pictures in all. Inferior to Van Eyck in nothing as a craftsman, he surpasses him in feeling. He paints velvets and flesh with a rarer, nobler tenderness that makes him the keenest poet of the Flemish school.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-edward-:
Henry Edward Manning, second Archbishop of Westminster, was born in 1808 into a banking family and educated at Harrow and Balliol College, Oxford. There he took a first in classics in 1830 and shone in debate. After a short post in the Colonial Office he felt called to the ministry and was ordained in the Anglican Church in 1832. He spent seventeen years as rector of Lavington in Sussex, where his parish work showed zeal for the poor and for reform.

Appointed Archdeacon of Chichester in 1841, Manning threw himself into visitations and charges that foreshadowed his wider work, while the Oxford Movement drew him toward Rome. Newman's submission in 1845 came after years of conviction, and the account stresses that such a conversion is often a matter of time rather than a sudden step. The entry follows Manning through this Anglican period, tracing the path out of the Church of England.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hong-kong:
Hong Kong island was ceded by China to Great Britain in January 1841 under restrictions, with cession completed by the Treaty of Nanking in August 1842. Gregory XVI named a prefect apostolic under the bishop of Macao in 1846. A vicariate apostolic was created in 1874 and entrusted to the Milan Seminary of Foreign Missions, present in the city since 1850.

Giovanni Timoleone Raimondi, Acanthus's titular bishop, served as first vicar apostolic until his death at Hong Kong in 1894. His successors were Luigi Piazzoli and Domenico Pozzoni, elected in 1905. The vicariate counted twelve European and ten native priests, over fourteen thousand Christians, twenty-six churches, and dozens of schools, plus Canossian, St. Paul, and native sisters, across Hong Kong, Lautau, and three mainland districts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hunting:
Hunting has been forbidden to clerics in one form or another from early times. The Corpus of Canon Law forbids all servants of God to hunt or range the woods with hounds, and to keep hawks or falcons. The Fourth Lateran Council under Innocent III interdicted hunting and hawking to all clerics.

Trent worded its decree more mildly: clerics should abstain from illicit hunting and hawking, implying not all hunting is illicit. Canonists generally split noisy hunting, called clamorous, from quiet hunting, allowing the latter but not the former. Ferraris held hunting lawful for clerics if rare, for sufficient cause such as need, use, or honest recreation, and with becoming moderation, though Ziegler disputed that reading.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-lelon:
French bibliographer Jacques Lelong was born at Paris on 19 April 1665. He died there on 13 August 1721. At ten he entered the Knights of St John of Malta. After a brief and unhappy stay in Malta, he studied at Paris. He left the knights and entered the Oratory in 1686. He taught at Juilly college in the Meaux diocese. He was ordained priest there in 1689.

Later he served as librarian at Notre-Dame des Vertus seminary in Aubervilliers near Paris. In 1699 he moved to the St Honoré Oratory at Paris. He remained its librarian until death twenty-two years later. His first famous work was the Bibliotheca Sacra, a two-part bibliography of sacred texts and versions in every language. It listed the best editions and manuscripts with historical and critical notes. The entry presents a librarian who mapped the Bible's printed world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jakob-wimpfel:
Jakob Wimpfeling, humanist and theologian, was born at Schlettstadt in Alsace on 25 July 1450 and died in the same town on 17 November 1528. He went to school at Schlettstadt under Ludwig Dringenberg. Starting in 1464 he studied at Freiburg university, taking a bachelor's degree in 1466. Afterward he studied at Erfurt and Heidelberg, taking a master's degree in 1471, and then he spent three years on canon law, followed by theology.

Speyer's cathedral preachership came his way in 1483, and in 1498 Elector Palatine Philip summoned him to Heidelberg as rhetoric and poetry professor. From 1513 he dwelt at Schlettstadt, where pupils and admirers gathered round him, until Lutheran disputes broke apart that literary circle. He died lonely and embittered. His early works pressed for synods held more often, for devotion to Mary, and for better clerical discipline.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-bede-pol:
John Bede Polding was the Benedictine monk who became the first Archbishop of Sydney and Primate of Australia. Born at Liverpool in 1794, he was schooled at the Benedictine house at Acton Burnell and took the habit in 1810. He was ordained in 1819, serving as parish priest, prefect, novice-master, and sub-prior. First chosen for Madras, he was instead sent to New South Wales, consecrated in London in 1834.

Reaching Sydney in 1835, he found just three priests in New South Wales, plus one in Tasmania. He worked like a parish priest himself, saying Mass in stations and convict prisons, teaching, hearing confessions, and visiting the dying. Between 1836 and 1841 seven thousand convicts made retreats under his guidance. After a visit to Rome in 1841 he returned as archbishop of a new hierarchy, governing Australian Catholicism until his death in 1877.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-hardyng:
John Hardyng was an English chronicler and soldier whose chronicle is shadowed by his own forgeries. Born in 1378, he served Henry Percy, known as Hotspur, and Sir Robert Umfreville. He fought at Homildon Hill in 1402 and Shrewsbury in 1403, became constable of Warkworth Castle, and fought at Agincourt in 1415.

Henry V employed him to fetch Scottish documents proving Scotland's subjection to England, rewarding him with the manor of Geddington. Hardyng's conduct on this mission is indefensible: he forged many documents, some still in the Record Office, and claimed reward for the fraud. As constable of Kyme Castle he compiled his chronicle in three versions: Lancastrian to 1436, Yorkist, and a third dedicated to Edward IV running to 1461. It is valuable for his acquaintance with the leading statesmen of the age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-mensing:
John Mensing was a Dominican theologian and celebrated opponent of Luther in Germany. Born probably at Magdeburg, he entered the Dominicans in 1495, studied at Wittenberg, and took his licentiate in 1517 and doctorate at Frankfurt-on-the-Oder in 1518. He lived when controversy was rife and reformers' teachings spread rapidly through every province.

From 1522 to 1524 he held the Magdeburg cathedral pulpit and wrote his first defenses of the Sacrifice of the Mass. Enemy boldness then forced him to Dessau, where he aided Princess Margaretha von Anhalt against heresy. Professor at Frankfurt-on-the-Oder in 1529, theologian to the Elector at the Diet of Augsburg in 1530, provincial in 1534, and suffragan Bishop of Halberstadt, he took a leading part with Eck. He played that part at the Worms and Ratisbon conferences of 1540 and 1541. He died about 1541.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-ming:
John Ming was a Swiss Jesuit philosopher who wrote on evolution, socialism, and ethics for American Catholics. Born at Gyswyl in Unterwalden in 1838, he was educated at the Benedictine college at Engelberg, then entered the German Jesuit novitiate in 1856. At Aachen he studied philosophy, and theology at Maria-Laach, and taught theology at Gorz before coming to the United States in 1872.

After two years in pastoral ministry he taught theology at Milwaukee, then philosophy for twenty-one years, chiefly at Buffalo, Prairie du Chien, and St. Louis. Once he had mastered English he wrote for the Messenger and the American Catholic Quarterly Review on evolution and socialism, the two great questions facing American Catholics. He produced a treatise on the temporal power and his Data of Modern Ethics Examined, then studies of the characteristics, religion, and morality of modern socialism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-of-victr:
John of Victring was an Austrian Cistercian chronicler and confidential secretary to dukes of Carinthia. Born probably between 1270 and 1280, he became abbot of Victring in 1307 and served as chaplain and secretary to Duke Henry of Carinthia. After Henry's death in 1335 he defended the duke's daughter Margaretha's claims at Linz. Albert II and Otto of Austria took the lands and made him their valued counselor.

Frequenting Vienna as their secretary until 1341, he withdrew to his monastery to compose the history of his own age. His Book of Certain Histories, first a history of Austria and Carinthia from 1231 to 1341 based on Ottocar's rhyming chronicle and his own collections, grew in 1342. It became an imperial chronicle from 1217. In 1343 it grew into one from Carolingian times. Learned in Latin and Greek poets, lucid in narrative and impartial in judgment, he stands among the most important chroniclers of the late Middle Ages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-epping:
Joseph Epping was a German Jesuit astronomer who decoded Babylonian sky records. Born at Neuenkirchen in Westphalia in 1835 and orphaned young, he studied mathematics at Münster, joined the Society of Jesus in 1859, and taught mathematics and astronomy at Maria-Laach. In 1872 he went to Quito to teach at Ecuador's new Polytechnic.

Driven home by unrest after President Moreno's murder, he spent his last years teaching younger Jesuits in Holland. With Father Strassmaier he found the key to Babylonian moon tables and matched ancient planet names to Mars, Saturn, and Jupiter. His 1889 book on Babylonian astronomy mattered for both astronomy and chronology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kwang-tung:
Kwang-Tung is a prefecture apostolic covering its whole Chinese province except districts held by Macao and Hong Kong. St. Francis Xavier tried to enter it in 1552 but died on Shang-sch'wan island before preaching there.

Father Melchior Barreto reached Canton in 1556 and debated science and morals with mandarins, and Father Ruggieri won leave to open a chapel in 1581. Matteo Ricci, the real founder of Christianity in China, arrived at Canton in 1582 and planted settlements toward Kiang-si and Nanking that still stand. After dependence on Macao until 1658, French mission priests joined Jesuits, Franciscans, and Dominicans. Persecution in 1742 expelled all missionaries, though native priests kept some 7,000 to 8,000 Christians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-linkoping:
Linköping, in Sweden, originally included Östergötland, Gotland, Öland, and Småland.

Benedict, 1220-1237, was the first of a long line of prelates who built and endowed the cathedral, begun in 1150 but unfinished at the Reformation. Among them was Blessed Nicholas Hermansson, 1374-1391, who had tutored St. Bridget's sons Charles and Birger, and received her body at Vadstena. He composed an Office in honour of St. Bridget. The last Catholic bishop was Hans Brask, bishop 1513-1527, died 30 July 1539. He championed the Old Learning, and had to leave in 1527, when the Diet of Westeraas made Lutheranism the state religion. The religious houses set up between the twelfth and sixteenth centuries included the cathedral chapter and the Cistercians. The Cistercians had three houses for men: Alvastra, Nydala, both founded in 1143, and Gutvalla, or Roma, in Gotland.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luke-wadding:
Luke Wadding was an Irish Franciscan historian and theologian, born at Waterford in 1588 and dead at Rome's St. Isidore College in 1657. Eleventh of fourteen children, he learned Latin prose and verse by thirteen, lost both parents at fourteen, and studied philosophy in Ireland before Lisbon's Irish seminary.

Joining the Friars Minor at Matozinhos in 1605, he specialized in Scotist philosophy and theology, then built St. Isidore's College at Rome as a home for Irish Franciscans. His Annals of the Friars Minor, his edition of Duns Scotus, and his histories of the order made him the age's great Franciscan scholar. His work still anchors the study of Scotus and the Irish mission.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lying:
Lying, as Aquinas defines it, is a statement at variance with the mind. That beats the common formula of a false statement meant to deceive. One may lie while telling truth he believes false, and a known liar, believed by nobody, still lies when his words clash with his thought.

Following Augustine and Aquinas, moralists split lies into injurious, officious, and jocose kinds. Harmful lies, white lies of excuse or benefit, and jokes told for fun fall in these classes, though mere obvious jest carries no malice. Aristotle and Kant allowed no lie ever. Plato let doctors and statesmen lie for good, and modern writers split the same way, with Paulsen and most non-Catholics admitting the lie of necessity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martin-john-s:
Martin John Spalding was seventh Archbishop of Baltimore, born at Bardstown, Kentucky, in 1810 and dead at Baltimore in 1872. His forebears left England for Maryland in the seventeenth century, his grandfather moving to Kentucky in 1790. He entered St Mary's College, Lebanon, in 1821, taught mathematics there at fourteen, and graduated in 1826.

After four years at Bardstown seminary he entered Rome's Propaganda in 1830, was ordained in 1834, and won a theology doctorate defending 256 theses. Back at Bardstown he pastored the cathedral and edited the Catholic Advocate from 1835. He became Louisville vicar-general in 1844, coadjutor in 1848, and bishop in 1850. He brought Xaverian Brothers to Louisville in 1854 and founded Louvain's American College, opened in 1857. Succeeding at Baltimore in 1864, he organised the St Vincent de Paul Society, founded the House of the Good Shepherd and St Mary's Industrial School, and finished the cathedral. He presided over the Second Plenary Council of 1866, which backed his Catholic university idea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-matthew-lang:
Matthew Lang moved between chancery desk and bishop's throne with rare ease. Born at Augsburg in 1468, he studied at Ingolstadt, Tubingen, and Vienna, then served as secretary to Emperor Maximilian I in 1494, imperial councillor in 1501, and chancellor in 1508. Though named Prince-Bishop of Gurk in 1505, he stayed at court as a layman and never once visited that diocese.

Made cardinal in 1511, he ran imperial talks with France, Venice, Hungary, and the pope, and became Archbishop of Salzburg in 1519. He helped put Charles V on the imperial throne, pushed measures against Luther, crushed the Peasants' War in his lands, and held reform synods at Muhldorf. A lover of letters and a proud prince of the Church, he acted more from statecraft than from piety.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-matthias-doer:
