Matthias Doering, a Franciscan historian and theologian born at Kyritz in Brandenburg between 1390 and 1400, died there in 1469. He joined the Friars Minor at home, studied at Oxford, took his doctorate at Erfurt in 1424, and taught theology and Bible study. In 1427 his order chose him provincial for Saxony, and in 1443 the Conventuals made him minister general.

Doering threw himself into the Council of Basle's cause, backing a council's power over the pope, and he helped depose Eugene IV and elect the antipope Felix V in 1439. Excommunicated by Magdeburg's archbishop, he appealed to Rome, resigned in 1461, and spent his last years writing at Kyritz. Works tied to his name include a Confutation of papal primacy, a defence of Nicholas of Lyra, a lost book on church perplexities, and a chronicle continuation to 1464.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-men-of-unders:
The Men of Understanding, or Homines Intelligentiae, were a heretical sect cited before the Brussels Inquisition in 1410-11. Their leaders were Egidius Cantoris, an illiterate layman, and the Carmelite William of Hildernissen. The sect, kin to the earlier Brethren of the Free Spirit, taught the final salvation of all people and even demons. It held that bodily sin cannot stain the soul, and believed in a mystical illumination and union with God.

That union, they claimed, was so perfect it freed them from all moral and church laws and pledged salvation infallibly. Both leaders gloried in visions they claimed to enjoy. Cantoris, in religious exaltation, ran nude through Brussels streets proclaiming himself mankind's saviour. About 1410 Peter d'Ailly, Bishop of Cambrai, moved first against the heresy. William retracted, though doubtfully, in 1410, and again in 1411, when he was sentenced to three years in a castle and then exile outside the diocese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michael-waddi:
Michael Wadding, also called Godinez, was a mystical theologian born at Waterford, Ireland, in 1591 who died in Mexico in December 1644. Orphaned young, he studied two years at Salamanca's Irish seminary and entered the Society of Jesus in 1609. After Villagarcia's novitiate he won leave for Mexico's missions, taking the name Godinez, by which he is best known. He made his profession in 1626.

He gave years to Sinaloa's rough mission, worked among the Mayos and Tephanes in 1620, took charge of the Comicaris, and with much labour won over the Basiroas to Christian tribes. In his Teologia mistica he recounts, as one who bore them, the missionaries' privations and sufferings. He taught for years in Mexican colleges. Famed for deep knowledge of supernatural states and rare prudence in guiding souls, his Practica de la teologia mistica, published in 1681, ran through ten editions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-munich-freisi:
Munich-Freising is a Bavarian archdiocese that grew from the ancient Diocese of Freising. Its church goes back to Saint Corbinian, who came in 716 to organise Bavarian Christianity. He raised a Benedictine monastery and school on a mountain near Freising. When Saint Boniface ordered Bavaria's church affairs in 738, Corbinian's brother Erembert became first Bishop of Freising, suffragan to Mainz.

The diocese then stretched across the Upper Isar country to the Inn and the watershed, gaining convents at Tegernsee, Moosburg, Schliersee and elsewhere. Bishops such as Joseph of Verona and the learned Aribo shaped its early learning. The entry follows Freising through medieval prince-bishops, secularisation, and its union with Munich as an archdiocese in the nineteenth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-otto-of-freis:
Otto of Freising was a bishop and historian born between 1111 and 1114 and dead at Morimond in Champagne on 22 September 1158. Son of Saint Leopold of Austria and Agnes, daughter of Henry IV, he was half-brother of Conrad III and uncle of Frederick Barbarossa through his mother's first marriage. Destined young for the priesthood, he became provost at Klosterneuberg, studied at Paris, and with fifteen noblemen entered the Cistercian order at Morimond on his way home.

Within three years he was abbot, then bishop of Freising in 1137 or 1138, still wearing his order's habit. He founded and reformed monasteries, brought Aristotelian thought and Paris-style debate to Freising, and won back church lands lost in the investiture strife. His Chronicle frames history as a clash between the earthly city of Babylon and the divine city. His Deeds of Frederick, covering peace years 1152 to 1156, stays a prime source for Barbarossa's reign.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patrick-flemi:
Patrick Fleming was a Franciscan friar born at Lagan in County Louth on 17 April 1599 and dead on 7 November 1631. His father descended from Lord Slane's line, his mother from Robert Cusack, baron of the exchequer. In 1612, amid fierce Irish persecution, young Fleming went to Flanders, studying first at Douai, then at Louvain's College of Saint Anthony of Padua. He took the Franciscan habit in 1617 and made solemn profession a year later.

Baptised Christopher, he took Patrick as his religious name. After studies at Rome's Saint Isidore College and ordination, he lectured on philosophy at Louvain, winning repute for learning and administration. When Strict Observance Franciscans opened a Prague college, Fleming became its first superior and theology lecturer. Fleeing Saxon invaders in 1631 with Matthew Hoar, he was killed by armed Calvinist peasants on 7 November.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pickering:
Thomas Pickering was an English Benedictine lay brother and martyr, born about 1621 to an old Westmoreland family. Sent to St. Gregory's at Douai, he took vows as a lay brother in 1660 and went to London in 1665 as steward to the Benedictines serving the queen's chapel royal. There he became known to the queen and Charles II, and when Parliament drove the Benedictines out in 1675, he alone was allowed to stay, probably as no priest.

Titus Oates's pretended revelations of 1678 accused him of plotting the king's murder. No evidence but Oates's word appeared, and the queen publicly believed him innocent, yet the jury condemned him with two others to hanging, drawing, and quartering. Charles twice reprieved the three, then yielded to Commons' petition of April 1679. Pickering alone was executed, on 9 May 1679, his blood-stained cloth kept at Downside.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-religious-pai:
Religious painting has accompanied the Church's life since the Catacombs, serving ecclesiastical ornament, and for centuries after Constantine it was the only art in the Christian world. Until the Renaissance the Church monopolized painting: profane painting in Europe is only five centuries old and took the lead in the nineteenth century alone. Through the whole Christian era, then, the history of painting has been the history of religious painting, still fertile, though diminished.

The survey follows its changing faces, above all the Virgin, to whom art sang tender hymns. The Byzantine Panagia and the medieval Throne of God and Queen of Heaven gave way to the Mother. Bernard, Francis of Assisi, and Bonaventure made devotion to the Madonna a Christian devotion. Schools vied to paint the holiest Virgins, Siena's among the charming, and the entry closes wondering what future awaits an art that once expressed every shade of human nature.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-religious-son:
Religious song, or sacred song, is the name for poetical and musical creations used in public worship but kept outside the official liturgy for their freer, more subjective character. It springs from the faithful's desire, encouraged yet guided and controlled by the Church, to take an active part in ceremonies. While psalms were sung traditionally at early Eucharistic celebrations and love-feasts, the agapae, assemblies soon improvised songs of their own, religious in burden but spontaneous beside the psalms.

Missionaries turned the people's familiar melodies to Christian use, setting Christian texts to them to wean converts from pagan belief and practice. That habit led an emotional people to vent growing religious feeling in words and melodies of their invention. By the latter part of the ninth century vernacular words were mingled with liturgical chant. The name Leisen marks the vast song literature of the period that followed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-flemi:
Richard Fleming, Bishop of Lincoln and founder of Lincoln College, Oxford, lived through the turbulent years of the Wycliffite dispute. A Yorkshire man educated at University College, Oxford, he first came to notice as a young university officer. In 1409 he sat among the commissioners who examined the writings of John Wyclif. Later, as bishop, he carried out the order to burn Wyclif's exhumed body in 1428.

His enduring mark was educational rather than judicial. Fleming attended the Council of Constance and rose through church offices to the see of Lincoln. He used his position to found a college at Oxford meant to train clergy against heresy. The entry also traces his benefices and rectorships, including Boston, and notes that early suspicion of sympathy with Wyclif never hardened into doubt about his own orthodoxy. It is a useful portrait of a bishop-administrator in a divided church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-nutter:
Robert Nutter and Edward Thwing were English martyrs executed together at Lancaster on 26 July 1600. Nutter, born at Burnley about 1550, entered Brasenose College, Oxford, and then the English College at Reims. Ordained priest in December 1581, he returned to England and was committed to the Tower in 1584. There he spent forty-seven days in the pit, forty-three in irons, and twice suffered the scavenger's daughter torture.

Shipped to Boulogne with twenty priests in 1585, he revisited Rome, then was imprisoned again at Newgate under the alias Rowley, at the Marshalsea, and at Wisbech Castle. Thwing, of a Heworth family, studied at Reims and Pont-a-Mousson, taught Greek, Hebrew, rhetoric, and logic, and was ordained at Laon. After a stay at Spa for a knee ulcer, he went on the mission in 1597. Both men escaped to Lancashire, were arrested in May 1600, tried for being priests, and suffered on the same day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rudolph-willi:
Rudolph William Basil Feilding, eighth Earl of Denbigh and ninth Earl of Desmond, was born 9 April 1823 and died in 1892. He was educated at Eton College and Trinity College, Cambridge, where he took a Master of Arts. He entered the Church in 1850 and worked energetically for many Catholic charities under Cardinal Wiseman.

As Viscount Feilding he served as honorary treasurer of the Peter's Pence Association, jointly with Viscount Campden and Archibald J. Dunn. He showed great courage and independence of character. Such qualities were needed in the mid-nineteenth century, when English Protestant feeling ran high against the restored Catholic hierarchy. To mark his conversion with thanks, he built the Franciscan monastery at Pentasaph in North Wales.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-chrodegang:
St. Chrodegang, also called Godegrand, Gundigran, Ratgang, Rodigang, and Sirigang, was bishop of Metz. He was born at Hasbania, in today's Belgian Limburg, at the start of the eighth century, to a noble Frankish family. He died at Metz on 6 March 766. This entry follows a boy educated at Charles Martel's court, who served as his private secretary, then chancellor, then prime minister in 737.

On 1 March 742 he was appointed bishop of Metz, keeping his civil office at Pepin's request. In his influential position Chrodegang laboured earnestly for Church and State, and was ever solicitous to strengthen the union between temporal and spiritual rulers. In his diocese he introduced the Roman liturgy and chant, and community life for his cathedral clergy, with a special rule he wrote for them. He founded the Abbey of Gorze near Metz in 748, and remained its friend and protector.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-stephen-ha:
Stephen Harding, third abbot of Cîteaux, held the young Cistercian reform to strict observance through near collapse. Born at Sherborne in Dorset about the middle of the eleventh century, he studied at Sherborne, Paris, and Rome. Stopping at Molesme on his return, he joined Robert's community, practised great austerity, and became Robert's chief supporter.

He was one of twenty-one monks who retired to Cîteaux under Hugh of Lyons to found a stricter house. When Robert was recalled to Molesme in 1099, Stephen became prior under Alberic, and on Alberic's death in 1110 he was elected abbot. With monks few and the duke of Burgundy offended, he begged alms door to door rather than relax the rule. He died on 28 March 1134, after welcoming Bernard and his companions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-wolfgang:
Wolfgang, bishop of Regensburg from 972 to 994, counts with Ulrich and Conrad among the three brilliant stars of tenth-century Germany. Born about 934 to Swabian counts of Pfullingen, he had a cleric tutor at seven and then attended the celebrated monastic school on Reichenau. There he befriended Henry, brother of Poppo of Würzburg, and followed him to Würzburg's cathedral school.

There he heard the noted Italian grammarian Stephen of Novara. When Henry became archbishop of Trier in 956, he called Wolfgang to teach in the cathedral school and labour for diocesan reform, despite enmity. Wolfgang's Trier years deepened his monastic and ascetic bent. Later bishop of Regensburg, he reformed clergy and monasteries and preached in Hungary and Bohemia. He died at Pupping on 31 October 994.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-temiskaming:
Temiskaming is a Vicariate Apostolic of Canada, suffragan of Ottawa, bounded by Hudson Bay and the Great Whale River in the north and by 72° and 91° west longitude. It was erected on 22 September 1908 by dividing the Diocese of Pembroke. Fathers de Bellefeuille and Dupuy first preached there in 1836, with yearly visits to Indians at Hudson's Bay Company posts. Oblates took charge in 1843 under Father Laverlochère, settling at Fort Temiskaming in 1863 and moving to Ville Marie in 1886.

Lumbering followed the fur trade, then agriculture drew settlers to Lake Temiskaming's fertile shores. Railways and the silver and gold finds of 1903 advanced the Ontario section. Catholics number about 20,000, including some 5,000 Indians. Haileybury is home to the first vicar, Elie-Anicet Latulipe, named in October 1908 and consecrated that November. The vicariate holds 17 parishes, 20 missions, and many stations, served by 21 secular priests, 4 Sacred Heart missionaries, and 9 Oblates, with convents, hospitals, and schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-ewing:
Thomas Ewing, jurist and statesman, was born in West Liberty, Virginia, in 1789 and died at Lancaster, Ohio, in 1871. Raised in pioneer hardship in the Muskingum Valley, he learned to read from his sister and worked in the Kanawha salt works by furnace light. In 1815 he took the first degree ever given by a college in the western country, at Ohio University. He was admitted to the bar the next year.

Entering the Senate from Ohio in 1831, he stood with Webster and Clay against Jackson and backed Clay's protective tariff. The entry also follows his children, including sons who served as generals and a daughter, Eleanor, who married William Tecumseh Sherman and wrote her father's memorial in 1872.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-flemin:
Thomas Fleming, Archbishop of Dublin, was born in 1593, son of the Baron of Slane, and died in 1665. He studied at the Franciscan college of Louvain, became a Franciscan priest, and taught there for years before Urban VIII named him to Dublin in October 1623. His appointment angered opponents of the religious orders, and the priest Paul Harris attacked him in print.

Fleming called a provincial synod at Dublin in 1640. When the Confederate war broke out he backed the Confederates, sending a procurator to Kilkenny in 1642 and attending the general assembly that October. A man of peace by temper, he sought settlement at almost any price and opposed the thorough policy of the Old Irish party, signing the 1643 commission to treat with Ormond.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-hardin:
Thomas Harding, a controversialist born at Combe Martin, Devon, in 1516, became the Catholic champion against Bishop Jewel. A Winchester scholar from 1528, he entered New College, Oxford, in 1534, became Hebrew professor under Henry VIII in 1542, and served as chaplain to the Marquess of Dorset. He first leaned to reform, but under Mary declared himself Catholic and took a divinity doctorate in 1554.

Elizabeth's accession cost him his preferments and brought imprisonment, and he retired to Louvain, where he served St. Gertrude's church and devoted himself to controversy. His 1564 Answer to Master Jewel's Challenge opened a long exchange with the bishop of Salisbury. Harding died at Louvain in September 1572.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-thomas-th:
Thomas Thwing was a Yorkshire priest executed at York in 1680 during the panic over the alleged Popish Plot. Born at Heworth Hall in 1635, he trained at Douai and worked in his native county, serving as chaplain at Carlton Hall, opening a school. Later ministering to the Institute of Mary community at Dolebank, where three of his sisters lived.

Arrested there in 1679, he was caught up in accusations by two dismissed servants who claimed a plot to murder the king. His relatives were acquitted in London on the same evidence, but Thwing, tried again at York, was convicted. The king first reprieved him, then issued the warrant after Parliament protested. On the scaffold he declared his innocence, his loyalty, and his charity to his neighbour.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vicariate-apo:
Eastern Shan-tung is a Chinese vicariate separated from Northern Shan-tung in 1894, covering the prefectures of Yen-chou, Lai-chou, and Teng-chou, with about ten million inhabitants and a very healthy climate. It was entrusted to the Franciscans under Mgr Caesarius Schang, resident at Chefoo.

Its modern history turned on violence: in November 1897 two German missionaries, Francis Xavier Nies and Richard Henle, were murdered at Chang-kia-chwang. The killings led Germany's fleet to occupy Kiao-chou days later. In 1899 the German-held territory was detached to Southern Shan-tung. By 1909 the mission counted twenty-two priests, nine thousand Catholics, nearly twelve thousand catechumens, thirteen churches, 138 chapels, and 350 stations, plus schools, hospitals, and orphanages.

Northern Shan-tung is a Chinese vicariate erected by Gregory XVI in 1839 under its first vicar apostolic, Louis de Besi, formerly pro-vicar of Hu-pe and Hu-nan. It endured many wars and persecutions, was divided into northern and southern Shan-tung in 1885, and lost its eastern portion to a new vicariate in 1894.

Entrusted to the Franciscans under a vicar apostolic resident at Tsi-nan-fu, it enjoys a salubrious, temperate climate and numbers eleven million inhabitants. Growth was rapid: in 1904 it counted eleven European Franciscans, eighteen native priests, 18,000 Catholics, 13,900 catechumens, and 134 churches and chapels. By 1910 twenty-nine European fathers, nineteen native priests, 28,000 Catholics, 20,000 catechumens, and 187 churches and chapels.

Southern Shan-tung is a Chinese vicariate. Its Catholic faith had scarcely been preached in its southern districts before Father John Baptist Anzer of the Steyl Seminary was sent there as pro-vicar in 1882. With another Steyl missionary he began the work, and in 1886 the vicariate was erected, later gaining the German-held districts of Kiao-chou, Tsi-me, Kau-mi, and Chu-chong in 1898.

Entrusted to the Divine Word priests of Steyl under Mgr Augustine Henninghaus, resident at Yen-chou-fu, it held twelve million inhabitants in a temperate climate. In 1908 it counted forty-six European and twelve native priests, over 35,000 Catholics and nearly 40,000 catechumens. 131 churches and chapels, seminaries, Chino-German and catechumen schools, a college for European girls, asylums, and a hospital.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wheeling:
Wheeling is a diocese comprising West Virginia except eight eastern counties in Richmond diocese. It also covers twenty-four Virginia counties and part of Craig County, 21,355 square miles in West Virginia and 7,817 in Virginia, 29,172 in all. Formed from Richmond by apostolic letters of July 1850, its first bishop was Richard Whelan, transferred from Richmond, where he had been consecrated its second bishop in March 1841.

The earliest Wheeling chancery record notes Francis Rolf appointed pastor in 1829, recording a baptism on 3 November 1828, with evidence of earlier priestly visits. Wheeling town, established in 1795, is said by one vague tradition to take its name from a Father Whelan who ministered occasionally to his flock. Western Virginia, which became West Virginia in 1863, never held many Catholic settlers nor many professing any religion. In 1912 its Catholic population, institutions, and clergy are set out in the entry's closing statistics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wood-carving:
Wood-Carving covers making art objects from wood with knife, chisel, file, or drill. This entry treats only artistic work: plastic pieces such as statues and crucifixes, called wood-sculpture, and arabesques and rosettes for cabinets, called wood-carving proper, though the two often merge. Wooden god-statues served religion in antiquity, above all in Egypt, but wood-carving flowered only in the Christian era.

Perishable timber leaves scant early Christian remains, yet wood served church uses as today: Bawit saints at Cairo, Saint Sabina's door at Rome, wooden reliquaries, and Maximianus's ivory-clad chair at Ravenna. German art began in wood, churches and fittings alike, dressed with animals and interlaced geometry. Almost all is lost save Radegunde's desk at Poitiers and a Lombard door at Parma, with low-relief chests like Terracina's and Puy's door signed Godfredus made me.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wyoming:
Wyoming, the forty-fourth state, takes its name from the Delaware word Maughwauwama, mountains with large plains between. It spans 41 to 45 degrees north and 27 to 34 degrees west of Washington, bounded by Montana, South Dakota, Nebraska, Colorado, Utah, and Idaho. It measures 355 by 276 miles across 97,883 square miles, larger than New York and Pennsylvania together. Its face is mountainous, with valleys, plains, and plateaux.

Ranges run northwest to southeast in broken spurs: the Rockies end in the Wind River Range, with Big Horn, Owl, Rattlesnake, Medicine Bow, Teton, Yellowstone, and Black Hills beside it. Rivers rising here include the Yellowstone, Big Horn, Snake, Green, Cheyenne, Belle Fourche, and Powder, none navigable but prized for irrigation and timber. Lakes include Yellowstone, Jackson, Shoshoni, Lewis, Madison, and Fremont, and Yellowstone Park, set apart by Congress at 3575 square miles, shows geysers, springs, lakes, and woodlands.
chekhov-tales-garnett-1916-darling:
Constance Garnett published The Darling and Other Stories in 1916, a volume of Anton Chekhov's tales in her translation. Garnett's many volumes introduced Chekhov to the English-speaking world. Her Chekhov arrived in the middle of the First World War and found eager readers.

The title story follows Olenka, a woman who takes on the views and work of each man she loves, losing any self of her own. Other stories in the volume show Chekhov's doctors, teachers, and clerks in quiet crises. His scenes end without verdicts, leaving readers to judge. Garnett's plain English let that restraint speak, and the volume helped change what English short fiction could be.
children-s-internet-protection-act-cipa-:
The United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania issued this opinion on May 31, 2002, striking down parts of the Children's Internet Protection Act. Chief Circuit Judge Becker wrote for a three-judge court with Judges Fullam and Bartle. The American Library Association and Multnomah County Public Library led the plaintiffs. Federal library funding, through the E-rate and LSTA programs, stood behind the law.

Findings of fact run for hundreds of pages: how the Internet is indexed, how much explicit material exists, and how filtering software harvests and sorts web pages. Overblocking, the court found, was inherent to the technology. The analysis applies strict scrutiny to a content-based limit on a public forum. The government appealed, and the Supreme Court reversed the judgment a year later. As hosted, the opinion is a landmark record of libraries and the early web.
cleveland-past-and-present-its-represent:
Cleveland Past and Present: Its Representative Men, by Maurice Joblin, was published in 1869 and photographically illustrated by E. Decker. Its preface sets the book against Colonel Whittlesey's Early History of Cleveland, which closed with the War of 1812. Cleveland then was a pioneer settlement of a few families.

Joblin covers what followed: growth to a village, then a commercial port, then a flourishing city of a hundred thousand people. His method is biography. The city's history is written in the lives of its pioneer settlers and prominent citizens, trade by trade. One sketch follows Mr. Dickman, United States District Attorney for the Northern District of Ohio, who resigned early in 1869 for private practice.
comfort-pease-and-her-gold-ring:
Comfort Pease and Her Gold Ring, by Mary Eleanor Wilkins Freeman, is a story of a New England childhood built around a christening gift. Aunt Comfort gave her namesake a gold ring and a gold dollar for her name. Both treasures live in Mrs. Pease's little rosewood work box, alongside her best cameo brooch and a lock of hair from a baby brother who died.

The ring was bought large on purpose. A real gold ring, Aunt Comfort argued, must not be outgrown, and Comfort's father came of a well grown family. So the child may look but never wear. At eight she is small for her age and can crowd two fingers in. Later chapters send her over cold roads, searching where the ring cannot reasonably be, driven by a hope that reason cannot touch.
coming-to-the-king:
Coming to the King, by Frances Ridley Havergal, is a short book of devotional verse. Its opening poem retells the Queen of Sheba as a figure of the soul. The speaker came, but not like Sheba's queen, alone: no stately train, no costly gifts, no friend at court save one, the King. Requests and deep questions are spread before his throne.

The King answers with guidance, victory over doubts and fears, and quiet rest. His house appears with strong foundation and living stones, and his loyal ones dwell with him for aye. A later hymn walks the desert road behind a blessed guide. Golden towers rise ahead, mansions stand ready, and on the King's hands a name is graven that he can never forget.
count-bunker-being-a-bald-yet-veracious-:
J Storer Clouston subtitled Count Bunker a bald yet veracious chronicle, continuing the two gentlemen of his earlier Lunatic at Large. Baron Rudolph von Blitzenberg, appointed attache to the German embassy in London, arrives with estates the size of an English county and a flutter of society excitement. The baron is partly an imposture, and his friend Mr Bunker manages the performance.

Scottish country houses, a countess reading novels between meals, and letters that arrive after the events they might have changed carry the intrigue. Clouston, a Scots writer of light fiction, keeps the tone arch and the plot moving like a stage farce. The von Blitzenberg books were Edwardian favorites, gentle ancestors of Wodehouse.
craftsmanship-in-teaching:
Essays on the craft of teaching by William Chandler Bagley make up this book, printed by the Macmillan Company of New York. Copyright was taken in 1911 and the text was reprinted through May 1912. Bagley had written before on the educative process and classroom management.

Twelve chapters treat optimism in teaching, the force's efficiency, and the test of good supervision. Others take up how children may be trained to study, and the new attitude toward drill. One pleads for what is definite in schooling, and one asks how science bears on the teaching of literature. The closing chapter sketches the ideal teacher. The book speaks to teachers who want their daily work treated as a skilled craft.
daddy-takes-us-skating:
A winter tale for young children by Howard R. Garis fills this 1914 book. Hal Blake and his sister Mabel, called Mab, walk home from school with red noses in the cold. Their father, Daddy Blake, can tell them everything, or so Hal stoutly claims.

Skating is the sport at the heart of the book. Daddy takes the pair out on the ice and answers their questions as they go. Ice fishing comes in too, with lines set so a bell rings when a fish bites. Garis wrote many such Daddy books. The tale is short, warm, and built to teach small facts about winter while it entertains.
dahcotah-life-and-legends-of-the-sioux-a:
Life and legends of the Sioux around Fort Snelling fill this book by Mrs Mary Eastman. Captain Eastman, her husband, made the drawings. Mrs C. M. Kirkland wrote the preface, and the book is inscribed to Henry Sibley of the House of Representatives.

Eastman says she wrote to stir care for the moral wants of the Dakota people. Tales in the book include Wenona, who paddles toward the rapids while her husband calls in vain from the shore. Chapters mix camp life, custom, and story. The record keeps the author's own spellings and frame, those of a white officer's wife of her time. Readers get both the legends she gathered and the lens she gathered them through.
darkest-india-a-supplement-to-general-bo:
A plan to carry the Salvation Army's social gospel to India fills Darkest India, by Commissioner Booth-Tucker, dated 1891. It stands as a supplement to General Booth's In Darkest England and the Way Out. Booth-Tucker says Indian readers need a bullock charter as England needs a cabhorse charter.

He holds that Booth's scheme can be taken up in India almost as it stands. Monthly report forms to Government show the work in course, among them a Jail Gate Brigade at Colombo. Tables of rupees and counts of men helped fill such pages. The book mixes plea, plan, and Army bookkeeping. It shows how the Army hoped to fight want in India with English methods.
doe-osti-17070151-toolkit-for-agentic-al:
Toolkit report ANL-26/74 from Argonne authors Khanh Nguyen, Paul Fischer, and Mi Sun Min presents NekMeshPy, a Python toolkit for building all hexahedral meshes for fluid simulation. A mesh divides a shape into small cells; hexahedral cells are six sided blocks prized for accuracy. The toolkit offers building blocks rather than one push button mesher.

Parts include lofting, tagging, attaching, and boundary layer skinning, plus quality checks that guide an AI coding agent toward valid meshes. The authors then let such an agent build examples. Simple shapes came together from short prompts by reusing prior examples. Complex shapes still needed step by step guidance from a person who knows meshing, and agent written code needed human cleanup.
doe-osti-17076584-investigating-optical-:
Katherine Johnson, Hunter Andrews, Avery Wood, and colleagues studied light based monitoring for Oak Ridge IOTA Lab in report ORNL/TM-2026/4805, dated September 2026. The lab tests iodine capture from the off gas of used fuel reprocessing. Watching iodine levels live, without taking samples, would aid process control and rule compliance.

Two laser methods were tried as partners. Raman spectroscopy, done outside the gas stream, correctly identified iodine reacted phases on silver and copper sorbents, but in stream use was blocked by probe and window limits. The second method, LIBS, spotted gas phase iodine in helium at 3 parts per million and in argon at 5, but not in air at 100 or below.
doe-osti-17084204-multiphoton-diagnostic:
Christopher Kliewer and David Chandler of Sandia test whether entangled photons can boost chemical sensing in project 241580, reported in SAND2026-26916R. Laser spectroscopy reads chemistry by light, but weak signals limit what it can unravel. Entangled photon pairs were claimed in past papers to raise nonlinear absorption by huge factors, though later theory disputed those claims at practical light levels.

The team measured second harmonic generation, a nonlinear mixing process, driven by a pulsed entangled pair source. Mixing probability came out 50 to 400 times the classical value across the tested fluxes. Total second harmonic output ranged from 80 down to 20 nanowatts as flux varied. The report frames the result as evidence in a live debate.
doe-osti-17116336-district-geothermal-he:
Final report from Anna Wagner and colleagues covers geothermal district heating for extreme cold, dated September 2026. Wagner's team sits at the Army Cold Regions Research and Engineering Laboratory. National Laboratory of the Rockies staff also took part. The demonstration site is Fort Wainwright, Alaska, where heating is a survival need. Project EW22-7479 pairs ground source heat pumps with heat stored underground.

Heat stored in a field of boreholes banks summer warmth for winter demand. The method is called borehole thermal energy storage. The team gathered energy use data from existing buildings. It modeled cuts in primary energy for heating and cooling. Design documents at 35 and 65 percent completion tie a heat pump system into the post heating plant. Cost analysis and public works support were also project goals.
doe-osti-17197708-ultra-high-performance:
Samantha Sabatino, Mohammed Alnaggar, Zipporah Harlan, and colleagues design shipping containers from ultra high performance concrete. Their September 2025 report, from Oak Ridge, serves the Office of International Nuclear Security. The containers would move advanced and small modular reactors. Such reactors may ship as large units. The container must guard them against crash, fire, and attack. Ultra high performance concrete offers extreme strength in thin sections.

Chapters review the material's structural, blast, and ballistic behavior, plus heat and fire resistance. Test panels were scanned in 3D. Slab thickness was matched against striking velocity for varied ammunition. The design method builds the container around a standard shipping form. Conclusions stress alignment with industry needs and list extensions for later work.
doe-osti-2575198-two-project-concepts-on:
Final scientific and technical report DE-FE0032346, from Resources for the Future under Daniel Raimi with Jacob Greenspon and Zachary Whitlock, covers April 2024 to March 2025. Fossil fuel workers face an uneven energy transition: oil and gas extraction jobs fell from about 200,000 in 2015 to 120,000 in 2023 even as output hit records. The study asks which new jobs actually fit the skills those workers already have.

Using O*NET occupational data, the team identified common fossil fuel occupations and computed the skills gap between each one and candidate jobs. Matches were graded, with lists of good-match occupations for fossil workers, including in low-emissions energy sectors. The analysis then turns to training: what postsecondary programs exist for the low-carbon technologies involved, and where completions fall short. Two project concepts for an equitable transition close the report, framed for policymakers, labor groups, and the communities that host fossil industries.
doe-osti-2583537-residential-electrifica:
QuitCarbon's home electrification planner got a technical and messaging review from two national laboratories under CRADA CRD-23-24266. Report NREL/TP-5500-95022, dated April 28, 2025, records the work, led by Ben Park at NREL with Pacific Northwest National Laboratory as co-party. The connection came through the American Made Challenges EAS-E Prize, which pairs competitor teams with laboratories. QuitCarbon's tool generates automated plans for swapping a home's fossil systems for electric ones.

The laboratories evaluated the planning model's algorithms, inputs, outputs, and underlying assumptions, checking accuracy and compliance. The point of review is trust at scale: a homeowner acts on the plan's numbers, so the numbers must survive expert scrutiny. Strengthening the tool's technical foundation strengthens every plan it issues. The project sits inside a larger push to make residential electrification a guided, ordinary transaction rather than a research project per house.
doe-osti-2584243-integration-of-electric:
Technical report NREL/TP-5500-93766, by Andrew Speake, Anthony Fontanini, Rajendra Adhikari, and colleagues, wires electric vehicles into ResStock, NREL's residential building stock model. A house with an EV is a different load than the same house without one, and stock models that ignore charging will misjudge neighborhood demand as adoption spreads. The project characterizes the baseline EV stock first: ownership patterns, charger types, battery sizes, miles traveled, and the fraction of charging done at home.

Stakeholder engagement shaped an integration plan, and the modeling work routes EV data through HPXML files into EnergyPlus simulations. Battery capacity is sampled from ResStock's own input files; charge rates follow charger level, while energy use per mile adjusts with outdoor temperature from empirical curves. Outlet access, a quiet determinant of who can charge at home, gets its own analysis. The result lets building researchers simulate homes and their cars as one system.
doe-osti-2586393-floating-offshore-wind-:
Jeremy Stefek of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory is the technical contact on this final report, NREL/TP-5000-95792, issued in August 2025 for CRADA number CRD-23-23782. Alexia Aubault shares credit for the work. Under the American-Made FLOWIN Prize, NREL gave voucher technical support to Ocergy, maker of the OCG-Wind floating offshore wind platform.

NREL assessed the United States supply chain and workforce for that semi-submersible floater, and reviewed vessel needs for installation. Thirteen interviews covered steel distributors, forges, foundries, ports, and fabricators large and small. Three findings stand out. Assembly ports are the key barrier to domestic production of steel-based floating platforms. Domestic steel producers can supply the types and amounts of steel needed. And close coordination among stakeholders will be vital as the supply chain is built.
doe-osti-2586732-high-temperature-active:
Southwest Research Institute ran this project under Department of Energy award DE-EE0009823, from February 2022 through June 2025, with Aaron Rimpel as principal investigator. The goal was high-temperature active magnetic bearings for supercritical carbon dioxide machinery. Such machines promise better power cycle efficiency, and magnetic bearings can match gas bearings on losses while adding tunable control and no wear.

The team produced conceptual designs for radial and thrust bearings, sized on a sealed waste-heat recovery machine, and ran material tests at temperature. A radial bearing design aimed at 540 degrees Celsius proved feasible. The thrust bearing had to be limited to 315 degrees Celsius for high-speed running. The chosen magnetic alloy, Hiperco 50A, drove that limit through its behavior at high temperature. Oxidation and mass change data for candidate materials fill the testing chapters.
doe-osti-2588537-hadron-storage-ring-tra:
Henry Lovelace III of Brookhaven National Laboratory, with S. Berg, K. Drees, and colleagues, wrote this technical note, BNL-228874-2025-TECH, in September 2025. It tackles transition crossing in the Hadron Storage Ring of the future Electron-Ion Collider, for the yellow only configuration. The ring reuses the RHIC tunnel and most of its yellow ring magnets.

As hadrons accelerate, they cross a transition energy where the ring's behavior flips. Crossing it badly costs beam quality. The fix is a gamma-T jump, shifting the transition energy with dedicated quadrupoles. The note works with one optics set. Its phase advances per arc cell are 87 degrees horizontal and 85 degrees vertical. Those values cancel the beta and dispersion waves the jump excites and hold the tune shift down. The total gamma-T change is one unit. Rebuilt insertion regions break the old RHIC symmetry, so quadrupole placement is reworked region by region.
doe-osti-2588656-fy-25-progress-on-compu:
Zhiee Jhia Ooi, Qiuping Lv, Matthew Jasica, Darius Lisowski, and Rui Hu of Argonne National Laboratory wrote this progress report, ANL-ART-311. It covers modeling of the water-based Natural Convection Shutdown Heat Removal Test Facility, Argonne's rig for proving natural convection alone can carry reactor decay heat away, with no pumps to fail.

Fiscal 2025 modeling used RELAP5-3D on a new tank configuration, its inlet lowered by 45 inches. Stability maps divide behavior into five operational modes. They run from stable single-phase liquid through twin-peak and sinusoidal oscillations to stable two-phase flow and non-uniform oscillations. Two experimental runs were simulated. Run-104, with riser inlet throttling, matched the data well and exposed tank backflow into the chimney. Run-99 was a decay heat test, and the lowered inlet predicted it more accurately than the earlier mid-tank configuration had. Exploratory studies add downcomer heating and a bypass channel.
doe-osti-2589172-floating-offshore-wind-:
Aubryn Cooperman, Daniel Mulas Hernando, and Nick Riccobono of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory are the technical contacts for this CRADA final report, NREL/TP-5000-96830, dated September 2025. The partner's technology came from Aikido, a floating offshore wind platform developer. The task: plan, schedule, and price the full United States manufacturing and installation chain for its design.

The study builds a hypothetical project in one of the California lease areas off the central coast. It then plans each step in detail: manufacturing, assembly, load-out, transportation, upending, turbine integration, and offshore transport, with schedule and cost estimates for each, compared against conventional floating platform designs. Modeling ran in ORBIT, NREL's open-source offshore installation simulator, customized for Aikido's process. The changes added a transportation stage for finished substructures and wet storage capacity at the staging site, and re-timed the turbine integration sequence.
doe-osti-2589601-learning-quantum-comput:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2025-11852R, by Timothy Proctor, teaches neural networks to describe the errors of a quantum computer in plain terms. Error learning drives hardware progress, but the standard approach, tomography, grows impossibly costly as qubit counts rise. Simpler noise models scale, yet they blind users to whole classes of real errors.

The work builds an interpretable network design, called a QPANN, that estimates error parameters directly from circuit data. Tests use a hypothetical four-qubit system with crosstalk, where qubits disturb their neighbors. Training circuits were each run 10,000 times, and a noiseless-training case set the ceiling. Network estimates tracked the ideal benchmark closely in the tests shown. If the approach scales, labs could read a machine's faults from a model simple enough to understand.
doe-osti-2589610-material-control-amp-ac:
Ramon Pulido, Tania Rivas, and Nathan Shoman build accounting models for a factory that makes TRISO fuel, in Sandia report SAND2025-11726. TRISO particles carry uranium kernels inside layered coatings and are a leading fuel form for high-temperature reactors. The generic factory studied here would use high-assay low-enriched uranium, which raises tracking duties.

Modelers walked the full process line, from kernel production through coating, pressing, and heat treatment. Steps that only bake the material, such as carbonization and annealing, are modeled as simple time delays, since the fuel's makeup does not change there. The model shows where material sits, in what form, and for how long. Safeguards planners can test camera, scale, and record-keeping choices against it before a real plant is built.
doe-osti-2997454-snakes-for-the-hadron-s:
Brookhaven National Laboratory technical note BNL-229010-2025-TECH, also numbered EIC-ADD-TN-141, by Kiel Hock and Vadim Ptitsyn, covers the spin rotators, called snakes, for the Electron-Ion Collider's Hadron Storage Ring. Polarized proton and helion beams lose their spin alignment as they circle and speed up. A snake twists the spin by 180 degrees at each pass, canceling that drift.

Six full helical snakes are planned, each built from four helical dipole magnets. Four come straight from the existing RHIC collider, and two more will be built from rotator magnet coils on hand. One of those must use left-handed coils to keep enough spares, a mix never flown before. Simulations with Opera field maps in the zgoubi tracking code show the left-handed snake reaches the needed spin axes for both protons and helions on existing power supplies.
doe-osti-2997806-super-efficient-air-con:
Baryon Inc.'s final report on award DE-EE0009683 covers a super-efficient air conditioning project. Jeffrey Premer of Wilmington, Delaware, led work that ran from October 2022 with an extension to March 2025. The design centers on a cooler, called the BDC unit in project records, built around heat and mass exchangers, a membrane system, and a water distribution system. Every milestone in the plan is marked accomplished.

First-year work delivered thermal models of the cooler and a flow model of the water distribution. A model of the membrane system followed. Each was checked against literature data or simple experiments within stated bands of 5 to 10 percent. Candidate exchanger materials ranged from treated textiles to rigid Kraft paper, with uneven water spread noted as a flaw to fix. The second year reached the project's second go/no-go gate, a laboratory prototype judged against 70 percent of the target effectiveness.
doe-osti-2998579-integrated-molten-salt-:
Argonne National Laboratory report ANL/NSE-25/71, also issued as INL/RPT-25-88160, by Travis Mui, Daniel O'Grady, Thanh Hua and co-workers, sums up recent molten salt reactor modeling work. The work sits in NEAMS, the Energy Department program that builds computer tools for advanced reactor designs. Its focus is thermal hydraulics, meaning how heat moves through flowing reactor coolant.

The team coupled two codes, SAM and Pronghorn, through an interface named Saline, with salt properties taken from a molten salt database. Both codes run on the MOOSE framework. Checks covered heated pipe flow in one dimension, natural convection loops in three dimensions, and cases based on the Molten Salt Reactor Experiment. The coupled system stayed stable and matched the benchmark results well. Designers gain one tool chain that joins whole-plant modeling with detailed core modeling.
doe-osti-3000794-phase-ii-field-demonstr:
The Electric Power Research Institute issued this final report for award DE-FE0026140 on 29 August 2025, with Robert Trautz as principal investigator. It closes a decade of work at the Lansing Smith Generating Plant in Southport, Florida. Reporting ran from September 2015 to May 2025. The project belonged to the Brine Extraction Storage Test program. When carbon dioxide is pumped underground at scale, pressure builds in the receiving rock. Pulling brine out relieves it.

The demonstration tested pressure management in the field and priced the brine problem it creates. Extracted brine is costly to handle. Treating it for beneficial use, such as power plant cooling water, can change the economics. Desalination options for salty water were assessed alongside. Modelling for an electromagnetic monitoring campaign appears. Three rounds of crosswell surveys were judged best for tracking the plume. Surface to borehole data was dropped as poor value.
doe-osti-3001099-confirmation-using-gamm:
Peter Marleau of Sandia summarises COGNIZANT in SAND2025-13642R, dated October 2025, a confirmation system with a privacy trick at its core. Arms control inspectors may need proof that an object matches a declared nuclear item, without learning anything else about it. Zero-knowledge methods promise exactly that: a yes-or-no answer and nothing more. COGNIZANT encodes gamma-ray signatures in time patterns, using an anti-mask approach so the measurement itself cannot be reverse-engineered into design information.

The final summary walks through the system's design, its concept of operations and laboratory demonstrations. Use case studies show where the method fits treaty monitoring, and a measurement campaign at the Pantex plant tested it against real-world conditions. The work builds on the earlier CONFIDANTE line of research. Marleau's report is a compact capstone for a system meant to let rivals verify each other without spilling secrets.
doe-osti-3002245-development-of-high-tem:
Anthony Birri, Holden C. Hyer, Daniel C. Sweeney, and colleagues work on sensor attachment in Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/4061, dated August 2025. Strain gauges and fiber sensors must be bonded to metal that will run extremely hot, inside reactors or test rigs. Ordinary adhesives fail at those temperatures. The team developed bonding methods that hold for both steady and rapidly changing strain readings.

Tests compared bond materials and application steps under heat. A good bond passes the metal's true strain to the sensor without slipping or cracking. The work builds on the group's earlier embedded fiber sensor studies in printed metal parts. Reliable high-temperature strain data feed the digital models used to predict component life. The report gives practitioners a tested starting point instead of trial and error.
doe-osti-3003005-practical-probabilistic:
Noam Steiner Tomer and Samuel D. Pollard present a programming system in Sandia report SAND2025-13969R, printed November 2025. The system is Roulette, a language for probabilistic programming: writing models where quantities are distributions, not fixed numbers. Such programs let analysts compute with uncertainty directly instead of bolting it on afterward.

The report documents Roulette's design and its standard library. Discrete and continuous distributions are covered, along with an embedded tool called Disrupt for building domain-specific languages. A worked discretization example shows the error sources honestly: the trapezoid-rule area error and the rationalization error are drawn and measured. The library implements a catalog of distributions with their support limits. The intended readers are Sandia analysts who need auditable uncertainty calculations in a practical tool.
doe-osti-3003768-holographic-quantum-sim:
Shyam Shankar and Andrew Potter of the University of Texas at Austin give the final technical report for DOE award DE-SC0022102, submitted December 1, 2025. The project ran from September 2021 to August 2025 under the Basic Energy Sciences program. It pursued holographic quantum simulation: using a small quantum processor, plus classical help, to mimic strongly correlated electron systems that defeat ordinary supercomputers.

Three tasks structured the work. The first prepared ground and thermal states holographically, covering frustrated magnets, the Fermi-Hubbard model, and fractional quantum Hall systems. The second simulated long-time dynamics away from equilibrium. The third built holographic versions of embedding methods used for complex materials. Target applications include high-temperature superconductors and perovskite photovoltaics. The report lists the team of postdocs and students who carried the work.
doe-osti-3004821-doe-fair-surrogate-benc:
Geoffrey Fox and Gregor von Laszewski of the University of Virginia give the final report for DOE grant DE-SC0023452, dated November 17, 2025. The award ran from September 2022 to August 2025. The project, the Surrogate Benchmark Initiative, built a shared library of benchmark data sets for AI surrogate models: neural networks trained to stand in for expensive supercomputer simulations.

The repositories follow FAIR principles, keeping data findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable, with code and artifacts beside the numbers. Partners included Argonne, Indiana University, Rutgers, and the University of Tennessee at Knoxville. Surrogates can speed some computations by orders of magnitude, but only shared benchmarks let the field compare them fairly. The report closes with the catalogue, middleware, and web presence the team built.
doe-osti-3005543-final-technical-report-:
Paul J. DeMott and Sonia M. Kreidenweis of Colorado State lead the final report for DOE award DE-SC0021116, which ran from September 2020 to August 2025. The project traced natural aerosol sources: the dust, sea spray, and biological particles that seed clouds. Those particles decide how many droplets a cloud forms, which shifts its brightness, lifetime, and rain.

Observations spanned both hemispheres, drawing on ARM campaigns over land and ocean. The team used Energy Department value-added products for cloud condensation nuclei and specialized in ice-nucleating particles, the rare particles that start ice in mixed clouds. Conference records in the report range from agricultural ice nuclei to marine variability studies. Better source accounting feeds climate models whose largest uncertainty remains exactly this aerosol-cloud link.
doe-osti-3006211-fundamental-research-ai:
Final report DE-SC0018087 comes from Pennsylvania State University. Alexey Silakov led the project, with John Golbeck, Donald Bryant, Paul King, and Michael Gorka. It asks whether sunlight that plants cannot use can be rerouted to make fuel. Photosynthesis often takes in more light than the plant can spend, and the excess is thrown off through non-productive paths. Earlier work by the team attached a catalyst to photosystem I and made hydrogen from light. This project, running from September 2017 to August 2024, genetically fused parts of photosystem I with a recently found oxygen-tolerant [FeFe] hydrogenase.

The summary judges the approach plausible: the modified photosystem can divert energy to non-native electron-accepting pathways, and viable [FeFe] hydrogenases were identified as building blocks for a robust hybrid system. The work leaves a test bed for later optimization rather than a working fuel-producing cell. Fourteen publications are listed.
doe-osti-3006225-metal-organic-framework:
Final report dated September 19, 2025, from Shengqian Ma at the University of North Texas, with Argonne as partner, closes a HyMARC seedling project on hydrogen storage materials. The idea joins frustrated Lewis pairs, acid and base sites kept from neutralizing, inside metal-organic frameworks. These FLP@MOF sorbents aim at DOE's 2025 targets of 5.5 weight percent hydrogen and 0.040 kilograms per liter, at room temperature and under 100 bar.

Phase I synthesized varied FLP@MOF systems and studied how much FLP loading helps. Uptake data were cross-checked at other labs, against a first milestone of 1.5 weight percent reversible capacity. Phase II tuned measurement protocols against a reference sample and moved to high surface-area frameworks. It used in-situ infrared study and computation to pin down how hydrogen binds. The mechanism work is framed as the base for a sorbent that stores hydrogen without deep cooling or very high pressure.
doe-osti-3006292-comsol-simulation-of-op:
Fermilab documentation FERMILAB-FN-1278-SQMS-STUDENT, by Xiaoyu Chen, dated August 18, 2025, records COMSOL simulations of a whispering gallery mode resonator. The model couples a silicon nitride bus waveguide to a lithium niobate ring of radius 2.48 millimeters in size. The core is 2.00 micrometers wide and 0.80 high, set 0.10 micrometers from the ring, at the 1.55 micrometer design wavelength. Printed values give a material-limited quality factor of 1.11 x 10^8 and a free spectral range of 8.70 gigahertz between modes.

The conclusion contrasts the two polarizations. The TE00 mode stays tightly confined in the core, overlaps the ring weakly, and couples poorly. The TM00 mode leaks more field into the cladding and reaches strong coupling resonances. A separation scan finds critical coupling at a gap near 0.20 micrometers to 0.22 micrometers, with over-coupling below and under-coupling above. Changing waveguide thickness shifts resonance positions. Refined 3D models will be needed for quantitative matches to experiment.
doe-osti-3007930-reliable-and-efficient-:
Machine learning that scientists can trust is the aim of Qiang Du of Columbia in a November 2025 final report for DOE grant DE-SC0022317. The work builds math tools for learning systems whose answers must be exact, clear, and in line with the laws of physics.

Three fronts were covered: pulling features from fast-changing data, the theory of finding dynamics with neural nets, and rigorous optimization. One product is a two-stage algorithm for stretched non-negative matrix factorization. It beat the existing NENMF method on real diffraction data in both precision and speed. Theory results sharpen optimal transport bounds used in uncertainty estimates.
doe-osti-3012686-optimizing-enzymes-for-:
Nicholas Gauthier of Dana-Farber Cancer Institute prepared this final technical report for award DE-SC0022024, covering 2021 to 2025, with partners at the National Renewable Energy Laboratory and Harvard. The project aimed to design better enzymes for breaking down PET, the polyester in drink bottles, of which about 65 million metric tons are made yearly. Enzymes offer a recycling route that could return plastic to high-quality feedstock.

The team paired machine learning protein design with high-throughput lab testing, including a low-cost robotic platform. They built and characterized hundreds of new PET-cutting and partner enzymes, many matching the best performers in the published literature. Attempts at a droplet-based ultra-fast assay hit real obstacles, which the report records plainly alongside the design tools released to other researchers.
doe-osti-3013233-comstock-measure-docume:
National Renewable Energy Laboratory report NREL/TP-5500-92502, by Jie Xiong and Janghyun Kim, dated November 2025, documents a ComStock modeling measure: lighting control for load shedding. ComStock simulates the whole U.S. commercial building stock. This measure asks how much peak demand falls when buildings dim or switch lighting during grid stress events.

The documentation lays out the baseline lighting assumptions, the control strategies modeled, and the dispatch windows when shedding is called. It also records the measure's limits, including how sensitive results are to the chosen dimming percentage and dispatch schedule method. Stock-level results compare annual utility bills and site energy against the baseline. Modelers use the document to apply the measure consistently and judge where its savings claims hold up.
doe-osti-3016026-findings-from-large-ben:
Savannah River National Laboratory report SRNL-STI-2026-00017, by Dylan D Rodene and Edelmy J Marin Bernardez of that lab, plus Michael D Clark and David Genders of the Electrosynthesis Company. It dates to January 2026. It reports large bench-scale tests of denitration electrolyzers for the EDCGe project at the Hanford site. Denitration strips nitrate out of nuclear waste liquid using electric current.

Phase 1 tests checked how well the electrolyzer worked on simulated waste supernatant, the liquid layer above settled tank waste. The team tracked operating settings and reaction products, and flagged ammonia handling as a key open problem for the full-scale system. Findings cover how robust the process looks and what steps come before a plant-scale build. Waste managers get early proof of whether electric denitration plus caustic generation can pretreat Hanford waste.
doe-osti-3016089-floating-offshore-wind-:
Jeremy Stefek, Lucas Eshuis, Brinn McDowell, Frank Oteri, and Bailey Pons were the National Laboratory of the Rockies technical contacts for this January 2026 cooperative research final report, NLR/TP-5000-98563. The work supported a team in the American-Made FLOWIN Prize for floating offshore wind readiness. It focused on the INO floating platform design and its path to United States production.

Two questions drove the support. First, how many workers, in which trades, full-scale production and deployment would need. Second, which domestic suppliers could make the main components. The team mapped supply chain limits and gaps at regional and national level. Feasibility of training the needed skilled trades varied by location, so each area's strengths and gaps were charted. Builders of floating platforms get a plain view of the workforce and supplier work still ahead.
doe-osti-3017348-volumetric-subtractive-:
Dongping Terrel-Perez of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory wrote this February 2026 report, LLNL-TR-2012546, on volumetric subtractive manufacturing, project 24-LW-069. Making small negative features, holes and voids, is a standing weakness of additive manufacturing. Overcuring, diffusion, and refractive index changes make the smallest printable void always worse than the smallest solid feature. Multi-scale parts in one exposure are also hard.

The project developed a hybrid method that works both ways. Positive features are printed by photo-polymerization, hardening resin with light. Negative features are printed by photo-degradation, breaking material down with light. Together the two tools let builders carve structures top-down as well as build them up. The report presents complex objects made with the combined approach. Designers of microfluidics and small mechanical parts get a route to voids and channels that printers alone could not hold.
doe-osti-3017766-white-rock-canyon-ripar:
Bridget Lorraine Bloodwood, Kaya Osita Krantz, and Jessica Carla-Claire Celmer of Los Alamos National Laboratory wrote this riparian monitoring report, LA-UR-26-20926, issued February 6, 2026. The laboratory's eastern boundary runs along the Rio Grande in White Rock Canyon, about four miles of river frontage. Feral cattle have been documented along that stretch since the 1980s, and cattle are especially hard on riparian land.

Riparian zones are biodiversity hubs and crucial habitat, including for the endangered Southwestern Willow Flycatcher and Yellow-billed Cuckoo on laboratory property. Surveyors walked transects running parallel and perpendicular to the river. They scored six types of cattle impact, including grazing evidence, browse pressure, and ground cover disturbance intensity. The monitoring gives land managers a measured record of damage in a canyon they are charged to protect, and a baseline for judging whether control efforts work.
doe-osti-3018059-fy25-task-5-small-scale:
Austin A Bachman, Amy M Westesen, and Richard C Daniel of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory led this October 2025 report, FY25 Task 5: Small-Scale Mixing. Six authors are named in all. The work serves Hanford tank waste processing, where settled solids must be resuspended before waste can be moved. Small-scale tests let engineers find the mixing energy that full-scale tanks will need.

Early runs used glass beads as a clean stand-in waste. Attention settled on the critical velocity, the flow speed at which solids lift and stay suspended. That behavior was pursued further with real mineral simulants. Gibbsite and boehmite were chosen because those mineral phases are known to be present in actual tank waste. The same equipment and method carried across all materials, so results compare cleanly. Tank designers get scale-up data grounded in the minerals that actually sit in the tanks.
doe-osti-3018688-a-comprehensive-framewo:
Montana Technological University closed award DE-SC0021090 with this final report on validating power-plant simulation models. Daniel Trudnowski led the project, following Joshua Wold, with Ronald Hruban, Rayce McCord, and Nolan Wanner. Grid planners rely on phasor simulations, and regulators let utilities validate plant models against recorded disturbances. How accurate those validation methods are was unmeasured. The project used Monte-Carlo Experimentation to answer. A laboratory mock plant was built: a generator and prime mover, synchronized to the grid, with switched load banks for repeatable transients.

Repeated experiments on the mock plant produced statistics on validation accuracy. Real plants cannot be experimented on that way, so the team built a Monte-Carlo Simulation framework that mimics the process. The simulation version needs less data and can run on plants. Utilities gain a way to check their checkers. The framework and the mock plant are the project's deliverables.
doe-osti-3018757-dynamic-networks-experi:
Stephen L Heck and Louis Quinones of Sandia measured how detection errors poison seismic event association in SAND2026-16532, printed January 2026. Associators group phase detections into events. Two algorithms faced the test: PEDAL and GaMMA. The Dynamic Networks Experiment 2 supplied ground-truth data with known events. The team then degraded the inputs in controlled ways. Dropout rates, added noise, and detection precision were varied across datasets. Bulletin quality was scored beyond simple precision and recall.

One result cuts against intuition. GaMMA's recall improved when noise increased, without producing more false events. False split events, where one real event breaks into two, were mapped for both algorithms. Their location densities show where each associator is fragile. For monitoring networks, the lesson is budgetable: this is how much association quality a given detection error rate costs. The experiment design lets other associators be graded on the same scale.
doe-osti-3020125-mcgrath-community-energ:
McGrath Community Energy Planning records an Energy Technology Innovation Partnership Project (ETIPP) planning effort for McGrath, a remote interior Alaska community of about 300 people on the upper Kuskokwim River. The town runs on an isolated diesel microgrid, and fuel costs are high. A McGrath Energy Committee formed in 2023 brought together the city, the Native Village Council, the local utility, and regional partners.

Residents ranked alternatives to diesel as their top improvement priority in a 2021 survey. The plan assesses local energy resources and then studies focus areas in depth, including a solar photovoltaic and battery storage system sized with the REopt tool. It lays out practical steps for cutting diesel use while keeping the isolated grid reliable.
doe-osti-3020280-enhanced-simulation-too:
National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-6A40-95007, by Jennie Jorgenson, examines how power system models should schedule long-duration energy storage paired with solar power. Standard models plan one day at a time, so they charge and discharge storage too shortsightedly and undervalue it. The project compared four fixes, from multi-day look-ahead windows to ending charge targets borrowed from simpler simulations.

The other two methods price the future value of stored energy directly, or vary the model's time detail so critical hours stay sharp. Each involves trade-offs in computing cost and ease of use. The team also tested how long-duration storage supports the grid during a severe winter storm modeled on 2021's Storm Uri, in a projected 2035 system. The report recommends methods by system size so planners can credit storage fairly.
doe-osti-3021633-a-computational-workflo:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report by Ruonan Wu, Jianqiu Zheng, Winston Anthony, and Yuliya Farris, dated September 2025, builds a computational workflow for a hidden player in soil carbon: viruses. Soil microbes drive carbon cycling, and viruses infect those microbes, killing some and reprogramming others. The project links viral data into models of how soil communities answer experimental warming, bridging microbial modeling to carbon and mineral modeling.

The workflow integrates metagenomic data across samples from an in-situ warming experiment. Weighted read coverage for representative microbial genome bins spanned from 6.8 to 238.1. Virus-host associations proved extensive, with over 1.2 million linkages involving 96 viral contigs. Infections skewed lytic by count, meaning viruses bursting their hosts, but coverage-weighted analysis showed lysogenic infections, viruses lying dormant in host genomes, contributing about equally.
doe-osti-3021639-low-valent-actinide-com:
Progress report on low-valent actinide chemistry describes a project building uranium(III) complexes on carborane-based ligands, boron-carbon cages called dicarbollides. These cages act as 3D cousins of the flat cyclopentadienyl ligands common in organometallic work. The project's aims were to tune the complexes' electronic and redox traits through ligand decoration, test small molecule activation, study magnetic behavior, and in time extend the chemistry to transuranic elements.

The team worked out reliable synthesis for both uranium(III) and uranium(IV) metallacarboranes. Adding groups to the cage at boron vertices, away from the metal, shifted the uranium center's oxidation potential in a predictable way while leaving its shape unchanged. That split between electronic tuning and structural change is the project's central result. It lets the team isolate how ligand electronics alone shape actinide bonding. Binding energies and frontier orbital trends across the swapped series back the pattern.
doe-osti-3021699-rotators-for-the-hadron:
Brookhaven National Laboratory technical note BNL-229478-2026-TECH, also numbered EIC-ADD-TN-140, by Kiel Hock, dated February 2026, designs spin rotators for the Hadron Storage Ring of the Electron-Ion Collider. The collider needs hadron beams whose particle spins point lengthwise along the beam at the collision point. Rotator magnets on either side must deliver that longitudinal polarization across the full energy range, for protons and for helium-3 nuclei alike.

Helions rotate 1.56 times more per unit of magnetic field than protons, because their gyromagnetic factor, charge, and mass differ. The note tabulates working rotator configurations for helions at 41, 100, and 183 GeV per nucleon, with alternate solutions noted. Current settings for the inner and outer power supplies of the sector 5 and 6 rotators are charted across energies. The result: longitudinal polarization is achievable at all planned energies for both species.
doe-osti-3022243-multi-scale-model-infor:
A University of Massachusetts Lowell final technical report, led by project lead Fanglin Che under award DE-SC0025553, tells of work on plasma-nanoparticle interactions aimed at cleaner hydrogen output. The target process is cracking ammonia into hydrogen for ship fuel, using non-thermal plasma with nanoparticle catalysts to cut the energy cost.

The work joined quantum chemistry, plasma kinetics, and physics-informed deep learning across scales. Its inverse design strand used a diffusion model whose loss function carries a correction steering generated alloys toward a nitrogen adsorption energy near minus 0.9 electron volts. Fifteen bimetallic candidates emerged, most built from earth-abundant elements. Named examples include CoFe, NiFe, CoMo, NiMo, and FeCu. The models are offered as portable tools for predicting plasma kinetics and catalyst behavior together.
doe-osti-3022533-blueprint-for-doe-quant:
A multi-lab blueprint lays out how the Department of Energy should prepare for fault-tolerant quantum computing. It was written by a DOE laboratory quantum supercomputing team led by Ryan Bennink. Contributors came from eight laboratories and several universities. Its goal is quantum scientific utility: solving scientifically valuable problems that classical computers cannot reach. First demonstrations are due in the late 2020s, with maturity in the early to mid 2030s.

The strategy asks DOE to deploy first-generation scientifically relevant machines with at least 100 logical qubits. It targets initial deployment in 2028. The machines would be folded into the national scientific computing infrastructure the department already runs. Research directions, milestones, and workforce needs fill out the plan. Its argument is that tying in with supercomputing centers, not standalone machines, is where the scientific payoff will come from.
doe-osti-3025199-leveraging-reveal-for-d:
Gabriel Zuckerman, Victor Igwe, and Travis Williams of the National Laboratory of the Rockies presented these slides in March 2026 on using the reVeal platform to site data centers. reVeal, an open-source tool released under a BSD-3 license, breaks national or regional load growth down into fine-grained local estimates. Its guiding question is practical: where can a strained grid add tens to hundreds of gigawatts of data center load quickly?

The framework steps through site feasibility, favorability, site selection, and integration. Exclusion screens remove airport footprints, Defense Department clear zones, wetlands from the national inventory, and conservation lands, and they set new load back 3.7 kilometers from missile silo sites. A case study walks the screens through to candidate sites that power system models can then use.
doe-osti-3028178-white-rock-canyon-ripar:
Bridget Bloodwood, Kaya Krantz, and Nicoli Carr of Los Alamos National Laboratory's Environmental Stewardship Group report riparian monitoring in White Rock Canyon, LA-UR-26-22543, dated February 26, 2026, for the lab's field office. Riparian strips along the canyon's water are thin, rich habitat in dry country, and repeat monitoring shows whether they are holding their cover and species mix.

Method sections fix the field protocol. Each plot carries three transects, photographed from set points in all four cardinal directions, 36 photographs per plot in total. Line-point intercept readings were taken every meter along each transect, recording vegetation class and species plus litter. Shrubs and trees up to ten feet tall that crossed the lines fed a canopy gap assessment, a densitometer measured canopy cover meter by meter, and grazing or trampling disturbance was noted.
doe-osti-3030847-roadmap-for-assessing-f:
David Christopher Horvath, Guy L. Fredrickson, Toni Y. Karlsson, and colleagues at Idaho and Argonne national laboratories chart a research roadmap in report INL/RPT-25-83615, dated July 2025. The topic is pyroprocessing, a way to recycle used nuclear fuel inside molten fluoride salts. Both labs share the work. Their aim is to name the research and development gaps that block the method, so funders can close them in a sane order.

Candidate steps get a hard look. Electrowinning must be proven at bench and then engineering scale. Oxide precipitation could drop fission products out as solids for disposal, sorted by how strongly each grabs oxygen. Melt crystallization can clean salt for reuse; Idaho has shown it in chloride salts, but fluoride salts still need tests for recovery, scale-up, and tuning.
doe-osti-3252740-automatic-image-point-m:
Orrin Thomas, Kjell Ryerson, Christopher G. Tate, and Gene Bailey of Oak Ridge National Laboratory survey image matching in report ORNL/SPR-2024/3272, dated December 4, 2023. Sparse image point matching finds the same spot across many photos. That one skill underpins photo triangulation, structure from motion, simultaneous location and mapping, and data fusion for maps and robots. The report explains how the field moved from hand-written rules to learning systems.

Rule-based matchers cannot take in as much training input, or grow as complex, as deep learning matchers, the authors note. The survey walks the learning methods in time order, since each fed on the last. For each, it covers which pipeline step the network replaced, what training data it ate, how its cost function was shaped, and how it was tested against rivals.
doe-osti-3362565-graduate-traineeships-i:
Rasha Morsi of Norfolk State University reports the university share of a graduate traineeship in accelerator engineering and physics, under award SC0022533. The wider effort joined Old Dominion University, Hampton University, and Jefferson Lab to train students for accelerator work, the machines behind much of physics and medicine. Norfolk State supported one graduate student, Bryan A. Belcher, who finished his computer science master degree on time in July 2024.

Belcher thesis tested whether adding sentiment awareness improves paraphrase detection by transformer language models such as BERT, RoBERTa, DeBERTa, and ELECTRA. Adding the sentiment signal helped the tested models. He also trained at a national accelerator school session in June 2023 and presented at a December 2024 computing conference. The report is candid that no further United States citizen students at the school took up the traineeship.
doe-osti-3362790-water-vapor-isotopic-me:
Joseph Galewsky of the University of New Mexico reports on isotope measurements in report DOE/SC-ARM-26-010, dated May 2026. A Picarro L-2130 analyzer was placed at the Kennaook Cape Grim station in northwest Tasmania, a baseline site that samples clean Southern Ocean air. The visit rode along with the CAPE-K cloud and precipitation campaign run by the Atmospheric Radiation Measurement facility. Isotope ratios in water vapor act as fingerprints for where the water evaporated and how it traveled.

Calibration runs anchor the record. In February 2025 the routine was set with water jugs from the South Pole and Hawaii. Sealed standards named USGS45, USGS47, and W-64444 were run in sequence on March 20, 2025, and again across October 13 to 15. Stable reading windows and vapor levels near 9,000 to 11,000 parts per million mark the checks.
doe-osti-3363534-degradation-science-int:
Pranjali Khajanji, a doctoral candidate at the University of California San Diego, files this May 2026 annual progress report. It covers corrosion in an additively manufactured high-entropy alloy. The alloy is a nano-lamellar material known as AlCoCrFeNi2.1. It offers strength, ductility, and wear resistance even when hot. But its behavior in aggressive acids across length scales was poorly understood.

Built by laser powder bed fusion, the alloy's fine layers let a chromium rich film cover both phases quickly, stabilizing its corrosion potential. Annealing changed the picture. Five hours at 600 degrees Celsius coarsened the layers and raised the corrosion current. One hour at 1000 degrees coarsened them most and left the matrix nearly continuous. The report ties each microstructure to its measured attack pattern.
doe-osti-3367007-multiscale-and-machine-:
Idaho National Laboratory report INL/PRT-25-88167 applies the MALAMUTE modeling framework to predict microstructure in additively manufactured metals. Sudipta Biswas, Somayajulu Dhulipala, Peter German, and Michael McMurtrey wrote it, with Purna Vindhya Kota of Johns Hopkins. A printed part's grains and phases are set by its thermal history, layer by layer. If simulation can predict them from process settings, qualification stops depending on printing and cutting test coupons forever.

The work couples multiscale physics with machine learning: process simulations feed thermal fields, microstructure models evolve grains, and learned surrogates speed the chain. September 2025 progress covers the framework's methods and demonstrations.
